Ghana News.title: NDC Regional Elections: Walewale supporters allege sabotage after former parliamentary candidate wins Regional Secretary
Ghana News.content:
Supporters of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) in Walewale have accused officials of the North East Regional Coordinating Directorate of deliberately frustrating celebrations following the election of former Walewale parliamentary candidate, Abubakari Abdallah, as the party's Regional Secretary.

The supporters allege that electricity supply to Walewale was deliberately disconnected shortly after the party's regional executive elections on Saturday, November 14, 2026, to prevent them from celebrating Mr Abdallah's victory.

Power went off in the township a few minutes after the election results were declared, with Mr Abdallah and several other candidates emerging victorious.

JoyNews checks confirmed that the outage affected Walewale, while electricity supply in other parts of the region remained uninterrupted.

Power was subsequently restored to the township at about 11:00 a.m. on Sunday, November 15.

The incident has triggered angry reactions among Mr Abdallah's supporters, many of whom have taken to social media to condemn what they describe as an attempt to undermine the former parliamentary candidate.

Some have accused officials of the Northern Electricity Distribution Company (NEDCo) of allowing the electricity distribution network to be drawn into what they consider a political vendetta against Mr Abdallah, who has contested the Walewale parliamentary seat three times.

One supporter directly accused the North East Regional Minister, Ibrahim Tia, of being behind the alleged blackout, although no evidence was provided to substantiate the claim.

However, there is no independent evidence to establish that the outage was politically motivated or that any government official or NEDCo personnel deliberately disconnected electricity to frustrate the celebrations.

Several attempts by JoyNews to reach NEDCo officials in Walewale for comments were unsuccessful. Rauf Tanko retains regional chairmanship amid inducement allegations

Meanwhile, incumbent NDC North East Regional Chairman, Abdul Rauf Tanko Ibrahim, has retained his position after securing 146 votes.

His re-election has, however, attracted attention following his admission during an interview with journalists that he distributed motorbikes and other forms of support to delegates ahead of the elections.

Responding to questions about allegations of vote-buying, Mr Tanko acknowledged distributing motorbikes but defended the gesture as part of his responsibilities as the incumbent regional chairman.

"It is not only motorbikes that were given to delegates," he told journalists.

"Don't forget that I am the incumbent Regional Chairman. Before winning this election, it was my duty to finance or fund the party's activities in the region. So, I don't think it is misplaced for me to buy motorbikes for executives to enable them to carry out party activities across the region," he added.

Full list of elected NDC North East Regional Executives

The November 14 elections produced the following winners:

Regional Chairman

Abdul Rauf Tanko Ibrahim – 146 votes

Regional Vice Chairman

John Bibirim – 100 votes

Regional Secretary

Abdallah Abubakari – 114 votes

Deputy Regional Secretary

Thomas B. Jayen – 95 votes

Regional Organiser

Godfred Mayeem – 124 votes

Deputy Regional Organiser

Mohammed Akunloya – 97 votes

Regional Treasurer

Ibrahim Rasheed – 94 votes

Deputy Regional Treasurer

Nurudini Abdul-Rahaman – 136 votes

Regional Communications Officer

A. Abdul Gafaru Mohammed – 108 votes

Deputy Regional Communications Officer

Hamza Iddrisu Salifu – 70 votes

Regional Women's Organiser

Sumaya Ligbi Salifu

Deputy Regional Women's Organiser

Asana Yidana

Regional Youth Organiser

Fatawu Karandey Amidu

Deputy Regional Youth Organisers

Kamil Dabri Ibrahim

Yussif Sulemana Saeed

Zongo Caucus Coordinator

Tahiru Rafiu – 80 votes

A total of 231 delegates participated in the regional elections held at the Nalerigu Senior High School. More than 200 police officers were deployed to the election grounds to maintain security.

The officers arrived unarmed, with the police commander explaining that the arrangement was intended to ensure a peaceful and impartial electoral process. He said armed personnel remained on standby to respond to any eventuality.

The elections form part of the NDC's internal reorganisation ahead of the party's national executive elections scheduled for December 19, 2026.

Abuba's victory comes against the backdrop of tensions with Regional Minister

Mr Abdallah's election as Regional Secretary comes against the backdrop of a prolonged political disagreement between his supporters and North East Regional Minister Ibrahim Tia, largely centred on influence within the NDC and access to government appointments.

The tensions became increasingly public in November 2025 when supporters of Mr Abdallah accused the Regional Minister, the Regional Chairman and other party executives of deliberately frustrating the former parliamentary candidate's attempts to secure a government appointment.

The aggrieved supporters also complained that several grassroots activists who worked for the party during the 2024 general elections had been overlooked in government appointments, while individuals they considered less active in the party had been rewarded with influential positions.

Some further accused regional party executives of circulating damaging reports about Mr Abdallah and his associates, including allegations that some of them engaged in skirt-and-blouse voting during the 2024 elections.

Mr Tia rejected the allegations, insisting that neither he nor the regional executives had deliberately worked against the former parliamentary candidate.

In an interview with JoyNews on November 19, 2025, the Regional Minister argued that contesting parliamentary elections or supporting the NDC did not automatically entitle anyone to a government appointment.

"He is not the only one who contested and hasn't been appointed," Mr Tia said, citing other former parliamentary candidates in the region who had also not received government positions.

He also denied claims that regional executives had submitted reports to discredit Mr Abdallah, explaining that the party obtained information about constituency activities through several channels, including national-level party officials.

The disagreement subsequently spilled into the party's grassroots structures in Walewale, with aggrieved supporters threatening to boycott party activities over what they described as the marginalisation of loyal members.

On December 7, 2025, regional executives, including Mr Tia and Regional Chairman Rauf Tanko, held an emergency meeting with aggrieved party members in Walewale.

The meeting followed weeks of agitation over government appointments and allegations that influential regional figures were sidelining Mr Abdallah and his supporters.

A joint committee comprising regional executives and constituency representatives was established to examine the complaints and recommend measures to address the divisions.

Mr Abdallah's victory in the November 14, 2026 elections is therefore politically significant, particularly against the backdrop of competing interests within the party in the constituency.

Ghana News.title: The stench of cocaine and Ghana’s new cedi – Occasional Kwatriot Kwesi Yankah writes
Ghana News.content:
On my global rounds last year, I was shocked to see at airport shops perfume names that shook me to the core: a perfume called ‘Cocaine,’ then another designer perfume. ‘Opium.’ But the killer of them all was ‘Sinners Perfume,’ apparently the fastest ticket to Hell.

Surprisingly, the accompanying aromas were smooth, except that no Daddy in his right senses would want ‘Cocaine Perfume’ even mistakenly seized by Customs officials.

Those were on sale for $175 to $200, and attracted a small queue of young men.

The trip to the cocaine world is not as long as you thought. Who knows if we have a cocaine heritage on our hands in Ghana, in search of heritage items on a new currency.

Our beloved country has now launched new currency bank notes, called the ‘heritage series’: a label we are scratching our heads to understand. Are the current cedi notes that weak and fragile, their batteries about to die? Or does the Bank of Ghana seek an excuse to print new money and fill the till to rescue 2028? ‘There is no money in the system,’ market women complain of low sales; so ‘let’s simply print more money and give it an elegant pseudonym, Heritage? Were the signs not clear? Did you notice the speed, the rush, the sense of urgency, and eventually the anti-climax: a comedy of errors on our sovereign cedi. National mourning, indeed, tears for a sinking Ghana.

For once, the entire public is part of this debate on our national heritage; and we are together debating wrong faces matched to human names on new currency notes; and we lament essentials missing in the national heritage.

Indeed, faces on our new cedi notes have sparked so much debate that we forget the likelihood that Artificial Intelligence may have fooled us all.

Let Ghana wait until rumours spread that the man we see as Kofi Annan on the new 100 cedi note is really not Kofi Annan but our friend Kevin Taylor; and that the lady displayed as Justice Annie Jiagge on the new 10 cedi note is ‘before God and man,’ probably Akosua Jollof? Simply imagine the stampede online.

It is now unclear whether the Bank of Ghana will swallow its pride and go back to school for remedial education: honouring the name Theodocia Okoh with the true Face of Theodocia Okoh, the true designer of the national flag. Letitia Obeng, the mistaken identity, was well known to us fellows of the Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences.

She was an award-winning scientist who, in 2006, succeeded Nana Dr S.K.B. Asante as the first female President of the Academy. ‘Auntie Leti’ must be stirring in her grave over her mixed identity with Theodosia.

Then comes, of late, a damning verdict on the picture representation of Cardinal Peter Dery on the two cedi note.

Says a worried Ghanaian: “It is simply disheartening and baffling that a national tribute meant to honour an iconic figure of our faith, the late Cardinal Peter Dery of blessed memory, could be marred by such a glaring oversight.”

Cardinal Peter Dery

Then was this blatant omission of five of the Big Six on the heritage bank notes, leaving a lone Kwame Nkrumah. Remember the Big Six statue in Accra was demolished in 2024 by an anonymous Ghanaian at dawn, who had enough time to videotape the entire event in full view of cheering spectators.

It was during the Nana Addo era. No arrests were made by the police, who were three hundred meters away. When the Mahama party won power in late 2024, the Big Six roundabout was redesigned, with the Big Six statue conspicuously deleted. The Big Six with Nkrumah, Danquah, Edward Akufo Addo, Obetsebi Lamptey, Ako Adjei, and William Ofori Atta, is apparently no longer a heritage priority? But wait till power changes hands in 2028; Ghana’s toy play may bounce back.

And what do we do with this bizarre incident? 2021 one Esther Bosha a Zimbabwean national and crew member of Emirate Air, visits Ghana as tourist, poses for a picture among market women in Accra; then says a word or two in praise of Ghana. A kind-hearted Bank of Ghana adds her picture among traders, as qualified to stick on Ghana’s one cedi banknote. Esther Bosha as Ghana’s heritage icon? Zimbabwe currently chuckles hearing this.

I myself visited Zimbabwe in 2006 and felt at home seeing Mugabe’s Zanu-PF headquarters in Harare, hoisting the Red Cockerel flag of Kwame Nkrumah’s CPP. I warmly applauded, but did that qualify me to appear on the Zimbabwean currency?

Where is our state protocol? Our parliament? Ghana, when did we drop the baton and lose the plot? And how did we sink this low? Our state emblems now run the ship of state aground, and all is quiet? Akom ko, the elders say. ‘The pristine dance of the high priest is no more, leaving the field for those that merely twirl around in raffia skirts…

Ghana is no longer the state we knew: now plunged into a crisis of identity, prewired with a badge of dishonour. We miserably flopped at the soccer World Cup, but beat our chest with pride, excelling in a global cocaine league. Daily news breaks of Drugs shipped through our ports, sometimes officially escorted. Our port officials see no cocaine, speak no cocaine, smell no cocaine and do no cocaine. But kids do cocaine at home and school. The scandal breaks only after the horse has left the stable…When cocaine arrests are made, no names and no faces.

Indeed, a silent cocaine prosecution in a nation that is not angry enough to crack the whip. Yes, we have a heritage to protect, and display on bank notes, but it is Negative Heritage.

A sordid heritage of moving sewage that was once called rivers; a heritage of toxic streams, poisoned crops, dangerous turbidity. No river has been spared, including the great Volta River, and with it the diverse fish species it hosts. The school kids are busy too, learning the sport of poisoning; they have abandoned school and now mine in poisonous waters.

After all this, we finally set our sights on the sea, to seal the shipment of floating sewage.

But we shouldn’t omit pedophilia among the emerging heritage. Our moral compass is gone; elders and security now look on while school kids are defiled. Is anybody home, Ghana?

A new cedi note has been launched in the filth of a negative heritage. That is the legacy we leave for future generations: the stench of cocaine across the landscape, in schools, a nation high on drugs, and a polluted banknote that says it all: A rotten heritage can only be returned to the Sender.

How much has Ghana lost in all this?

There is something they call Financial loss to the state. Hello Attorney General!

Ghana News.title: Ghanaian community leaders in Toronto urged to step up as gun violence claims young lives
Ghana News.content:
AI-generated illustration.

The growing number of young people losing their lives to gun violence in parts of Canada has prompted renewed calls for Ghanaian parents and community leaders to take a more active role in protecting the next generation.

The appeal, directed at parents, traditional authorities and community associations in Toronto, comes amid grief over the reported killings of young people, including Javits Frimpong in New York, 18-year-old Malik Abass in Toronto and, most recently, Brandon Blake in Etobicoke.

For Kwei Armah, a member of the Ghanaian community, the deaths should serve as a wake-up call to families and leaders who may not be paying enough attention to the challenges confronting young people growing up abroad.

In an emotional appeal, he urged parents to look beyond providing their children with material needs and become more involved in their everyday lives.

“Dear parents and leaders of our Ghanaian community, please wake up and take your children's and siblings' security seriously as the devil is at work!” he said.

He believes parents must make time to understand their children's experiences, friendships, difficulties and concerns, rather than assume that providing food, clothing and education is enough to secure their future.

“Please engage your children in more conversations as to how you can raise them well, train them well and educate them well by paying more attention to their needs than attending funerals, parties and barbecues,” he appealed.

His comments reflect growing concern about the vulnerability of some young people in immigrant communities, where parents may be balancing demanding work schedules, family responsibilities and the challenges of raising children in a different social environment.

For many Ghanaian families who moved to Canada in search of better opportunities, securing a brighter future for their children remains a central part of the migration dream.

But the recent deaths have brought a painful reminder that access to education, employment and other opportunities cannot guarantee a future if young people are exposed to violence and other dangers.

Another young life lost

The latest concern follows the fatal shooting of 18-year-old Brandon Blake of Barrie near Martin Grove Road and Finch Avenue West in Toronto.

According to a Toronto Police Service news release published on Wednesday, November 11, officers responded to reports of gunshots at about 12:56 a.m. on Tuesday, November 10.

Officers found Blake suffering from gunshot wounds. Despite life-saving efforts, he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Police said two suspects fled before officers arrived.

Investigators have identified 19-year-old Joseph Kunene of Toronto as a suspect wanted for first-degree murder. Police have released his photograph and described him as armed and dangerous.

A second suspect, described as a white male wearing black clothing, a hood and a face mask, remains unidentified.

The killing was recorded as Toronto's 34th homicide of 2026, according to the police release.

The deaths of Blake and Abass, alongside the reported killing of Frimpong in New York, have intensified concerns among sections of the Ghanaian community about the safety of young people.

Although the circumstances surrounding the separate incidents remain subject to police investigations, the tragedies have prompted questions about how families and community institutions can better support young people and help prevent violence.

A call for stronger community involvement

Mr Armah believes the responsibility for protecting young people should not rest with parents alone.

He is urging chiefs, religious leaders, community associations and other influential members of the Ghanaian diaspora to make youth welfare a consistent priority.

He argues that community engagement should go beyond organising social gatherings and coming together to mourn after a tragedy.

“Let our future leaders live. Brood over them, let them go to school and take advantage of the wonderful career opportunities that abound in this country,” he said.

His appeal is for more deliberate conversations, mentorship and guidance to help young people navigate the pressures and risks they encounter.

For Ghanaian community leaders, this could mean creating more opportunities for young people to speak openly about their experiences, connecting them with trusted mentors and strengthening support systems for families.

The challenge is to ensure that youth safety becomes a shared responsibility rather than an issue that receives attention only when another life is lost.

The Ghanaian community in Canada has worked over the years to preserve its cultural identity, support families and create opportunities for the next generation.

Mr Armah's message is that these efforts must also place greater emphasis on the safety, wellbeing and upbringing of young people.

His appeal is simple: parents must be present in their children's lives, community leaders must take a more active interest in their welfare, and families must act before another tragedy strikes.

Ghana News.title: The right diagnosis, an incomplete cure – Frimpong Boateng writes on 2027 budget
Ghana News.content:
Professor Kwabena Frimpong-Boateng

"These boom-and-bust cycles must cease"

On the evening of Thursday, November 12, 2026, the Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, when presenting the 2027 budget, told Parliament that Ghana's boom-and-bust cycles must cease. Few Ghanaians would disagree. Too many times we have lived through hope followed by hardship, a stable cedi followed by sharp depreciation, and a recovery followed by another crisis.

I have read the full 2027 Budget Statement, and I want to answer one question. Does the Minister appreciate why the boom-and-bust cycles happen, and does his New Economy programme remove the cause?

My answer is that the Minister has made the right diagnosis but prescribed an incomplete cure. The budget sees two causes clearly. It misses a third, and the third is the one that will bring the next bust.

What the budget gets right

The budget statement is more candid about the causes of our instability than most budgets before it. It says the cedi came under pressure "when prices dropped or fiscal discipline weakened" (para. 161). It concedes that "temporary booms had financed permanent commitments" (para. 168), and it blames reckless spending, weak revenue and expensive debt for the crisis of 2022.

Most importantly, the budget statement admits that past governments repaired the public finances "but did not use the recovery to alter the structure of the economy," and so "the cycle began again" (paras. 186–187). It even pledges that fiscal discipline "will apply throughout the election cycle" (para. 239).

So the Government does understand two causes: our dependence on raw commodity exports, and fiscal indiscipline. I accept both. My quarrel is with what is missing.

The machine that is not in the plan

Read the eight pillars of the New Economy and one thing stands out. The only imports the budget counts as a drain on the cedi are things we consume: rice, sugar, poultry, fish, vegetables and medicines. It says the food import bill "weakens the cedi" (para. 260). It promises that when Ghana grows and processes more, "the cedi will face less pressure" (para. 336). It demands that every cedi of fiscal space answer the question: "what imports will it replace?" (para. 191).

The budget never asks that question of the factories themselves. Throughout the statement, machines are things to buy and finance:

the "manufacturer investing in new machinery" is offered equipment leasing (paras. 228, 231);

the rice hubs receive tax incentives for "irrigation, mechanisation, silos, modern mills" (para. 276);

GH¢800 million is allocated "to procure agricultural machinery" (para. 1543);

the review of Chapter 98 of the Customs Tariff concerns duty concessions on imported "machinery and other inputs" (para. 860);

the textiles pillar promises jobs for machine operators, not machine makers (para. 448);

for the nuclear plant, "international partners will only provide technology, finance, engineering and specialist services" (para. 380).

Cocoa grinding mills, gold refineries, alumina plants, rice mills, garment lines and pharmaceutical plants are all capital goods. Ghana makes almost none of them, and few of their spare parts. Every one will be imported and paid for in dollars, and every one will be kept running with imported spares, also paid for in dollars.

The arithmetic

The budget's own figures show where the capacity to make machines stands in the Government's order of priorities.

2027 allocation

Amount

New Economy programme, 2027 outlay (para. 249)

GH¢30 billion

Procurement of agricultural machinery (para. 1543)

GH¢800 million

Completion of the Foundry and Machine Tooling Centre (para. 1582)

GH¢51 million

GRATIS Foundation, whole year, no capital expenditure (Appendix 4A)

about GH¢3 million

The Foundry and Machine Tooling Centre is the one line in this budget about making machines rather than buying them. The Centre dates from my time as Minister for Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation, and six years after I left office, it is still waiting to be completed. In 2027 it receives about 0.17 per cent of the New Economy outlay, and one-sixteenth of what we will spend on imported farm machinery in the same year. GRATIS, built to carry engineering capability into the regions, receives less than half of one per cent of the machinery budget.

Nothing in the New Economy programme is set aside for machine tools, foundries, spare parts or engineering manufacturing.

How the next bust will come

Suppose the New Economy succeeds exactly as planned. By 2030 Ghana processes all its cocoa, refines all its gold, processes all its manganese and bauxite and mills its own rice. Food imports fall, export earnings per tonne rise, and the cedi strengthens.

But each of those plants was built with imported equipment, and each needs a steady flow of imported spares, replacement parts and, in time, replacement machines. When a mill breaks down, it cannot wait for the cedi to recover. It must buy the part at whatever the exchange rate happens to be. This demand for foreign exchange is stubborn, and it grows with every factory we open.

The budget itself names commodity price volatility as the first of its five principal risks (para. 1025). When commodity prices next fall, export earnings will drop, but the bill for machines and spares will not. The cedi will come under pressure again, and the cycle will begin again, at a higher level of output but under the same ceiling. That is the trap of an economy that assembles but does not make. Value addition on imported capital goods moves the bottleneck; it does not remove it.

There is a fiscal test as well. The programme is financed partly by lowering the primary surplus target by one percentage point of GDP (para. 247), beginning in the year before an election. The Government will answer that a surplus of at least 0.5 per cent of GDP remains (para. 221), and that is a fair answer. But the pledge of discipline "throughout the election cycle" will be tested in 2028, and Ghanaians have heard such pledges before.

What a complete cure would require

The modern world economy is knowledge-based and driven by science and technology. Societies that produce, adapt and commercialise knowledge have achieved sustained growth and rising living standards. Raising money to pay foreign contractors to build infrastructure, good as the projects may be, cannot by itself lead to sustained economic development. Ghana has to develop the capacity to build the machines its industries run on.

The cure is not to abandon value addition. It is to add the pillar the plan lacks: the capacity to make the machines.

Make capital goods a ninth pillar of the New Economy, with its own budget, targets and delivery unit, as the other eight have.

Fund the Foundry and Machine Tooling Centre to operate, not merely to be completed, and link it to the processing enclaves as a supplier of spare parts.

Establish the Design and Manufacturing Technology Centre called for at the conference of Ghanaian scientists and engineers that the Ministry of Environment, Science, Technology and Innovation and the Ghana Institution of Engineering convened at Peduase in January 2019. The foundry can cast and machine parts; the Centre would let Ghana design the machines themselves, working with the processing enclaves on the equipment they need.

Apply the budget's own local-preference principle to machines. If public money spent on rice must buy Ghana rice (para. 283), public money spent on silos, mills, dryers and processing equipment should, where quality allows, buy from Ghanaian fabricators: Suame Magazine, the regional centres of GRATIS, KNUST's Technology Consultancy Centre, and the private engineers who have already shown what they can do.

Reform Chapter 98 so that duty concessions on imported machinery are matched by incentives to make the same machinery here, and are phased down as local capacity grows.

Judge every New Economy project by its import content, not only by the jobs and exports it creates.

The question every factory must answer

The Minister asked every cedi of fiscal space to say which imports it will replace. I ask the same question of every factory the New Economy will build. Until Ghana can make at least some of the machines that make its goods, our booms will be paid for in dollars we will not have when the bust comes.

The diagnosis in this budget is right. The cure is not yet complete.

Ghana News.title: GES warns public against fake teacher recruitment links circulating on social media
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Education Service (GES) has cautioned the public against fake teacher recruitment links circulating on social media, stressing that its recruitment exercise has not yet commenced.

In a statement issued on Sunday, November 15, the Service said it had received reports of links being shared across various social media platforms, falsely claiming to originate from the GES in connection with teacher recruitment.

Management clarified that the recruitment portal is not open and urged prospective applicants to disregard any messages or online forms purporting to be part of an official recruitment exercise.

"The public is assured that when the Service is ready to commence the recruitment exercise, an official announcement will be made through all its authorised communication channels," the statement read.

It further warned that individuals who access suspicious links or provide personal information through unofficial online forms without verifying their authenticity do so at their own risk.

GES advised the public to exercise caution and rely only on its official communication platforms for information regarding future teacher recruitment.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Africa CDC says Ebola outbreak in DR Congo ‘still not under control’
World.content:
‘If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak,’ Africa ​CDC director says.

Share Africa CDC says Ebola outbreak in DR Congo ‘still not under control’ on social media

Africa’s top public health agency says the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is still not under control six months after it was declared.

“If we don’t stop this outbreak now, it would be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have,” Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told Reuters news agency on Sunday.

Since the outbreak was announced on May 15, more than 11,200 cases and 5,500 deaths have been recorded, according to government data.

Kaseya said that more than “80 percent of ‌new cases emerge outside contact lists and over 65 percent of deaths” have occurred in the community outside health centres.

Cases have now been reported in East, Central and West Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.

“We are all in agreement today to say that this outbreak is still serious, and is ⁠still not under control,” Kaseya said.

The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which can trigger haemorrhagic fever.

It is the second-largest and second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, behind only the 2014-2016 West African outbreak. That epidemic infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000.

Eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces have been affected in the ongoing outbreak, and many deaths have occurred outside treatment centres.

Delayed detection, conflict and strained health services have led to a more rapid spread of the virus than in previous outbreaks.

Kaseya said coordination between DRC and donors remained a problem, calling it “a collective failure”.



Only $1.3bn of the $2.9bn pledged by donors to fight Ebola has been released, according to Kaseya.

“We are not pointing fingers,” he said, adding that Africa CDC was working closely with Kinshasa to ensure money isn’t wasted ‌through ‌duplication and that the DRC was working to digitise the payroll to health workers who “hadn’t been paid for months”.

Containment has been especially difficult because no vaccine or treatment has been developed specifically for the Bundibugyo strain, which kills about half of the people it infects.

Earlier this month, the World Health Organization (WHO) approved clinical trials of two new Ebola vaccines and said it expected results in early 2027.

“Transmission is slowing in several early epicentres, and clinical trials, including the Tumaini trial and new vaccine candidates, are advancing rapidly”, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote in a post on X.

The WHO said at least 3,000 people have recovered from Ebola virus disease in DRC and returned home.

World.title: Prince Harry in Ukraine meeting Invictus 2027 hopefuls
World.content:
British Royal says he’s ‘taken a risk’ in fourth surprise visit to Ukraine since 2022 to meet wounded veterans.

Britain’s Prince Harry has met wounded veterans and medics in Ukraine during a surprise visit.

The royal family member attended Ukraine’s National Invictus Games and a conference for medics in the western city of Lviv on Saturday. It was organised by Superhumans, a clinic that specialises in the rehabilitation of war-wounded.

“Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth,” Harry said, adding that he’d “taken a risk to come here”.

Ukraine has about 1.4 million combat veterans, more than 10 percent of whom have disabilities.

“You’re going to win the war,” the 42-year-old British royal said during his fourth trip to the country since the start of the conflict with Russia in 2022.

The prince watched wheelchair rugby players competing for a place in Ukraine’s team for next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham in England.

Around 500 people have registered to compete to qualify for the 60-member squad – the largest ever team – that Ukraine is planning to send to the 2027 event.

“You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success,” he said.

Prince Harry is the founder and patron of the Invictus Games Foundation, which he established in 2014 to support wounded, injured and recovering military service personnel and veterans through adaptive sports, e-sports and recovery programmes.

“When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,” Harry told wounded veterans later on Saturday.

At a rugby game, he hugged Valery Odainyk, a contestant at the Invictus Games in Canada last year. The leg amputee is “still an active serviceman” in the Ukrainian forces.



“So when do you find time to train?” Harry asked in surprise.

The 41-year-old Odainyk said he told Harry that his involvement in disability sport “all started and continues with the Invictus Games.”

They feature a mix of adaptive core and winter sports, such as alpine skiing, archery, track and field, cycling, wheelchair basketball, rugby and tennis.

World.title: Estonia to close border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker
World.content:
Eight arrests made in connection with an attempted arson, which Tallinn says was ordered by Russian intelligence.

Share Estonia to close border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker on social media

Estonia will close its border crossings with Russia, after an attack on an Estonian defence company that Tallinn blames on Moscow.

The foreign minister made the announcement on Sunday, after eight people were detained overnight in connection with an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.

Estonian authorities said the attacks had been ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence. There was no immediate comment from Moscow.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote on X, “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.

“Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia’s ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention.”

He did not specify how long the border closure would last.

Latvia’s Interior Minister Janis Dombrava thanked Estonia’s Internal Security Service on X, saying that several “Latvian citizens and non-citizens” were arrested.

“Since the collapse of the USSR, there have been people among us who are willing to commit serious crimes in Russia’s interests. We will continue our work to ensure that such people cannot endanger the lives of those who love Latvia and want to live in safety,” Dombrava wrote.

‘Shadow war’

Estonia, a European Union and NATO member state and a strong ally of Ukraine, currently has three open border crossings with Russia at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula.

Marko Mihkelson, chairman of the Estonian Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, told Al Jazeera that the arrests demonstrated that Estonia was “prepared to respond swiftly to such attacks”.



“It is essential that Russia’s state-sponsored campaign of terror does not remain merely a matter of diplomatic protests, either in Estonia or among our allies elsewhere,” Mihkelson said.

“Russia is waging a shadow war to divide Europe and undermine support for Ukraine. European countries must respond with asymmetric measures of their own. Closing borders with Russia is one such measure.”

Nearly 1,500 migrants reach Spain’s Canary Islands in one day

NewsFeed Nearly 1,500 migrants reach Spain’s Canary Islands in one day

Nearly 1,500 migrants were rescued off Spain’s Canary Islands in a single day, marking the highest daily total since 2020. A total of 1,488 people arrived in 14 boats, with most coming from Senegal, The Gambia and Guinea.

World.title: Morocco becomes first Arab nation in FIFA’s top five men’s rankings
World.content:
Morocco becomes the only Arab country, and first African nation since Nigeria in 1994, to be ranked fifth in the world.

Share Morocco becomes first Arab, second African nation in FIFA’s top five on social media

Morocco have become the first Arab country to enter FIFA’s top five men’s team rankings after moving up by two places from their previous best position of number seven.

The two-time World Cup quarterfinalists leapt ahead of Brazil and Portugal on points on Sunday, following their strong performance in recent continental football matches.

Morocco are also the first African and Arab country to reach back-to-back quarterfinals at the World Cup, where the continent’s top-ranked nation was knocked out by France in consecutive tournaments.

The Atlas Lions’ 2026 finish did not improve or match their semifinal run at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where they surpassed all expectations to become Africa and the Arab world’s first semifinalists and the darlings of the tournament.

Following the World Cup in North America, Mohamed Ouhabi’s team have maintained a 100 percent record in the current round of qualifying matches for the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) 2027.

Morocco thumped Niger 5-0 in their latest qualification match on Friday, as the star-studded lineup shone in front of a raucous home crowd in Rabat.

AFCON’s defending champions lead Group A by nine points.

However, their AFCON title is contentious and is subject to a hearing at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) following an appeal by losing finalists Senegal.

Senegal were stripped of this year’s AFCON title and Morocco were declared champions by the Confederation of African Football (CAF), despite Senegal beating the hosts ⁠⁠⁠⁠1-0 after extra time in January’s final in Rabat.



Senegal walked off the pitch for 14 minutes ‌‌‌‌after a penalty was awarded against them late in regulation time, with several players returning to the dressing room in protest before they resumed play.

Morocco missed the spot kick, sending the match into extra time, where Senegal scored the winner to secure victory.

However, they were stripped of the title two months later after CAF’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match by walking off the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 victory to ⁠⁠⁠⁠Morocco.

The controversial 2025 title was the northwestern African side’s second AFCON title since 1976.

Morocco is one of the cohost nations for the FIFA World Cup 2030.

World.title: Israel Kidnapped Iranian Generals in Hunt for Ron Arad
World.content:
Gen. Abdullah Saberi, an Iranian commander, stepped out for a jog early one morning in an upscale diplomatic quarter of Syria’s capital. Israeli intelligence officers waited nearby. Posing as movers, they had slipped past the neighborhood’s security checkpoints.

As he headed for a nearby park, General Saberi passed two men who carried an oversize refrigerator box. In a flash, the men restrained the general, drugged him, threw the box over his head, shoved him into a white van and left as if nothing had happened.

He was whisked to Israel for interrogation, according to numerous officials in the Middle East, including senior Iranian officials close to General Saberi and a Syrian official who reviewed video of the September 2021 kidnapping.

As a veteran of Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, General Saberi knew many secrets. But his interrogators were interested in only one.

World.title: In Banff, a Grizzly Bear Known as ‘the Boss’ Rules the National Park
World.content:
To the scientists and wardens of Banff National Park he is grizzly bear 122. But to everyone who lives in or near Canada’s oldest national park, and many of its 4.5 million annual visitors, he is the Boss.

He has been struck by a freight train without apparent ill effect. He has shrugged off being hit by cars. Scientists have confirmed that he killed and snacked on a black bear at least once, and he is believed to have fathered many, if not most, of the bears in his 2,000-square-kilometer territory.

Most of all, the Boss has become Canada’s 700-pound celebrity bear king. When he strolls along the Trans-Canada Highway looking for dandelions, “bear jams” swiftly follow. His battles with a rival bear known as Split Lip are legendary. (He caused the split lip.) His annual awakening from hibernation, usually in March, is reported by news outlets across Alberta.

World.title: Iran Attacks Bahrain for the Second Time in Days
World.content:
A spokesman for Iran’s Foreign Ministry, Esmaeil Baghaei, said on Sunday that Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the United States or others.

Asked in a news conference in Tehran whether the Iranian attack in Bahrain signified a change to the country’s approach, and whether Iran was still awaiting an official American response in the negotiations, Mr. Baghaei said that Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on safeguarding its security.

Mr. Trump has zigzagged over whether or not he might order a return to full-blown war. The initial campaign failed to compel Iran to abandon its nuclear program but did ensnarl global energy markets, which contributed to a resounding defeat for the Republican Party in the recent midterm elections.

It is far from clear whether a new U.S. or Israeli attack on Iran could force Tehran to make new concessions. The country has said it has rebuilt its military capabilities during the truce, and U.S. and Israeli officials will also have to consider whether they are willing or able to contend with Iranian missile and drone attacks across the Middle East, given their depleted stores of aerial interceptors.

Mediators from Qatar and Pakistan have shuttled to Tehran in recent weeks in an effort to avert a return to all-out war. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, will travel to Pakistan and Oman in the coming days, Mr. Baghaei said on Sunday.

World.title: Saudi-Backed Forces Retreat in Yemen, Leaving Key Strait in Houthi Control
World.content:
Forces backed by Saudi Arabia in Yemen said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from the country’s Red Sea coast, where they have been fighting for weeks to retake strategic territory from the Iran-aligned Houthi militia.

A group of fighters called the Southern Armed Forces, who are allied with the government of Yemen, said in a statement that they were “redeploying” to protect the interim capital, Aden, citing recent battlefield developments and “threats targeting” the city.

Aden has been the seat of the internationally recognized government for more than a decade, since the Houthis seized control of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital.

The retreat is a blow for the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia as the balance of power in Yemen continues to tilt toward the Houthis, analysts said.

World.title: Is Italy the Model for Europe’s Future?
World.content:
When I first moved to Rome, I spent my time living in the past.

At the turn of the century, I drifted through a vintage postcard of postwar Italy: old women sitting around tables they had dragged into the street, old men playing cards in caps, cats arching their backs on the hoods of snub-nosed Fiats.

As newspapers filled with talk of Silvio Berlusconi, a media mogul with ambitions and appetites worthy of a Roman emperor, my meanderings inevitably took me toward Tiber Island, a sliver of land in the middle of the river that divides Rome.

An ancient bridge on the island’s left bank had a strange statue of weather-beaten faces positioned back-to-back as if they couldn’t stand one another. The heads rose out of the shared torso of a square pillar and represented Janus, Rome’s god of the past and future, the deity of transitions and change.

World.title: In Europe, an Emboldened Iran Contributes to a Sense of Anxiety
World.content:
On Veterans Day this past week, President Trump declared that his decision to go to war with Iran had been a complete success.

“When this conflict is over, and it will be soon,” he said, speaking on a blustery morning from Arlington National Cemetery outside Washington, “the entire world will be a much safer and better place, more peaceful place.”

That is not how it feels in Europe.

A growing number of attempted terrorist attacks across the continent and in Britain, including a foiled plot against a major American military base, arson attacks on Jewish community sites and cyberattacks that raised temperatures in refrigerators and blood banks are rattling national security officials and unnerving the public. Many have been attributed to Iran or to proxies acting on its behalf.

The sense of global unease was heightened when the U.S. government grounded all air travel for hours on Friday in what officials later said was a technical issue.

World.title: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
World.content:
Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.

“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.

But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.

“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”

World.title: ‘Get Focused on London’: How Iran’s Agents Attacked European Targets
World.content:
Within days of the war starting, Mr. al-Hassani and at least two associates, including an operative for Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, began plotting the attacks in Europe, prosecutors said. The men talked about procuring drones and missiles from contacts in Iran. They pored over a map of London, with one saying they should “get focused” on targeting the British capital. Soon after, attacks hit temples and other Jewish sites in London.

In the fight against much stronger conventional forces, Iran has found ways to impose costs on its adversaries without inviting a full military response. One major aspect of Iran’s strategy is its embrace of small-time criminals to conduct low-cost assaults against vulnerable targets that are part of everyday life.

Since the U.S.-Israeli war began, Iran and its proxies — who sometimes act on their own — have stepped up such attacks, particularly in Britain, which has allowed the United States to use its military bases to strike Iranian forces. By hitting American allies, Iran aims to sow fear and try to weaken their support for the U.S. and Israeli military deployments, experts said.

“What we are seeing right now is the application of a playbook Iran has refined over decades,” said Adrian Shtuni, an associate fellow with the International Center for Counter-Terrorism. In addition to the criminal attacks, he also cited Iran’s efforts to build proxy militant networks outside Iran and enhance its abilities to carry out cyberattacks.

World.title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
World.content:
Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.

The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.

Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".

It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.

The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.

On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".

"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.

On Friday Zelensky said speed limits of around 100mph had been enforced on the network since Monday, but only in Russian-occupied areas and not the whole of Ukraine.

"It already has political implications. If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporary occupied territories as not ours," the New York Times reported him as saying.

World.title: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
World.content:
Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.

The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.

Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".

It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.

The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.

Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.

As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.

Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."

In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."

Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.

The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.

Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

World.title: Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over fatal church mass shooting
World.content:
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.

The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.

Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts".

The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.

Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.

CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.

World.title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
World.content:
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.

The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.

Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.

"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.

He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.

"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.

The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.

The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".

Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.

The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

World.title: Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America.

Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory".

On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire.

There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love."

The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope.

He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.

Read more on the significance of the Pope's visit to Peru

World.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
World.content:
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

World.title: Czechs rally against plan to switch funding of public media
World.content:
Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the licence fee and use the state budget to fund public media.

Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom.

The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.

Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests.

Czech households currently pay â 205 crowns ($9.44; Â£7.06) a month for public TV and radio.

Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended.

"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency.

"If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."

World.title: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay
World.content:
Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage.

Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend.

The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (Â£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP.
