Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (Â£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis.

On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in.

A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.

Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out.

He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest".

World.title: JUST IN: Gov Sanwo-Olu rewards Flamingos with ₦300 million, iPhones
World.content:
Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu has announced a ₦300 million reward for Nigeria’s victorious U-17 women’s national team, the Flamingos, following their historic triumph at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco.

Under the package announced Sunday at the Lagos House in Marina, each player and member of the coaching crew will receive ₦10 million.

The players will get an iPhone and headphones along with the cash reward.

The latest reward adds to the recognition and financial incentives the team has received following its historic achievement, which made Nigeria the first African country to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.

The development comes days after President Bola Tinubu announced a ₦100 million Federal Government Savings Bond for each squad member at a reception for the team in Abuja.

The President also approved ₦100 million in cash for head coach Akeem Ishola Busari, while the technical crew received ₦50 million each.

The First Lady, Oluremi Tinubu, announced the package on the President’s behalf on 11 November.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Senate had also pledged ₦100 million to the team in recognition of its achievement.

How the Flamingos made history

The Flamingos secured their first FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup title after defeating Japan 2-1 in the final in Rabat on 7 November.

Nigeria took the lead through Awawu Bashiru in the 39th minute before Oluebube Umejiaku doubled the advantage shortly after the restart.

Japan reduced the deficit through Fuki Ito in the 80th minute but could not find an equaliser as Nigeria held on to claim the trophy. Umejiaku was named Player of the Match.

The victory in Morocco was particularly remarkable because Nigeria recovered from a 2-1 defeat to Poland in their opening match to win six consecutive games.

They subsequently defeated Puerto Rico and defending champions Korea DPR in the group stage before overcoming Mexico and Venezuela in the knockout rounds.

The team then beat Brazil 3-1 in the semi-finals to reach its first final in the competition, where the victory over Japan secured the title.

Nigeria’s victory also marked the first time an African country had won the tournament since its introduction in 2008.

While the various awards by the Federal Government and now the Lagos State government have been applauded, the need to sustain investment in women’s football and the development of emerging talents has also been advocated for by key industry figures.

World.title: 2027: Political violence could ruin investor confidence ahead of elections – CPPE
World.content:
The Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise (CPPE) has warned that mounting political violence, intimidation and inflammatory rhetoric ahead of the 2027 general elections could erode investor confidence.

The free enterprise advocacy group also cautioned on Sunday about the adverse implications of the trend for businesses and economic stability if the current wave of political unrest spirals out of control.

It urged political leaders, political parties and state institutions to exercise restraint, uphold the rule of law and shield the business environment from the consequences of political tensions.

Muda Yusuf, its CEO, made the call in a policy brief on Sunday, following reports of attacks on opposition parties’ political gatherings earlier this month.

“Political violence must be unequivocally denounced, regardless of its perpetrators or beneficiaries. Electoral ambition must never take precedence over the security of lives, property and investments,” the group said.

Politically motivated violence does not merely threaten democratic governance, it noted, but also risks investment, business operations, employment, and economic growth.

It warned that political instability could discourage new investments, delay business expansion plans, and increase the risk premiums investors sometimes demand for extra comfort in a tense political climate.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to CPPE, political clashes, insecurity, and violent protests can disrupt supply chains, logistics, and market access, while prolonged instability could accelerate capital flight and intensify foreign exchange volatility.

It said the economic impact could be particularly severe for small businesses, informal enterprises and investors with significant fixed assets that could not be easily relocated.

Institutional neutrality

CPPE called on security agencies to act proactively and impartially to forestall violence and ensure that perpetrators and their sponsors are held accountable.

It stressed the significance of protecting the independence and neutrality of key state institutions, notably the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), security agencies, the judiciary, regulatory bodies and the civil service.

“The politicisation of these institutions creates risks that extend well beyond the electoral process,” the group asserted.

“It weakens the rule of law, undermines regulatory predictability, increases the perception of arbitrary government action and erodes confidence in the protection of investments and contractual rights.”

The organisation further said INEC must operate independently and professionally, free of political interference. At the same time, security agencies should protect political actors, electoral officials, citizens, and economic assets without partiality.

It also urged the judiciary to remain independent and accessible to resolve electoral disputes on time, warning against using regulatory and law enforcement institutions for political intimidation or partisan advantage.

To prevent political tensions from undermining economic activities, the organisation outlined five priority actions for political leaders and state institutions.

These include adopting zero tolerance for political violence, protecting institutional independence, promoting responsible political communication, safeguarding economic activities and preserving policy and administrative stability.

CPPE urged political leaders to place national economic stability above partisan interests, insisting that Nigeria’s democracy should be strengthened through credible institutions and peaceful political competition rather than violence and institutional partisanship.

Earlier, PREMIUM TIMES reported incidents of political violence ahead of the 2027 general elections, including attacks on opposition supporters at a town hall meeting in Lagos on Thursday and Peter Obi’s convoy in Cross River on 4 November.

Violent clashes during Nigerian Democratic Congress and Obidient Movement processions on 7 November in Asaba left one person dead and five others injured.

World.title: How to grow Africa’s fashion industry, by CAFA
World.content:
The Confederation of African Fashion (CAFA) has called for increased investment in manufacturing, improved access to finance and stronger market connections to unlock the economic potential of Africa’s fashion industry.

The organisation made the call during the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) WKND 2026, recently held in Lagos, where industry discussions focused on the structures required to expand Africa’s creative economy.

Although Africa has a large pool of fashion designers, artisans and entrepreneurs, the industry still faces challenges, including limited textile manufacturing capacity, inadequate infrastructure and difficulty accessing finance and international markets.

CAFA said addressing these gaps was essential to building a competitive fashion industry capable of creating jobs, expanding trade and retaining more economic value within the continent.

Strengthening manufacturing capacity

Speaking at the event, CAFA’s Mission Coordinator, Reginald Ekeanyanwu, highlighted the need to make large-scale fashion manufacturing more accessible to emerging and established designers.

He said improving production infrastructure, manufacturing standards and market opportunities would help African fashion businesses compete more effectively.

The organisation is pursuing this objective through its Seed to Wear Programme, a 10-pillar roadmap designed to strengthen different segments of the African fashion value chain.

The programme covers cotton cultivation, fibre processing, textile production, fashion design, financing, and distribution.

According to CAFA, developing these interconnected sectors would help address existing production gaps and create a more sustainable manufacturing ecosystem.

Investment critical to industry growth

The discussions at CANEX also highlighted the importance of financing in expanding Africa’s fashion industry.

Investments are needed to improve textile production, modernise factories, introduce new technologies and establish distribution networks capable of serving larger markets.

CANEX WKND brought together creative entrepreneurs, investors, financial institutions, and other industry players to explore opportunities to develop Africa’s creative industries.

Its business programme, which included a Finance Summit and Deal Room, provided a platform to connect creative businesses with potential investors and financing opportunities.

For CAFA, attracting investment into the fashion industry requires looking beyond individual designers and collections to the wider infrastructure needed to support production and trade.

Seeking access to global markets

CAFA also identified market access and regional cooperation as important priorities for the industry’s development.

It is advancing this agenda through its African Fashion Industry Growth Charter, which seeks to promote policy alignment and cooperation among African countries.

The initiative is expected to support efforts to address barriers affecting manufacturing, investment and trade across the continent.

The organisation is also advocating stronger industry standards, intellectual property protection and distribution systems to improve the competitiveness of African fashion products.

These initiatives support CAFA’s ambition to grow Africa’s fashion economy from an estimated $60 billion to $500 billion by 2036.

Next steps

CAFA’s participation in CANEX WKND 2026 provided an opportunity to present its industry development agenda to manufacturers, investors, policymakers and other players in the creative economy.

The organisation said continued engagement with these groups would be necessary to translate discussions on manufacturing, financing and market access into practical partnerships.

Achieving a more competitive African fashion industry, it added, would require coordinated efforts from governments, manufacturers, financial institutions, designers and investors.

World.title: 2027: Governor Namadi flags off zonal campaign in Gumel, receive defectors
World.content:
The All Progressives Congress (APC) in Jigawa State has kicked off its 2027 governorship and presidential campaigns, with Governor Umar Namadi calling on supporters to deliver massive votes for President Bola Tinubu and all APC candidates in the state.

Starting in the North-West Senatorial District, the campaign took the party’s mobilisation drive to Gumel, where the governor presented APC flags to candidates contesting on the party’s platform and received over 1,000 defectors.

Addressing supporters, Governor Namadi renewed his commitment to education, job creation, agricultural development, and youth empowerment, maintaining that his administration remains focused on improving the lives of ordinary citizens.

According to the governor, his administration has fulfilled its previous campaign promises, and he pledged to generate more employment, strengthen the agricultural sector, and expand economic opportunities across the state.

Delivering a message on behalf of President Tinubu, Governor Namadi announced Federal Government plans to establish agricultural warehouses in Jigawa to improve the storage of farm produce. He noted that a committee has been constituted to drive the initiative, alongside efforts to encourage private companies to purchase produce directly from farmers at competitive prices.

He added that this measure will reduce post-harvest losses, shield farmers from poor market pricing, and boost their earnings. Consequently, the governor urged farmers to increase production, assuring them of sustained federal support.

Prior to arriving at the campaign venue, Governor Namadi paid homage to the Emir of Gumel to seek royal blessings for the political engagement.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The rally subsequently drew a large crowd of supporters who welcomed the governor with party flags and chants backing President Tinubu and other APC candidates.

In his remarks, the Jigawa APC Chairman, Ahmad Garba, stated that the party will sustain its development programmes if re-elected and urged residents to vote for all APC candidates. Similarly, the Director-General of the state campaign council, Lawan Yau Roni, highlighted the administration’s 12-point development agenda as evidence of the party’s dedication to Jigawa’s progress.

Other party leaders and political stakeholders also used the platform to appeal for voter support, emphasising the need for continuity in governance.

A major highlight of the event was the defection of 1,103 members of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) to the APC—a development the ruling party described as a major boost to its political strength ahead of the 2027 general election.

The Gumel rally marks the commencement of the APC’s zonal campaign tour as the party seeks to consolidate its grassroots base and secure another mandate in Jigawa State.

World.title: ‘Why Nigeria may miss gas flaring stop date’ – NUPRC
World.content:
Ibrahim Illo, a senior manager in the Sustainability, Health, Safety and Environment Department of the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC), disclosed this in an interview with PREMIUM TIMES at the ongoing COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye.

Mr Illo said that although the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) provides mechanisms to discourage gas flaring and promote the commercial use of associated gas, financing remains a challenge for operators seeking to execute gas utilisation projects.

“Some of the operating companies are also making an effort to see how they can source funds to execute this project,” he said.

“Oil and gas projects are not cheap projects; you need funding.”

He attributed the financing difficulty partly to the global energy transition, which he said was constraining funding for fossil fuel projects.

Mr Illo said the NUPRC was participating in international climate discussions, including COP31, to present Nigeria’s initiatives and government commitments and explore opportunities for collaboration to support emissions reduction.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nigeria’s gas-flaring record

The financing concerns come amid a deterioration in Nigeria’s recent gas-flaring performance.

The World Bank’s 2025 Global Gas Flaring Tracker reported that Nigeria’s gas flaring increased by 12 per cent in 2024, marking the second consecutive year of rising volumes.

The country recorded an eight per cent increase in flaring intensity, from 11 cubic metres per barrel of oil produced in 2023 to 12 cubic metres in 2024, more than twice the global average.

The report attributed 60 per cent of Nigeria’s gas flaring in 2024, and 75 per cent of the increase recorded that year, to facilities operated by the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) and several smaller, mainly indigenous companies.

It noted that some of these companies might lack the technical expertise and funding required to undertake capital-intensive gas utilisation projects.

The report also identified the commercial and regulatory challenges associated with using captured gas for electricity generation, alongside limited project financing and infrastructure constraints.

Nigeria has previously struggled to meet its gas-flaring commitments.

In 2016, the country launched the Nigerian Gas Flare Commercialisation Programme (NGFCP), targeting 2020 as the deadline for ending routine gas flaring. The target was missed, and the programme subsequently faced implementation delays.

Nigeria also endorsed the World Bank’s Zero Routine Flaring by 2030 initiative in June 2016.

Regulatory measures

Despite the implementation challenges, Mr Illo said the PIA had strengthened the regulatory framework for addressing gas flaring by empowering the commission to take ownership of gas that operators would otherwise flare and make it available to third parties willing to utilise it.

He said the provision had deterred operators, while the law also required oil and gas companies to pursue gas monetisation.

Under Section 105(2) of the PIA, the NUPRC has the right to take, free of charge, natural gas destined for flaring and make it available for commercialisation.

The 2023 Gas Flaring, Venting and Methane Emissions (Prevention of Waste and Pollution) Regulations also require producers to submit plans to eliminate and monetise gas flaring, maintain emissions records, and comply with reporting requirements.

However, PREMIUM TIMES reported in an October 2026 investigation that implementing the anti-flaring framework faced regulatory delays and gaps in methane monitoring.

The investigation found that the NUPRC issued permits to 28 companies in December 2025 to commercialise flare gas, more than four years after the PIA was enacted.

It also found gaps in the commission’s publication of emissions data and in operators’ submission of mandatory methane information, raising concerns about monitoring compliance with existing regulations.

Mr Illo said reducing emissions would require sustained cooperation among government agencies, operators and other stakeholders.

He also cautioned that climate action would not end with the 2030 deadline.

“Climate change issues are continuous. Even if you get to 2030, there will still be emission reduction efforts that we need to do,” he said.

Host community obligations

Beyond gas flaring, Mr Illo said the PIA introduced provisions to address environmental degradation and improve conditions in communities hosting oil and gas operations.

He identified host community development, environmental remediation and the decommissioning of oil and gas facilities as key measures under the Act.

Under Chapter Three of the PIA, oil and gas companies must contribute three per cent of their annual operating expenditure to host community development trusts.

The funds are intended to finance projects identified through community needs assessments, including healthcare, education and infrastructure.

Mr Illo said more than 174 host community development trusts had been incorporated across oil-producing areas, with some already implementing and commissioning projects.

He added that the framework had improved cooperation between communities and operators and helped reduce vandalism of oil and gas assets.

Asked how the commission holds operating companies accountable for fulfilling these obligations, Mr Illo said compliance was built into the regulatory approval process.

He explained that companies must incorporate host community development trusts and commit to environmental remediation and decommissioning plans before their field development plans can be approved.

He also said operators were required to make financial provisions for environmental restoration in the event of pollution incidents and for the decommissioning of facilities after production ends.

However, he did not provide specific examples of enforcement actions or sanctions against companies that failed to meet their environmental and host community obligations.

World.title: Ebola: DRC cases surpass 11,000; insecurity hampers response
World.content:
Insecurity has been identified as one of the “greatest obstacles” to containing the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where more than 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths have been reported.

The World Health Organisation (WHO), in a news release published on 15 November, said attacks on health workers and facilities, displacement and difficulties reaching remote communities were disrupting efforts to contain the outbreak.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, has spread to 67 health zones across eight provinces, with between 400 and 500 new cases reported weekly.

“Children account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and one third of deaths. Seven in 10 children under five with confirmed Ebola have died,” it noted.

Attack on healthcare

According to the WHO, a recent armed attack in Cantine-Aloya killed 66 civilians, including three health workers, while three health facilities were looted.

The attack also resulted in more than 1,000 contacts being lost to follow-up, with three confirmed cases still unaccounted for. Another attack on the town was reported on 11 November.

According to WHO, more than 80 attacks on healthcare have been recorded since the outbreak was declared.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“A halt in hostilities is urgently needed to protect communities and health workers, and to safeguard the progress made over the past six months,” it noted.

The WHO said about two-thirds of confirmed deaths occurred in communities, suggesting that many infections were being identified too late for patients to receive timely treatment.

Cross-border transmission concerns

WHO also highlighted the risk of the outbreak spreading beyond the DRC, following recent imported cases in Kenya and Nigeria.

The agency said cross-border collaboration has strengthened surveillance, information-sharing and coordination among affected and at-risk countries.

“Recent imported cases in Kenya and Nigeria underscore the continuing risk of spread beyond national borders. Delays in paying frontline health workers and responders create tension and slow the response,” it said.

WHO said the developments underscored the need for neighbouring countries to maintain surveillance and preparedness, particularly around high-risk border areas.

Response gains

Despite the challenges, WHO said efforts had slowed transmission in some of the outbreak’s initial hotspots, including Mongbwalu, Nyankunde, Nizi, Rwampara and Butembo.

Diagnostic capacity has expanded from two laboratories to more than two dozen, while nearly 2,000 treatment beds are available across 104 treatment and transit centres.

About 3,000 people have recovered from the disease, while more than 17,000 community health workers and 46,000 community actors have been trained to support the response.

WHO said sustained funding, safe access for health workers and greater community participation would be essential to reaching areas that remain difficult to access and bringing the outbreak under control.

READ ALSO: WHO urges concrete action on antimicrobial resistance worldwide

Nigeria records no new infections

In Nigeria, the index patient evacuated to Switzerland has recovered and been discharged from hospital. At the same time, all 62 people identified as contacts have completed the mandatory 21-day monitoring period without any secondary infection.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) disclosed this on 13 November, saying the patient tested negative for the virus after receiving further treatment in Switzerland.

NCDC Director-General, Jide Idris, said 13 of the 62 contacts developed fever or other symptoms during monitoring, but all tested negative. Seven suspected Ebola cases reported in five states were also investigated, with none testing positive.

“However, it is important to note that the completion of contact monitoring does not, by itself, constitute a formal declaration that an outbreak is over. Such a determination must be based on the applicable public health criteria and the findings of ongoing surveillance,” it noted.

“Nigeria therefore remains vigilant, particularly given the continued occurrence of Ebola virus disease in the DRC.”

World.title: WHO urges concrete action on antimicrobial resistance worldwide
World.content:
The World Health Organisation (WHO) has emphasised the need for countries to translate global commitments to tackle antimicrobial resistance (AMR) into concrete action.

It warned that inadequate financing, weak surveillance and poor coordination continue to undermine progress.

The call comes as the world prepares to mark World AMR Awareness Week (WAAW), from 18 to 24 November, against the backdrop of an estimated 4.7 million deaths associated with bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2021.

“AMR is one of the most urgent global health threats and development challenges. It threatens our ability to treat infections, protect animal and plant health, and produce safe food, and also has an impact on the environment,” said Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, Director a.i. (ad interim) of WHO’s Department of Antimicrobial Resistance.

Mr Nyemazi spoke at the sixth Annual Global Media Forum on AMR, ahead of this year’s awareness week, themed “One Health, One Action: Prevent AMR Now”.

He said the figures represent real consequences for patients, families, farmers and communities, stressing the need to move beyond global commitments to practical action.

“However, let’s be honest. The gap between commitments and pledges versus implementation remains wide,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

At the 2024 United Nations General Assembly High-Level Meeting on AMR, world leaders adopted a political declaration committing to reduce deaths from bacterial AMR by 10 per cent by 2030, from a 2019 baseline of 4.95 million.

They also pledged to ensure that at least 60 per cent of countries have funded national AMR action plans by 2030 and called for at least $100 million in catalytic funding, including through the AMR Multi-Partner Trust Fund.

Gaps undermining progress

WHO’s Senior Technical Officer and Lead of Multisectoral Coordination in its AMR Department, Kefas Samson, said progress remained uneven across countries.

He identified inadequate financing, gaps in surveillance of antimicrobial resistance and use, weak infection prevention in healthcare facilities, limited diagnostic capacity and unequal access to quality-assured medicines as major challenges.

Mr Samson said WHO is supporting governments to assess their needs, cost interventions and adapt their plans to local circumstances and available resources.

The organisation is also strengthening surveillance to track implementation of the updated Global Action Plan on AMR for 2026–2036 and measure progress towards the 2030 targets.

Other targets include ensuring that 70 per cent of antibiotics used in human health belong to WHO’s Access group, which comprises antibiotics recommended for first- and second-choice treatment of common infections.

Countries are also expected to strengthen their capacity to test for priority bacterial and fungal pathogens, with a target of at least 80 per cent of countries having the required testing capacity by 2030.

Mr Samson described the updated global action plan as a framework for translating the 2024 political declaration into measurable action at country level. The plan adopts a One Health approach, bringing together human, animal, agricultural and environmental sectors.

Livestock, environmental concerns

The Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO) warned that failure to improve animal health and farming practices could further increase antimicrobial use.

Junxia Song, FAO’s Deputy Chief Veterinarian and Chief of its One Health and Disease Control Branch, said global antibiotic use in livestock could rise by nearly 30 per cent by 2040 without intervention.

However, she said improved animal health and farm management practices could reduce antibiotic use by up to 57 per cent.

“Prevention must become central to the global fight against antimicrobial resistance, with farmers placed at the heart of the response,” she said.

The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) also warned that environmental pollution could undermine efforts to contain AMR.

Aitziber Echeverria, UNEP’s AMR Coordinator in its Chemicals and Health Branch, said the environment played a role in the emergence, transmission and spread of drug-resistant microorganisms.

She identified pharmaceutical manufacturing, agriculture and food systems, healthcare, and municipal waste and wastewater management as priority areas requiring intervention.

“The environment and AMR cannot be treated separately. That is the One Health concept,” she added.

Animal health

Jane Lwoyero, a programme officer at the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), said investment in preventing animal diseases could generate significant economic returns.

“For every US$1 that is invested in prevention of animal diseases and for better animal health systems, we are assured of getting a return of US$28,” she said.

She said fewer than 20 per cent of WOAH member countries vaccinated animals against notifiable diseases, while animal diseases caused estimated annual losses of up to $300 billion globally.

However, she noted some progress in reducing antimicrobial use in animals. WOAH data showed global antimicrobial use in animals declined by three per cent between 2019 and 2024.

The organisation also reported that 74 per cent of countries did not use antimicrobials for growth promotion. In comparison, 19 per cent still permitted the practice, and seven per cent had not reported their position.

Abuja conference to review global progress

Nigeria is expected to host the fifth Global High-Level Ministerial Conference on AMR in Abuja from 6 to 8 December.

The meeting is expected to review progress, address implementation challenges and renew political commitment to tackling AMR. The updated Global Action Plan for 2026–2036 and the proposed Independent Panel on Evidence for Action against AMR are also expected to feature in discussions, with possible launches at the conference.

Mr Nyemazi said the meeting would provide an opportunity to assess whether global commitments were producing results in communities.

He urged journalists to sustain public attention through accurate and evidence-based reporting.

“You make visible what is often invisible. Your accurate, evidence-based and solution-focused reporting shapes public understanding, sustains political attention and holds all of us accountable,” he said.

The Global AMR Media Alliance Chairperson, Shobha Shukla, said the challenge was no longer simply getting countries to recognise AMR or develop national action plans, but ensuring they had the funding, surveillance systems, laboratory capacity and accountability mechanisms to implement them.

She also called for a people-centred response that prevents “unnecessary antimicrobial use” while ensuring that those who need effective medicines can access them.

World.title: Three killed, many abducted in Sokoto attack – Police
World.content:
The police in Sokoto State have confirmed the killing of three people and the abduction of several residents during an attack by suspected bandits on Yartsakuwa community in Rabah Local Government Area.

The attackers reportedly invaded the community in the early hours of Sunday, killing residents and stealing livestock.

The state police spokesperson, Ahmad Rufai, confirmed the incident to THE PUNCH, saying three people were killed, while others were kidnapped.

However, a resident who survived the attack, Najeeb Yartsakuwa, reported a higher death toll of four, comprising three men and a woman. Daily Trust also reported four deaths.

In a Facebook post cited by PUNCH, Mr Yartsakuwa said the attackers entered his family home and abducted his sister and four sisters-in-law.

He said other women were also taken from the community, although the total number of abducted residents had not been established.

The resident appealed for prayers for the victims and the safe return of those kidnapped.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The police have yet to reconcile their casualty figure with the resident’s account. The identities of those killed and the total number of abducted residents also remain unclear.

Previous attacks

The latest incident follows a series of deadly attacks on rural communities in Rabah, where residents have faced repeated killings, kidnappings and livestock theft.

In September, PREMIUM TIMES reported that suspected bandits attacked Tofa community in the same local government area, killing residents and abducting dozens of others.

Accounts of that attack put the death toll at between seven and 10, while estimates of those kidnapped ranged from 35 to about 40.

Earlier, on 30 August, eight farmers were killed and five others injured during an attack on Ghandi community, also in Rabah.

Security forces subsequently reported intercepting armed men advancing towards Ghandi, but the operation did not prevent the later attack on Tofa.

The renewed violence comes despite military and police operations aimed at dismantling armed groups operating across parts of Sokoto State.

On 9 November, the Sokoto police announced the rescue of two abducted residents during an operation targeting suspected bandits’ hideouts in Yabo Local Government Area.

The police said the operation also led to the destruction of structures allegedly used by the armed group.

It remains unclear whether security personnel have been deployed to Yartsakuwa following Sunday’s attack or whether an operation has begun to rescue the abducted residents.

World.title: Lagos prosperity driven by public servants’ dedication — Hamzat
World.content:
Hamzat

By Olasunkanmi Akoni

Lagos State Deputy Governor, Dr. Obafemi Hamzat, has attributed the state’s economic prosperity and development to the dedication, professionalism and contributions of its public servants.

Hamzat spoke on Saturday while leading more than 4,000 civil and public servants in a fitness walk organised by the Lagos State Government as part of activities marking the 2026 Public Service Week.

The exercise, which began at the Adeyemi Bero Auditorium, Alausa, Ikeja, featured aerobics and a brisk walk through Alausa and adjoining communities, promoting physical fitness, healthy living and workplace wellness among public sector employees.

The deputy governor was accompanied by the Head of Service, Mr. Bode Agoro, and the Principal Secretary to President Bola Tinubu and former Lagos State Head of Service, Mr. Hakeem Muri-Okunola.

Also in attendance were members of the Body of Permanent Secretaries, heads of extra-ministerial departments and offices, as well as civil and public servants from the mainstream public service, commissions and local governments across the state.

Participants commenced the exercise with aerobics sessions before embarking on the fitness walk around the Alausa-Ikeja communities.

Addressing the participants, Hamzat commended the workers for their impressive turnout, stressing the need for public servants to prioritise their health and wellbeing.

He said the exercise reflected the health and dignity component of his PROMISE campaign, particularly the first pillar, People First agenda.

“They say health is wealth. So, a healthy Lagos is a wealthy Lagos, and you are an important part of that promise,” he said.

The deputy governor also acknowledged the strategic role of the public service in implementing government policies and programmes, describing the civil service as the machinery of government.

According to him, without a functional and effective civil service, government activities and development initiatives would suffer.

“Without a functional and effective civil service, nothing gets done,” Hamzat said, urging public servants to take pride in their contributions to governance.

He noted that public servants were responsible for documenting government decisions and ensuring their implementation.

Making reference to the ongoing electioneering period, Hamzat also responded to comments made during a political debate the previous day, where the civil service was reportedly identified as one of the challenges confronting Lagos State.

He disagreed with the assessment, insisting that public servants remained indispensable to the delivery of government policies and development programmes.

Hamzat further stressed the need to extend the benefits of economic prosperity to more households and businesses across the state.

Earlier, Agoro disclosed that the exercise attracted more than 4,000 participants, expressing optimism that subsequent editions scheduled for January and February would record even greater participation.

He commended the commitment of the workforce and reiterated the importance of collective involvement in activities that promote staff wellbeing.

Also speaking, Muri-Okunola described public servants as key implementers of government policies and programmes.

He commended their contributions to Lagos State’s development and urged them to sustain their commitment to effective service delivery.

The fitness walk formed part of activities lined up by the Lagos State Government to promote a healthier workforce, strengthen camaraderie among public servants and reinforce the importance of staff wellbeing in effective service delivery.

World.title: Sanusi, Ladoja warn against politicising traditional institutions
World.content:
Emir of Kano, Muhammadu Sanusi II

By Adeola Badru

The Emir of Kano, Muhammadu Sanusi II, and the Olubadan of Ibadanland, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, have called for national healing, peaceful coexistence and stronger bonds among Nigeria’s diverse ethnic and religious groups, warning against the politicisation of traditional institutions.

The two traditional rulers spoke on Sunday in Ibadan when Sanusi paid a courtesy visit to Ladoja at his palace in Oke-Aremo, where they stressed the need for traditional institutions to remain above partisan interests and serve as instruments of reconciliation, mutual understanding and national unity.

Sanusi, who was in Ibadan to honour an invitation from the League of Imams and Alfas in South-West Nigeria, said his visit reflected his belief in a country where ethnic, religious and political differences would not determine relationships among citizens.

He described the engagement as one of the positive developments needed to bridge Nigeria’s regional and cultural divides, stressing that national unity, progress and prosperity could only be achieved when people from different backgrounds deliberately reached out to one another.

The Emir said although other engagements had emerged, he considered it important to honour his earlier commitment to attend the conference, even if his participation would be brief.

“We fixed this date a long time ago, and even though other events came, we considered it important to honour our promise to appear at the conference, even if it is for a brief period, because they have been expecting me to come.

“This invitation is part of the positive developments we have been yearning for to build a bridge where Nigerians from different parts of the country reach out to each other and come together in the interest of the unity, the progress and the prosperity of our dear nation,” he said.

Sanusi also apologised for the delay in visiting Ladoja following his appointment and coronation, explaining that certain circumstances had prevented him from attending earlier.

He congratulated Ladoja on his ascension to the throne of his forebears and prayed for divine protection, a long and peaceful reign, as well as prosperity for Ibadanland and Nigeria.

The Emir described the courtesy visit as necessary, given the longstanding relationship between the two traditional institutions and their respective communities.

Reflecting on his relationship with Ibadan, Sanusi recalled his longstanding connections with the ancient city dating back to his days at First Bank, his association with the late Aare Musulumi of Yorubaland, Alhaji Abdulazeez Arisekola Alao, and his subsequent tenure as Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria.

He said Ibadan had remained a familiar destination over the years, adding that he had maintained close relationships with several indigenes of the city.

Sanusi also expressed his readiness to host the Olubadan in Kano, saying reciprocal visits would further strengthen the longstanding bonds between the two communities and promote understanding among Nigerians from different regions.

Responding, Ladoja identified political interference in traditional institutions as a major concern, calling for deliberate measures to insulate traditional rulers from partisan politics and arbitrary decisions capable of destabilising established traditional structures.

He warned that political actors who interfere in traditional institutions often take decisions without fully appreciating their historical significance and the far-reaching consequences for affected communities.

Specifically, the Olubadan expressed concern over developments surrounding the Kano Emirate, arguing that an institution with more than 1,000 years of history should not be subjected to arbitrary fragmentation.

He urged those involved in the controversy to allow reason to prevail, expressing hope that peace and the historical integrity of the Kano Emirate would be restored.

“We have a lot in common. And we have to find a way of insulating the position of the traditional rulers from partisan politics, failure of which they continue to take decisions whose consequences they don’t even understand.

“From history, we know that Kano has been there for more than 1,000 years. And for somebody to wake up and say he is going to break it doesn’t seem to be reasonable. We pray that reason will prevail in the Kano Emirate to restore what we used to know Kano for,” Ladoja said.

Recalling the Maitatsine crisis, which originated in Kano, the Olubadan stressed the need to sustain peace in the ancient city, describing it as a major commercial centre whose stability has implications for the wider northern region and Nigeria.

He noted that Kano and Ibadan were widely regarded as two of the country’s most accommodating cities, adding that Kano remained a major convergence point for Hausa- and Fulani-speaking communities.

According to him, Kano’s importance as a commercial hub extended beyond Nigeria, making peace and stability in the city a matter of national importance.

Ladoja also commended Sanusi for relinquishing his position as Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria to ascend the throne of his ancestors, describing the decision as a reflection of his character, convictions and commitment to traditional service.

He noted that the CBN governor occupied a strategic position in the management of Nigeria’s economy, adding that Sanusi’s decision to leave the office for the Kano throne demonstrated the importance he attached to his traditional heritage.

The Olubadan further recalled admiring the Emir’s spiritual devotion during their encounters in Medina while performing Umrah, saying Sanusi remained committed to prayer even when he occupied the country’s foremost banking position.

“Whoever is heading the Central Bank is virtually heading Nigeria’s economy, so to have left that office to become the Emir of Kano shows who you are. I used to admire him any time I went to Umrah; even as the Central Bank Governor, he was always on the same spot in Medina for hours praying,” he said.

Ladoja, who disclosed that he was still in the first year of his reign, also explained the distinctive traditional succession system in Ibadanland, which operates a republican arrangement without a clearly defined ruling house.

He said the emergence of an Olubadan followed a lengthy progression through the traditional chieftaincy hierarchy, requiring aspirants to climb 22 or 23 successive stages before attaining the throne.

The monarch disclosed that his journey towards becoming Olubadan began in 1993 and lasted 32 years, expressing gratitude to Almighty Allah for making his ascension to the revered stool possible.

“Ibadan, as you know it, is republican. There is no defined ruling house, and it is only the Almighty Allah that crowns the Olubadan of Ibadanland because you have to climb 22 or 23 ladders before you become the Olubadan.

“I started my journey in 1993; that is a journey of 32 years. For that, I thank God that I am the Olubadan today,” he said.

The Olubadan also pledged to reciprocate Sanusi’s visit by travelling to Kano, while recalling his longstanding friendship with a Kano elder, Yusuf Garba Ali, dating back to 1972.

World.title: NDC candidate in Kwara pledges N120,000 minimum wage for workers
World.content:
The governorship candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Kwara, Prof. Abdulmumin Ajia, has pledged a minimum wage of N120,000 for workers in the state.

Ajia made the pledge on Sunday in Ilorin while unveiling the NDC’s 2027 Gubernatorial Campaign Council manifesto, tagged ‘Forward Kwara Agenda’.

He proposed a N120,000 public-service minimum wage benchmark and a cost-of-living adjustment framework for workers and pensioners.

He said his administration would verify the payroll, assess the financial implications, consult labour unions and publish an implementation and funding timetable.

On pensioners, Ajia promised to verify outstanding gratuities and publish a schedule for settling validated arrears.

He also pledged to establish a predictable payment timetable for newly due pension obligations.

Ajia said he entered the governorship race to make public institutions work reliably for all Kwarans, regardless of political affiliation.

“I am running to make public institutions work that way. If entrusted with office, I will serve people who support me, people who oppose me and people who have never attended a political meeting,” he said.

He said his experience as a teacher, researcher and university administrator had taught him to ask critical questions, examine evidence and take responsibility for results.

Ajia, who led a School of Business and mentored young people, said his visits home exposed him to the challenges facing unemployed graduates.

He said many young people could hardly predict when fair employment opportunities would become available.

According to him, government has a responsibility to ensure that citizens understand how to access assistance, eligibility requirements and appeal procedures.

He said access to public services should not depend on personal relationships with the governor.

Ajia said the Forward Kwara Agenda outlined six areas of governance, anchored on stronger institutions, greater opportunities and shared prosperity.

On security, he said farmers should access their farms, children should travel safely to school and traders should return home safely from markets.

NAN reports that the event attracted hundreds of NDC stakeholders from the state’s 16 local government areas.

World.title: ‘Xavi wants to play Xavi-style football’ – Klopp praises Netherlands coach
World.content:
Germany’s newly appointed national football team head coach Jurgen Klopp gestures as he addresses a press conference at the headquarters of the German Football Federation (DFB) in Frankfurt am Main, western Germany on July 24, 2026. Jurgen Klopp was named as the new head coach of the German men’s national football team on July 24, replacing Julian Nagelsmann who was dismissed after the team’s disappointing World Cup performance. Klopp, famed for his success during stints as coach at Borussia Dortmund and especially Liverpool, has been in talks with the DFB about trying to lead Germany — long a football powerhouse — back to prominence. (Photo by John MACDOUGALL / AFP)

Germany coach Jurgen Klopp praised Xavi Hernandez on Sunday, saying the new Netherlands coach already had the Dutch playing in his own image after just five games in charge.

Speaking in Berlin ahead of Monday’s meeting between the two old rivals, Klopp pointed to Friday’s 7-0 thumping of Greece in Amsterdam and said the former midfielder had made an impression.

Considered among the best midfielders in the history of the game, Xavi formed the core of a possession-dominant Barcelona side who won four Champions League titles. He also won the World Cup with Spain.

“They simply played some electric football,” Klopp said, adding: “Xavi wants to play Xavi-style football…

“He’s a coach who really pushes his approach to the limit. And that’s exciting. I always loved playing against teams who play like this.”

Third in the group with only the top two reaching the quarter-finals, Germany will need to beat the Netherlands to give themselves a chance.

“They’re a team who really come alive in European football,” Klopp said of the Netherlands.

“It’s one of the fiercest rivalries in football. It’s a great honour for me.”

Appointed in August, the Spaniard said he was beginning to understand the nature of the rivalry with Germany.

“Now I can understand more because I’m here and I feel this kind of rivalry. It will be a really good test for us,” Xavi said.

In his press conference, Xavi deflected Klopp’s praise and said the Netherlands’ big win over Greece was down to his players.

“It’s not Xavi-football. It’s all about the players. They are the most important. I don’t need to convince them to play this style of football, they have the capacity to play like the last game.

Germany and the Netherlands played out a 1-1 draw in Amsterdam in September, the first match in charge for both Klopp and Xavi.

Xavi said he would try and do the unexpected on Monday, but acknowledged it would not be easy against the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach.

“It’s difficult to surprise a coach like Jurgen Klopp,” Xavi said.

“He’s one of the best coaches in the past few years. And it’s an honour to come up against him tomorrow.”

Vanguard News

World.title: APC mocks NDC over campaign spending claims
World.content:
APC National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka.

By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA — The All Progressives Congress (APC) has mocked the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) over its criticism of the Federal Government’s spending priorities, accusing the opposition party of focusing on the ruling party’s campaign activities instead of preparing for the 2027 general election.

The APC National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka, described the NDC’s claims as “comical”, saying the party had appointed itself “Nigeria’s auditor-general of campaign financing” despite what he described as its limited electoral presence.

Morka was reacting to a statement by the NDC National Campaign Council spokesperson, Dr Chiogo Constance Ikokwu, who accused President Bola Tinubu’s administration of prioritising political publicity and patronage over critical sectors of the economy.

Ikokwu had alleged that substantial resources were being spent on political publicity and the distribution of vehicles, laptops, sewing machines and food items by groups supporting Tinubu, while essential public services remained underfunded.

She also questioned the government’s spending priorities in view of additional revenue accruing from the removal of the petrol subsidy and changes in taxation.

On security and healthcare funding, the NDC spokesperson claimed that only about seven per cent of the Defence Capital Budget was released in 2025.

She further alleged that only N36 million out of the N218 billion allocated to health capital expenditure was released in the same year, citing a reported disclosure by the Minister of Health.

The opposition party also accused some APC-controlled state governments of similar spending practices, warning that political publicity and patronage could not conceal the consequences of poor governance.

But dismissing the criticism, Morka said the NDC lacked the electoral footprint and political relevance to question the APC’s campaign activities.

“It is rather comical that the NDC, a party that has no electoral footprint and is still struggling to establish its political identity and relevance, has suddenly appointed itself Nigeria’s auditor-general of campaign financing,” he said.

Morka argued that the opposition party had become preoccupied with the APC’s campaign activities instead of developing its own platform and preparing for the forthcoming election.

“The NDC has yet to initiate or show any capacity to conduct nationwide campaign activities as expected of any serious party. Instead, the party has continued to display its obsession about APC and its legitimate campaign activities,” he said.

He added that the NDC was distracted by what he described as the APC’s coordinated campaign activities across the country.

“The NDC is only jittery and dazed by the APC’s focused and well-coordinated campaign activities across the country rather than expend its energy crafting its own campaign platform ahead of the 2027 general election,” Morka said.

World.title: NDDC allegation: Akpabio challenges Amaechi to produce evidence
World.content:
By Henry Umoru

ABUJA — President of the Senate, Senator Godswill Akpabio, has challenged former Rivers State Governor and African Democratic Congress (ADC) vice-presidential candidate, Rotimi Amaechi, to provide documentary evidence to substantiate his allegation that Akpabio introduced a 50 per cent deduction from payments to contractors of the Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC).

Akpabio said public accountability required evidence rather than campaign declarations, insisting that allegations of wrongdoing must be supported by verifiable facts and subjected to appropriate investigation.

He also said Amaechi’s eight-year tenure as governor of Rivers State deserved public scrutiny, particularly regarding expenditure and outcomes of major projects initiated by his administration.

The Senate President’s position was contained in a statement issued on Sunday by his Special Adviser on Media and Publicity, Hon. Eseme Eyiboh, in response to remarks attributed to Amaechi at an ADC political rally in Bauchi on Saturday, November 14, 2026.

According to the statement, Amaechi had alleged that Akpabio introduced a 50 per cent deduction from payments due to NDDC contractors.

Akpabio described the allegation as serious but said Amaechi had not provided contract documents, payment records, identifiable transactions or other verifiable details to support it.

He challenged the former governor to identify the contracts involved, the affected contractors, when the alleged deductions occurred and the payment arrangements through which they were allegedly made.

He also asked Amaechi to provide evidence establishing Akpabio’s personal involvement in the alleged deductions.

The statement quoted Akpabio as saying: “Mr Amaechi is entitled to raise concerns about public administration. He is equally obliged to distinguish what he can substantiate from what he merely alleges.

“The same standard applies to every public officeholder. We therefore invite him to place any credible documentary evidence in his possession before the appropriate authorities so that the issues he has raised may be examined objectively and in accordance with the law.”

He added that public accountability was strengthened when allegations were tested against evidence, public expenditure examined against outcomes and institutions allowed to discharge their responsibilities without political interference.

Amaechi’s Rivers record deserves scrutiny — Akpabio

The Senate President said Amaechi’s tenure as Rivers State governor between 2007 and 2015 was also a legitimate subject of public examination, particularly concerning the cost, completion and sustainability of projects undertaken during the period.

He specifically cited the Port Harcourt monorail project and the Malaria-Free Rivers State initiatives as examples of projects whose implementation and outcomes, according to him, raised questions about public expenditure and value for money.

On the monorail project, Akpabio said its reported cost, incomplete implementation and inability to deliver the anticipated public transportation service warranted examination.

He raised questions about the amount spent on the project, the extent to which its original objectives were achieved and the institutional and contractual decisions that contributed to its difficulties.

According to him, public accountability should extend to every public official entrusted with public resources and authority, irrespective of political affiliation.

“The credibility of a public allegation must rest not on the volume of its delivery, the status of its author or the occasion on which it is made, but on the quality of the evidence supporting it. Let the facts speak,” he said.

2027 elections

Akpabio acknowledged that political disagreements would intensify as the country approaches the 2027 general elections, describing such disagreements as normal in a democracy.

He, however, cautioned political actors against making unsubstantiated allegations capable of undermining public confidence in institutions.

He said allegations concerning the NDDC’s contracts, finances and administration should be addressed through credible investigative processes rather than turned into instruments of political confrontation.

The Senate President stressed that the people of the Niger Delta deserved functional infrastructure, transparent procurement, completed projects and measurable development outcomes.

He added that the interests of the region should remain central to discussions about the commission and its responsibilities.

World.title: 2027: NDC accuses Tinubu of prioritising campaign propaganda over budgets
World.content:
President Tinubu

By Henry Umoru

ABUJA — The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has accused President Bola Tinubu’s administration of prioritising campaign propaganda and political patronage over funding critical sectors of the economy, alleging that the huge spending on political publicity explains the poor implementation of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 budgets.

The opposition party challenged the Federal Government to publish verifiable figures showing how much had been released for critical capital projects and administrative subventions in the three fiscal years, compared with expenditure on political s and patronage.

The NDC made the allegations in a statement signed on Sunday by the Spokesperson of its National Campaign Council, Dr. Chiogo Constance Ikokwu, titled, “Dear Mr. President: The Huge Cost of Your Campaign Propaganda Testifies to Why You Failed to Adequately Fund 2024, 2025 and 2026 Budgets.”

The party said its assessment of what it described as a barrage of political s, donations, vehicles, laptops, sewing machines, food items and other gifts distributed by groups and individuals claiming to support Tinubu had raised questions about the administration’s spending priorities.

It alleged that despite increased government revenue following the removal of fuel subsidy and higher taxation, critical social and physical infrastructure, national security and citizens’ welfare had not received adequate funding.

Ikokwu said: “For instance, despite the palpable insecurity confronting the nation, only about seven per cent of the Defence Capital Budget was reportedly released in 2025.

“Even more disturbing was when the Minister of Health reported that only ₦36 million out of the ₦218 billion allocated to Health Capital expenditure was released in the same 2025.”

The party argued that the alleged low releases for defence and health raised questions about the government’s commitment to addressing insecurity and improving public services.

It also expressed concern over the implementation of the 2026 budget, which it claimed had received inadequate attention, and accused the APC of devoting substantial resources to campaign publicity and political patronage ahead of the 2027 elections.

Questioning the administration’s spending priorities, Ikokwu asked how a government benefiting from fuel subsidy removal and increased taxation could plead a lack of funds for national security, healthcare, education, federal roads and the welfare of ordinary Nigerians while political activities appeared to attract substantial resources.

The NDC also alleged that several state governments, particularly those it claimed had been pressured into joining the APC, had poor records of budget implementation but had sufficient resources for campaign propaganda.

The party further linked what it described as poor governance and deteriorating infrastructure to the rising incidents of political intimidation and violence, alleging that such developments could be aimed at discouraging voters from participating in the January 2027 elections.

It, however, warned that propaganda, political patronage and intimidation could not permanently conceal the consequences of poor governance.

“The NDC therefore challenges the Tinubu administration to explain its budgetary priorities and demonstrate, with verifiable figures, how much has actually been released for critical capital projects and administrative subventions in 2024, 2025 and 2026, as against the resources expended on political publicity and patronage by sundry characters,” the statement said.

The party also declared that its presidential candidate, Peter Obi, and running mate, Rabiu Kwankwaso, would prioritise accountability, public service funding and a transition from a consumption-driven to a production-based economy if elected in 2027.

“The Obi/Kwankwaso administration will be accountable; will fund public services and move the country from consumption to production,” it added.

World.title: Lagos APC faults Obi, NDC over singing old national anthem
World.content:
…Questions opposition’s focus on national development

By Olasunkanmi Akoni

LAGOS — The Lagos State chapter of the All Progressives Congress, APC, has criticised former Labour Party presidential candidate, Peter Obi, and members of the Nigerian Democratic Congress, NDC, over their singing of Nigeria’s former national anthem at a recent town hall meeting.

The party’s spokesman, Seye Oladejo, who reacted to the development, described the action as political theatrics and nostalgia rather than a focus on national development.

Oladejo argued that national symbols should not be used selectively for partisan purposes, noting that Nigeria adopted its current national anthem through a lawful process.

He said the incident reflected what he described as a pattern in which Obi’s public conduct appeared influenced by the immediate sentiments of his political audience.

According to him, aspiring to lead a country of more than 200 million people requires independent judgment, intellectual discipline and respect for established national institutions.

“A president must possess the temperament to listen to his supporters without becoming captive to their sentiments,” Oladejo said, adding that leadership required providing direction even when it differed from the immediate expectations of supporters.

The APC spokesman also questioned the consistency of Obi’s political alignments and policy agenda, citing reports that the former Anambra governor had described his current presidential ambition as a “valedictory shot” at the presidency.

He maintained that the office of the president required a clear and implementable development programme rather than symbolic gestures.

Addressing the NDC, Oladejo said political parties were expected to present credible policy alternatives and provide clear direction on governance rather than operate as what he described as “cultural nostalgia clubs.”

He argued that singing the former national anthem would not address pressing national challenges, including unemployment, insecurity, infrastructure deficits and economic hardship.

The Lagos APC urged Nigerians to scrutinise the policy positions, consistency and respect for national institutions demonstrated by those seeking political leadership, while reaffirming its commitment to what it described as forward-looking governance.

World.title: MTN Defends Data Billing, Says Apps Driving Rapid Consumption
World.content:
Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt

The Mobile Telecommunications Network (MTN) Nigeria has defended its data billing practices, insisting that it does not “steal” customers’ data, but acknowledged growing concerns among subscribers over unexplained data depletion.

The telecom giant made the clarification in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, during its “Data on Trial” initiative, a courtroom-style engagement designed to allow customers to question MTN officials over how their data is consumed.

The event, held at the weekend, featured customers and content creators as the prosecution, while MTN executives constituted the defence team.

MTN’s Chief Customer Relations and Experience Officer, Ugonwa Nwoye, said the initiative was a response to persistent complaints from customers who wanted greater visibility into their data consumption.

According to her, “customers have been telling us that they want to know what uses their data,” adding that the company had embarked on sensitisation campaigns for about two years before deciding to introduce face-to-face engagements. What we want is a better understanding for our customers about how their data is used, how they can track the use of their data on their phone or on platforms that we have built for them.”

MTN Nigeria’s General Manager, Network Performance and Quality Assurance, Mike Ndukwe, attributed increasing data consumption largely to the migration from older network technologies to 4G and 5G, alongside the rapid growth of smartphones, social media and high-definition video content.

He disclosed that Nigeria consumed about 13.2 million terabytes of data in 2025, while consumption in the first half of the current year had already reached 8.52 million terabytes, representing about 43 per cent year-on-year growth compared with the corresponding period.

World.title: Keyamo Insists NDC Erred in Singing Old National Anthem During Townhall Meeting in Lagos
World.content:
Chinedu Eze

The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, has repudiated those who try to justify the singing of old national anthem by the National Democratic Congress (NDC) by saying that All Progressives Congress (APC) also sing ‘On Our Mandate’, insisting that Senator Seriake Dickson led party was wrong, after all.

On Thursday, November 12, NDC held townhall meeting at the Classic Event Centre, Oregun Ikeja, Lagos, where old national anthem was sung instead of the new; although party members claimed that the new national anthem was sang later.

However, Keyamo, in his verified X (Twitter) account insisted that NDC was wrong and rejected the attempt to justify their action by the NDC party members, saying that APC also sing ‘On Our Mandate’.

The Minister explained, “Let me educate some mischievous persons who try to equate singing the on your mandate song, which is used to serenade President Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu, with singing an outlawed anthem in place of a legally approved National Anthem.

“At no time have supporters of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu sung on your mandate in place of the National Anthem. At every occasion, the National Anthem is always sung as a mark of recognition of one of our most important national symbols, and then the President is serenaded by his supporters with on your mandate.”

He said that nobody stops Peter Obi from adopting a song, even the old anthem, as his own song. But it must be sung either before or after the legally recognised National Anthem is given its due recognition.

“Again, as part of presidential protocol, whenever the President walks into an event or gets up to speak, the Police Band usually plays any instrumental to herald his presence or speech. They simply choose anyone they fancy. Check all videos of Presidents Obasanjo, Yar’Adua, Jonathan or Buhari entering the National Assembly or getting up to speak. It must be preceded by an instrumental from the Police Band. In this case, the Police Band sometimes plays the on your mandate instrumental to herald the President’s speech. This comes after the national anthem has been played,” he said.

Keyamo also noted that many states in Nigeria today have their own anthem, but it is always sung after the National Anthem has been rendered.

“Singing an outlawed anthem in place of a legally approved national anthem by the NDC is surely an expression of a desire to have a separate country, and that is an ingredient of a secessionist group,” Keyamo insisted.

World.title: Uwaleke Lists Options for Infrastructure Financing Beyond Govt Borrowing
World.content:
* Says growing debt burden demands urgent, fundamental rethink

Ndubuisi Francis in Abuja

Renowned financial expert, Prof. Uche Uwaleke, has stated that Nigeria’s growing public debt burden has made an urgent case for a fundamental rethink of how the country finances infrastructure.

He stated that the Nigerian capital market offers viable alternatives through infrastructure bonds, infrastructure funds, infrastructure investment trusts and other structured investment vehicles that can attract institutional investors and ordinary Nigerians into commercially viable projects.

In an article, ‘Beyond Government Borrowing: How the Capital Market can Unlock Opportunities to Finance Nigeria’s Infrastructure,’ he argued that the whole idea was to move beyond a model in which government borrows and carries most of the financial risks, towards one in which government uses its institutions, assets and regulatory influence to attract private investment.

Citing statistics by the Debt Management Office (DMO), Uwaleke noted that Nigeria’s total public debt rallied to N166.79 trillion by June 30, 2026, representing an increase of N14.39 trillion, or 9.4 per cent, compared with the N152.40 trillion recorded a year earlier.

“Of this amount, domestic debt accounted for N91.59 trillion (54.91 per cent), while external debt stood at N75.20 trillion (45.09 per cent).

“The debt stock also increased by N7.44 trillion in just three months, from N159.35 trillion at the end of March 2026. The pressure is compounded by the cost of servicing these obligations: Nigeria is projected to spend about US$11.6 billion on debt service in 2026, close to half of expected government revenue,” he said.

Against this backdrop, the one-time finance commissioner in Imo State said the question was no longer how much more government can borrow, but how it can mobilise long-term domestic and international capital to finance critical infrastructure without further deepening the public debt burden.

According to him, the Nigerian capital market offers viable alternatives through infrastructure bonds, infrastructure funds, infrastructure investment trusts and other structured investment vehicles that can attract institutional investors and ordinary Nigerians into commercially viable projects.

Properly structured, he explained that these instruments can channel private savings into productive infrastructure, while ensuring that long-term project financing was supported by the revenue streams generated by the assets themselves, making such investments financially sustainable and, in the case of project-backed bonds, potentially self-liquidating rather than an additional burden on general government revenues.

“The whole idea is to move beyond a model in which government borrows and carries most of the financial risk, towards one in which government uses its institutions, assets and regulatory influence to attract private investment.

“Properly structured infrastructure bonds, for example, can provide long-term financing whose repayment is supported by the cash flows of the infrastructure project itself. Where tolls, user charges, power-purchase agreements or other predictable revenues are sufficient to meet interest and principal repayments, the borrowing can become self-liquidating rather than a continuing claim on general government revenues.

“Infrastructure funds and investment trusts can go further by allowing investors to acquire an economic interest in infrastructure assets and share in the income they generate, while diversifying risk across a portfolio of projects,” the Professor of Capital Market at the Nasarawa State University, Keffi and President of the Capital Market Academics of Nigeria (CMAN) said.

Uwaleke explained that a good example of how the government can use external financing and a relatively modest initial budget contribution to deliver major infrastructure was the Abuja-Keffi-Akwanga-Lafia-Makurdi road, adding that the project was executed by China Harbour Engineering Company under an Engineering, Procurement and Construction with Finance (EPC+F) arrangement.

He said 85 per cent ($460.8 million) of the contract sum of $542.14 million was financed through a China Exim Bank facility, while the Federal Government provided the remaining 15 per cent ($81.32 million) as counterpart funding.

“The project demonstrates the potential benefits of using structured financing to reduce the immediate call on government budgetary resources. Rather than financing the entire construction cost from public funds, government contributed a fraction of the initial financing requirement and obtained a major transport asset.

“The broader lesson is that infrastructure should be structured around identifiable revenue streams and repayment capacity. This is where the Nigerian capital market can play a much more significant role,” he stressed, adding that infrastructure bonds could be issued to finance projects with predictable cash flows, while infrastructure funds can pool capital from several investors and allocate it across different projects.

“Infrastructure investment trusts offer another opportunity by enabling investors to acquire units in a professionally managed vehicle that holds income-generating assets such as toll roads, power transmission facilities, ports and other infrastructure. Instead of government carrying the entire cost of building and maintaining these assets, private investors can provide capital in exchange for a share of the income generated.

“International experience shows how a sovereign investment institution can help make this model work. India provides a particularly instructive example through its National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF), a sovereign-anchored investment platform established to mobilize domestic and international capital for infrastructure and other nationally important sectors,” he said.

Citing several models and examples from India, he noted that the examples were particularly relevant because Nigeria already has an institution with a mandate to perform a similar catalytic role–the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA), which was established to manage public investment funds and support long-term economic development, including the development of domestic infrastructure.

“Its three core funds include the Stabilization Fund, the Future Generations Fund and the Nigeria Infrastructure Fund (NIF), with the latter specifically mandated to invest in Nigerian infrastructure.

“The NIF’s stated investment sectors include motorways, healthcare, power and agriculture, among others. More importantly, its investment strategy already provides for direct investment in infrastructure projects and companies, co-investment through investment funds, and the creation of institutions that support infrastructure development.

“This means Nigeria does not necessarily need to establish another government-owned infrastructure fund. A more practical approach would be to strengthen the existing Nigeria Infrastructure Fund and position the NSIA as a major anchor investor, sponsor and catalyst for infrastructure investment vehicles that can raise additional capital from the market.

“The NSIA could commit a portion of its infrastructure allocation as seed capital to a regulated infrastructure fund or investment trust, while inviting pension fund administrators, insurance companies, banks, asset managers, international development finance institutions and other long-term investors to participate.

“Once the vehicle has an appropriate governance structure, a credible pipeline of projects and a clear investment mandate, it could raise additional capital through private placements or public offerings on the Nigerian Exchange, subject to the relevant regulatory requirements.There is also a compelling opportunity to bring ordinary Nigerians into this process,” Uwaleke noted.

World.title: Nigerian-Born Chemist Advances Global Drug Safety, Plans US Testing Lab
World.content:
A Nigerian-born chemist working in the United States, Kaothar Olurode Adeleke, has announced plans to establish an independent contract analytical testing laboratory to help prevent drug shortages and expand quality-control capacity in the pharmaceutical industry.

Adeleke, who currently works as a Quality Control Chemist at Tower Laboratories Ltd in the United States, observed inadequate testing facilities often slow down pharmaceutical production, leaving patients without timely access to safe medicines.

At Tower Laboratories, Adeleke conducts analytical tests to verify the potency, stability, and shelf life of medications before they reach pharmacy shelves.

Her work includes screening products for major companies such as Pfizer, Bristol Myers Squibb, and Thermo Fisher Scientific, testing drugs used to treat malaria, diabetes, and common headaches to ensure they are effective and free from harmful impurities.

According to Adeleke, every medicine must undergo strict laboratory verification to protect patients from substandard products, stressing her goal to use science to solve practical problems and improve human lives.

Before joining the U.S. pharmaceutical sector, Adeleke built her scientific foundation in Osun State, earning both her National Diploma and Higher National Diploma in Science Laboratory Technology from The Federal Polytechnic, Ede.

She credits the practical laboratory training she received at the institution with equipping her for international industry standards.

She later moved to the United States, where she earned a Master of Science degree in Chemistry from the University of New Haven, Connecticut.

During her postgraduate studies, Adeleke focused her thesis on converting carbon dioxide, a major greenhouse gas linked to global warming, into methanol, a useful chemical and potential fuel.

She noted that the project reinforced her view that academic research must translate into practical solutions that protect the environment and improve daily life.
