Addressing young Nigerians pursuing careers in science, research and innovation, Adeleke urged them not to be discouraged by the scale of challenges facing the scientific community.

“Do not be intimidated by the big problems. Start where you are. Learn what you can. Every expert you admire today was once a beginner,” she said.

She added that young Africans possess the intellectual capacity to contribute to global scientific advancement if they pursue opportunities with confidence.

“Nigeria has brilliant young scientists. What we need is to believe that we belong in these spaces: in the best laboratories, working on the biggest problems. Because we do,” she pointed out.

World.title: NDC: Tinubu Spends Big on Campaign Propaganda, Neglects Security, Health Budgets
World.content:
* Opposition party questions release of only 7% of 2025 defence capital allocation

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has accused President Bola Tinubu’s administration of prioritising campaign propaganda, political s and patronage over critical national development needs.

The opposition party argued that the government’s spending priorities explain the persistent underfunding of essential sectors of the economy.

The opposition party alleged that the All Progressives Congress (APC) and groups claiming to support Tinubu’s re-election were committing enormous financial resources to political publicity, donations and distribution of gifts.

The National Campaign Council Spokesperson of the party, Dr. Chiogo Constance Ikokwu, made the allegations in a statement issued Sunday.

The NDC claimed that critical sectors such as defence, healthcare, education and infrastructure remained inadequately funded.

The party, which described the situation as a disturbing reflection of the administration’s misplaced priorities, challenged the Federal Government to publish verifiable figures showing the actual releases for capital projects and administrative subventions in 2024, 2025 and 2026, alongside its expenditure on political publicity and patronage.

The NDC statement questioned how an administration benefiting from the removal of fuel subsidy and increased taxation could continue to plead paucity of funds for essential public services.

Ikokwu said the party had observed an avalanche of political s, donations and gifts, including vehicles, laptops, sewing machines, food items and other forms of largesse distributed by different groups and individuals claiming to be acting in support of Tinubu’s mandate.

According to her, the scale of such political activities raises serious questions about the government’s priorities, particularly against the background of inadequate funding for national security, healthcare and other essential services.

Part of the statement read: “Nigerians are naturally wondering how an administration with so much money from removal of fuel subsidy accruals and high taxation has jettisoned funding critical social and physical infrastructure, as well as the welfare of the greatest number of Nigerians.

“At the same time, the APC has devoted humongous money to campaign publicity and political patronage.”

The NDC spokesperson cited what she described as disturbing figures from the 2025 budget implementation, particularly the alleged poor release of funds allocated to defence and healthcare capital expenditure.

She said that despite the worsening security challenges confronting the country, only about seven per cent of the Defence Capital Budget was reportedly released in 2025.

Ikokwu also expressed concern over the reported release of only N36 million out of the N218 billion allocated to health capital expenditure in the same fiscal year.

“Even more disturbing was when the Minister of Health reported that only N36 million out of the N218 billion allocated to Health Capital expenditure was released in the same 2025,” she said.

She argued that the figures illustrated the extent of the government’s alleged failure to translate budgetary allocations into actual funding for critical public services.

The opposition party also extended its criticism to state governments, alleging that several administrations, particularly those it claimed had been pressured into joining the APC, were equally demonstrating poor commitment to budget implementation while allegedly making resources available for political campaigns.

“Most worrisome is that most state governments, especially those coerced into APC, have scant records of budget funding like their master, but have surplus for campaign propaganda,” she alleged.

The NDC further questioned the rationale behind the Federal Government’s repeated borrowing requests amid what it described as extravagant expenditure on political activities.

It asked how an administration benefiting from increased revenue following the removal of fuel subsidy and imposing higher taxes could continue to cite financial constraints when confronted with demands for improved security, healthcare, education, federal roads and social welfare.

Ikokwu maintained that the government’s alleged failure to adequately fund critical sectors, coupled with deteriorating infrastructure and poor governance, was contributing to the growing political tension in the country.

She linked the situation to what the party described as increasing incidents of political intimidation and violence ahead of the January 2027 general election.

According to her, such developments were capable of discouraging voters from participating in the electoral process, thereby undermining democratic competition and the credibility of the forthcoming elections.

“The NDC warns that no amount of propaganda, political patronage or intimidation can permanently conceal the consequences of poor governance,” she said.

The party’s spokesperson, however, projected the NDC as an alternative, promising that an administration led by its presidential ticket, Peter Obi and Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, would prioritise accountability, public service delivery and productive investment.

“The Obi/Kwankwaso administration will be accountable; will fund public services and move the country from consumption to production,” she declared.

The party consequently challenged the Tinubu administration to provide a comprehensive account of its budget implementation over the past three fiscal years, particularly the amounts released for critical capital projects and administrative subventions.

It also demanded that the government demonstrate, with verifiable figures, how much public resources had been committed to political publicity and patronage by various groups and individuals purportedly campaigning for the president.

The NDC said transparency over budget implementation had become necessary to reassure Nigerians that public resources were being deployed in accordance with national priorities rather than partisan political interests.

World.title: Edo Defends Yari’s Food Availability Claims, Says 2.5m Votes Possible for Tinubu in 2027
World.content:
Felix Omoh-Asun in Benin City

The Edo State government has defended the Director-General of Tinubu’s Presidential Campaign Council and former Zamfara State Governor, Abdulaziz Yari, over his assertion that Nigerians should still visit markets and find food to buy, insisting that the statement should be understood within its proper context.

The Edo State Commissioner for Information and Strategy, Kassim Afegbua, explained that Yari was not suggesting that Nigerians were free from economic hardship, but was making the point that food remained available in Nigerian markets, unlike in some foreign countries where consumers reportedly experience shortages of essential grocery items.

Afegbua argued that food affordability and availability were two different issues, noting that while economic challenges had made it difficult for many Nigerians to afford basic food items, the commodities remained accessible through various markets.

Afegbua, who spoke on Arise Television’s Sunday morning programme, monitored in Benin City, added that consumers could obtain food at relatively cheaper rates by patronising local markets and buying directly from farmers rather than relying exclusively on high-end supermarkets and other expensive outlets.

The commissioner also attributed the gradual improvement in agricultural activities in some communities to improved security, which he said had enabled farmers to return to their farmlands and resume production.

However, he acknowledged that Nigerians were still grappling with significant economic difficulties, maintaining that the Federal Government was pursuing reforms aimed at addressing the challenges and stabilising the economy.

He also defended Governor Monday Okpebholo’s pledge to secure 2.5 million votes for President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 presidential election, describing the figure as an ambitious but achievable target that would be driven by aggressive voter mobilisation and the state government’s development strides.

He said the target was informed by Edo State’s growing voter population, pointing out that the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) had put the state’s eligible voters at 2.865 million.

He maintained that the state government was committed to mobilising, sensitising and persuading voters to support Tinubu’s re-election, insisting that the administration’s investments in infrastructure and social development had provided sufficient reasons for the electorate to endorse the president for a second term.

“The context at which we made that statement is the fact that we are setting a target for ourselves. After all, the new voters, as at last week when INEC released the figures, is 2.865 million people. What happens if we get 2.5 million? Is it a crime?” he asked.

Highlighting the state government’s development initiatives, Afegbua said the administration had intensified efforts in infrastructure, education, healthcare and other critical sectors.

“We are doing so much, we are working so much, we are building infrastructure, we are touching the social development aspect, we are building schools, health sectors, and all of that,” he said.

The commissioner argued that the Federal Government’s increased allocations to states, alongside the development opportunities they provide, should encourage Edo voters to support Tinubu’s continued leadership.

According to him, the state government’s task was to convince the electorate that continuity in federal leadership would translate into more development for Edo State.

“Our responsibility is to woo them, plead with them, appeal to them that they should allow the man who is providing the funding with respect to increased allocation to the state to continue so that they can see more development,” he said.

Afegbua also warned that frequent changes in government could undermine economic stability and disrupt the implementation of policies, arguing that continuity was essential to sustaining the gains of ongoing reforms.

“It is even dangerous for economic growth of any country for you to disrupt the flow or the process as it were now, when things are getting stabilised,” he said, reaffirming the state government’s determination to deliver Edo State for Tinubu in 2027.

He further disclosed that Governor Okpebholo was expected to embark on a statewide tour of the 192 polling wards to canvass support for the president ahead of the election.

Afegbua said the state government will intensify its grassroots mobilisation efforts to persuade voters and ensure that their votes counted.

“Edo people are ready. We are going to deliver Edo State to President Tinubu, and we are very proud of it, and we are going to work assiduously,” he declared.

World.title: Ex-INEC Commissioner Urges Trump To Tie US Policy To Credible 2027 Polls
World.content:
Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja

A former Electoral Commissioner of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Mike Igini, has called on the United States of America’s President Donald Trump to adopt a ‘No Mandate From Fraud’ doctrine ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 presidential election, insisting that his administration would not do business as usual with any government produced through electoral fraud.

In the letter dated November 15, 2026, Igini said the US government should make the announcement before the election and not after.

The former INEC national commissioner argued that Nigerians are not leaving Nigeria because they do not love their country, but because decades of electoral malpractice, corruption, insecurity and weak accountability.

This, he noted, has destroyed confidence in government and forced thousands of professionals, students and families to seek refuge in the United States.

Igini added: “Border enforcement alone cannot solve this. We must address the cause at the source.

“Nigeria has the population, oil, gas and talent to be one of the richest nations on earth. But [it has been] undermined by [a] leadership recruitment process that has rendered the country a plundered wilderness, littered with the debris of missed opportunities.”

Igini urged the Trump administration to dispatch a senior US delegation to engage President Bola Tinubu, presidential and governorship candidates, INEC, political parties and other relevant institutions, to communicate clearly that credible elections, peaceful competition and respect for constitutional rights are core US national interests tied to bilateral engagement, migration and stability.

In consultation with European partners, igini stressed that the U.S should issue a clear warning to the INEC Chairman, national commissioners, resident electoral commissioners and ad hoc staff drawn from federal agencies and universities.

He said officials who engage in deliberate manipulation of results, falsification of electoral records or other serious electoral offences established by credible evidence should face individual consequences, including visa restrictions and, where legally justified, targeted financial sanctions and asset freezes.

Igini also proposed extending consequences to the immediate family members where applicable.

While stressing that judicial independence is indispensable, Igini said it must not become a shield for deliberate corruption or subversion of electoral justice.

He maintained that judicial officers whose deliberate corruption or other sanctionable misconduct is established by credible evidence should face visa restrictions and asset seizures.

Igini stressed that the Nigeria Police Force, Department of State Services (DSS), armed forces, Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) and other security institutions have a duty to protect citizens and obey the law impartially, not politicians, and to stem growing violence and thuggery since campaigns commenced.

He emphasised that senior officers and commanders whose authorisation or facilitation of voter intimidation, electoral violence, unlawful suppression of opposition or manipulation of outcomes is established by credible evidence should face visa restrictions and other sanctions.

He noted that the police and DSS are currently headed by two officers with enviable records of service.

Igini maintained that the US should support credible domestic and international observers to monitor the process before, during and after the election, with particular attention to voter intimidation, impartial conduct of security personnel, publication of polling-unit results, transparent collation and resolution of electoral disputes.

Igini argued that the doctrine serves Trump’s America-First agenda in four ways: Reduces migration pressure as credible elections produce good leaders.

He explained that good leaders fix the economy, saying when Nigeria works, Nigerians will stay home and many in the US diaspora will return.

Igini said it would also help the US to stop legitimising and funding governments that lack the consent of their people.

World.title: Nigeria’s Oil Sector Shifts to Local Repairs As Operators Seek Lower Costs, Cut Imports
World.content:
Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt

Nigeria’s drive to reduce dependence on imported oil and gas equipment and lower operating costs is gaining momentum as indigenous engineering firms expand local capacity to repair and maintain critical equipment used across the industry.

The latest development is the inauguration of a new engineering service centre by Chesdon Engineering Limited in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, aimed at providing specialised equipment repair and testing services for onshore and offshore oil and gas operations.

The facility offers electric motor overhaul, valve repair and recertification, as well as specialised hose assembly and testing, providing operators with a local alternative to the costly replacement of damaged equipment.

Speaking at the official opening and dedication of the service centre and head office, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Chesdon Engineering, Nnazoba Dunu, said the investment reflected the company’s transition from an equipment procurement business to an integrated engineering services provider.

“What you see behind me today is a major milestone in our strategic evolution, transitioning Chesdon Engineering from a pure procurement partner into an end-to-end service and solutions company,” Dunu said.

He said the changing ownership structure of oil and gas assets and growing pressure on indigenous operators to improve efficiency were creating new opportunities for local engineering companies.

According to him, the industry is increasingly moving away from expensive equipment replacement towards high-reliability repairs that can reduce both capital and operating expenditure.

“The market is shifting from expensive equipment replacement to high-reliability repairs, cutting both capital expenses (CAPEX) and operating expenses (OPEX),” he stated.

Dunu said despite significant progress in Nigerian content since the enactment of the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development Act in 2010, substantial opportunities remained in equipment maintenance, technical services and engineering support.

“The facility can overhaul and repair electric motors of up to 1,000kW, undertake valve repairs and recertification across all classes, and assemble and test hoses of up to eight inches.

“It is also equipped with a DNV-certified 10-foot test bench for onshore and offshore applications, alongside specialised calibration equipment for instruments, motors and remote valve testing,” he said.

Dunu said the company had supported some major indigenous oil producers since 2024 and was investing further in testing equipment while expanding its technical workforce.

He stressed that developing Nigerian manpower was central to the investment.

“What we prefer to do is take up young graduates, train them and get them to do exactly that work that can be done anywhere outside this country.”

Chairman of the event and former Director-General of the Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency (NIMASA), Dr. Dakuku Peterside, described the investment as evidence of organisational growth and the ability of indigenous companies to respond to changing market demands.

“Organisations are wired for growth; else, they die or are acquired. Chesdon is growing because people refer to them and demand for them,” Peterside said.

World.title: Not just a crown: Miss SA misses out on luxury car and penthouse
World.content:
Miss SA winners will reportedly no longer recieve a luxury apartment or car as part of the prize package. Images via IG

It’s not just a crown that Miss SA 2026 Tiyani Makamu has forgone under the pageant’s new ownership. The new queen has also missed out on a posh penthouse and luxury car too, which were previously included in the prize package.

MISS SA NO LONGER INCLUDES CAR AND APARTMENT AS OFFICIAL PRIZES

Many South Africans have expressed their disappointment that Tiyani Makamu was not given the pageant-worthy crowning moment she deserved after receiving an underwhelming headpiece.

But that’s not all she’s missing out on. Under the new ownership of the Motsepe family, the new Miss SA’s prize package no longer includes the use of a luxury penthouse and car for the duration of her reign.



Up until this year, winners were granted the use of three-bedroom apartments in luxury estates, as well as various luxury Mercedes-Benz models.

According to Miss SA chairperson, Dr Precious Moloi-Motsepe, who took over ownership late last year, the pageant’s new model featured fewer luxury lifestyle benefits and more investment in leadership, entrepreneurship and measurable community impact.

“Our ambition is not simply to crown a woman, but to support a generation of women leaders who will help shape South Africa’s future”, Moloi-Motsepe told the public.



The Miss SA winner will also no longer compete in international pageants such as Miss World, Miss Universe, and Miss Supranational, and will focus more on domestic endeavours.

Miss SA used to have sponsors for Skin Care, Make-Up, Dental cover, clothing from YDE and Truworths I think, shoes, Mercedes car, an apartment, Jewellery from Pandora etc keep your crown!! #MissSA2026 — Yolanda_N2Lee (@symo_summer) November 14, 2026

WHAT HAS SHE WON?

Apart from the title of Miss SA, the new queen receives a R1 million cash prize and R500 000 in dedicated funding for her social-impact projects.



The first princess, Cwenga Koyana Kotu-Rammopo, receives a R250 000 cash award and a dedicated R150 000 Impact Fund, whilst the second princess, Lesego Khumo Nyathela, gets a R150 000 cash award and a dedicated R100 000 Impact Fund.

The top three contestants will also receive executive development opportunities, mentorship, wellness support, access to regional and international leadership networks, and the chance to lead initiatives in education, entrepreneurship, health, and youth development.

World.title: Palesa to Mowana: Miss SA crowns over the past decade [photos]
World.content:
Miss SA crowns over the past decade. Images via Miss SA

The Miss SA pageant has been trending on social media after it crowned its new queen, Tiyani Makama, with a headpiece resembling a party favour from a fast-food restaurant.

Unlike years before, the organisation – now run by the Motsepe family – failed to showcase the significant piece of jewellery, which is considered a symbol of national identity, heritage, and the responsibility that comes with representing the country.

WHAT HAPPENED TO MISS SA AND MOWANA?

Over the weekend, the Miss SA organisation trended online after chairperson, Dr Precious Moloi-Motsepe, gifted Tiyai Makema a makeshift crown and a cape.



The organisation later claimed that the headpiece was a “temporary ceremonial crown”, and invited designers to collaborate with it to create an official piece of jewellery.

#MissSA #MissSouthAfrica2026 this years crown 👑 is a joke though 😭, the Burger King Crown pic.twitter.com/78GgjzSXLO — Lady_L_ (@Lee_Raa_Tuu) November 15, 2026

Did you guys see the back of the crown for Miss South Africa 2026? Omg! Embarrassing 💔 pic.twitter.com/DF0W1KKKQr — Lihle (@Cebe_Lihle23) November 15, 2026

Later, Nungu Diamonds set the record straight, stating that Miss SA had failed to renew its sponsorship agreement to continue using its Mowana crown.

Nevertheless, it had offered the use of the crown to the pageant, in good faith, as negotiations continued.

However, Miss SA organisers decided against using the crown and were likely left scrambling for a replacement.



CROWNS OVER THE PAST DECADE…

Take a look at some of the crowns worn by Miss SA winners over the years…

Palesa : 2014 – 2015

Created by Jack Friedman Jewellers and Malcolm Kluk, the crown featured titanium designs of indigenous South African plants.

The crown was worn by Rolene Strauss and Liesl Laurie.

Enhle: 2016 – 2018

Jack Friedman Jewellers and Howard Friedman created a sterling silver crown which included three large purple sugilite stones, associated with love, protection and healing, as well as an amethyst and white quartz crystals.

The crown was worn by Ntandoyenkosi Kunene, Demi-Leigh Nel-Peters, and Tamaryn Green.

Have you heard? The #MissSA2016 crown has been named "Enhle". pic.twitter.com/0kXtkPzXbn — Miss South Africa (@Official_MissSA) February 28, 2016

Buhle: 2019 – 2022

American Swiss, in collaboration with Johan Louw, created a sterling silver crown featuring 2,500 cubic zirconia stones.

It was inspired by the Ndebele culture and was designed to resemble shooting stars.

It was worn by Zozibini Tunzi, Shudufhadzo Musida, Lalela Mswane and Ndavi Nokeri.

They say that a girl can't love anything more than diamonds, but we love our @AmericanSwiss created Buhle crown just a little bit more. pic.twitter.com/g8VPPfCePK — Miss South Africa (@Official_MissSA) November 11, 2019

Mowana: 2023 -2025

Nungu Diamonds created the last crown – a silver frame featuring hundreds of diamonds, gemstones and cubic zirconia.

It was inspired by the baobab tree, indigenous to Limpopo and was worn by Natasha Joubert, Mia Le Roux and Qhawekazi Mazaleni.

World.title: A home you can buy for nothing goes on sale this week
World.content:
Home goes to auction with no reserve. Image for illustration purpose only. Image: Pexel

Of all the homes in South Africa going to auction this week, only one doesn’t have a reserve price.

This home in a middle-income suburb has no asking price.

Buyers could get the bargain of a lifetime: a home below R1 000.



But there are conditions.

A home you could buy for free

This week, a home in Welkom makes its way to a sheriff’s auction. The home doesn’t have a price.

Instead, bidders decide how much they’re willing to pay.

The sheriff has to accept the highest bid, regardless of the amount.

Of course, when the final hammer falls, the bidder will be responsible for paying the sheriff’s commission and settling the balance.

The auction will take place at the Welkom Sheriff’s Office: 366 Stateway, Doorn, Welkom, Free State, on Wednesday 26 November at 11:00.



The home going under the hammer is a 3-bedroom, 1-bathroom property with a garage on Van Wyk Louw Street in Jan Cilliers Park.

It’s a suburb where homes start at R650 000, and the average sale price is R1.1 million.

But this property is sold as-is, and buyers cannot inspect it before bidding.

The downside of buying at auction

Auction properties are routinely damaged by former occupants, and when the property isn’t vacant, buyers will have to spend money evicting the residents.

The buyer is also responsible for paying any municipal debt.

The home going to auction this week has R332 763 in municipal debt.

What is a no-reserve auction and what will you pay?

Before a bank can take a property to auction, it approaches the court.

In court, a judge sets a reserve price.

The reserve price is the lowest bid needed for a transfer of ownership.

To take possession of the home, a buyer must bid more than that price; otherwise, the bank becomes the owner.

But a no-reserve auction means there’s no minimum.

In theory, a bidder could bid R1 000.

If no one places a higher bid, they become the owner.

Because property owners can still owe the bank money after their home sells at auction, courts often place a reserve price, even if it’s R50 000.

World.title: Springbok and wife make miracle baby announcement
World.content:
Springbok Willie le Roux and his wife Holly Clare are expecting their first child. Images via IG

Springbok Willie Le Roux and his wife, Holly Clare, have announced their pregnancy, just months after sharing their struggle with infertility with the public.

The rugby player and the professional nutritionist – who wed two years ago – have been together since 2019.

WILLIE LE ROUX AND WIFE HOLLY CLARE ARE EXPECTING!

In their Instagram post, Willie Le Roux and wife Holly Clare went public with news of their first pregnancy.



“Some dreams take a little longer”, Holly shared.

The couple announced the news with a tennis-themed celebration with friends and family – including fellow Springbok Handre Pollard- at the Nieuwe Sion Estate near Franschhoek

The “Le Roux Open” featured a fun day of games and drinks between pals.



In February, Holly Clare shared her infertility struggle.

The Springbok WAG revealed she had suffered from “silent endometriosis” and had undergone an “exploratory” operation.

Holly Clare shared that the recovery was long and painful. However, she was using her platform to encourage women in similar situations to explore their options.



She shared at the time: “You don’t get given any promises in infertility, but the days you feel hopeful, you grab them. Children are the biggest blessing, and I am hopeful we will have our own one day”.

SPRINGBOK BABIES ON THE WAY

Willie le Roux is one of several Springboks whose wives are pregnant.

Others include Kwagga Smth – also set to become a first-time dad – and Jasper Wiese.



Other players like Makazole Mapimpi, RG Snyman and Vincent Tshituka have also recently welcomed their bundles of joy.

World.title: Pitso Mosimane on Lyle Foster’s quality
World.content:
Bafana Bafana coach Pitso Mosimane enjoyed the moment Foster chose to pass the ball to Relebohile Mofokeng instead of going for goal himself.

Mofokeng made no mistake with the opportunity, putting South Africa 2-1 ahead in the 76th minute at the Orlando Amstel Arena.

Foster had come on as a substitute in the second half and was making his first appearance under Mosimane.



PITSO MOSIMANE EXPLAINS FOSTER’S ASSIST

The Houston Dynamo striker had missed the coach’s opening three matches following his club move and returned to the squad after a difficult 2026 FIFA World Cup.

He had already come close to scoring after receiving a delivery from fellow substitute Puso Dithejane, but his effort went narrowly wide.

The next opportunity was different. Instead of trying to finish the move himself, Foster picked out Mofokeng. The striker then ran towards the technical area, where Mosimane embraced him.

Speaking to FARPost, Mosimane explained that the celebration was mainly about Foster’s decision to put the team first.

The coach felt the striker could have tried to score himself, but was pleased that he chose to give Mofokeng the opportunity.

“He showed me that he’s not here for himself. Normally, he would not pass that ball back… So he shows that he wants to play for the team and he shows that he’s not selfish. And that’s the embrace. I appreciate that.



Mosimane also praised Mofokeng’s finish, describing it as a quality goal.

He explained that while he would have been happy to see Foster score, the decision to create an opportunity for a teammate made the moment even better.

“Well-taken goal, world-class finish. I celebrated with Rele a lot. But more to Lyle, to say, ‘You really show that you want to play for the country,’ Mosimane added.

FOSTER SENDS A MESSAGE TO HIS TEAMMATES

Mosimane believes players show their attitude through what they do on the pitch.

For him, Foster’s decision was an example of how a striker can contribute to the team even when he has an opportunity to score himself.

“And that’s the only message you can send. You send the message on the pitch by your behaviour. The behaviour tells everything. If he scores without passing it, it’s good also. But it’s also sweeter when we score when he passes, because normally strikers don’t pass.”

Foster’s first appearance under Mosimane therefore gave the coach something positive to take from an otherwise disappointing evening.

Bafana had taken the lead through an own goal before Kenya fought back to level matters.

Mofokeng then restored South Africa’s advantage with his 76th-minute goal, but the hosts could not hold on.

Ryan Ogam scored a late equaliser to make it 2-2 and ensure Kenya left Soweto with a point.

The two teams will meet again in Nairobi on Tuesday, where Foster could get another opportunity to make an impression under the Bafana coach.

World.title: Hlaudi Motsoeneng confirms coalition agreement with ANC
World.content:
Former South African Broadcasting Corporation (SABC) chief operating officer Hlaudi Motsoeneng has confirmed that his party, the African Content Movement (ACM), will work with the African National Congress (ANC) to govern Maluti-a-Phofung Local Municipality in the Free State.

This comes as political parties continue coalition negotiations to reach possible agreements in hung councils following the 2026 local government elections held on 4 November.

HLAUDI MOTSOENENG AND ANC REACH COALITION AGREEMENT

Speaking to the SABC in Johannesburg on Sunday, Motsoeneng said the ACM had initially planned to win all the seats in the municipality. However, voters had decided that the party would have to work with other political parties.



He said the ANC had approached the ACM to engage on addressing challenges and leadership in municipalities.

“For us, what is important is service delivery for as long as the ACM is in power. I told the people that I’m not promising them, but there will be water, roads, electricity in Maluti-a-Phofung, and we must create employment.

“Those are the issues that occupy our minds because we want to change the lives of people in Maluti-a-Phofung,” he said.

“The ANC and ACM will work together in Maluti-a-Phofung,” he added.

Hlaudi Motsoeneng also revealed that the two parties had not yet discussed the allocation of leadership positions, including who would be appointed mayor and deputy mayor, as well as other positions within the municipal leadership.

World.title: Mamelodi Sundowns legend suffers injury on African duty
World.content:
The Sundowns legend was forced off during Uganda’s 1-1 draw against Botswana in their 2027 AFCON qualifying match.

Onyango lasted just 42 minutes before being replaced by 22-year-old Kingdom Osayi, who currently plays for Swedish third-tier outfit Assyriska FF.

The injury is another concern for Sundowns, particularly with the veteran goalkeeper yet to make an appearance for the club this season.



Onyango has been included in Miguel Cardoso’s matchday squad on four occasions but is still waiting for his first minutes in the current campaign.

MAMELODI SUNDOWNS LEGEND’s INTERNATIONAL RETURN

The former Uganda captain came out of international retirement after four years to help the Cranes prepare for the 2027 AFCON tournament, which they will co-host.

Head coach Paul Put wanted the experience of the veteran goalkeeper as Uganda looked to bring younger players into the national team.

Onyango has started eight of Uganda’s last 14 international matches since returning, keeping two clean sheets.

The goalkeeper previously explained why he believed having experienced players alongside younger footballers was important.

“Of course every team needs senior players and young blood because the young blood gives more energy and the senior players help the players to calm down when there is pressure to help them to manage the game,” he said last year.



“The game requires a lot of experience but it also requires a lot of running which is done by the young ones and that is what we share.”

His comments came after Put made it clear that experience would be important in helping the next generation of Ugandan players.

SUNDOWNS LEGEND NEARING THE END

Onyango’s future at club level has also been a talking point after Cardoso previously explained the role of the experienced goalkeeper and captain Themba Zwane in the Sundowns squad.

Both players understand their positions within the team, with the coach having to manage an experienced group alongside younger players.

There is also the possibility that the upcoming AFCON tournament could be Onyango’s final appearance at the competition.

The 2027 edition would be his fifth AFCON tournament, with the veteran expected to consider bringing his international career to an end afterwards.

Uganda remain in a good position in Group H despite the draw against Botswana.

The Cranes have collected five points from their opening three matches and currently sit at the top of the group.

However, Sundowns will be hoping Onyango’s injury is not serious as they prepare for the demanding fixtures ahead.

The goalkeeper has been an important figure at Chloorkop for several years, and his experience remains valuable even as his playing time has reduced.

World.title: Explainer : Why your child may end up in a different school
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Gauteng Education is racing against time to place pupils in schools for the 2027 Academic Year.

While some households will receive a notification of a successful placement at a selected school, others will have to adjust to a whole new school.

Gauteng Education MEC Lebogang Maile revealed that more than 77,000 applicants are yet to be placed, with Grade 8 pupils making up the largest share.

According to Maile, the department has identified more than 139,000 available spaces, but acknowledges that these are not necessarily in the schools or communities where demand is highest.

READ | Over 77,000 pupils in Gauteng remain unplaced

To date, 278 schools have reached capacity, including 174 primary schools and 104 secondary schools.

Pressure, according to Maile, remains concentrated in key urban centres, with the highest volumes recorded in districts located within the metropolitan municipalities of Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni.

This revelation by the provincial government may leave many parents, some still clinging to their phones for a notification, with one question: When and where will my child be placed?

Maile indicated that unplaced applicants who cannot be accommodated at these 278 schools are being transferred to the next closest school with available space.

“Gauteng does not experience uniform pressure across its schooling system. Some schools have available capacity, while others receive substantially more applications than they can reasonably accommodate. “Consequently, the challenge is not simply to count available spaces. It is to align those spaces with learner demand, geographical accessibility, school infrastructure and the practical circumstances of families,” Maile explained.

Maile said areas of high demand must be understood within the country's broader spatial and geo-social realities.

READ | Gauteng's 2027 school placement scramble

Not only does Gauteng have the highest population, but it also experiences a significant in-migration, with many turning to the province for employment or to improve their livelihoods.

These implications, according to the MEC, are evident in the province's schooling system.

“With an annual population growth of 1.6%, which outpaces the national average of 1.2 %, the province’s growth results in greater demand for schools, classrooms, educators, transport and associated infrastructure, "Maile added.

Maile said these pressure areas remain the primary focus for placement interventions, capacity optimisation and transfer management to maximise available spaces and reduce the number of unplaced applicants.

He said as of 13 November 2026, the Department commenced issuing transfer offers.

These offers are intended to help address outstanding placements, particularly where schools originally selected by applicants have reached capacity.

World.title: Gauteng's 2027 school placement scramble
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Parents and guardians of Grade 1 and Grade 8 pupils who have not been placed at their desired school due to capacity will be issued transfer offers to alternative schools.

They will then have seven days to accept or decline the offer.

This is according to Gauteng Education MEC Lebogang Maile, who gave an update on placement for the 2027 academic year, scholar transport as well as school funding.

Maile said the issuing of transfer offers began on 13 November and forms part of the admission process.

To date, more than 77,000 applicants are yet to be placed, with Grade 8 pupils making up the largest share.

READ | Over 77,000 pupils in Gauteng remain unplaced

The department says it has identified more than 139,000 available spaces, but acknowledges that these are not necessarily in the schools or communities where demand is highest.

“We understand that receiving an offer from a school other than a preferred institution may not be preferable. However, it is important to recognise that the Department must balance individual preferences with the available capacity of schools and the obligation to provide access to education across the province,” he said.

Parents and guardians who want to challenge placement outcomes will also be given an opportunity to raise objections and appeals through an established process.

An objection may be lodged within the prescribed seven-day period, with the Department required to consider and determine it within the applicable 14-day period.

World.title: KZN residents urged to keep stormwater drains clear
World.content:
ETHEKWINI - With heavy rain expected, eThekwini Municipality says it is investing millions in road, water and sanitation infrastructure.

The money will also ensure the maintenance of drainage systems and widening canals to reduce the risk of flooding.

But the city says infrastructure alone is not enough, urging residents to stop dumping litter and building materials into stormwater drains.

World.title: The new Miss SA and the missing Mowana crown: Nungu Diamonds explains
World.content:
JOHANNESURG - Tiyani Makamu is South Africa's new beauty Queen.

But the 27-year-old's crowning on Saturday night was not without controversy, as social media attention turned to the crown on her head.

While many hailed the moment, others questioned why she did not wear the iconic Mowana crown by Nungu Diamonds.

Nungu Diamonds, which took note of the commentary, broke their silence on Sunday in a statement, explaining the crown and their relationship with the Miss South Africa Organisation.

READ | Miss SA 2025 | Qhawekazi Mazaleni crowned new queen

The fine jewellery company set the record straight, saying Nungu Diamonds did not design, craft, or supply the 2026 Miss South Africa crown.

This follows the non-renewal of a sponsorship agreement with the Miss South Africa Organisation for the 2026 pageant.

“Negotiations were conducted in good faith and continued into the final days before the finale; the parties were ultimately unable to reach a mutually beneficial agreement,” the statement read.

The company says its representatives had initially granted Miss South Africa permission to use the Mowana Crown at the finale on the understanding that sponsorship discussions would resume after the event.

However, it seems Miss SA opted otherwise

“The decision not to use the Mowana Crown rested solely with the Miss South Africa Organisation. We respect that decision,” Nungu Diamonds said.

The partnership between the Miss South Africa Organisation and Nungu Diamonds spans more than three years, starting in 2023.

Natasha Joubert became the first Miss South Africa to wear the Nungu Diamonds Mowana crown in 2023.

Miss South Africa 2024 Nia Le Roux and Miss South Africa 2025 Qhawe Mazaleni then wore it.

READ | WATCH | Women's month | Sign language is now official in SA

The crown, dubbed Mowana, is inspired by the baobab tree of Limpopo and stands as a symbol of strength, resilience and transformation

It features over 800 stones, including diamonds, gemstones, and cubic zirconia, with the largest weighing 15 carats.

Despite the controversy surrounding her crown, Makamu has her sights set on entrepreneurship during her reign as Miss South Africa.

World.title: Thwake Dam project reaches 94pc completion
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Thwake Multipurpose Dam, which is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment.[File,Standard]

Thwake Dam is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment as residents seek a review of alleged construction-related damage claims.

Principal Secretary for Water and Sanitation Julius Korir told the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Blue Economy, Water and Irrigation that construction had reached 94.2 per cent.

The dam is being built at the confluence of the Athi and Thwake rivers along the Makueni-Kitui border. It is designed to provide water for domestic use, irrigation and electricity generation.

Martin Kimeu, a resident of Wote, said the project would improve access to water for farming in the region.

“Ukambani is fertile. Water has been the biggest impediment to the realization of our agricultural potential. Thwake Dam water is the clear solution to this,” he said.

Kimeu also defended the compensation process, saying he had followed the project since its inception and believed the exercise had been conducted properly.

Jacob Mwanzia, a resident of Madangi Village, said households in his area had been assessed and compensated. He argued that outstanding complaints should be addressed without delaying the project.

Mariam Mwikali, another resident, said assessments had been conducted on affected properties and residents given an opportunity to raise concerns.

However, some households have complained that construction-related blasting damaged their homes. Residents have reported cracks in walls, windows and foundations as well as dust, noise and ground vibrations.

In August 2026, residents from villages in Mavindini Ward, organised under the Thwake Dam Blasting-Affected Community Committee, sought an independent review by the African Development Bank (AfDB).

The residents alleged that some properties had been left out of assessments and compensation. They also sought access to assessment reports, photographs, measurements, valuation records and estimates for repairs or reconstruction.

A project official said the dam's safety department invited competitive bids for an independent assessment of properties potentially affected by blasting. Agile Consulting was selected to conduct the exercise.

The official said the consultant assessed 330 households within a two-kilometre radius of the construction site and submitted its report to the project implementation team. A large proportion of those assessed were satisfied with the exercise, the official added, without giving a breakdown.

Ben Mwongela, a director at Agile Consulting, said the assessment reviewed blasting records, vibration data and compliance with regulatory standards.

The exercise also involved documenting households, classifying structural defects and preparing bills of quantities and cost estimates for repairs or reconstruction, he said.

The AfDB conducted a field mission to the project between September 21 and 25, with its report published on October 21, 2026.

The bank's team, led by project task manager Nancy Ogal, met residents whose homes had been affected by blasting and identified outstanding health, safety, environmental and social issues, including homeowner grievances.

The bank called for timely compensation and continued monitoring of the project's environmental and social performance.

During a stakeholder engagement visit to Mavindini in October, Korir said the government had secured additional funding after the project experienced cash-flow constraints.

“When we ran short of cash, we engaged with our development partners, and they allocated additional funding, and this money will now go towards total completion of the project,” he said.

In June 2026, the AfDB approved additional financing of €68.39 million to support completion of the first phase, alongside funding from the Kenyan government.

The bank said the financing would support engineering refinements and safety works, including strengthening foundations, raising the dam and constructing two additional saddle dams.

The project has four phases. The first involves construction of the dam, while the subsequent phases cover hydropower generation, water supply and sanitation infrastructure, and irrigation.

The dam is approximately 80.5 metres high and has a planned storage capacity of 688 million cubic metres.

Once the water supply component is operational, the project is expected to provide 150,000 cubic metres of treated water daily to an estimated 1.3 million people in Makueni and Kitui counties and Konza Technopolis in Machakos County.

The irrigation scheme is designed to cover 40,000 hectares, equivalent to about 100,000 acres of agricultural land.

The project is also designed to generate 20 megawatts of hydropower.

The water supply, irrigation and hydropower components require infrastructure beyond the dam structure, including treatment and distribution networks and power generation facilities.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”

The report shows how widespread the abuse is. “Twenty-six percent of women age 15–49 have ever experienced technology-facilitated violence from any perpetrator,” the report says, and 21 per cent experienced it often or sometimes in the 12 months before the survey. Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced it at the hands of a current, most recent or previous partner.

The burden is not spread evenly, the report states that Nairobi City records the highest lifetime experience from any perpetrator at 33 per cent, followed by Murang’a and Baringo at 32 per cent each.

“For abuse by an intimate partner, Homa Bay 36 per cent and Baringo 35 per cent lead, while in the 12 months before the survey Trans Nzoia topped the list at 31 per cent. At the other end, Mandera and Wajir report just 3 per cent, a figure that may say as much about silence as about safety,” the report says

The picture is similar among young people. A 2024 rapid study by the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, working with the UNFPA and Women Economic Empowerment, found that nearly 90 per cent of young adults enrolled in three Nairobi tertiary institutions had witnessed TFGBV, and 39 per cent had experienced it personally.

Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced gender violence committed by a current, most recent or previous partner, and 22 per cent did so in the past year. When women were asked who was responsible, the answer was blunt. Current husbands or intimate partners accounted for 61 per cent of perpetrators, former partners for 22 per cent and strangers for just 13 per cent.

Women who have never been married or had a partner face a different threat. For them, the most common perpetrators are strangers at 45 per cent, online attackers at 23 per cent and friends or acquaintances at 20 per cent.

Warning signs

Control is the common thread. The report describes such behaviours by a male partner as “important early warning signs that may escalate into violence within a relationship.”

Sixty-one per cent of ever-partnered women say their current or most recent partner has shown at least one controlling behaviour, and 27 per cent report three or more. Half say he has been jealous or angry when they spoke to other men, and 36 per cent say he insists on knowing where they are at all times. Others describe partners who demand passwords or read messages without consent.

Age and marital status matter. Technology-based gender violence is lowest among girls aged 15–19 at 10 per cent and highest among women aged 20–24 at 37 per cent. Forty-one per cent of divorced, separated or widowed women have experienced it, compared with 27 per cent of married women and 19 per cent of the never married.

Yet the digital rights advocate Cherie Oyier, a programmes officer at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), says the low figures in some places should not be read as safety. Much of the abuse happens where nobody can see it.

“Closed applications, meaning like WhatsApp, those are the ones that most people, intimate partners will usually use,” she says. “Even as you are scrolling the internet to look for these instances, we may not be able to catch it. But it does not mean that it is not happening or that it is at a lower level.”

Culture also silences women. “Most women are told just endure, this is what marriage is about,” Oyier says. “Sometimes they don’t know, it’s so overt, like it doesn’t come out clearly that this is abuse. So most of the times, it is not reported.”

Online, abuse has been turned into entertainment. “It has become banter,” she says. “Even the people who are experiencing it have trivialised it. It’s now ingrained to you, like this is something that happens, you should expect it actually. If you post a picture, one of the things that you are thinking about is what kind of comments am I going to get.”

A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: Not so fast: Court slams brake on ARA over wealth forfeiture
World.content:
Felix Mecha Nyakundi could not provide a plausible explanation for how he amassed his wealth.

The Court of Appeal has ruled that the government cannot go after a person’s wealth without prior investigations to establish reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property constitutes proceeds of crime.

In a landmark judgment, Justices Patrick Kiage, Jamila Mohammed and Nduma Nderi said that although it does not require a person to be charged for a crime for the Asset Recovery Agency (ARA) to come knocking, it bears the responsibility to link the wealth or cash to a crime.

World.title: Back to sender: Aisha Jumwa returns to UDA
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto welcome former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa has returned to President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA), ending a three-month political fallout with the ruling party that saw her join opposition outfit Wiper Patriotic Front and declare support for the one-term movement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

President Ruto welcomed Jumwa back into UDA at State House, Mombasa, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in a political reunion that could reshape alignments in Kilifi County and the wider Coast region as parties position themselves for next year's elections.

The reunion comes barely three months after Jumwa dramatically announced her departure from UDA, accusing the party leadership of frustrating her political ambitions and failing to support her quest for the Kilifi gubernatorial seat.

On July 30, 2026, Jumwa announced her resignation during a press conference at her Kakuyuni home in Malindi, saying her attempts to have her grievances addressed by the President had repeatedly been unsuccessful.

Among her concerns was what she described as humiliation and rejection within the ruling party, including an alleged incident in which she was chased out of State House during a meeting between Ruto and Coast leaders.

She also accused sections of the ruling coalition of undermining her gubernatorial ambitions, claiming that the political arrangements being pursued in Kilifi were designed to deny her an opportunity to contest for the county's top seat.

President William Ruto recieve former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Jumwa, who was among UDA's founding members and one of Ruto's most vocal mobilisers at the Coast during the 2022 elections, said her loyalty to the people of Kilifi outweighed her allegiance to any political party.

"My loyalty to the people of Kilifi will always be greater than my loyalty to any political party. The voice of the people of Kilifi is louder than the voice of UDA," she declared during her exit announcement.

Her departure marked a significant political shift, particularly given her central role in mobilising support for Ruto in the Coast region.

In August, Jumwa turned to the opposition, where she was warmly received by Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, who visited her at her Kakuyuni residence on August 14 alongside a delegation of party leaders, including Nyali MP Mohamed Ali, Kitui Senator Enoch Wambua and Wundanyi MP Danson Mwashako.

Kalonzo subsequently proposed Jumwa for the position of Wiper Deputy Party Leader, citing her political experience and influence, while also backing her ambition to contest the Kilifi governorship on a Wiper ticket.

Jumwa embraced the new political alliance, declaring support for the one-term movement and threatening to mobilise UDA supporters in Kilifi to deregister from the ruling party and join Wiper.

"We are the ones who registered UDA members in Kilifi, and we are embarking on a grassroots campaign to deregister them from UDA and join Wiper," she said at the time.

On September 8, she attended a meeting involving Wiper leaders and Coast gubernatorial aspirants, including Mohammed Ali and Danson Mwashako, as the party intensified efforts to expand its influence in the region.

However, the political alliance has now taken another turn, with Jumwa returning to the party she had accused of frustrating her ambitions.

Announcing her return, President Ruto welcomed the former Cabinet Secretary back into UDA, signalling renewed efforts to consolidate the ruling party's support in the Coast region.

"I look forward to working with her to advance the party’s transformation agenda at the Coast and across the country. We remain committed to uniting leaders and Kenyans around our shared vision of a united, inclusive and prosperous Kenya," the President said.

Her return comes as Ruto steps up political mobilisation in the Coast region ahead of the 2027 elections, with Kilifi emerging as an important battleground for competing political formations.

Jumwa's political journey has been characterised by shifting alliances. She previously served under the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), representing Malindi in Parliament before becoming Kilifi's first Woman Representative between 2013 and 2017.

She later became one of Ruto's key political allies and served in his Cabinet.

World.title: Buxton estate tensions escalate after county officials attacked
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

A dispute over the multibillion-shilling Buxton Point housing project in Mombasa turned violent after county officials were allegedly attacked while enforcing a government order suspending construction over outstanding contractual obligations.

The confrontation came a day after County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Lands, Housing, and Urban Development Mohamed Hussein ordered GulfCap Real Estate to halt all construction activities pending the resolution of disputes involving the county government and hundreds of former Buxton Estate residents.

The officials were reportedly pelted with stones as they attempted to serve the developer with an enforcement notice, with allegations that individuals linked to businessman Suleiman Shahbal were involved in the confrontation.

Hussein condemned the incident, saying attempts to intimidate government officers would not derail efforts to enforce the law and protect public interests.

"Let them bring goons, machetes, and stones if they want. I am not intimidated. I will execute my duties, and nobody will threaten me. The law must be followed, regardless of who you are or how much money you have," he said.

"We are here for the people of Mombasa, and we will ensure their rights are protected. Nobody is above the law," he added.

The November 10 enforcement notice, issued by County Director of Physical Planning Qassim Ali, directed GulfCap Real Estate to stop further development activities and obtain valid construction permits.

The notice, issued under Section 72(1) of the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, cited construction under a varied development plan without county approval and an ongoing dispute involving the developer, former tenants, and the county government.

The notice was reportedly received by the project's manager, Billy Okendo.

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county government and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units and commercial spaces developed in the first and second phases.

An addendum to the agreement signed on January 15, 2020, outlines the county's entitlement, with the allocation expected to be transferred upon completion of the second phase.

In a letter dated April 30, 2025, the county demanded 10 per cent of the proposed 1,800 housing units, translating to 180 apartments. The demand was renewed in February 2026, with the county seeking details on how the allocation would be implemented.

However, in correspondence dated September 22, 2026, the Department of Lands, Urban Planning and Housing expressed concern over what it described as the developer's failure to provide substantive responses to previous demands.

The county also questioned whether GulfCap had provided performance security equivalent to 10 per cent of the total construction cost for each phase, as required under the agreement.

It further demanded proof of payment of the Project Development Fee, which is payable in instalments as the project progresses.

The county said it had also raised technical and planning concerns during a meeting with the developer on April 15, 2026, including the need to address outstanding issues and resubmit the masterplan application.

But the dispute goes beyond the county's financial and contractual entitlement, with more than 500 former residents accusing the developer of failing to honour promises made when they were displaced in 2019.

John Tsuma, Secretary-General of the Buxton Tenants Welfare Association, said former residents had waited for more than seven years to return to their homes despite assurances that they would be prioritised once construction was completed.

"We are very disappointed by what happened. We had a meeting with the CECM, and he made it clear that all construction activities should stop until the outstanding issues are resolved. We did not go there to fight anybody. We wanted the directive implemented," Tsuma said.

He accused the developer of benefiting from the project while former residents continued to struggle to secure the houses they were promised.

"The developer has benefited from A to Z. He was given land by the county government, and the houses were sold off-plan. Yet, when it comes to fulfilling the promises made to former residents, we are still being taken around in circles," he said.

Tsuma said residents were not demanding free houses but wanted the affordable tenant-purchase arrangement they were promised before leaving the estate.

"We are not asking for free houses. We want the tenant-purchase arrangement that was promised to us so that we can pay for the houses and return to our homes," he said.

He also questioned why the developer had allegedly failed to surrender the county government's 184 housing units under the joint venture arrangement.

Mohamed Mzee Rubea, chairman of the evicted Buxton residents, said the money paid to the families during their displacement was a relocation allowance and not compensation for their homes.

He said the former tenants were given Sh240,000, with assurances that they would rent alternative accommodation for 12 months and return once the houses were completed.

"What we received was relocation money, not compensation for our houses. We were told to take the money and rent houses for 12 months and that we would be the first people to return once construction was completed. But here we are, more than seven years later, still waiting," Rubea said.

He said the original agreement involved 522 former tenants who were promised priority access to houses under the redevelopment.

Rubea added that each household was also promised Sh60,000 as a deposit towards acquiring a house under the tenant-purchase scheme.

"We were promised Sh60,000 as a deposit for those who would take up the houses. The developer later said the money would only be given to those who actually acquired the units. We are still waiting, and many of us have not received anything," he said. At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

He further claimed that the county had written to the developer in 2023, 2024, and 2025 seeking engagement over the outstanding commitments.

Mutua Mutia, another former resident, said the prolonged dispute had left families frustrated, especially after they were promised they would return within a year.

"I have lived in Buxton since I was a young boy. My firstborn child is now more than 30 years old, and the history of Buxton is one that pains us. We were evicted with the promise that we would return after one year, but today it is seven years and we are still struggling," Mutia said.

The former residents are also demanding the reconstruction of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) centre demolished to pave the way for the project, as well as the construction of a promised community social centre.

Hussein said the county had yet to receive either facility or its share of the housing project.

"The county has not received its 10 per cent share to date. There was an agreement that the demolished ECD centre would be reconstructed and handed over to the county, alongside a community social centre, but we have not received either," he said.

The first phase of Buxton Point delivered 584 housing units in 2023, while the second phase is expected to provide between 1,400 and 1,500 additional apartments. Completion had been scheduled for August 2027.

However, GulfCap Real Estate Chief Executive Officer Chris Ochieng defended the developer's position, saying 492 housing units would be handed over to buyers by December.

While urging the county to stop politicising the project, Ochieng warned that the ongoing controversy risks disrupting the project’s completion and affecting hundreds of workers who depend on it for their livelihoods.

He said the county government's 10 per cent share would be transferred upon completion of the project.

He also maintained that the developer had supported displaced residents by providing Sh240,000 for relocation and offering them preferential rates to purchase apartments.

Ochieng said the continued involvement of county officials in the dispute was unfortunate, particularly at a time when 492 homeowners are expecting to take possession of their houses in December.

He noted that the controversy was not only creating uncertainty among prospective homeowners but also threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of people employed directly and indirectly through the project.

“It is very unfortunate that Mombasa County officials are bringing politics into a national project. We have 492 homeowners who expect to take possession of their units by December. Beyond the homeowners, hundreds of people depend on this project for employment and their daily livelihoods,” said Ochieng.

He called on the county leadership to allow the project to proceed without unnecessary political interference, arguing that Mombasa has previously witnessed housing projects that stalled despite significant public interest.

World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses opposition divisions as 'polygamous family' rivalry
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County on November 8, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims of divisions within the Opposition, describing the disagreements among its leaders as normal sibling rivalry in a polygamous family, while insisting that the coalition remains united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua said the Opposition leaders were committed to working together to challenge President William Ruto, despite their differing opinions on the timing of selecting a joint presidential flagbearer and occasional disagreements among their political camps.

Speaking during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County, the former Deputy President likened the political differences to children from the same father competing for attention but eventually uniting whenever an external threat emerges.

“The Opposition is united to a man, and we have agreed that we will have a single presidential candidate. Everybody is committed, and we talk on a daily basis. The only challenge is normal petty problems,” he said.

He added that the disagreements should not be interpreted as a breakdown of the coalition, maintaining that such differences were healthy and expected in a broad political alliance.

“Ile shida kidogo ni ya boma, watoto wengi wa baba mmoja. Watoto huko ndani, oh, baba anakupenda kuliko mimi. Mbona ulinunua kiatu kabla mimi? Si hiyo ni kawaida kwa polygamous family?” he posed.

Gachagua said the bigger threat to Opposition unity was not necessarily disagreements among its principals but the conduct of their supporters, social media influencers and political bloggers, whom he accused of fuelling unnecessary tensions through insults and online confrontations.

He cautioned Opposition leaders against allowing overzealous supporters to dictate their political relationships, warning that unchecked political attacks could eventually weaken the coalition and undermine its common objective.

“If there is anything to separate us, it is our supporters and social media bloggers. Wanawakisha moto hakuna, watu wangu na wa Matiang'i wanatukanana na sisi tunakula breakfast pamoja,” he said.

He further claimed that some political influencers associated with his DCP party had been recruited and allegedly paid by individuals opposed to him to attack his leadership and the party.

Gachagua urged coalition principals to exercise restraint and avoid reacting to every provocation from supporters, insisting that political leaders must remain focused on the bigger picture.

“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.
