But for years, there were no rules or regulations making the federal government actually enforce those protections.

Until the spring of 1977, when a band of activists with disabilities decided to do something about it. Led by Heumann and Kitty Cone, activists took over the former Department of Health, Education and Welfare building in San Francisco for nearly a month — widely considered the longest sit-in of a federal building in U.S. history.

People across disability groups — from wheelchair users to people with intellectual and health-related disabilities — camped out, demanding, and eventually winning the passage of rules that made Section 504 enforceable. The protests paved the way for federally funded institutions like schools, libraries, city buildings and other entities to be made accessible for disabled people.

toggle caption i HolLynn D'Lil/Getty Images

"Judy always said, 'disability only becomes a tragedy for me when society fails to provide the things we need to lead our lives' — job opportunities or barrier-free buildings, for example," says former NPR correspondent Joe Shapiro, who covered disability and was a friend of Heumann's until she died in 2023.

Regarding disability rights as basic civil rights was a novel concept at the time, but has remained core to the movement today.

Shapiro says Heumann was fueled by the idea of a generation of young disabled people who would come of age under the ADA: "They see the ADA as a floor, not a ceiling, and Judy loved that there's this new generation demanding more."

Sponsor Message

With the film having opened in theaters this month and now streaming on Apple TV, NPR sat down with some members of the ADA generation to talk about Heumann's legacy, and the threats they see today to the movement she helped launch.

"It is our job to carry on her legacy and keep that fire burning all these decades later," says Kaleigh Brendle, who started a disability rights organization called Judy's League to push back against the Trump administration's efforts to roll back protections attached to Section 504.

Last month, a federal judge dealt a blow to disability rights activists by agreeing to strip out mentions of "integration" of people with disabilities from Section 504 regulations. This erased some of the very language Heumann and her movement had helped win 50 years ago.

As she watched Being Heumann, Brendle says she "felt simultaneously sad that we're here again because I know she would be hurting to see so much of what she fought for at risk. But it also strengthened my resolve."

Brendle, who is blind and has other disabilities, held a watch party of Being Heumann with four other members of Judy's League. They spoke to NPR about their impressions.

These are excerpts from that conversation, edited for length and clarity.

On what stood out most about Being Heumann:

Liam Holland, 25, Philadelphia: The very first line of the movie is Judy chanting "[Sign 504]!" That gave me chills right away, because almost 50 years later, 504 is the exact reason we founded Judy's League. Seeing her lead the chant hit home because we are still fighting those exact same battles today.

Cricket Bidleman, 27, Baltimore: Like Liam said, seeing history come full circle was not particularly encouraging. But we did it once, so we can do it again. We can save 504.

Kaleigh Brendle, 23, Berkeley, Calif.: What I loved seeing over and over on display was just the unshakable resolve that Judy showed, that fire that would not be extinguished … And I think right now we're seeing relentless challenges to our rights from this administration, from every direction. ... It really gave me hope and renewed what I feel we need to be doing right now.

Sponsor Message

Ellana Crew, 30, Baltimore: I feel I've never seen so many real disabled people on screen in one place ... They are laughing, they are swearing, they're telling dirty jokes … That was one of my favorite things, honestly, it was just like, 'OK, wow, I didn't expect that to be in this movie.' They are not shying away from disabled people as sexual and romantic beings, which is rarely something that society lets us talk about. And ... it's remarkable how many of the sentiments in the movie, based on this time in the 1970s, still feel so relevant today.

On what parts of the disability rights movement back then still feel relevant:

Ellana Crew: A lot of attitudes expressed by non-disabled people [in the film] felt fairly indistinguishable from the attitudes I hear today. Like some of the same sentiments, some of the same opinions of pity, charity-based mindsets of like, "Oh, well we feel bad for you, but we can't do anything about it, it's just too hard." I think people would be amazed how often that still happens today, or maybe they wouldn't.

Cricket Bidleman: It's amazing to see how in some ways we've made so much progress. I mean, now we have computers and technology that work for us, and autonomous vehicles and things like that. But the discrimination hasn't really changed that much.

Kaleigh Brendle: What really moved me was hearing Judy lead the "Sign 504" chant because I, along with several other people in Judy's league ... we were in Austin, Texas on the Capitol steps this July. And all these years later we were having to chant "Hands off 504."

On how the legacy of Judy Heumann and other activists has shaped the disability rights movement today:

Liam Holland: Every week, I roll a mile and back [in my wheelchair] by myself to get chicken for my dinner puree. That trip has a lot of curb cuts. Before 504, sidewalks did not have ramps, which stopped disabled people's access to sidewalks. The [1977] sit-in forced the government to mandate public access. So every curb I go over is directly tied to that fight. ... The people at the deli see me come in every week by myself. They fist-bump me, get my card from my wallet, put it back ... And then I roll home over curb cuts listening to music. So what Judy means to me, quite simply, is independence and normalcy.

Sponsor Message

Leigh White, 30, Galloway, N.J.: Unfortunately, history rhymes. And we're not right back where we started, but we are in the crucible, if you will, where we're kind of being fired at on all sides. And it's important to remember her grit and her tenacity and her true dedication ... Disabled individuals are the largest minority group in the United States. And it crosses all genders and all races and everything. So by fighting for the rights of people with disabilities, it kind of raises all boats.Kaleigh Brendle: I always say to other people that don't understand the disability experience: If you broke your arm tomorrow, you would expect that the world would accommodate you. You would expect to have the accommodations that you needed as you navigated that temporary disability. Why is it wrong for us to expect what you would expect in that situation?

Cricket Bidleman: We've made so many advancements because of people like Judy and because of … all these activists and advocates who came before us. And although I do have to struggle with people to obtain access to media or textbooks or the standardized testing to get into various education, it's still nothing compared to some of the things we saw in the movie

Leigh White: Us being part of the 'ADA generation,' we're able to reap the benefits. And with hindsight we're really able to appreciate the work that she's done and then kind of carry the torch into the future. So that the struggles we're going through right now, hopefully the next generation of disabled youth don't have to go through the same things.

World.title: Trump blasts judge for halting his Washington golf project and says he will appeal
World.content:
Trump blasts judge for halting his Washington golf project and says he will appeal

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a "highly destructive and political decision" from a federal judge after she ordered a two-week delay on renovations at a historic Washington public golf course that he has been trying to redevelop into a championship-level venue.

In a social media post, Trump said his administration will "immediately appeal, on an expedited basis" the temporary restraining order from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, which she issued just before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months.

Sponsor Message

"It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court," said Trump, who spent much of the weekend posting photos on his social media site of the golf course. "They don't call it Trash Island for no reason!"

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

Trump had announced work on the site along the Potomac River would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that the president's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something Trump has denied. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the judge's decision.

Reyes, in her ruling Saturday, noted that those posts presented a problem for the government, indicating that Trump's redevelopment plan was final and that the National Park Service "will close the Park to implement it."

Sponsor Message

Both points, she wrote, "favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

The order is in effect through Nov. 28. The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.

Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.

World.title: FAA ground stop disrupts college football
World.content:
FAA ground stop disrupts college football

toggle caption i Justin Ford/Getty Images

The Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop on Friday has led not only to travel headaches, but also schedule changes and delays in college sports.

Many college football teams were in airports Friday on their way to upcoming games when the nationwide ground stop was issued and thousands of flights were canceled. The FAA on Saturday said airports were returning to normal operations, but that delays and cancellations would continue through the day.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the ground stop's impact on college football. Several games on Saturday were delayed for hours.

"If you look at the cost of what happened yesterday, we're talking if you like football — I know we've had some disruptions to the college football schedule. Some games are being moved," Duffy said during a news conference Saturday. "That's not the most important thing, but we do want to move teams around the country so we can have playoffs happen."

Sponsor Message

Utah, ranked No. 2 in the College Football Playoff Rankings, will kick off against Arizona in Tucson at 8:30 p.m. local time — a three-hour delay. The Auburn vs. Mississippi State game was pushed back more than four hours to start at 3:15 p.m. local time in Mississippi because of the ground stop. The Florida Atlantic Owls were also unable to fly to Oklahoma on Friday ahead of their game against the Tulsa Golden Hurricane. Saturday's game, which was supposed to begin at 2:30 p.m. local time, was moved to 6:15 p.m. local time.

While other college teams were able to arrive at their destinations and proceed with games on Saturday, the University of Mississippi did not.

Ole Miss, ranked No. 19, was not able to fly to Oklahoma as planned on Friday for its matchup with the University of Oklahoma Sooners. The game between the two teams, which was scheduled to occur Saturday, will now take place on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET, according to the Southeastern Conference. The game will compete with several NFL games that will be televised at the same time. NFL teams were largely unaffected by the ground stop.

In order to help alleviate fans' frustration, the Sooners on Saturday announced "fan appreciation" promotions for the rescheduled game. Oklahoma students can go to the game for free with their student ID and there will be reduced prices on concession items such as $2 for popcorn or a 16-ounce beer.

World.title: Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law
World.content:
Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law

toggle caption i Alex Wong/Getty Images

One of the first casualties of a new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives is a St. Patrick's Day parade in a beach town that has been celebrating its Irish American community for nearly 60 years.

The city of Delray Beach announced this week that it was canceling its popular St. Patrick's Day festivities in compliance with a new law that takes effect on Jan. 1. The city will also withdraw its sponsorship of LGBTQ Pride celebrations in June, officials said.

The law, backed by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is part of the state's ongoing crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives that the governor has called discriminatory and said have "no place" in public institutions.

Sponsor Message

The city lawyer for Delray Beach, a community in southeast Florida with picturesque beaches and a historic downtown, told the mayor that any government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that are not a national holiday (for example: Independence Day) could run afoul of the new anti-DEI law. So, Mayor Tom Carney said, he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city's biggest events of the year.

In past years, the parade, an annual event since 1970, wound its way through the downtown core of Delray Beach with spectators lined up several-people deep along the route. Local businesses and organizations sponsored floats and giveaways. School bands played as they marched through the streets. Participants included members of the Ancient Order of Hibernians, the largest and oldest Irish Catholic organization in the country.

"I've said it's engrained in the DNA of Delray and I do mean that. It's one of our signature events," Carney, a Republican, told NPR.

The mayor said he's hopeful that the city can find a path forward — and a way to preserve the event.

If a private sponsor were to volunteer to take over the St. Patrick's Day parade, or the June Pride celebrations, Carney said, the city would gladly hand over the reins and support the continuation of these festivities.

Sponsor Message

"These types of events we should be celebrating because in this country, people can have these events. In other countries, you can't do this. We have great freedoms here," he said. "And if the community wants something and it's not against public policy then I would support them to do it if they're using private dollars. If we can do it, we should do it."

Carney, who is of Irish descent, said the parade was privately run until about eight years ago — so returning to a private-sponsorship model would be a callback to the parade's origins. His own family, he said, was involved in keeping the parade going during the 1980s and 1990s.

Delray Beach officials said they have been inundated with emails, calls and social media messages from constituents who are angry that the community's decades-long celebration had been axed.

"It was kind of a call to action to me," Carney said. "The community really wants to have it, so we should go ahead and have it, we just need to get it privately funded."

The governor, meanwhile, has accused Delray Beach of weaponizing the new anti-DEI measure to make a political point. DeSantis said the city was "engaging in "malicious compliance" in a message he posted on X following the city's cancellation announcement.

"What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law," the governor wrote. "It's just an attempt to make a political point — a point that legacy media will no doubt try to amplify. We've seen these stunts throughout the years. Rinse and repeat."

The mayor said the city is merely trying to stay out of trouble with the law. The measure, SB1134, asserts that any official that violates the provision could face civil or legal consequences.

"The legislation has unintended consequences. The governor may genuinely believe what he believes and I take him at his word; our city attorney came up with a different conclusion," Carney said. "I'm going to leave it at that."

World.title: Russia will not compete at world junior hockey championship in Alberta, IIHF says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The International Ice Hockey Federation has confirmed in a statement that Russia will not have a team at the world junior hockey championship next month in Alberta, citing government restrictions in Canada.

The IIHF says Russia will not be able to play at the tournament starting Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer, despite a mandate for the country's reinstatement from the Court of Arbitration for Sport, following restrictions put in place by the federal government.

The organization says Canada will remain as host despite going against the CAS's ruling.

"After carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer," the IIHF said in the statement released Sunday.

"All participating MNAs have been informed and an updated competition schedule will be posted shortly."

In a statement Sunday, the Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable" and "unlawful."

"The IIHF's decision was made solely due to political reasons, in violation of a binding and effective ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport — which stated that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to participate in international competitions — as well as an agreement between the IIHF and RIHF, under which the international federation committed to implementing the CAS ruling with immediate effect"

The RIHF said it will make a joint appeal with the Russian Olympic Committee to the International Olympic Committee and will "pursue all available legal avenues to ensure the enforcement of the CAS ruling, the restoration of the rights of Russian athletes and reparation for the harm caused."

Russia and Belarus have been banned from competing in international hockey tournaments since 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The CAS mandated Russia's immediate reinstatement in an Oct. 30 ruling. The ruling would be in effect for the world junior championship and would affect four other tournaments, including the women's world championship set for November 2027 in Quebec City.

The federal government pushed back quickly, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying Nov. 3 at a meeting of Commonwealth countries in Antigua that Russians and Belarusians would be barred from competing in Alberta regardless of the CAS's decision.

"While Russia and Belorussia (sic) are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Carney said.

"So if you're asking specifically about the world juniors, the Russians will not be there."

The CAS's decision was met with immediate pushback. Finland's hockey federation said Nov. 2 that its national teams would not play Russia in international tournaments as long as the war in Ukraine continued. Sweden, Czechia and Latvia were among the other countries to follow Finland's lead over the next few days.

The ice hockey federation of Sweden, the defending world junior champion, said: "The Swedish line was and is crystal clear — Sweden will not play ice hockey matches against Russia in the situation we are in right now."

The court later defended its decision, saying the IIHF failed to provide sufficient evidence to justify continuing its ban on Russian teams, noting the ruling was based strictly on legal arguments and evidence presented.

But Ottawa maintained its stance, clarifying later that even Russian players with valid visas to compete in Canada would be barred from the world juniors.

The impasse left the tournament in limbo, with Norway's federation saying it would be bumped from the competition in favour of a Russian team, a decision that was never confirmed publicly by the IIHF.

Meanwhile, hockey officials in Russia vowed to respond. Russian ambassador to Canada Oleg Stepanov criticized Ottawa's decision, accusing the government of bringing politics into sports.

Russian hockey federation president Vladislav Tretiak threatened to seek compensation from Canada and push for relocation or cancellation of the Alberta world juniors if Russia was barred from competing.

He also asked the IIHF ethics council to investigate and punish national federations organizing boycotts of games against Russia.

World.title: Scientists race to discover and protect what lives in the ocean
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Scientists say not knowing what lives in our oceans is holding back efforts to protect them. Because of that, many are racing to discover and document the wild and diverse species in marine environments that are often hard for humans to access.

Ocean Census, a global collaboration of scientists and non-profit organizations, estimates that scientists have documented less than 10 per cent of some 2.2 million fish, marine mammals, shellfish, plankton, squid, jellyfish and other species that live in our oceans.

"It's very difficult to protect what you don't know," said Michelle Taylor, head of science at Ocean Census.

A sea cucumber with horned appendages, nicknamed Loki, and a bright red-orange coral with fans of slender branches are among 57 new species announced and identified in October from an Ocean Census expedition off Argentina last year.

This new sea cucumber species was nicknamed Loki because of its prominent horned appendages, reminiscent of the god in Norse mythology. It was found in the Mar del Plata submarine canyon off Argentina. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

A striking, bright red-orange octocoral was photographed nearly 2,000 metres below the surface of the ocean in Argentina's Mar del Plata canyon. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

A landmark UN biodiversity agreement in 2022 committed to protecting 30 per cent of the world's land, water and marine areas by 2030 , but has been falling short on ocean protection , with just 12 per cent of oceans (compared to 27 per cent of lands) set to be protected by 2030.

Canada has so far protected 15.5 per cent of its oceans, according to the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society (CPAWS).

Claire Goodwin, a research scientist at Huntsman Marine Science Centre in St. Andrew's, N.B., said the goal is to protect areas with high biodiversity.

"But if you're not surveying some of your marine life and you don't know what's living there, you can't say which those biodiverse areas are."

A cone jelly captured by the remotely operated vehicle SuBastian off the coast of Argentina. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

Sponges that eat meat, provide housing

The problem is that even within Canada, many areas are difficult to explore. Goodwin was part of an expedition in the Saguenay Fjord in Quebec in 2023.

On its steep walls, where only one species of sponge had previously been recorded, her team discovered 20 or 30 sponge species, including some new to science.

Carnivorous sponges were found in Quebec's Saguenay Fjord in 2023. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC)

Among them were carnivorous sponges that trap shrimp with glass, velcro-like appendages to engulf and digest slowly, "which was really exciting," said Goodwin, since most sponges are passive filter feeders.

Goodwin says sponges have important roles in the ecosystems — as food for sea stars, homes for some worms and a place to lay eggs for some fish. Sponges in Canadian waters can also grow to half the size of an adult human.

Claire Goodwin collects sponges in the Bay of Fundy off the coast of New Brunswick. (Torben Brydges/Fisheries and Oceans Canada)

The sea slug Dendronotus yrjargul was recorded on a recent expedition led by the Innu Nation. It was the first time the species has been found off the coast of Canada. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC/Innu Nation)

Now Goodwin is working with the Innu Nation in Labrador to survey uncharted waters in their territory. "We literally don't know what the seabed's going to be like, let alone what's going to be living on it."

Climate change impacts and solutions

The race is on to find out as the ocean warms rapidly , and climate change shifts where species are found.

Already, Goodwin says, some species have completely disappeared from regions where they were once common. She points to basket stars, "really cool sea stars that have branching arms," which were once common around St. Andrew's, but haven't been seen there since a rapid warming around 2016.

A basket star, Gorgonocephalus arcticus, is seen in the Saguenay Fjord. The species used to be common in the Bay of Fundy but seems to have disappeared due to climate change. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC)

Loïc Jacquemot, a postdoctoral researcher at Université du Québec à Rimouski, said in many areas, we don't even have much of a baseline from which to compare changes.

He's currently surveying Baffin Bay off the coast of Nunavut using a technique called eDNA, which identifies species from DNA shed into the water by organisms' skin, poop and tissues. That way, they can be surveyed without actually seeing or catching them — all you need is a water sample.

Loïc Jacquemot samples water for eDNA in B.C.'s coastal fjords. (Submitted by Loïc Jacquemot)

He said species adapted to colder waters are expected to move into a smaller and smaller area "because, of course, they cannot go much more north," while warmer water species may expand their range.

That can have big impacts on things like the food chain — including fish and shellfish humans eat — and on the way carbon is moved around the ocean by zooplankton species that migrate each day between the depths and the surface.

"It's important for the climate because all these changes impact the way carbon is stored in the ocean," Jacquemot said.

This tiny copepod is one of 20 new species identified by the Ocean Census in October. These organisms are among the zooplankton that move carbon between the surface and depths of the ocean. (The Nippon Foundation-Nekton Ocean Census/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

Photosynthetic algae called diatoms from fjords in Greenland. Diatoms are important for capturing carbon dioxide in the oceans. (Submitted by Loïc Jacquemot)

The carbon stored by the ocean and its species is known as blue carbon. So far it includes 30 per cent of carbon dioxide generated by humans, along with 90 per cent of the excess heat trapped by climate change, said a recent UN report , which warned that the ocean's ability to absorb more CO2 and heat is weakening.

Meanwhile, coral reefs, known as biodiversity hotspots with the ability to store huge amounts of carbon , are one of the ecosystems most threatened by climate change .

The impact of the ocean and its species on climate change are at the forefront of this year's UN climate summit, COP31, underway in Antalya, Turkey. Protecting marine ecosystems and "unlocking blue carbon for climate resilience" is one of 10 items on the meeting's " action agenda ."

This week at COP31, former U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and groups representing island states pushed for a strong reference to oceans in next year's global "stocktake" of climate policies, supported by the European Union and African countries.

This grenadier fish was observed with parasitic copepods attached to its head during a 2025 Ocean Census expedition off Montagu Island near Antarctica. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

This marine worm, Harmothoe imbricata, was found off Canada's Atlantic coast. (Christy Carr/HMSC)

For the 'biogeochemical functioning of our planet'

Taylor with Ocean Census said marine ecosystems are important for humans — even people who live far from the sea, not just for producing food and medicines, but also on a bigger scale. "You know, it's part of the biogeochemical functioning of our planet. We're very reliant on it, whether we realize it or not."

Taylor, Goodwin and Jacquemot all hope that by sharing with people the amazing diversity of life in the ocean, they can help people appreciate the importance of saving it.

"When we show people pictures and videos of what's underwater, they're always amazed by what we actually have down there," Goodwin said.

Michelle Taylor, head of science for Ocean Census, checks out views from the cameras on the ROV SuBastian during a mission to catalogue deep sea species. (Paul Satchell)

Taylor describes them as an incredible diversity of "wild looking creatures" and says for some of them "you wouldn't believe they were of this planet."

She said she's very worried about coral reefs especially, but "you have to have the attitude that there are solutions to this." In the meantime, she added, "we need to find as many species as we can, so we can understand diversity on this planet before it is lost."

This is part of a series of articles highlighting the work of scientists looking at disappearing groups of species you may not have thought much about. It's a chance to get to know them and how they impact our lives, and find out what can be done to keep them around.

World.title: Trump breaks silence on nationwide ground stop, demands more money for FAA infrastructure from Congress
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday broke his silence on the nationwide ground stop that snarled airline travel this weekend, using the incident to push Congress on money to fully upgrade America's air traffic control system.

The Republican president has been conspicuously quiet on the ground stop since it began Friday afternoon, instead issuing statements on social media about completely different topics as frustrated passengers were left stranded at airports and his government scrambled with airlines to restore normal travel.

Trump said in a new post on his social media platform that his administration has begun upgrading that system, but that the task should not be done in "drips and drabs."

Congress, which the Republican Party has controlled for nearly two years, approved $12.5 billion US for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) as part of the party's sweeping tax cut package last year, but Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has repeatedly characterized that funding as a down payment on a broader overhaul of the aging system.

"If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently," Trump wrote on social media Sunday. "It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old — RIDICULOUS!"

In another post, he complained about how his Democratic predecessor had maintained the FAA and the air traffic control system, accusing Joe Biden's administration of making an "old and broken system worse than when they began."

WATCH | Here's what caused the nationwide ground stop in the U.S.: Routine maintenance to replace telecom line led to air traffic control outage: U.S. transportation secretary | Duration closed caption 3:40 U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told a news conference that a contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration was working at a remote location to replace a copper line when an unknown issue overloaded the aging air traffic control system, forcing the FAA to keep planes on the ground nationwide.

Biden signed a massive infrastructure bill into law in the first year of his presidency, which set aside $25 billion US for the FAA to improve airports and its traffic control towers, to redevelop airport terminals and "upgrade the foundation" of the air traffic control system, according to the FAA.

Duffy was the administration’s public face on the ground stop across the Sunday news shows, pressing Congress for billions of dollars for upgrades to the air traffic control infrastructure.

"I can’t apologize for what was passed on to us. And I can't blame Republicans or Democrats, because it's all of them. It goes back 20, 25, 30 years of a lack of investment," he told NBC's Meet the Press.

In a post on the social media platform X, Duffy said contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. had secured two routers from FAA facilities in Texas and Arkansas and was conducting "deep diagnostics" on the equipment. He has said the problem began when L3Harris was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fibre wire, somehow causing the system to overload.

WATCH | Was a lack of funding to blame for the glitch that led to Friday's ground stop?: Did a lack of funding lead to the order to ground aircraft across the U.S.? | Duration closed caption 1:31 Several experts who spoke to CBC News say a lack of funding for new technology partially led to the U.S.-wide grounding of aircraft that caused travel chaos across the country and beyond. Former airline pilot and accident investigator John Cox speaks to some of those funding challenges over the decades.

After the wire was replaced at the site in El Dorado, Ark., and the router was turned on, a problem then cropped up at a facility in Amarillo, Texas, cascading into the ground stop. "We didn't think that should or would happen, he told ABC's This Week.

As for the travelling public, Duffy told CBS's Face the Nation that "we have some delays in the airspace right now," but looking to the end of the day and into Monday, "we should be running at full capacity."

In a ground stop, airplanes and crews are taken out of position, he said, "so it takes a little bit of time for the airliners to get back … at full capacity and operation but we're well on our way."

World.title: Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony full of emotions as Phil Collins, Queen Latifah, more inducted
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Phil Collins gave a tearful acceptance speech and got an electrifying tribute from Cynthia Erivo, Oprah Winfrey inducted the late Luther Vandross, the crowd yelled along with Billy Idol, and Wu-Tang Clan crowded the stage for a rowdy celebration at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony on Saturday night.

Queen Latifah, Oasis, MC Lyte, Sade, Joy Division/New Order and Iron Maiden were also inducted during the ceremony at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, along with producer Rick Rubin, who got a long-bearded tribute from the Red Hot Chili Peppers.

A night that beforehand felt like it might fall flat with the absences of key inductees was as lively and overloaded as the induction ceremony ever is.

U2 was the night's surprise opener, playing their new single Silencio while surrounded by dancers in riot squad gear. They then launched into their 1984 classic Pride (In the Name of Love) as singer Bono alternately raised a peace sign and fist.

Run DMC and Aerosmith were the surprise closers with a loud jam of Walk This Way, their 1986 classic collaboration, produced by Rubin.

Queen Latifah, left, and Megan Thee Stallion perform during the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony on Saturday in Los Angeles. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

Collins gets emotional, Idol gets wild

The 75-year-old Collins, whose mobility trouble and other health problems kept him from performing, took the stage slowly using a pair of canes and cried at a huge ovation from a crowd that included his daughter, actor Lily Collins, and four other children.

Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker inducted Collins and praised him for his unprecedented dual stardom as a drummer and a hit-making pop singer in the 1980s.

"I grew up just wanting to play the drums," Collins said. "Everything else has been a really happy accident. I can't believe, when I look back, how life has gone."

Phil Collins, left, is introduced by Blink-182 drummer Travis Barker during Saturday's ceremony, before Collins shared a tearful speech. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

Collins was already in the hall as a member of Genesis, but now gets the solo honour.

Hours later, the crowd leapt to its feet and shouted along with White Wedding during the induction of Idol — one of the few artists ticket buyers knew for sure would show up and perform.

He was inducted along with his longtime guitarist Steve Stevens by No Doubt members Gwen Stefani and Tony Kanal, who joined Idol for a duet on Eyes Without a Face.

Oprah inducts Luther Vandross

Winfrey said with relish that Vandross was "the maestro of the love song" and said he was once correctly named "the top artist that people make love to."

Vandross, an R&B singer with a velvet voice, was one of the definitive singers of the 1980s and '90s. He died in 2005.

"Luther Vandross sang with such passion and soul it could reach something deep inside that you didn’t even know needed to be reached," Winfrey said.

Hip-hop acts make their presence known

Wu-Tang Clan, the hip-hop collective from New York's Staten Island, filled the stage with its 10 current members, giving a memorable acceptance speech and a performance that had the crowd on its feet dancing. Backed by a big jazz band, the musical medley included C.R.E.A.M., Method Man and late member Ol' Dirty Bastard's Shimmy Shimmy Ya.

"Wu-Tang rewrote the rules of hip-hop and did it without a big machine behind them," said comedian Chris Rock, who inducted them.

Audience members put up Wu-Tang Clan hand signs as the Wu-Tang Clan performs during the ceremony on Saturday. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

MC Lyte, a trailblazing female rapper starting in the late 1980s, was the first artist inducted, with hip-hop star Remy Ma doing the honours. Her contemporary and fellow groundbreaker Latifah was inducted later in the evening by Megan Thee Stallion, who said Latifah "taught us to recognize royalty within ourselves."

Latifah said that for a long time, she would not have believed this night was possible.

"It's difficult enough being a woman in hip-hop," she said, "let alone being a hip-hopper in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame."

Inductee Queen Latifah speaks during the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony on Saturday in L.A. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

Latifah and MC Lyte then took the stage together to perform a medley of their hits, including Latifah's U.N.I.T.Y. and MC Lyte's Ruffneck.

They entered the hall as recipients of the Early Influence Award along with posthumous inductees Gram Parsons, Fela Kuti and Celia Cruz, who were all inducted via video tribute.

A stage full of Rick Rubins

Legendary rock, hip-hop and country producer Rubin accepted his induction with a one-sentence acceptance speech.

"You can't kill rock 'n' roll," he said, and left the stage.

The Red Hot Chili Peppers dressed as Rick Rubin during their performance at the ceremony on Saturday. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

The Red Hot Chili Peppers then appeared, all four of them wearing white wigs and long white fake beards to match Rubin's signature look as they played their 1991 breakthrough hit Give It Away, one of many he produced for them.

Oasis and the other no-shows

Oasis, the youngest of the inductees, didn’t show up. Guitarist Noel Gallagher was playing a gig back home in Britain, and his younger brother, Liam Gallagher, has said he just didn't want to come.

"Anybody surprised they didn’t show up?" asked actor and Oasis superfan Bob Odenkirk, who inducted them. "It would’ve been out of character if they had. I would've been worried."

Iron Maiden, the quintessential British heavy metal band of the 1980s, as well as iconic singer Sade weren't at the event. Joy Division and New Order got a joint induction, with only the bassist for both bands, Peter Hook, showing up at the ceremony.

After streaming the ceremony live for the past few years, the hall returned to its previous format, where the public won't see it until an edited version airs on ABC and Disney+ on Dec. 9.

World.title: Carney cites her award-winning book on encampments. Here's what she says of his plan to end homelessness
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of Canada's leading authors on homelessness says the prime minister's plan to end it is an "ambitious goal" that has potential, but won't actually go all the way.

Prime Minister Mark Carney introduced his government's second budget last week, which features a big headline promise: end homelessness in 10 years.

Governments sometimes tease big pledges in the run up to tabling a budget. That wasn't the case with this year's signature pledge, but there was an Easter egg that could have pointed to this new policy focus.

Earlier this year, Carney told the Globe and Mail that he was reading Encampment by Maggie Helwig , which won this year's Shaughnessy Cohen Prize for political writing.

Encampment tells the story of Helwig's activism and effort to keep her Toronto churchyard open to those in need. The award jury called the book "a necessary, on-the-ground view of Canada's homelessness crisis."

November's budget went on to propose a $11.2-billion cash injection to tackle homelessness, one of this year's largest line items.

Carney is not the first politician in Canada's history to set this target, but with Canadians facing an escalating affordability and housing availability crisis, the stakes are high.

Helwig gave her assessment of Carney's plan to CBC's chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton.

"I think that the commitments which have been made are serious commitments. They are constructive commitments. They are not at a scale which would end homelessness," Helwig said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live.

"If we are able to significantly reduce levels of homelessness, especially unsheltered homelessness, that's a big deal."

Helwig says Canada faces a very difficult situation with homelessness growing exponentially.

A national homelessness count in 2025 found that more than 65,000 people were homeless on a given night in Canada, a 59 per cent increase over five years. The share of unhoused people living in unsheltered locations, including encampments, had also increased from 23 per cent to 27 per cent.

What's needed in the Liberal plan?

Helwig's broad critique of the Liberals' proposal is that it should not overlook the straightforward need for more basic housing.

"I worry that there's a bit too much emphasis on mental health and addictions, as if those were the primary drivers of homelessness," she said.

Helwig says sometimes the issue is just needing a place someone can afford to live, since long-term homelessness itself is "fantastically destructive to people's mental and physical health."

Helwig helps move a resident's belongings as Toronto city workers prepare to clear an unhoused persons encampment at St. Stephen-in-the-Fields Church, in Toronto, on Oct. 16, 2025. (The Canadian Press)

Helwig points to Dunn House in Toronto as an example of a housing program where the focus is not exclusively on mental health and addiction, but which takes a more holistic picture of what people need when coming out of chronic homelessness.

It features direct access to doctors, nurses and a host of other health professionals with the goal of improving their health and alleviating pressure on hospitals.

"No one wants to move into the crazy house for the crazy people, right?" Helwig said, referring to projects that could over-emphasize mental health language.

Helwig says the reality is that some people do need intensive mental health support but it must be provided in a way that does not stigmatize individuals.

Influence on Carney

The day after making this pledge public, Carney cited Helwig during an announcement in Winnipeg.

While downplaying Barton's questions about whether she had a direct role in motivating Carney's new ambition, Helwig said it's nice to think her book may have contributed to it.

While listening to Carney speak publicly about the goal for the first time, Helwig noted Carney's use of language emphasizing Canada becoming a community that takes care of each other — a central theme to her book.

She said she's less concerned about whether the Liberals' plan will actually end all homelessness, compared to whether it will do good for the people who are sleeping on the streets right now.

"In a situation where we have seen so much stigmatizing language, so much demonizing language, so much emphasis on getting these people somewhere that's out of sight, to talk about this in terms of community and care, that in itself is actually quite important."

World.title: Satellite limitations imposed by Musk's SpaceX pose danger for Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield satellite communications system are hindering its ability to intercept Russian drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.

He warned that limitations on the system, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, could weaken defenses around Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid.

Ukraine's interceptor drones continue to lose contact with their operators when flying faster than 161 km/h along the front line and over Russian-occupied territory, leaving them unable to catch Russian Shahed drones, Zelenskyy said.

"We are counting on these restrictions to be lifted," he wrote on social media. "The protection of lives and Ukrainian energy infrastructure before winter depends on this. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the President's Office have been instructed to work closely with the American side and SpaceX.

"It is important to be on the right side of history. We need to help Ukraine."

Zelenskyy questioned Saturday whether the problem was technical, saying the restrictions appeared to have been imposed by SpaceX despite earlier assurances from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Starshield was more under U.S. government control.

Outages after Russian strike on power facility

Meanwhile, a Russian strike on Chornomorsk, a port city in Ukraine's Odesa region, injured six people and damaged energy infrastructure, regional head Oleh Kiper said Sunday on Telegram.

The blast and falling debris also damaged a gas pipeline and nearby residential buildings, while two parked cars caught fire.

The strike hit a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks, temporarily leaving about 41,000 customers without power, Kiper said.

A woman walks at the site of a building damaged during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the city of Chornomorsk, Odesa region, on Nov. 15, 2026. (Nina Liashonok/Reuters)

Overnight Russian airstrikes on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured another six people, including a two-year-old boy, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Sunday.

Russia launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 guided aerial bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian attack kills 1 in Russia's Rostov

Ukrainian drone strikes damaged two electrical substations in Russia's Rostov region, killing a chief engineer, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said Sunday.

Four people were injured when drone debris fell on their cars, Slyusar wrote on social media. A fifth person was wounded when debris struck a "production facility" in the village of Troitskoye, he said.

Ukrainian forces also targeted Russia's Tatarstan region, officials said. Radmir Belyaev, mayor of Nizhnekamsk, the region's third-largest city, said a "large-scale and prolonged attack" damaged its industrial zone.

Six people were injured, and heating and hot water supplies were disrupted in parts of the city, he said.

Ukraine's General Staff said it had hit two sites in Nizhnekamsk: Nizhnekamskneftekhim, one of the largest petrochemical complexes in Europe, and a production site operated by petrochemical company Sibur. An oil refinery in the area was also hit, it said.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces shot down 533 Ukrainian drones overnight across 13 Russian regions, the Russian-annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.

Drones damage Black Sea ships, Romania says

Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said Sunday that three commercial vessels in the Black Sea were struck by drones overnight, the latest in a string of attacks that have raised fears of the war spilling over into NATO territory.

"Once again, maritime security in the Black Sea has been threatened," Niculescu wrote on X.

Romania's Ministry of National Defense said a Greek-flagged oil tanker was struck by a drone, sparking a fire that was extinguished by the crew. Two more ships were later struck by drones, and their crews also extinguished fires onboard, the ministry said. No casualties were reported and the ministry did not state the origin of the drones.

"These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law," Niculescu said, adding that they "reflect the deteriorating security situation caused by Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine."

A rescuer works at the site of an apartment buildings damaged by a Russian air strike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Nov. 14, 2026. (Reuters)

Last month, a string of cargo ships and tankers were struck by aerial or naval drones near the Bulgarian and Romanian coastlines. At least 30 sailors on commercial ships were confirmed dead or reported missing.

"We will continue to take all necessary measures, alongside our Allies, to strengthen security in the Black Sea," Niculescu added. "This remains a key priority for the Government, in close co-operation with our regional partners and NATO."

Estonia threatens Russian border closure

Estonia's government said Sunday it would close all border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1, after the Baltic country's prime minister accused Moscow of attempting to sabotage an Estonian drone company a day earlier.

The government said an attempted attack had been carried out early Saturday against Threod Systems in Viimsi, north of the capital, Tallinn, "with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire."

"If Russia continues its hybrid operations in Estonia, and we know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people, we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face," Prime Minister Kristen Michal said in a statement.

"Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia's defense industry and defense capabilities are unacceptable," Michal added.

National broadcaster ERR reported Sunday that eight Latvian nationals have been detained after the attempted break-in.

World.title: Why researchers are using drones to keep polar bears and people apart
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Researcher Kyle Garrett is looking at the viewfinder as his drone takes off, making a loud whirring sound as it zips low over the subarctic tundra in Churchill, Man.

Soon, he spies a lone adult polar bear, which looks right at the drone's camera.

"We want to see, does it scare them?" said Garrett. "Does it steer them into places we want them to go?"

For a split second, the bear ducks its head and broadens its stance defensively, as it assesses a foreign object it's likely never encountered before.

Garrett, a master's student from Utah's Brigham Young University, is experimenting with aerial drone hazing, an emerging wildlife management technique currently being used by the U.S. Department of Agriculture and Federal Aviation Administration.

An adult polar bear stares up at the camera of a drone. (Polar Bears International)

While studies have shown drone hazing to be effective on black bears, Garrett is trying to see if it works with polar bears — a bigger, more curious and more aggressive species. The goal is to adapt the technology to Canada's North and try to take some of the risk out of managing the bears.

Why bear deterrence is a pressing concern

Around Churchill, polar bear deterrence is a serious issue requiring serious balance.

The town, which is located on the southwestern shore of Hudson Bay, roughly 1,000 kilometres north of Winnipeg, is the self-proclaimed polar bear capital of the world.

It sits in the middle of the migration path for one of the largest populations of the largest land predator on earth. And every fall, thousands of people come to watch the bears gather on the shores of Hudson Bay to wait for it to freeze.

LISTEN | How bear hazing went high-tech: Quirks and Quarks 9:08 Bear hazing goes high-tech with drones

The bears spend their winters hunting on the sea ice, though the warming climate has meant the bay ices over less predictably and later in the fall.

"The longer the bears are off the ice the more likely the bears are to come where people are," said Doug Clark, an expert on polar bear-human conflicts at the University of Saskatchewan.

"These aren't just skinny desperate bears, it's all bears, they all will come around [and] that creates situations that you certainly need to be on guard in."

The polar bear experiment

This fall Garrett is running the experiment in Churchill along with a couple of communities in northern Ontario and Nunavut.

In his drone video from the field, the bear begins to look curious as Garrett flies closer and directly over it, turning and braking the drone to make more loud whirring sounds.

The drone is far enough away to not touch the bear, but close enough to make it uncomfortable, and soon the bear starts to walk in the direction that Garrett is trying to nudge it.

"Once it kind of realizes, 'hey, I don't really like that,' then they move on their way," said Garrett.

One day, he says, it might be possible for a conservation officer to deter a bear from coming too close to humans from the safety of their office.

"We're mainly thinking about the distance we can be from the animal while hazing it out of areas."

Polar bears have been known to approach and attack people. This time of year, residents leave doors unlocked in case someone needs to get away from a bear quickly.

WATCH | Why more polar bears are encountering humans: As ice floes shrink, more polar bears are encountering humans | Duration closed caption 2:44 Researchers used to think that polar bears were coming into contact with humans more frequently because they were starving and searching for food. But new research suggests that's not the case.

The Manitoba government tracks "bear occurrences" in Churchill. An occurrence can range from simply a bear sighting to an actual confrontation.

According to the province's latest report, this bear season there have been nearly 300 occurrences. Fifteen of those have resulted in bears being captured by conservation officials, either to be relocated or held in Churchill's special "polar bear jail," a facility in an old military hanger where problem bears can be held until the ice forms.

WATCH | A polar bear gets a lift out of 'bear jail': Watch a polar bear air lift from Churchill's 'bear jail' | Duration 0:42 Two bears with a history of causing trouble in town. One committed a couple of B&Es. The other has been lifted out of town, but keeps coming back. The helicopter will take them 50 miles out, hopefully to a spot that's safer for them, and for humans.

The town runs a Polar Bear Alert program, which has long relied on the public and conservation officers to call in bear sightings. Now, PBI is looking to technology.

In addition to drones for deterrence and surveillance, it is also experimenting with what it calls Bear-dar, a radar system focused on detecting bears nearing town along with a network of mobile surveillance cameras it's calling Bear-vision.

"We want to bring additional eyes to the table," said Geoffrey York, vice president of science and policy for PBI.

"This would allow conservation officers to have a fairly low cost system that could be portable, something they could deploy in the field that would give them eyes on kind of problem spots."

A 'Bear-dar' system is installed near Churchill. (Elbert Bakker/Polar Bears International)

Questions the research still has to answer

As for the drone, Garrett says there is still a lot to learn about its limitations in Canada's rugged north, including how reliable the equipment is in the cold.

But the biggest questions are about the bears themselves — how they react and possibly adapt. It's possible that something that works now may lose its effectiveness over time.

"If a certain bear is droned often or daily it very well could become habituated to it," said Garrett.

But he says early results are promising.

"Be safe, and keep the bears wild. That's what we're hoping for."

World.title: Canada's health-care spending tops $10,000 per person this year. Where is the money going?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada is spending more on health care than ever. Whether Canadians are getting more care for their money is another question.

A new report from the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) , an independent, non-profit organization that collects and analyzes data on Canada's health-care system, projects health-care spending will reach a record $433 billion in 2026, or $10,398 per person, an increase of 4.8 per cent over last year.

For the first time since the pandemic, inflation-adjusted spending per person is expected to surpass its previous peak, reached in 2021.

But Canada already ranks among the higher-spending countries in the developed world, while patients continue to struggle with long wait times, overcrowded hospitals and difficulty finding family doctors.

That raises a central question: Is Canada spending enough on health care, or does the problem lie in how that money is being spent?

"I believe that these records of spending are just buying us more of the same right now," said Jason Sutherland, a professor at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver and director of the Centre for Health Services and Policy Research.

He argues that without substantial changes to how health care is organized and delivered, additional spending is unlikely to produce meaningful improvements for patients.

WATCH | 1 in 10 ER patients waiting more than 14 hours for care, report finds: 1 in 10 Canadians waiting more than 14 hours in emergency rooms: report | Duration closed caption 6:56 A new report by the Canadian Institute for Health Information says that in 2024-2025, one in 10 patients in emergency departments end up spending more than 14 hours there waiting for care. Dr. Michael Herman, a spokesperson for the Canadian Association of Emergency Physicians, says the report's findings aren't a surprise.

Is $10,000 per person a lot?

The $10,398 figure represents the combined cost of publicly and privately funded health care, including hospitals, doctors, prescription drugs and services paid for through private insurance or directly by patients. It is not the amount each Canadian pays in taxes.

While the figure may seem substantial, international comparisons provide important context.

According to the CIHI report, Canada devoted 11.5 per cent of its gross domestic product to health care in 2024, compared with an OECD average of 9.3 per cent .

That placed Canada alongside other high-spending countries, including France at 11.3 per cent and Sweden at 11.2 per cent, but below Germany at 12.2 per cent and the United States at 17.2 per cent.

"We are not cheap in our health-care spending," Sutherland said.

LISTEN | Ontario doctors demand an apology over provincial letters urging reduced hours and delayed care: Here and Now Toronto 7:49 Why is the Ontario Ministry of Health asking doctors to scale back their hours and delay patient care? Some Ontario doctors are demanding an apology from the province after receiving letters from the ministry asking them to scale back their hours and delay patient care. The Ontario Medical Association is worried the letters could scare doctors into doing just that. Dr. Rebbeca Hicks is the President of the OMA. She was on Here and Now.

Sara Allin, an associate professor at the University of Toronto's Institute of Health Policy, Management and Evaluation, agreed that Canada's spending is substantial. But she said the more revealing comparison is what countries achieve with their investments.

She pointed to data showing Canada performs relatively well on some measures, including life expectancy and vaccination rates, but continues to lag in important areas of access and service delivery.

"We have very persistently long wait times," Allin said. "We have persistent challenges with care co-ordination."

She described Canada's health system as generally a middle performer among countries with similarly high expenditures.

WATCH | Soaring cancer drug prices prompt warning over patient access: His cancer drug costs $90,000/month. Doctors say it’s greed | Duration closed caption 6:17 Cancer doctors across Canada are sounding the alarm over drug prices pushing public health care past a breaking point. CBC’s Christine Birak breaks down the numbers and hears from dozens of frontline oncologists about the impact of surging costs on patients.

More money, but where is it going?

The CIHI report identifies a potentially important change in how health-care spending is growing.

Inflation-adjusted spending per person is projected to grow 2.3 per cent this year, compared with just 0.4 per cent in 2025.

More significantly, CIHI estimates public-sector spending will increase by more than $5 billion beyond what is needed to keep pace with inflation and demographic changes.

Adam Rondeau, CIHI's manager of health spending and operations analytics, said the increase could be an early indication that governments are investing in additional capacity, new technologies and innovations in health-care delivery.

But determining precisely where that money is going is more complicated.

"It's difficult to say X number of dollars is net new and related to a given program of work," Rondeau said.

He explained that the report identifies additional spending but cannot establish whether that investment is producing shorter wait times, more available services or better patient outcomes.

Meanwhile, the report states that spending on physicians is projected to increase 8.3 per cent this year, substantially faster than overall health-care spending.

Yet access to primary care remains a major challenge. CIHI's research on primary care found that 17 per cent of Canadian adults reported having no regular health-care provider in 2023.

Sara Allin, an associate professor of health policy at the University of Toronto, says Canada spends more on health care than many comparable countries, but it continues to struggle with long wait times and access to services. (Submitted by Sara Allin)

Spending more isn't necessarily spending better

For Allin, the challenge isn't simply increasing health-care budgets; it's ensuring that additional investment produces measurable improvements.

"If we're spending this much, it's more perhaps how we're spending it than the level of spending at this point in terms of driving further improvements," she said.

One important difference between Canada and some comparable countries, she said, is how health care is financed.

According to CIHI's expenditure figures, 71.4 per cent of Canada's health spending is projected to come from public sources in 2026, with the remaining 28.6 per cent financed privately.

Allin said several other wealthy countries fund a larger share of health care collectively, allowing them to cover a broader range of services, including prescription drugs, dental care and mental health supports.

She said those differences have consequences for both efficiency and equity.

Publicly financed systems can negotiate lower prices and reduce some administrative costs, she explained. They can also reduce financial barriers that prevent patients from accessing needed services.

WATCH | Health-care workers hold rally after 3.5 years without a contract: Hundreds of unionized health-care workers rally outside legislature | Duration closed caption 2:04 At least two health-care unions have gone three and a half years without a contract. On Wednesday, hundreds rallied outside the legislature demanding the government take action.

Allin said gaps in Canada's public coverage mean people without adequate private insurance can face substantial costs for necessary services, particularly prescription drugs and mental health care.

She also questioned whether Canada's health-care financing arrangements provide sufficient incentives to improve patient outcomes.

Rather than simply paying providers according to the volume of services delivered, Allin said governments could do more to link funding with measurable improvements in care.

Sutherland similarly argued that governments need to rethink where additional resources are directed.

He pointed to home care, assisted living, long-term care and other community-based services as areas where greater investment could help keep patients out of overcrowded hospitals and emergency departments.

Both experts also raised concerns about the pressure that rising health-care spending could place on other public priorities, including education, housing and social services.

Ultimately, Sutherland said, the figures should reassure Canadians that substantial resources are being devoted to health care while also prompting them to question whether those resources are being used effectively.

"I think they should be somewhat relieved that Canada is not underfunding this health-care system, but at the same time, they should be concerned that they're not getting great value for their money."

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
