Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Why Brazil?
World.content:
A sky that doesn`t charge to dream.

By Dany Cesario

HAVANA TIMES – Ever since I arrived in Brazil, there is one question I get asked repeatedly: “Why do so many Cubans come here?”

And every time I hear it, I think the question should be different: What is happening in Cuba that makes so many people decide to seek a different life?

The island is deteriorating, hardships are mounting, and people are wearing themselves out trying to get ahead. Yet the leaders’ worn-out rhetoric never changes, as if repeating the same slogans could feed a family, rebuild a country in ruins, or restore hope to those who have spent far too long waiting for change.

It outrages me that people are expected to make sacrifices without seeing them translate into a decent life. That expressing a different opinion becomes a problem, and that deciding one’s own future comes up against so many barriers.

Despite everything, there are still those who continue to justify this reality, as if defending a political narrative were more important than acknowledging the suffering of those who live it.

All of this makes me think of my mother and so many Cubans like her.

I wonder how many more years they will have to wait to live with the peace of mind they deserve. How many more promises will they have to hear before they can simply live, without worrying every day about what they will put on the table?

I’m not talking about privileges. I’m talking about rights: the right to live with dignity, to express what we think, and to make decisions about our own lives.

No government should take ownership of a people’s future or demand gratitude for what it is obligated to provide.

That is why Brazil, like any other country, does not have to be perfect for us Cubans to find what we have lacked for years: freedom, opportunities to grow, and the possibility of forging our own path without arbitrary restrictions.

It is not enough to talk about the homeland when the present is suffocating us and forcing us to pack our bags.

If we must emigrate to prosper, and if we have to seek new horizons to live with dignity, then the failure is not that of the people. It is the failure of a political system that has forced them to leave.

El destino comienza donde aprendemos a seguir..

Read more from the diary of Dany Cesario.

World.title: Cuba Revives Military Exercises after the US Elections
World.content:
A university student receives instructions from a Cuban Army instructor on how a rocket launcher works during a university defense exercise in Havana. The military exercises called during the first week of November are intended to strengthen the organization and coordination of Cuba’s defensive capabilities. Photo: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS

By Dariel Pradas (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – When Miriam Fuentes heard that the Cuban government had called military exercises the day after the midterm elections in the United States, her long-dormant fear of a military invasion by the neighboring superpower resurfaced.

“These military exercises wouldn’t surprise me if the Republicans had won the elections, but the Democrats swept them,” the 58-year-old Havana doctor told IPS, referring to the electoral debacle suffered by the ruling Republican Party in the November 3 elections.

On Wednesday, November 4, as media outlets around the world reported that the Democratic Party’s “blue wave” had swept even historic Republican strongholds and secured decisive majorities in the Senate, the House of Representatives, and state governorships, Cuba launched its “Moncada 2026” Strategic Exercise.

The nationwide operation lasted one day and was intended, according to the National Defense Council, to strengthen the preparedness and coordination of leadership and command bodies, troops, the territorial defense system, and the economy in the face of possible scenarios of aggression.

“We will defend every house, every neighborhood, every area until we defeat any Yankee who tries to take over Cuba,” declared Army Corps General Roberto Legra, first deputy minister and chief of the General Staff, in a video released on the social media accounts of the Ministry of the Revolutionary Armed Forces.

Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel, who participated in several meetings of provincial defense councils, also emphasized on his social media the importance of strengthening the country’s defensive capabilities “to confront any aggression against our homeland.”

Print media and local television reported how different Cuban provinces were preparing responses to possible scenarios of unconventional warfare and measures to neutralize aerial attacks by drones and manned aircraft, as well as the infiltration of commando units.

On Friday, November 6, the military exercises were followed by National Defense Day, during which many civilians were mobilized for military training with weapons, in accordance with Cuba’s Soviet-era defensive military doctrine known as the “War of All the People.”

These exercises have been repeated throughout 2026 as tensions between Havana and Washington have intensified.

Díaz-Canel had already indicated on March 20 that Defense Days were being held in 40,000 areas throughout the country.

“I’m really not too worried about a war breaking out. Although I begin my military service in December, and who knows what could happen,” said Dairon Rodriguez, an 18-year-old Havana student who graduated from a polytechnic institute.

Rodriguez will be drafted to complete two years of active military service, a requirement for men between the ages of 17 and 28, although shorter periods apply to those entering higher education, and exemptions exist for people deemed unfit for medical or other reasons.

“My mother, though, is worried all the time. She can’t stop thinking about it,” he added in his conversation with IPS.

*An army instructor shows a group of young people the features of an artillery piece during a university defense exercise in Havana. On Friday, November 6, a National Defense Day was held, during which civilians trained with weapons to respond to a potential military attack. Photo: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS*

Rising Tensions

The days leading up to the November 3 midterm elections in the United States were becoming increasingly tense, with the return of bellicose rhetoric not seen since early 2026.

Following the military operation that culminated in the abduction and detention of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro on January 3, US President Donald Trump insisted that Cuba would be next on the list of military interventions.

Two executive orders signed by Trump on January 29 and May 1, aimed respectively at blocking fuel shipments and threatening foreign investors, ultimately became the real attacks on the island, plunging it into unprecedented levels of a multidimensional crisis.

In fact, since June, Washington has approved sanctions almost weekly against officials and state-owned companies in this Caribbean island nation, located just 90 nautical miles (145 kilometers) from the United States.

In October, the sanctions were expanded further, with new restrictions on financial operations involving Cuba’s private sector, which the Trump administration had claimed it wanted to strengthen.

Bellicose rhetoric, however, had been largely absent during those months, at least until October 23, when Trump stated at an election rally in Florida that US warships would “pass by” Cuba after the war in Iran.

He added that his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, who is of Cuban descent and a fierce critic of the island’s government, would be responsible for resolving the country’s situation.

“What we’re going to do with Cuba is we’re going to bring those beautiful ships back from Iran, we’ll pass by Cuba, we’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards (45 meters) off the coast. They’ll raise their hands, and then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to close the deal,” the president commented.

Hours later, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez rejected “any threat involving US ambitions toward Cuba” in a social media post.

“Our coasts have beautiful beaches, but also sharp, jagged coastal rock formations, inhospitable to those who arrive with hostile intentions and ambitions of domination,” he added.

That same day, Rubio urged Cubans seeking to bring about a change of government to engage in “discreet cooperation with the CIA.”

Shortly afterward, the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) published instructions in Spanish for those wishing to contact it “securely,” along with recommendations for online communications involving the use of VPNs, secure networks, private browsers, and email accounts not linked to personal identities.

Rubio’s statements were mocked by Cuban officials and dismissed by the Cuban foreign minister in an interview published by *The New York Times* on October 29.

“Frankly, they don’t seem serious at all. They seem a little childish,” he said.

On October 31, Trump said that the Cuban government “is not going to last much longer” and that results would be seen “within these two and a half years, even before that.”

However, the US president suffered an unprecedented defeat in the midterm elections, meaning that beginning January 3, 2027, he will face a highly adversarial Congress that will reduce his ability to operate without constraints.

Some Cubans, including Dr. Fuentes, thought US policy toward Cuba would change in some way.

But it did not.

*Members of the Ministry of the Interior wave Cuban flags during a parade marking International Workers’ Day in Havana. Rising tensions between Cuba and the United States during 2026 have led to an increase in military exercises on the island. Photo: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS*

After the US Elections

On November 5, the United States again imposed sanctions on Cuban oil, technology, and maritime companies, as well as two Chinese firms — China National Electronics Import & Export Corporation and Beijing H&C Technologies — accused of supplying defense and security equipment to the Cuban government.

According to Rubio, the new measures seek to “put an end to the harmful activities of the Cuban regime.”

On Monday, November 9, Trump once again described the island as a “failed nation,” while Rubio released a video arguing that Cuba “has no future” under its current political and economic model and that it poses “a threat to US national security and interests.”

These were clear indications that the offensive against Cuba would remain unchanged unless Democrats impose some restrictions when they take control of Congress in January.

However, several international analysts warn that his party’s defeat in the November 3 elections could prompt Trump to shift his focus toward foreign policy, where he enjoys broader presidential powers.

Nor does support among the Cuban-American community for the policy against the island appear to have changed in Florida, a state that remains under Republican control and is home to the largest Cuban-origin electoral base, which supposedly inspires many of the White House’s decisions regarding Cuba.

The 2026 FIU Cuba Poll, released on October 27 by Florida International University, indicates that 77% of respondents agree with prioritizing maximum-pressure policies against the Cuban government, while 65% support blocking oil imports to the island.

The survey, which has tracked the political attitudes of Cuban-origin adults in Florida’s Miami-Dade County since 1991, interviewed 1,004 people by telephone between September 4 and 29 for this edition.

Among respondents in the latest survey, 73% support US military action to overthrow the Cuban government.

Of those respondents, 43% prefer a clandestine CIA operation or other covert activity; 28% favor bombing selected military targets; 14% support a ground invasion; and less than 1% approve of bombing urban areas.

Tensions in Cuba-US Relations Enter an Uncertain Phase

Nevertheless, the survey reveals that many of those who support maximum pressure and military action against Cuba are also among those who send the most remittances to relatives on the island and would like measures affecting the population to be eased.

“Cuban Americans want two things at once: a tougher stance toward Havana and a more bearable life for the Cuban people… The same respondents who support maximum pressure also support medicines, food, and assistance to Cuba’s private sector,” said Guillermo J. Grenier, one of the survey’s principal researchers.

First published in Spanish by IPS and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: How Cubans Can Face Up to 50 Days Without Electricity
World.content:
When a transformer explodes on their block

Citizen’s Report. Photo: AP / Ramon Espinosa

By Melissa Cordero Novo (El Toque)

HAVANA TIMES – Tulipan, in Cienfuegos, is a neighborhood in darkness, like the rest of the province and the country. Calling it a neighborhood in darkness is not just a descriptive expression. It means a whole lot of people who are fed up and beaten down by their inability to lead even a halfway normal life, forced to live in the 21st century as though they were in a cave during the Paleolithic era. Literally. No electricity. No water. Practically having to “hunt” for food. In the end, the Spanish words Cuba and cueva (cave) sound somewhat alike, and the two have much more in common than one might imagine.

From Tulipán, one family reports that scheduled power outages, complaints, and rights mean very little when a transformer breaks down on your block. That’s when another kind of hell begins. First, you have to call the Electric Company (UNE) and get someone to answer. The company says it is overwhelmed by demand, so it takes an extremely long time to respond — and even when it does, nothing gets resolved.

When residents finally managed to get through, they were told they “had to wait,” that no vehicle could be sent to assess the damage to the transformer. They were assured that theirs was “complaint number 16,000 this month,” and that the UNE had only two vehicles available to handle emergencies throughout the city.

Twelve days after the problem was reported — 288 consecutive hours without electricity — a vehicle from the electric company finally arrived in the neighborhood. The linemen climbed up, inspected the transformer, touched it in three places, and declared, “This can’t be repaired.” They put it back where it was, told residents they would have to wait for another crew to come and take it down because they couldn’t do it themselves, and left without saying anything else.

During another complaint call to the Cienfuegos electric company, residents questioned the absurdity of the linemen not removing the transformer while they were there. They were told that it would have to be transported to Santa Clara for repairs, pushing any solution even further into the future.

Residents are still waiting in darkness for that transfer to take place. The company cannot install a new transformer because none are available, nor can it repair the damaged one in Cienfuegos, known as the Pearl of the South. During the call, residents were also told: “We can’t give you a minimum or maximum timeframe for a solution because demand is very high.”

According to the experience of other residents whose transformer had exploded a few blocks away, the company told them that replacing it would take between 30 and 50 days. Saying “50 days” is easy. Living through them in complete darkness is another matter.

Explosions, Transfers, and Protests

Transformers exploding in Cuba no longer seem to be news. Unfortunately. A calamity should always be newsworthy. In Havana, according to the official Cubadebate, an average of 25 transformers break down every day, although on some days the number has exceeded 60. On October 30, 2026, Matanzas had 162 damaged transformers, according to the state-run newspaper Girón. The situation in the rest of the country must be just as bad, if not worse.

Public protests over broken transformers that nobody repairs have also become recurrent. On October 16, 2026, 45 families in Vertientes, Camagüey, had gone 51 days without electricity because of a transformer failure. Only after they protested publicly was another transformer installed. And on September 21, 2026, residents of El Condado, in Santa Clara, had to block the street to get the authorities’ attention after spending 36 hours without power following a transformer breakdown.

Nor is the Electric Company’s undeclared strategy of forcibly moving transformers from one location to another, without explanation, anything new. Several protests have also erupted for this reason. On July 29, 2026, for example, residents of La Gallega, in Guanabacoa, Havana, took to the streets to prevent authorities from removing transformers from their neighborhood.

The state-run press has reported on the establishment of workshops in certain locations, such as Holguín, to “restore” transformers. However, in Matanzas, Alejandro Rodríguez Azpeitía, director of the Provincial Electric Company, acknowledged that the province’s transformer factory was “practically shut down because it has no oil.”

Who Is Responsible for Transformer Explosions in Cuba?

An impoverished and obsolete electrical system is compounded by the overload transformers experience when power is restored after hours and hours of blackouts. The Havana regime has turned something inevitable into yet another problem: people rushing to plug in and charge their devices. Are they going to ask people not to do that, too?

Government specialists explain that “the simultaneous demand for electricity after prolonged hours without power” is what damages transformers and “other infrastructure in the distribution networks.” Luis Rodriguez, technical director of Havana’s Electric Company, told Canal Caribe that high temperatures were also part of the problem. Meanwhile, the director of the Matanzas Electric Company said that overloads were caused not only by storm damage but also by “the equipment people use for lighting (EcoFlow devices and portable power stations).”

But whatever causes the overload and eventual explosion of a transformer, responsibility lies with the Electric Company, the agency charged with preventing repeated system failures.

We spoke with a telecommunications and electronics engineer about the causes of transformer explosions on the island. The specialist confirmed that the main causes are, of course, overloads, extreme voltage spikes resulting from operations on the electrical grid, aging equipment, and the deterioration or lack of insulating oil. Both voltage spikes and overloads can heat the oil, cause it to evaporate, and ultimately lead to explosions.

Another phenomenon reflecting the extremes to which Cuba’s socioeconomic crisis is pushing people is the theft of transformer oil, which the regime classifies as sabotage. According to the engineer we consulted, the cooling oil extracted from transformers is “very clean” and “can be used as fuel for cars and motorcycles,” although he does not rule out the possibility that people are using it to cook food.

“Transformers consist of a laminated iron core designed to isolate eddy currents and coils, or windings, made of varnished copper wire. That copper is extremely expensive in the industry,” the engineer explained. For that reason, he doubts that the Cuban government has access to the amount of copper needed to repair so many transformers.

How quickly a transformer can be repaired depends on the extent of the damage. If it has not exploded, its “core and metal tank” might be reusable. Another major obstacle to repairs is rewinding the coils or windings — copper conductors wrapped around the iron core. This process must be carried out using specialized machines, known as winding machines, which require electricity to operate.

Importing transformers from abroad, which could be another solution, also seems impractical. In Mexico, for example, a pole-mounted transformer can cost between 60,000 and 100,000 Mexican pesos (approximately US$3,000 to $6,000), depending on its voltage rating. Just imagine: if Cuba cannot repair transformers consistently enough, how much money would be needed to import them from a nearby country like Mexico and replace the hundreds upon hundreds of broken transformers across the island?

Meanwhile, residents of Tulipán — along with those on dozens of other blocks and in other neighborhoods — remain in darkness, with no solution in sight.

Read more feature articles here on Havana Times.

World.title: Will There Be a Way Forward Tomorrow?
World.content:
Vías No Formales program (a state-run educational program for children ages six and under who are not enrolled in preschool or daycare).

By Lien Estrada

HAVANA TIMES – I walked past one of the little schools where I attended elementary school. It’s on Capitan Urbino Avenue in Holguín. I passed by in the afternoon and noticed a sign posted on the wall near the front door: “No Vías Today. Sorry.” Obviously, it meant there would be no classes in the

I laughed. Because my mind made a completely different association. I thought this announcement could just as easily have come from the Cuban state, addressing the people. Finally acknowledging its inability to solve the serious problems we face. A reality that has become almost suffocating in nearly every corner of the country.

We feel it in our bodies, often against our will, of course: the sense that we have no ways to save ourselves, no means of escaping what we have been forced to endure. A miserable existence takes hold day after day and night after night, amid blackouts and hunger, affecting a large percentage of the population. My mind kept telling me: Remove the word “sorry” from the end of the state’s acknowledgment of the terrible chaos we are living through. That word isn’t in its dictionary. Everyone knows that.

They have never shown remorse for the consequences the Cuban people have suffered because of government mismanagement. They never expressed it publicly (and we doubt they feel it privately) for the senseless persecution of homosexuals, religious people, and those who simply opposed their dictates. They even went so far as to establish a concentration camp for them in Camagüey Province.

Never, in their lengthy speeches or through their actions, have they acknowledged their disastrous economic decisions, driven by an unhealthy obsession with centralizing and controlling everything, like a feudal lord controlling merchants in the Middle Ages. Nor have they apologized for their disastrous military adventures, which have cost the people so much blood (they don’t produce anything; they give orders), with all the deaths in Africa and Latin America. They offer no apologies for the millions of Cubans who have been forced to leave this country, both in the past and today. In the past, those who left were called “scum.” Now, because the exodus has become so massive, they no longer attach a label to those who depart. After all, they need their remittances to survive.

And then there are the countless mistakes they have made over decades, invariably justified by the embargo imposed by US imperialism. They have managed to bury their own inefficiencies and those of others beneath that justification with a mastery that would astonish anyone. Because this hasn’t gone on for just a few days or a handful of years. It has lasted more than half a century.

The chaos has become so overwhelming that many people anxiously await an invasion of saviors, because we ourselves have been unable to put an end to the catastrophe we are experiencing.

I doubt anyone in Cuba could tell me I’m exaggerating. Unfortunately, I feel I’m not exaggerating in the slightest. Of course, powerful arguments both for and against this government that calls itself communist still coexist on the island. What cannot be denied under any circumstances is the utter disorder and chaos suffered by millions of people on this piece of land. It is more than evident, yet nobody takes responsibility for it.

Furthermore, the possible solutions that once seemed worth considering are fading away, like the morning fog dissipating as the day progresses.

Read more from the diary of Lien Estrada here on Havana Times.

World.title: US resumes flights after a four-and-a-half-hour shutdown caused by obsolete equipment
World.content:
US resumes flights after a four-and-a-half-hour shutdown caused by obsolete equipment

14th Saturday, November 2026 - 05:24 UTC Full article

Photo: AP / Ross Franklin

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday night lifted the nationwide ground stop it had ordered in the afternoon, after some four and a half hours of airspace closure that left thousands of flights cancelled. Donald Trump’s administration blamed the failure on overloaded, outdated analogue telecommunications equipment at air traffic control centres, ruled out a cyberattack for now and warned that the return to normal would be slow.

Airspace reopened at 8.15 p.m. Eastern time (10.15 p.m. in Montevideo), according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. According to his account at a White House press conference, at 3.36 p.m. radar and communications at control centres began giving inconsistent data, and shortly before 4 p.m. the FAA ordered that no aircraft take off. Duffy said the switches and routers of the old analogue telecommunications system became overloaded with data and began giving erroneous information. At that moment more than 3,500 aircraft were in the air, and they landed normally.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the failure was unrelated to Thursday’s global Microsoft outage and that, “as far as we have seen”, there was no cyberattack, although the investigation remains open.

More than 6,000 flights were cancelled and more than 25,000 delayed, according to FlightAware. Duffy spoke of “tens of thousands” of people stranded at airports, and the federal emergency agency, FEMA, activated its centres to ensure no passenger went without medication. Recovery will depend on the availability of pilots and crews, and flights that did not leave on Friday will be rescheduled from Saturday, less than two weeks before Thanksgiving.

Duffy used the briefing to ask Congress, which Democrats will control from January, for US$50 billion in emergency funding to build a new air traffic control system, on top of the US$12.5 billion already approved. According to the secretary, previous administrations received US$15 billion over 25 years and “barely anything was done”.

It was the third nationwide ground stop in US history, after the September 11, 2001 attacks and January 2023, when the pilot notification system failed.

World.title: US grounds all departing flights over an air traffic control communications failure
World.content:
US grounds all departing flights over an air traffic control communications failure

14th Saturday, November 2026 - 00:53 UTC Full article

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the failure affects the 22 regional centres that guide aircraft en route between airports and that FAA technicians are investigating

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday ordered a halt to all flights departing from the country’s airports “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”, following a communications failure affecting air traffic control centres. Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed and hundreds of thousands of passengers were stranded. The government has so far ruled out an attack.

The order took effect at around 4 p.m. US Eastern time (6 p.m. in Montevideo) and was extended until at least 11.30 p.m. Eastern time, according to TheStreet. “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis,” the FAA said, attributing the problem to a “temporary telecommunications outage” and saying it halted flights out of an abundance of caution. Aircraft already airborne continued to their destinations.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the failure affects the 22 regional centres that guide aircraft en route between airports and that FAA technicians are investigating. According to an internal Alaska Airlines message cited by CNBC, the problems affect communications and radar.

“There was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious act against us. It was just a telecommunication outage, as of right now,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House, though he said all possibilities were being examined. Mullin rejected comparisons with the 2001 attacks — “This is not the same as 9/11” — and warned that the problem “is not going to be resolved in an hour”.

The most affected airports were Atlanta, Chicago O’Hare and New York’s airports, according to FlightAware. Just over two million passengers fly domestically in the US each day, and the disruption comes less than two weeks before Thanksgiving, the busiest travel period of the year. United and American Airlines said international departures were also being handled case by case.

It is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a failure of the pilot notification system halted take-offs for hours, and before that since the September 11, 2001 attacks.

World.title: Microsoft restores services after a global outage hit Outlook and Teams in more than 70 countries
World.content:
Microsoft restores services after a global outage hit Outlook and Teams in more than 70 countries

13th Friday, November 2026 - 17:09 UTC Full article

In Australia, the outage affected the tax office, some courts, the Federal Police, the ASIO intelligence agency and the New South Wales state services platform

Microsoft said on Friday its services were recovering after a global outage that began on Thursday afternoon, European time, and for hours affected millions of users in more than 70 countries, including public bodies in Australia and Japan. The company ruled out a cyberattack.

The disruption hit Outlook email, the Teams work platform, SharePoint Online, the Copilot artificial intelligence assistant, the OneDrive and OneNote cloud services and the Microsoft 365 suite, widely used by businesses and governments. “We’re seeing continued progress in recovery across affected regions,” the company said, warning that some users could still experience intermittent problems. “We know our customers rely on our services to do important work every day, and we’re sorry for the impact these outages had,” it added.

“At this time, I can confirm there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity,” Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice-president for Copilot, Agents and Platforms, wrote on X. According to the company, several servers unexpectedly became unavailable and their load shifted to the remaining ones, in a domino effect that overwhelmed systems linked to Exchange Online, its email service. There is still no definitive analysis of what happened.

In Australia, the outage affected the tax office, some courts, the Federal Police, the ASIO intelligence agency and the New South Wales state services platform. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke activated a clause in the digital resilience agreement signed with Microsoft in June so that the country would receive priority in restoring services. In Japan, government spokesman Minoru Kihara confirmed that the government’s IT infrastructure was also disrupted, with no incidents at health facilities. Problems were reported in public services in Singapore and the Philippines, and in Thailand four major banks temporarily suspended email-dependent services.

Complaints on the Downdetector platform peaked first on Thursday afternoon, European time, and a second wave came on Friday morning, before returning to normal levels in the afternoon. According to the company, Microsoft 365 has more than 450 million corporate users and 95 million consumers, and Teams more than 320 million.

World.title: Chile tells Argentina “countries do not ask permission” for its ship bound for the Falklands
World.content:
Chile tells Argentina “countries do not ask permission” for its ship bound for the Falklands

13th Friday, November 2026 - 17:06 UTC Full article

The Chilean-flagged Danstar aims to restore a route suspended for some 15 years, carrying food, machinery and building materials as an alternative to supplies from Montevideo

Chile’s Foreign Minister Francisco Pérez Mackenna has ruled out asking Argentina for authorisation for the voyage of the Chilean vessel Danstar, which plans to reopen the commercial route between Punta Arenas and the Falklands in December, invoking the right of innocent passage recognised by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. “Countries do not ask permission,” he said, according to Argentina’s La Nación.

“Chile believes in the right to free navigation, which is guaranteed, the right of free passage, innocent passage, as it is called in UNCLOS maritime law. And we trust that right will be respected,” Pérez Mackenna said. He was responding to his Argentine counterpart, Pablo Quirno, who said on Monday on the A24 channel that the vessel must request permission to cross Argentine jurisdictional waters. “Thousands of ships pass through the Strait of Magellan every year. There are thousands of ships that ask for authorisation to cross when they leave for the Malvinas,” Quirno said. Since 2010, Argentina has required by decree prior authorisation for ships sailing between the mainland and the islands or crossing Argentine waters towards them.

The Danstar, a 72-metre Chilean-flagged cargo ship operated by Easter Island shipping company, aims to restore a route suspended for some 15 years with a cargo of food, machinery and construction materials, as an alternative to the supplies that arrive regularly from Montevideo. The private-sector initiative is promoted by the Falkland Islands Development Corporation and backed by Punta Arenas. “We want to be the islands’ big supermarket,” said its mayor, Claudio Radonich.

The Argentine government fears the route could provide logistical support to the Sea Lion oil project. Quirno recalled “the Chilean government’s commitment that this will not contribute logistically to the exploitation of natural resources” in the islands. According to La Nación, Chilean diplomats privately expressed “indignation” that Argentina has tolerated regular trade between the islands and Uruguay for years but concentrates its pressure on Chilean vessels. Argentina’s Foreign Ministry denies seeking to provoke an incident.

The exchange comes during a key week in the dispute over the islands. The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will announce on November 28 its decision on Argentina’s request to halt Sea Lion, after the hearings in Hamburg, and Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies is debating the sovereignty defence bill, which toughens sanctions on companies linked to resource exploitation in the archipelago. In October, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham raised with Chilean President José Antonio Kast London’s interest in the islanders’ right to self-determination.

World.title: Leo XIV to 52,000 young people in Lima: “Be passionate about everything worthwhile”
World.content:
Leo XIV to 52,000 young people in Lima: “Be passionate about everything worthwhile”

13th Friday, November 2026 - 02:58 UTC Full article

Photo: REUTERS/Yara Nardi

Pope Leo XIV met some 52,000 young people at Lima’s National Stadium on Thursday, according to El País, in the last event of his stay in the Peruvian capital before travelling to Chiclayo, the diocese he led as bishop. “Someone told me that Peru needs hope. You are the sign of hope,” he told them, to applause.

The young people came from the coast, the highlands and the jungle, many with parish groups and others on their own, and alongside Peruvian flags there were also Venezuelan and Chilean ones. The Pope entered the stadium track in the popemobile at around six in the evening, as the stands displayed signs asking for his blessing. The vigil included testimonies, a theatrical performance in which Peruvian saints came to the rescue of young people in crisis, music and scissor dancers, an Andean ritual.

At around half past seven, Leo XIV spoke with a message of comfort and encouragement. “Dear young people, when you suffer, turn to Jesus. Do not be afraid to speak to him sincerely. He knows our tears,” he said. “Be passionate about everything worthwhile. Cultivate your talents. Discover the richness of your culture. Do not settle for living according to what others expect of you.” He ended with an invitation to those who believe they are beyond redemption: “It is not too late to begin again.”

The Archbishop of Lima, Cardinal Carlos Castillo, recalled during the event Inti Sotelo and Bryan Pintado, the two young men of around twenty who were shot dead during the November 2020 protests. “In the recent history we have lived through in our country, young people often took to the streets to protest and in some cases several were shot. There are two martyrs: Inti and Bryan,” he said. Castillo said that after the crackdown many young people found in dance a form of expression that eventually reached the parishes. The testimonies included that of a young woman who lost a dozen relatives and of a nun who suffered abuse by a member of the Church.

Leo XIV, 71, who is recovering from lung cancer surgery, celebrates Mass on Friday at the Pampas de Pimentel, near Chiclayo, where nearly a million faithful are expected. On Saturday he will visit Cajamarca and Zaña, and on Sunday Cusco and Pucallpa, before returning to Rome on Monday, November 16.

World.title: British veteran returns to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took in 1982
World.content:
British veteran returns to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took in 1982

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 22:01 UTC Full article

Aged 18, Andy Gatrick found two wounded Argentine soldiers, later captured, at Mount Harriet in June 1982 and kept one’s helmet, which bore a name: Hector. Photo: Mick Dawson

A former Royal Marine has travelled to Argentina to return to an Argentine veteran the helmet he took during the Battle of Mount Harriet in the 1982 Falklands War, in a reunion filmed for a documentary, BBC Sussex reported.

Andy Gatrick, who was 18 at the time of the war, came across two injured Argentine soldiers during the Battle of Mount Harriet, fought on June 11 and 12, 1982. Both were captured by the Marines. Gatrick kept the helmet of one of them, which bore a name: Hector. Now 63, he managed to track him down and on October 23 flew to Gualeguaychú, in Entre Ríos province, to return it in person to Héctor Pereyra.

“I put my weapon down and as I bent down to put the strap over my shoulders, I saw movement and a cloth which looked like a white handkerchief. My eyes adjusted and there was two Argentinians, I didn’t know they were badly injured. I dived to the floor, weapon up. There was lots of shouting and swearing, bedlam,” Gatrick, from Bolton in northern England, said in footage sent to the BBC.

He was joined by another Royal Marine veteran, Mick Dawson, 62, who filmed the meeting for a documentary called Hector’s Helmet. According to Dawson, the British kit was poor and the Marines fought in berets, while the Argentines had American helmets, so Gatrick “borrowed” Pereyra’s. “In a very emotional day, he handed the helmet back in person to the guy he could have just as easily killed that night,” Dawson told BBC Radio Sussex. The two veterans “embraced like long lost brothers”, he said.

Dawson interviewed Pereyra about the moment when, wounded, he saw Gatrick emerge from the darkness. “He said, ‘I knew this man had the power of life or death over me and he chose life’,” Dawson recounted. “He then showed me a picture of his nine grandchildren and four children that wouldn’t have existed if Andy made a different decision that night. It was just the most amazing thing to witness.”

Dawson hopes to release the documentary next year. The 74-day war in 1982 left 907 dead: 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British personnel and three civilian islanders.

World.title: Lula to visit Madrid on Monday to meet Sánchez, two weeks before Spain’s election
World.content:
Lula to visit Madrid on Monday to meet Sánchez, two weeks before Spain’s election

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 18:02 UTC Full article

The visit will also include a political event at which Lula will expressly back the Socialist candidate, and Sánchez’s team had spent two weeks trying to arrange it

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will visit Madrid on Monday, November 16, to meet Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, less than two weeks before the snap general election on November 29, in which Sánchez is seeking re-election. It will be Lula’s first visit to Spain since he won Brazil’s election on October 25.

According to the Spanish government’s official statement, the two will hold a bilateral meeting at the Moncloa Palace to discuss relations between the two countries and coordination of initiatives such as Democracy Always and the Global Alliance against Hunger and Poverty. Lula will stop in Madrid on his way back from the UN climate summit, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, where he will also make a state visit to the Philippines.

According to the Spanish press, the visit will also include a political event at which Lula will expressly back the Socialist candidate, and Sánchez’s team had spent two weeks trying to arrange it. Sánchez has presented Lula’s re-election and the Democratic victory in the US midterms as proof that the advance of the radical right can be halted.

CNN Brasil reported that Lula will be accompanied by congressman André Janones, the architect of the digital strategy that helped his electoral comeback. The Spanish government and the Socialist Party insist that Janones is not advising Sánchez’s campaign and there are no plans for him to do so.

Polls show a slight recovery for the Socialists, so far insufficient to govern. A survey by 40dB for El País and Cadena SER shows the Socialist Party up almost two points, but the People’s Party and Vox would together win a comfortable absolute majority of more than 190 seats; 176 are needed to govern. The state-run Centre for Sociological Research shows a stronger Socialist recovery.

Neither Lula nor Sánchez attended the Ibero-American Summit held in Madrid last week. According to El País, Lula needed to rest and recover his voice after the campaign. Sánchez spoke by phone on Thursday with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum about bilateral relations and the outcome of the summit.

World.title: Paraguay’s banking superintendent arrested in the Ueno Bank investigation
World.content:
Paraguay’s banking superintendent arrested in the Ueno Bank investigation

12th Thursday, November 2026 - 11:20 UTC Full article

Insfrán was named in a criminal complaint expanded by opposition lawmakers last week, alongside the economy minister and other officials

Paraguay’s Superintendent of Banks, Holger Insfrán, was arrested on Thursday as part of the investigation into the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has already led to the pre-trial detention of former President Santiago Peña and former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, according to prosecution sources cited by the EFE news agency. The charges against him have not been disclosed.

The Superintendency of Banks, part of the Central Bank, is responsible for supervising and regulating Paraguay’s financial institutions, including Ueno. Insfrán was named in a criminal complaint expanded by opposition lawmakers last week, alongside the economy minister and other officials.

According to prosecutors, Ueno received large amounts of public funds during Peña’s term, including from five pension funds, while granting allegedly irregular loans to companies owned by its owners, the Vázquez Group. The bank had 2.94 million customers.

Peña, removed by the Senate on November 6, is charged with alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator, and could face a maximum sentence of 15 years, according to prosecutors. He says he is innocent. Carvallo, who headed the finance company from which the bank emerged before Peña appointed him to lead the Central Bank in 2023, is accused of breach of trust, producing false public documents and self-serving administration.

The Central Bank said on Wednesday that 100% of customers covered by the state guarantee have received an advance of up to 40 minimum wages, about 121.8 million guaraníes or roughly US$19,600, under the emergency law passed by Congress. It has until Monday to complete repayments up to the guarantee ceiling of 75 minimum wages, about 228.3 million guaraníes or roughly US$36,600.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Citing safety concerns, Acapulco cliff divers move to indoor municipal swimming pool
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

ACAPULCO, Guerrero — Organizers of the iconic La Quebrada cliff diving performances announced Tuesday that the world-famous show will permanently relocate to the municipal indoor swimming pool, citing improved climate control and a significantly reduced risk of hitting jagged granite outcroppings.

Starting next month, the divers, whose nighttime leaps from 115-foot coastal cliffs into a crashing Pacific ocean inlet have thrilled tourists since 1934, will transition to a 10-meter regulation platform. Event coordinators assured visitors that the experience will maintain every bit of its historic prestige, provided guests adjust their expectations regarding natural rock formations and ocean swells.

“La Quebrada was iconic, but the tide was remarkably inconsistent,” said lead coordinator Eduardo Ramos, standing beside the municipal center’s 12-foot deep end. “Here, the depth is fixed at 3.6 meters, the chlorine levels are monitored hourly, and our divers no longer have to wait for a swell to avoid breaking their legs. It’s better all-around, we think.”

To compensate for the loss of the Pacific breeze and dramatic natural canyon echoes, venue managers plan to play ambient audio recordings of crashing waves over the facility’s public address system. The traditional torch-lit evening performances will continue under the glow of energy-efficient overhead LED floodlights.

Divers have expressed enthusiasm for the move, noting that the controlled indoor setting allows them to focus on technical form rather than calculating wind shear or dodging territorial pelicans.

“The cliff had a lot of character, but it lacked basic amenities like warm showers and a designated locker room,” said veteran diver Javier Mendoza, who estimated he had leaped off the cliff face over 4,000 times. “Leaping from a fiberglass board into filtered, 78-degree water offers a level of professional predictability that raw nature simply cannot match.”

Local tourism officials remain confident that international visitors will continue to flock to the show, emphasizing that the ticket price will remain unchanged despite the move indoors.

“People come to Acapulco for authentic tradition,” Ramos said. “Whether that tradition occurs off a 35-meter sea cliff or next to a lane divider in pool three, the spirit of adventure remains entirely intact.”

World.title: Limited access: Reducing mobility issues for people with physical challenges
World.content:
After losing part of a leg following an accident as a teen, Juan Sánchez, 32, learned to adapt. He chose to use crutches instead of a prosthetic, and says he has gotten quite fast walking around his hometown of Tonalá. But tile floors, pieces of plastic on the ground and uneven sidewalks still cause problems.

“I’m careful,” he says. “I have slipped and fallen a few times.”

Sánchez is one of millions of people in Mexico living with mobility issues. According to the National Institute of Statistics, Geography and Informatics (INEGI), more than 6 million people in Mexico live with a disability.

Mobility challenges, such as walking, climbing or navigating stairs, are the biggest issues for people with disabilities. Negotiating uneven sidewalks, cobblestone roads and public transit is also challenging and, for some, limits their independence. Impairment, meanwhile, can make it difficult to control body movements or posture and can affect basic daily activities. A person with impaired mobility may use a wheelchair, crutches or other aids.

Already, more than half of those with disabilities are over age 60, and the population continues to get older.

Supreme Court mandate sets a new baseline

Recognizing mobility as a human right, Mexico amended its constitution in 2020 to grant every person the right to safe, accessible and efficient mobility. Since then, many improvement projects have focused on public transportation.

In January 2026, Mexico’s Supreme Court (SCJN) issued a ruling intended to transform the nation’s public transit system. The ruling aligns with the equality and nondiscrimination principles outlined in the constitutional amendment.

It’s a welcome development in the nation’s capital, where 71% of the population uses public transportation.

For instance, Mexico City Metro was ordered to ensure total accessibility for riders. That means doubling the number of seats reserved for people with disabilities, older adults and pregnant women, as well as removing physical barriers inside stations to reduce obstacles that hinder movement. This sets a precedent that the rest of the nation will need to follow.

Meanwhile, Metrobús is adding universal, inclusive design elements that anyone can use without assistance. Guadalajara is also improving public transit by modernizing and maintaining the elevators and escalators at transit stations. In preparation for the World Cup, Tlaquepaque trained hospitality workers to provide accessible and inclusive services.

A holistic approach to accessible infrastructure

While the SCJN ruling goes a long way toward improving transit systems, the bigger problem for many is getting to them.

Sánchez’s experience with uneven sidewalks and surfaces that cause his crutches to slip is not unique. Many cities have sidewalks that are uneven, narrow, lack ramps for wheelchairs or are routinely blocked by vehicles or other barriers. Often, roads aren’t any easier to navigate because of cobblestones, potholes or unsafe traffic patterns.

“We have to think about the whole trip, from the moment the person leaves home until they reach their destination,” says Dr. Rigoberto Antonio Cisneros García. He is one of the authors of the recently published “Proposal for Addressing Motor Disabilities in Mexico,” created jointly by the Centro Universitario de Ciencias de la Salud (CUCS) and the Mexican Foundation for Health, A.C. (Funsalud). The proposal hopes to improve the care and understanding of mobility issues in Mexico.

He highlights the need for accessible infrastructure that would allow more independence without relying on others for assistance.

“Mobility is a precondition for exercising almost every other right,” Cisneros García says. This includes receiving medical care, attending school, keeping a job and spending time in the community. He highlights the need for a collaborative network that complements public services and addresses the needs of affected individuals.

Overcoming distance to access key services

The System for the Development of the Family (DIF) is an important piece of infrastructure for those with mobility challenges. With locations throughout the country, DIF works to improve quality of life for people with disabilities. It distributes free assistive devices, such as wheelchairs, walkers and canes, and provides rehabilitation therapy.

But accessing these services often requires significant travel.

“It would be good if these places were closer,” Sánchez says, “because sometimes they’re located very far away.”

The offices he needs to access for disability paperwork and other services are about an hour’s drive or roughly two hours by public transit. For those with mobility issues, long trips are a barrier, especially if they need someone to assist them. That person may have to take time off work or plan around other obligations.

Sánchez has adapted well to his mobility challenges over the years. He wants others to have the same success and for his fellow citizens to be considerate of those with mobility issues. He notes that people often block ramps and sidewalks, making it more difficult for him to maneuver.

As a country, Mexico is making strides in accessibility but has much work to do. Prioritizing accessibility with a national network of services is key.

“We can’t expect to solve this problem if we design all our services from a desk or an office,” Cisneros García says. “Especially if we expect the most vulnerable people to come to us.”

Leanna Coy is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Trump renews tariff threats as Sheinbaum prepares for China
World.content:
Listen to this article

The second week of November started with news of the arrest of the CJNG operator known as “R2” following a shootout in Guadalajara on Sunday. The focus quickly turned to the economy on Monday, as President Sheinbaum announced a new record for formal employment levels in Mexico and sought to calm worries about the rollout of Mexico’s new Digital Economy Law, designed to phase out some cash payments.

U.S. President Donald Trump threatened Thursday to double tariffs on Mexican goods unless Mexico stops a migrant caravan heading north from Chiapas. The warning came as Mexico seeks lower U.S. duties on steel, aluminum and vehicles. President Claudia Sheinbaum replied that no caravan has reached the northern border during Trump’s second term.

The same trade talks frame her trip to China next week, where she will address APEC business leaders in Shenzhen and meet Xi Jinping. She says the meeting should not complicate negotiations with Washington.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Mexico-U.S. relations: Tariff threat and a wanted ex-prosecutor test bilateral ties

New revelations this week shed light on CIA operations in Chihuahua. The operations, which Mexican authorities call a sovereignty violation, came to light in April and have since been the focus of numerous government investigations.

The New York Times reported Tuesday that Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former Chihuahua special prosecutor, helped the CIA operate in Mexico in exchange for a U.S. visa. On Wednesday, Sheinbaum called the report “very interesting” and said the CIA’s participation in an April drug lab raid in Chihuahua violated the National Security Law. Former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui was detained last month on a treason charge tied to that raid. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said federal and state prosecutors hold outstanding warrants for Zuany.

On Thursday, Trump threatened to double tariffs in a Truth Social post, two days after a group of over 1,000 migrants left Tapachula heading north. The tariffs that could be affected include those on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles. Sheinbaum said Mexico will not use force against migrants, noting that no caravan has reached the northern border during Trump’s second term in office.

On Friday, after the Times reported that Zuany had fled to the U.S. and is under U.S. government protection, Sheinbaum said she would ask the Security Cabinet for more information. She called his alleged collaboration “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship,” but said she expects no friction because the matter has been discussed with the U.S. government.

China: Sheinbaum’s APEC pitch and a Yucatán research deal

As tensions with the U.S. simmer, Mexico continues to strengthen its relationship with China. On Nov. 6, Mexico’s Culture Ministry and INAH formalized a Maya archaeology project with Shandong University. The project grew out of residents’ objections to a quarry, which INAH sided with before the quarry proposal was quashed. Yucatán Governor Joaquín Díaz Mena then presented it to the Chinese Embassy, citing his aim of expanding Yucatecan exports to China.

At Thursday’s mañanera, Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Sheinbaum will be in Shenzhen Nov. 17-19. She will be the main speaker at an APEC Business Advisory Council event, where only she and Xi will address the plenary. She will pitch Plan México to investors and will not meet Trump in China, though she said she will “probably” meet him at the G20 summit in Florida in December. The stakes are tied to USMCA: the Trump administration decided in July not to renew it for 16 years, and U.S. concerns include Mexico’s trade relationship with China.

Economy: Record jobs and solar permits, rising inflation

Economic signals were positive throughout the week. On Monday, Sheinbaum said formal employment reached a record 23,088,353 at the end of October. The same day, inflation rose to 3.75%, above the 3.65% median forecast in a Bloomberg survey and a third straight monthly increase. The previous week, Banxico cut its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 6.25%. Sheinbaum credited the cut to the economy’s “good performance,” while the central bank said risks to its inflation outlook remain tilted to the upside.

The president also addressed the Digital Economy Law, which gives the Finance Ministry power to designate sectors where only digital payments are accepted. Openbank México CEO Juan José Galnares said it could cut cash use by up to 50% by widening access to credit, but warned against moving too aggressively. Sheinbaum said cash will not be phased out, though gas stations will go cash-free to curb fuel theft.

The MND Sheinbaum Index reflected the economy’s strength. It reached 71.5 for September, its highest score to date, driven by growth and employment data. Business confidence, at 48.4, remained below the 50 neutral benchmark.

In industry, the National Energy Commission approved six solar permits worth US $750 million, adding 649 MW from 2028. Only six of 57 applications met all criteria. Auto parts production hit a record US $11.118 billion in August, though U.S. imports of Mexican parts fell 1% in value in the first eight months. Parts enter the U.S. tariff-free if they comply with USMCA rules.

Tourism: Record totals, slower growth and fewer air arrivals

New data showed that visitation is up across the country, with new records in both arrivals and spending in September. Growth, however, has slowed compared to past years: spending rose 1.4%, against 6.1% a year earlier. Air arrivals, which account for 80% of tourism foreign exchange, have fallen two years running, and Cancún, Los Cabos and Puerto Vallarta airports handled 1.9 million fewer international passengers through October. Private-sector analysts cite the lack of promotion and a 17.8% Non-Resident Tax increase in January.

Mexico City expects 65.9 million tourist arrivals in 2026, up from 61.2 million in 2025. Officials credit concerts, sporting events and cultural activities.

A record-breaking year for sargassum is finally drawing to a close. Quintana Roo declared sargassum season over, a month later than in 2025, with over 150,000 tonnes of seaweed collected.

The influx of stinky algae weighed on Caribbean beach tourism this year, but failed to sink international visitation. Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez told the ITB Americas trade show in Guadalajara that culture was the main draw: About 36.3% of visitors came for it, more than double the 15%-16% who came for beaches.

Security: Arrests, an abduction and a homicide data gap

The weekend featured two dramatic security incidents. On Saturday, armed men abducted Río Bravo Mayor Miguel Ángel Almaraz on a highway between Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí. He was found Sunday at a Coahuila police checkpoint and said he escaped.

Also Sunday, the Navy arrested CJNG cell leader Rafael Álvarez Ayala, “R2,” and 19 others in Guadalajara after a shootout. García Harfuch said DEA intelligence helped locate him. He is the brother of the alleged mastermind of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo’s 2025 assassination.

On Monday, García Harfuch announced a 900-million-peso (US $48.2 million) package for Sinaloa, where 22,667 troops are deployed amid a rise in violence that has centered on the resort town of Mazatlán in recent months. Sinaloa’s homicides fell 18.8% in the first 10 months of 2026, yet it ranks fourth in total homicides nationwide.

Then, INEGI reported 29,488 homicides in 2025, 5,140 more than the federal count and the largest gap in more than a decade. INEGI shows a 12.1% decline from 2024; federal data show 21.2%. The Security Ministry says the sources use different methods but show the same trend. On Friday, Sheinbaum said a working group is reviewing the gap.

Good news: Young inventors, robotics wins and a World Cup bid

Looking ahead

At home, Mexicans are hitting their favorite stores as Buen Fin, the annual shopping discount extravaganza, kicks off.

President Claudia Sheinbaum travels to Shenzhen next week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, where she will court investors and strengthen ties with Asian leaders, including Chinese President Xi Jinping. A meeting with Trump is not on the agenda, leaving Mexico-China relations in the spotlight. However, Sheinbaum plans to meet the U.S. president in December at the G20 summit in Miami. Unresolved tariff and USMCA issues are likely to be on the table when they do.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: From the archive: The joy of having things made in Mexico
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in January 2025 — explores Mexico’s unique DIY economy, where virtually anything can be made to order.

It’s not that I’m embarrassed, but I do feel a little sheepish writing it: I have, apparently, abnormally large calves. At least for Mexico.

And let me tell you, that makes me pretty sad. I don’t know much about fashion — most currently fashionable clothing looks so silly to me — but I do love a sexy knee-high boot (no heels, please).

Alas, almost every knee-high boot I try on stops zipping up as soon as it hits my calf; they’re just not wide enough. And it’s heartbreaking, because I have seen some really cute boots out there.

But wait! It’s not the end!

Not too far from where I live is a town called Naolinco, famous for its leather products, mainly boots and belts. And if I decide to make a trip up to Naolinco, I can have a pair of boots made just for me! The style, the fit, the color — I can get exactly what I want with exactly the right fit.

Have I done this? Well, no. It’s a little pricey, yes, though not prohibitively expensive. The main thing is that you’ve got to make a day of it. It’s a bit of a drive, and then it’s figuring out exactly what you want and finding someone to make it for you. Then you’ve got to go back to pick them up. Mexico being Mexico, you’re definitely going to want to call and confirm they’re ready ahead of time, even if you’ve got a promised ready-by date.

But I could do it, and that’s the important thing.

And shoes aren’t all you can have made. The sky really kind of is the limit!

Having things made in Mexico: from plush carrots to custom furniture

When my daughter wanted “carrots” for her stuffed rabbit one Christmas, we had little stuffed carrots made. When she wanted “number blocks” from her favorite YouTube math singers, we had those made. And when her tastes became decidedly creepier, we had a bloodied “Canelita” from the “Animal Crossing: New Horizons” crossover made, complete with a detachable Velcro gun. She was over the moon. Oh, dear.

What else can you do? Well, there’s a seamstress a few blocks from my house, for example, who can “clone” clothing items. Just pick out the material, give her the original, and voilà! I’ve got a favorite dress and a favorite pair of pants that will be getting that treatment soon. After last year’s hellishly hot spring season and drought conditions, I’m going to be prepared for this one with the thinnest, lightest clothing I can find!

Speaking of drought, a water catchment system is another thing that you can have fitted to your home. This is something I’m personally dying to do; but alas, I rent. But aside from actual companies that can install these systems, it’s possible to find individuals who can do so, as well.

But the category of things I’ve had made the most of by far is furniture.

The importance of finding a good carpenter

It’s not the easiest thing in the world finding a good, reliable carpenter. So when you find one, hold on to this person for dear life! Because especially in a country where storage can be sparse, it’s important to be able to create options for yourself.

My favorite most recent carpenter-made piece of furniture is my standing desk. I bought the electrical base on Amazon, but skipped their overpriced desktops. Instead, I designed exactly the desktop I wanted, and a carpenter made it for me! We’ve also had a TV stand/bookshelf made to fit a tight living room, and a toy chest that I had fun painting once it was done. In the last house we lived in, I had a loft bed with built-in drawers and a desk made for my daughter. She loved the height and the cave-like feel underneath.

Why, you can even have beer made, a service my partner has provided. Got a restaurant or bar and want a special house recipe? There are people who can design and produce them for you. And of course, food, party favors and decorations for parties of any size can always be found. Themed t-shirts for the parents at birthday parties are currently a big thing in my city, actually. This is overkill if you ask me, but people seem to really get excited about it!

Will your own bespoke designs hit the nail on the head every time? Well, no. I found out a couple of times, for example, that my furniture-designing skills weren’t quite as professional as I thought they were. Fortunately, there are people who know much more about the things they make than we do. Trust them as guides.

The main trouble with having anything made, of course, is finding the right person or business. If you’re new in town or have limited Spanish skills, this can be tough. But if you have friends or at least know some people whose opinion you trust, then that’s your in. This is a country where everybody “knows a guy.” Ask around, and you’re sure to find someone!

And when in doubt or truly at a loss, take a look around Facebook or Instagram; many will have pages that display examples of their work.

So remember: there’s legwork, but it’s fun legwork. Think of it as an adventure and a chance to meet some cool new people. You might get your custom-made stuff and a new friend!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.
