World.title: The death of the night out? How Mexico City’s youth are socializing
World.content:
What if the problem isn’t that young people have stopped going out, but that we’ve been getting the night out wrong all along?

For decades, the formula seemed pretty straightforward: Friday night meant getting dressed up, meeting friends, drinking too much, dancing until the early hours and spending Saturday recovering. Going out was practically a weekend obligation.

But for a growing number of young people, getting wasted is losing its appeal. And the traditional clubbing experience is no longer the default way to socialize.

Instead, think dinner with friends, a long walk, a fitness class, a coffee that turns into a three-hour conversation, or a night at someone’s apartment. Alcohol hasn’t disappeared, and neither has the desire to have fun. But the priorities seem to be shifting.

So, is the night out dying? Or are we simply learning to have a good time differently? In Mexico City, where nightlife has long been part of the city’s appeal, I wanted to find out.

Is Gen Z drinking less?

There is evidence that young people are drinking less in several countries, although the trend isn’t universal. According to the European School Survey Project on Alcohol and Other Drugs, the proportion of European students who reported drinking alcohol in the previous month fell from 55% in 1995 to 43% in 2024. The figures concern school students across participating European countries, not all young adults worldwide.

Mexico offers another interesting example. The country’s 2025 National Survey on Drug, Alcohol and Tobacco Consumption (ENCODAT) found that the percentage of adolescents aged 12 to 17 who had consumed alcohol in the previous month fell from 16.1% in 2016 to 7.5% in 2025. That’s a substantial decline among teenagers, although it doesn’t tell us exactly how much Mexico City’s 20-somethings are drinking.

So, what’s behind the change?

Health consciousness is an obvious place to start. Fitness has become part of everyday life for many young adults, from Pilates and running clubs to strength training and early morning workouts. When your Saturday plans involve a long run rather than nursing a hangover, Friday night suddenly looks different.

There’s also a growing awareness of alcohol’s health risks. We know more about its relationship with sleep, physical performance and long-term health, including cancer. And when social media is full of people sharing their workouts, wellness routines and carefully curated lives, waking up feeling terrible can seem like a particularly bad trade-off.

But there’s a contradiction: The same social media that encourages us to go to bed early also makes us feel as though we should be doing something worth posting about. The perfect workout, the perfect job, the perfect group of friends and the perfect weekend have become another set of expectations to keep up with.

I still tell my friends to send me pictures when they travel. Increasingly, though, they would tell me they can’t wait to see my stories when it’s my turn to go somewhere. Sometimes it feels as if an experience isn’t quite complete until you’ve posted about it.

Could the pandemic have played a part, too? Young people who spent months isolated during formative years may have developed different social habits. But it would be too easy to blame COVID for an entire generation’s changing relationship with nightlife. Technology, money, work, wellness culture and shifting social norms may all be part of the picture.

And there’s another question worth asking: If drinking less is becoming more acceptable, does that mean we’re becoming less social, or simply less dependent on alcohol to socialize?

Everything in moderation

I’ve been doing Dry January for four years. Back in 2022, only one of my friends had even heard of it. She was the one who introduced me to the idea.

At the time, not drinking seemed strange unless you were taking antibiotics. How could you possibly go out and not drink? Every January, I’d find myself explaining why I was doing it and why taking a break from alcohol appealed to me. Most people weren’t particularly interested. They only wanted me to have a glass in my hand.

This year was different. By the end of January, I realized I didn’t really feel like drinking. I didn’t miss it at all, and when the month ended, I didn’t see a reason to start again.

I’d already been going out less, drinking fewer cocktails and mostly having wine when I went to restaurants. My first alcoholic drink of the year eventually came in May, at a friend’s wedding. I had a few cocktails, enjoyed myself and moved on.

What surprised me most wasn’t how easy it was to say no to alcohol. It was how much I enjoyed the mornings afterwards. Waking up after a fun evening with no hangover, enough energy to exercise, go for a walk or visit a museum felt like getting an extra day back.

Mexico City has also made it easier to experiment. There are bars and restaurants where alcohol-free drinks feel like a genuine part of the menu rather than an afterthought. A good mocktail can be just as enjoyable as a cocktail, without the alcohol.

Still, I don’t think everyone needs to give up drinking. If I go to Italy with my best friends, I’ll be more than happy to have a Spritz. At Christmas, I’ll gladly share a bottle of wine with my family.

For me, the shift has been about choice rather than restriction. I don’t want to drink just because everyone else is drinking, or because I’ve convinced myself that a night out requires alcohol. And I don’t think there’s anything wrong with someone who feels differently.

Perhaps that’s the real change: Not that drinking has become unacceptable, but that not drinking is becoming less of a big deal.

What do young people actually want from a night out?

To understand what’s happening in Mexico City, I asked young people about their habits, what they do instead of going out, and what would make them want to go out more often.

In my survey, 55% said they go out less frequently than they did three years ago. Respondents also described drinking less when they do go out. Their explanations were revealing.

Several said their friends simply weren’t interested in going clubbing as often. Instead, they preferred daytime plans, relaxed dinners or meeting at someone’s home. These gatherings felt more intimate and made it easier to catch up, have proper conversations and spend time together without feeling rushed.

Sports and wellness came up, too. For young adults juggling work, studies and other responsibilities, a weekend workout or an early start the next morning can take priority over a late night.

What stood out in my conversations was that the issue wasn’t always a lack of desire to socialize. It was a lack of enthusiasm for the available ways of doing it.

In my survey, respondents talked about wanting clubs closer to home, shorter queues and friends who were more willing to go out. Some described asking their friends to make plans and feeling as though they were begging.

That last detail stayed with me. Imagine wanting to go dancing, getting a group together and feeling as though you’re asking everyone for a favor.

But we should be careful not to confuse a preference for smaller gatherings with a rejection of nightlife altogether. People can want fewer nights out without wanting nightlife to disappear. They may simply be more selective about when they go, who they go with and what makes the evening worthwhile.

In fact, 65% of respondents in my survey said they still went to bars, clubs or parties at least once a week. That complicates the idea of a dying night out. Going out less often doesn’t necessarily mean giving it up.

Are bars noticing the shift?

If young people are changing their habits, what does that mean for the places where they spend their evenings?

I spoke to young people about what they drink and to bar and club owners in La Roma about what they have noticed since the pandemic.

In my survey, respondents described drinking less hard liquor and fewer cocktails, such as gin and tonics or rum and Coke. Beer and wine remained popular, while some said they alternated alcoholic drinks with water or delayed their first drink until later in the evening.

Others admitted that they didn’t particularly enjoy the taste of alcohol. For them, drinking was more about loosening up, feeling more sociable and having fun with friends.

Alcohol-free options therefore have an obvious appeal. But mocktails aren’t a complete replacement for the drinking experience: Some respondents said they found it boring to spend an entire evening drinking sodas or alcohol-free cocktails, particularly when everyone else was drinking.

The message isn’t necessarily that young people want bars without alcohol. They want more choice, a good atmosphere and a reason to stay.

The owner of a bar in La Roma that also serves food offered another perspective on the experience of running a venue where people can eat, drink and socialize. His observations, alongside those of a local club owner, suggest that the relationship between nightlife and the pandemic deserves a closer look.

The club owner described a shift after COVID, with fewer young people going out, while holidays and days off could still bring busy nights, including crowds of international visitors.

These are individual observations, not proof of a citywide decline. But they raise an interesting question for Mexico City’s nightlife industry: If people still want to meet friends, what kind of venues and experiences will persuade them to leave home?

The answer might not be another club with louder music and more expensive cocktails. It could be a place where the music is good but conversation is still possible, where food is as important as the drinks, or where people can spend an entire evening without feeling pressured to keep ordering alcohol.

What does the perfect night out look like now?

For many of the young people I spoke to, the ideal evening sounded surprisingly simple: dinner and drinks with friends, either at a restaurant or at someone’s home. Good food, music they actually like, an intimate atmosphere and, crucially, music that isn’t so loud they have to shout to hear one another.

They still enjoy dancing, meeting new people and discovering new places. But they also want to talk, catch up and feel comfortable.

Perhaps the problem with the traditional night out is that it sometimes asks us to choose between the things we want from socializing. We want music, but we also want conversation. We want to meet new people, but we also want to feel safe. We want spontaneity, but we don’t necessarily want to spend hours queuing or traveling across the city.

And Mexico City has no shortage of alternatives.

The night isn’t dead; it’s simply being redefined.

What if the best place to read were also the last place you’d expect to find a book?

From Tokyo to Amsterdam, book raves have been bringing reading into clubs and cultural venues, turning it into a collective experience. The idea is simple: a book, some music and the pleasure of being together, without the pressure to talk. Less noise, more pages. Silence, too, can bring people together.

Mexico City has its own version of this quieter pleasure. The city’s audioramas, including those in Parque México and Chapultepec, offer spaces where people can sit among the trees and listen to music. I discovered them recently and was fascinated by the idea of spending an afternoon there reading or even learning Italian, as I did on my last visit. Just watch out for the person beside you who might have decided to take a nap and start snoring…

Then there are running clubs, which have turned exercise into a social activity in its own right. From themed runs and coffee meet-ups to longer races that bring strangers together, the possibilities go well beyond a night at the club.

These activities aren’t necessarily replacements for nightlife. They’re reminders that socializing doesn’t have to revolve around alcohol, a late bedtime or a particular kind of venue.

Think about your own life for a moment. When you meet your friends, does it always involve drinking? Could it be a museum, a fitness class, a walk through Chapultepec, dinner somewhere new or a Sunday morning spent running and getting coffee afterwards?

None of these plans is inherently better than going dancing until sunrise. And there’s no reason we can’t enjoy both.

Maybe the death of the night out is really the death of the idea that there’s only one way to have a good time.

Young people still want connection, excitement, music, romance and stories to tell the next morning. They just seem increasingly willing to decide for themselves what those things look like.

So, no, I don’t think the night out is dead.

But perhaps the best night out is no longer the one you barely remember. It’s the one that leaves you with a good story, people you feel closer to and a Saturday morning you’re actually excited about.

And you? What’s your perfect night out?

Marta Delgado is a Spanish writer and marketing professional from Galicia, Spain, currently based in Mexico City. She writes about culture, lifestyle, and what it means to build a life abroad, drawing from her own time living in different countries.

World.title: I grew up watching Mexican stereotypes. Hollywood hasn’t changed much
World.content:
William Nericcio, like most of the roughly 500 million residents living in Mexico, the United States and Canada, grew up watching popular television shows and consuming major media outlets.

As a Chicano raised in Laredo, Texas — one of the most densely populated Latino cities in the U.S. — Nericcio regularly saw himself and his community reflected in popular media. Often, however, those portrayals weren’t very accurate or authentic, instead relying on repetitive tropes and one-dimensional stereotypes that Hollywood has been recycling for generations.

#NewProfilePic https://t.co/lbCa4WKiVl — William Nericcio (@eyegiene) July 6, 2026

Nowadays, as a professor of English and comparative literature at San Diego State University and co-author of “Talking #browntv: Latinas and Latinos on the Screen,” Nericcio’s work largely focuses on the historical depictions and evolving complexities of his community on the screen.

Predictable stereotypes

“There are particularly demented representations of your average Mexican (as being) violent, dirty, lazy,” Nericcio tells Mexico News Daily. “If they’re a woman, they like good sex. They’re gonna take things from you. They’re a spitfire. Temptresses (who) carry daggers. That’s the signifier of our violent deviance as Mexicans.”

While Nericcio admits that he likes shows such as “Breaking Bad” and “Narcos” — two popular series featuring prominent Latino characters — he says that representations of Latin Americans have largely remained stagnant and predictable.

“I watched ‘Better Call Saul’ (the ‘Breaking Bad’ spinoff) and after that, even I would cross the street (after seeing a Mexican person in public),” he jokes. “They don’t just kill. They kill with the artistic vision of Salvador Dalí. It’s killing cubed, masterful.”

Century-old tropes still being used

Of course, those kinds of derogatory character oversimplifications have existed for more than a century, going back to 1894, when the short film “Mexican Knife Duel” premiered, marking one of the earliest known forms of Mexican protagonists in U.S. media.

Quoting the scholar Gary D. Keller, the Library of Congress notes that “These films villainized Mexican men and sexualized Mexican women, a pattern that would recur all throughout the 20th century.”

My childhood through Hollywood’s Mexican lens

As a California-raised Mexican American myself, who came of age in the 1990s and 2000s, I can relate. For decades, Mexican characters have too often been minimized in U.S. media, flattened into binary archetypes. Think Speedy Gonzales, who’s portrayed as charming, quick-witted and brave, or his familial counterpart, Slowpoke Rodriguez, slow but cunning and dangerous.

Some of my earliest memories of action flicks are films like “Desperado” with Antonio Banderas and Salma Hayek. In it, Banderas plays El Mariachi, a stone-cold assassin who packs firearms in his guitar case. Hayek’s Carolina, meanwhile, causes car accidents when crossing the street because of gawking men.

Like Nericcio, however, I’ll admit that “Desperado” was one of my favorite movies growing up.

I can also recall films like “The Sandlot,” which featured the character Benny “The Jet” Rodriguez, a baseball-loving kid who, in retrospect, is arguably one of the most fleshed-out Chicano characters ever portrayed. Rather than focusing on his cultural differences or moral deficiencies, Benny is just a regular kid who dreams of making the big leagues. It felt relatable to me back then, and in many ways still does. Benny’s heritage is neither a strength nor a weakness, and besides the name on the back of his jersey, his latinidad was never a factor.

A.C. Slater, played by Mario Lopez in the popular TV series “Saved by the Bell,” was similarly down-to-earth in the ’90s.

Profit over authentic representation

But those examples of wholesome, fully dimensional Chicano and Chicana figures were hard to come by, in my memory.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Paul Shipper 🎨 (@paulshipper)

“It’s called show business, not show ethnography,” Nericcio says. “It demands a profit. What gets a profit? What has worked before. Hollywood is about rebroadcasting images that are tried and true: the criminality of the Mexican.”

Nericcio goes on to say, “It’s how Trump blasted his way into office. He hoodwinked Latinos by saying he’s good for the economy (and fueling media stereotypes about the threat of Mexican immigrants). Folks fall for this.”

In that sense, what’s shown on the screen has real-world consequences and larger implications. It’s not simply about wanting to see more diverse representations of Chicanos and Chicanas in popular media; it’s about how, by not diversifying characters, beliefs can be formed and popularized to negative ends.

Amongst this deluge of negative portrayals, there have been several authentic representations that, unlike A.C. Slater or Benny Rodriguez, also reflect on the lived experiences of Latin populations.

Nericcio points to two of his favorite examples: 2006’s “Children of Men” and 2008’s “Sleep Dealer.”

Both films are set against a dystopian backdrop, allowing social commentary about immigration, exploitation and labor to be at the core of the films’ messaging.

Perhaps more importantly, though, each film was directed by Latinos, with Alfonso Cuarón helming “Children of Men” and Alex Rivera crafting “Sleep Dealer.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by CALÓ News Arizona (@calonewsaz)

“It’s sci-fi about the future,” Nericcio says of “Sleep Dealer.” “It follows a cyber-bracero who plugs into the matrix and sells his labor by staying in Mexico. The film broadcasts corporate America’s biggest wet dream. Labor without the Mexicans. We don’t want their bodies; we want their food and their labor … we don’t want to hear them speaking. The film is a brilliant portrayal of Mexican subjectivity on the border in its complexity.”

The push for change in writers’ rooms

Those films, though, don’t often generate as much box office success. “Children of Men” was considered a commercial disappointment and was unable to recover its production budget during its theater run. This, despite receiving fairly critical acclaim and a cult following, including three Academy Award nominations, while being retroactively lauded as one of the best thrillers of its time.

“Latino filmmakers are making stories that feature Latino and Mexican actors, but with storylines that aren’t ripped from the tabloid headlines,” Nericcio says. “But most people don’t watch. The progress that will come, if it will come, will come from numbers. Are more Chicanos in film school? Are more of them breaking into creative spaces? The key is the writers’ rooms.”

In that case, the present and future look as grim as the past.

Under-representation in the film industry

In 2021, the Los Angeles Times reported that “Latino representation among film writers is even worse than Latino representation on screen: Since 2008, Latinos have never constituted more than 5% of employed Writers Guild of America (WGA) film writers, according to the available data.”

Earlier this year, the University of California, Los Angeles shared statistics from the LA Times’ De Los, which found that “in 2024, only 1% of leading roles went to Latinos; less than 5% of directors were Latino; and approximately 2% of writers were Latino. Latinos make up nearly 20% of the U.S. population.”

Same old Hollywood

In 2015, Nericcio attempted to do his part by developing his own show, “Mextasy,” that sought to “rewrite televised borders, rethink televisual borders or fronteras, revealing the pulsing, growing body of Latin America alive and thriving within and outside of Uncle Sam’s unknowing body to celebrate the Latino experience throughout the world.”

The show never took off. But the concept — and the intent — remains as urgent today as it did more than 10 years ago, when Nericcio pitched his idea to networks.

“I’m a Chicano from Laredo, Texas, who thinks I’m Anthony Bourdain,” Nericcio jokes. “But it didn’t get picked up. Hollywood will crush your soul.”

As ever, it’s up to consumers to dictate, through our wallets and watching power, what we do or don’t want to see.

It’s something I think about whenever I have the urge to watch the latest hit show or visit a theater (rare for me as the dad of a toddler, but still). Putting our money behind genuine creatives in the communities we’re from is one of the only ways we have to shift the tides.

Until then, Hollywood will continue Hollywood-ing when it comes to its interpretations of Mexican and Mexican Americans.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: US Jobless Claims Reach 200,000 in November
World.content:
Rio Times Markets · United States

Key Facts The figure New US jobless claims were 200,000 in the week ended 7 November 2026, seasonally adjusted.

Versus forecast Analysts expected 195,000, and the prior week was 191,000, so claims rose by 9,000.

The trend The four-week average held at 195,250, the same as the week before.

Why it matters Weekly claims are an early gauge of layoffs in the world’s largest economy.

What ends it A reading below 195,000 next week would show the rise was a blip.

New US claims for jobless benefits rose to 200,000 in the week ended 7 November 2026, above forecasts, though the four-week average did not move.

What Changed

New US claims for unemployment insurance, the weekly count of people applying for jobless benefits, were 200,000 in the week ended 7 November 2026. That was 9,000 more than the 191,000 of the previous week and 5,000 above the 195,000 consensus (average analyst forecast) on the RT economic calendar, our feed of official release dates and forecasts.

The figure is seasonally adjusted, which removes regular calendar patterns such as holiday hiring. The US Department of Labor, the federal employment agency, publishes it weekly, normally on Thursdays.

Where It Sits in the Trend

The Department of Labor series, as carried by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis’s FRED database, shows weekly claims of 198,000, 200,000, 195,000, 195,000 and 191,000 for the five weeks before this one. The new reading matches the 200,000 of the week ended 10 October and is higher than the other four weeks in that span.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on North America Email address Follow

The four-week average, which smooths out weekly noise, stayed at 195,250. That means one higher week has not yet changed the underlying picture.

Why It Moved

The release does not state a cause, so the reason for the rise is not confirmed. Weekly claims are noisy and can change by several thousand from one week to the next.

A single week above forecast is therefore a prompt to watch the next release, not a signal of a turning point.

What It Means for Readers Abroad

At this level, there is no sign of a wave of layoffs in the data released. For Latin America and Africa, US employment matters because it feeds into American consumer spending and the dollar.

A sustained climb well above 200,000 would be an early warning of slower US growth, which investors in emerging markets watch closely. This reading alone does not show that.

What Would End the Rise

A second week at or above 200,000 would suggest layoffs are edging up. A reading back near the 191,000 of the prior week would suggest the latest figure was a blip.

The next weekly report, normally due on Thursday, 19 November 2026, covers the week ended 14 November. A four-week average moving above 200,000 would be a clearer sign of change than any single week.

What Is Not Known Yet

It is not known which states or industries accounted for the rise, because the figures released here do not show that detail. The data also does not show whether people who lost jobs have found new ones.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many Americans filed new jobless claims in early November 2026?

There were 200,000 in the week ended 7 November, seasonally adjusted. That was 9,000 more than the previous week and 5,000 above the forecast.

What is the four-week average?

It averages the last four weekly readings to smooth out noise. It stayed at 195,250 in this release.

Why do jobless claims matter outside the United States?

They are an early read on US layoffs. Investors in Latin America and Africa watch them because US growth and the dollar affect emerging markets.

What would show whether layoffs are rising?

A second week at or above 200,000, or a four-week average above 200,000, would suggest so. A fall below 195,000 would point to a blip.

World.title: Argentina October Inflation Rises to 2.2%
World.content:
Rio Times Markets · Argentina

Key Facts The figure Argentina’s consumer prices rose 2.2% in October 2026 from September, and 33.1% from a year earlier.

Versus forecast Analysts expected 1.9% on the month and 32.7% on the year, so both readings came in higher.

The trend Monthly inflation sped up from 1.9% in September, while the yearly rate eased from 33.4%.

Why the two differ October 2025 saw a 2.3% monthly rise, so the 2.2% of October 2026 pulled the yearly rate down slightly.

What ends it A November monthly reading below 1.9% would show October was a one-month jump.

Argentina’s monthly inflation sped up to 2.2% in October 2026, above forecasts, even as the yearly rate slipped to 33.1%.

What Changed

INDEC, Argentina’s national statistics institute, reported that consumer prices rose 2.2% in October 2026 compared with September. That is faster than the 1.9% recorded in September and 0.3 percentage points above the 1.9% consensus (average analyst forecast) on the RT economic calendar, our feed of official release dates and forecasts.

Compared with October 2025, prices were 33.1% higher, down from 33.4% in September. Analysts had expected 32.7%, so the yearly reading was 0.4 points above forecast.

Where It Sits in the Trend

Monthly inflation moved the wrong way in October: from 1.9% to 2.2%, a rise of 0.3 points in one month. The RT calendar holds only the September reading for comparison.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on INDEC (Argentina) Email address Follow

The yearly rate moved the other way, from 33.4% to 33.1%. Both can be true at once, because the yearly figure drops the oldest month in its window and adds the newest.

Why the Two Numbers Differ

INDEC reported a 2.3% monthly rise for October 2025. When that month left the 12-month window and October 2026 at 2.2% entered, the yearly rate eased slightly, even though prices accelerated from September.

INDEC’s breakdown, as quoted in Argentine press, shows housing, water, electricity and gas rose 4.2%, the largest of any division. Core inflation, which strips out volatile items, was 1.5%, so the pickup came from items outside the core.

What It Means for Readers Abroad

A monthly rate of 2.2% would add up to roughly 30% over a full year if it were repeated every month, so the pace is still fast. For visitors, importers and investors, it means local prices keep rising fast.

The miss against forecast shows analysts had expected a calmer month. One reading is not a trend, but it makes the path of falling inflation harder to read in the short term.

What Would Confirm or End the Pickup

A November monthly reading at or above 2.2% would confirm that price pressure is building again. A reading back below the 1.9% of September would suggest October was a one-off.

The next yearly reading will drop November 2025 from the window, so it depends on both November 2026 prices and that earlier base.

What Is Not Known Yet

It is not known whether utility increases will keep pushing prices up in November. It is also unclear whether the pace will last beyond one month.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did prices rise in Argentina in October 2026?

Consumer prices rose 2.2% from September and 33.1% from October 2025. Analysts had expected 1.9% and 32.7%.

Why did the yearly rate fall if monthly inflation rose?

The yearly rate drops the oldest month and adds the newest. October 2025 had risen 2.3%, slightly more than the 2.2% of October 2026, so the yearly rate eased.

Who publishes Argentina’s inflation figure?

INDEC, the national statistics institute, publishes it monthly. The RT economic calendar tracks the release date and analyst forecasts.

What would show whether inflation is picking up again?

A November reading at or above 2.2% would suggest so. A figure below 1.9% would point to a one-off.

What to See & Do

FRIDAY IN SÃO PAULO

TODAY’S PICK — GALLERIES AND THE MERCADÃO Start at the Pinacoteca, finish at the Mercadão Go to the Pinacoteca de São Paulo in Luz, in Centro. It is open 10am-6pm and entry is R$40, free on Saturdays. Take the metro to Luz station, which sits a few minutes’ walk from the museum. A single metro journey costs R$5.40. Aim to arrive near 10am, when the rooms are quietest. Give it two hours. Then walk or ride to the Mercadão (Mercado Municipal) in Centro for lunch. It is open Monday to Saturday 6am-6pm, with free entry. If you want a second museum instead, the Museu da Língua Portuguesa is also in Luz. It is open 9am-4:30pm and costs R$25 on a Friday.

OUTDOORS — IBIRAPUERA Parque Ibirapuera is open every day from 5am to midnight, and entry is free. It is the natural choice if the sky is clear. MAC USP, in the Ibirapuera area, is open Tuesday to Sunday 10am-9pm and is free. It pairs well with a walk.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — PAULISTA AND LUZ We have not verified café or coworking hours today, so we name none. Japan House São Paulo on Avenida Paulista is open 10am-6pm on Fridays and is free to enter. Sesc Pompeia, in Pompeia, is open 10am-7pm on Fridays and is free. It is a calm place to sit between meetings.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — PAULISTA ART If you want a bigger, quieter-minded day, spend it at MASP on Avenida Paulista. It is open 10am-9pm on Fridays and entry is R$85. Entry is free on Tuesdays, so budget-minded visitors can wait for TUE 17, when it opens 10am-8pm.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Beco do Batman in Vila Madalena is an open-air street that is always open and free. It suits a wander after dinner. Sala São Paulo in Luz runs guided visits and ticketed concerts. Check the hall’s own programme for tonight’s performance.

On Avenida Paulista and around Luz, keep your phone in a front pocket on the metro platform and in crowds after dark.

Latin America feels like a continent holding its breath over money: governments are paying to keep prices calm, and households are not yet convinced.

São Paulo, Brazil’s financial centre. File photo.

The Continent’s Mood Today

On 12 November, the region’s front pages were about the cost of calm. Brazil’s Senate passed a savings package, Chile cut diesel prices, and Argentina learned that inflation is stubborn.

Underneath sits an old memory of prices running away. Governments from Santiago to Mexico City are spending political capital to avoid a repeat.

Brazil – Relief, With the Bill Still to Come

The Senate approved the base text of the fiscal adjustment bill of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by 45 votes to 31. The government says the package will improve the 2027 budget balance, and four amendment votes are set for Tuesday 17 November before it moves to the lower house.

The bill is known as PLP 299/2026. It still needs the lower house, where the government will need another majority.

Mexico – Two Warnings in One Week

On Thursday 12 November, President Donald Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico unless it stops migrant caravans marching north. More than 1,000 mostly Central American migrants left Tapachula, in southern Mexico, on 10 November.

The threat comes days after Mexican forces arrested ‘R2’, an alleged cell leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), in Zapopan on 8 November. For ordinary Mexicans, both stories touch daily life: trade, jobs and safety.

Chile – Paying for Peace on the Roads

The government agreed on Thursday 12 November to cut diesel by 142 pesos a litre (about US$0.14) and to freeze diesel prices against increases until March 2027, aiming to end a truckers’ strike. A motorists’ group, No + TAG, says its own protest against highway tolls will continue.

Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz puts the cost at about US$500 million over 2026 and 2027. Chileans remember the 2019 unrest and the trucker blockades, so many see this as a price worth paying.

Argentina – The Last Mile Is the Hardest

INDEC, Argentina’s national statistics office, reported October inflation of 2.2%, above the roughly 1.8% that economists expected. The monthly rate has stopped falling, and the weariness is easy to hear.

Argentines have been told for two years that the worst is over. A stalled monthly rate feels like a promise slowly breaking.

Colombia – Profits Up, Rubble Still Down

Davivienda, one of Colombia’s largest banks, reported a 38% rise in profit. Miner Mineros also hit a record profit.

Not every company shared the cheer, though, as cement maker Argos saw profit fall 29%.

Peru – A Budget Vote and a Cooling Mood

Congress set the 2027 budget vote for 20 November. Prosecutors are asking for double their budget, which shows how much institutions are fighting for money.

A poll found 53% disapprove of Fujimori. The pattern is familiar in Lima, where political approval has often collapsed within months.

The Shared Mood

From Brasília to Santiago, the feeling is the same: governments are buying calm and families are checking the price. Nobody wants to be the first to relax.

Hope exists, in rising bank profits and the Buen Fin sales weekend that starts today in Mexico. Patience is the scarce resource, and it is being spent faster than the budgets.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the mood in Latin America today?

Cautious and cost-conscious. Brazil’s Senate backed a fiscal package, Chile cut diesel prices to end a strike, and Argentina’s inflation stalled at 2.2%.

What did Brazil’s Senate approve?

It approved the base text of Lula’s fiscal adjustment by 45 votes to 31. Amendment votes are set for Tuesday 17 November, then it goes to the lower house.

What did Chile agree with truckers?

Diesel falls 142 pesos a litre (about US$0.14) under a deal announced on 12 November, and prices are frozen against increases until March 2027. The government expects Congress to vote on Tuesday 17 November.

01 The bond market flinches, and shares follow

Wall Street is giving back a little after Wednesday’s rally. The S&P 500 sits at 7,592 (-0.35%), the Dow at 52,297 (-0.36%) and the Nasdaq at 25,366 (-0.39%).

The falls are small, but the mood is nervous. The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, is at 18.7 (+6.92%) as investors pay more for protection after a week of violent swings.

The cause is the bond market. The US 10-year Treasury yield is 5.134% (+2.68%), and a yield that high makes future company profits worth less today.

Gold has lost its shine as a result. The spot price is $3,881/oz (-2.46%), another hard fall this week, because the metal pays no interest while Treasuries now pay over 5%.

The dollar adds to the pressure. The dollar index is at 103.146 (+0.23%), which makes gold and other dollar-priced assets dearer for buyers elsewhere.

02 A hot jobs market and a hawkish Fed

The labour market is why the Fed cannot relax. October payrolls rose 165,000 against a forecast of 65,000, and unemployment fell to 4.1%.

Traders have since begun to bet on a Fed rate rise rather than a cut. That sharp turn explains why the 10-year yield has pushed above 5%.

Weekly jobless claims rose to 200,000 in the week to 7 November against 195,000 expected, and continuing claims fell to 1.697 million in the week to 31 October, according to the US Labor Department’s series. Producer prices are the next test.

The US PPI arrives at 13:30 Lisbon (08:30 New York), with forecasts of 0.4% on the month after 1.3% last time, and 6.6% on the year after 6.3%. Core PPI, which strips out food, energy and trade, is forecast at 0.3% after 0.7%.

A figure above forecast would harden the case for a rate rise. Fed officials then take the stage.

Collins speaks at 14:10 Lisbon and Bowman at 15:50, with Jefferson just after midnight.

03 Brazil feels the squeeze from Washington

Brazil received a friendlier inflation print than the US did. Official October IPCA, reported by the statistics agency IBGE on Thursday, rose 0.14% on the month, after 0.82% in September.

The annual rate is what counts for policy. It edged up to 4.63% from 4.58% in September, still above the 4.5% upper limit of the central bank’s tolerance band.

Brazil’s central bank held the Selic at 13.75% on 4 November, ending five straight cuts, according to its own statement. With the US 10-year above 5% and the dollar index at 103.146, a pause is the comfortable option.

The real is the shock absorber. When US yields rise, investors demand more to hold Brazilian assets, and the currency usually weakens, which feeds back into import prices.

Brazil’s own data follow today. Retail sales are due at 12:00 Lisbon (09:00 Brasília) and business confidence at 14:00, forecast at 46.5 against 46.2.

Colombia reports retail sales and industrial production at 15:00 Lisbon (10:00 Bogotá). Forecasts are 8.7% and -0.8%, against 7.3% and -3.7% before.

Oil is a second pressure point for Latin America’s exporters. The US Energy Information Administration (eia.gov/petroleum/supply/weekly) reports commercial crude stocks at 414.4 million barrels for the week to 6 November, up 4.7 million.

Gasoline stocks rose 1.8 million barrels to 210.8 million, and distillates rose 4.1 million to 103.3 million. Builds like these weigh on crude.

In Europe, the UK economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, matching forecasts and beating the 0.5% before. The goods trade gap widened sharply to £22.29 billion (about US$29.5 billion) from £19.61 billion (about US$25.9 billion), which tempers the good news.

The three-month average growth rate was 0.7%, up from 0.6%. Japan sold five-year bonds at 2.186%, below the 2.379% of the previous auction.

In China, total social financing is forecast at 1,420 against 3,550 before, a drop that would signal weak credit demand.

World.title: The Perfect Family Beach Day at Playa Carrillo, Costa Rica
World.content:
This is between me and you. Don’t tell anybody else. We don’t want too many people overcrowding the places I’m about to tell you about. Here’s how to spend a perfectly wonderful day at the beach in Guanacaste with your family. My little family and I have done this a bunch of times, so we’ve now got it down to a science. We’re going to spend the day at Playa Carrillo.

This works best if you’re staying along the coast in the general Tamarindo/Playas del Coco area in which case it can be a there and back again day trip. Here we go. First, you and your significant other have to plan on leaving at a decently early hour in the morning. For us it’s something like 9am. This will allow you plenty of time for driving, lunching, beaching, and returning. Of course, you’ll never hit this lofty goal. Anyone with kids knows that a series of things will inevitably happen that will push back your departure time, but that’s life.

Once everybody’s finally in the car with seatbelts in place the drive begins. The drive is actually part of the fun of this day trip. The most common route takes you through the historic city of Nicoya. When I say through it, I mean wiggling your way through the city’s narrow, sometimes one-way streets, past all of the little stories, people selling things on the sidewalks, and a mix of contemporary and historic-looking buildings. If you feel like it, you can pull over at the park with the neat old church and buy the kids some ice cream. Even if you don’t stop, driving through the buzz of human activity has a nice vibe.

The nice drive portion of the day continues after you make it out of Nicoya. As soon as the city ends you drive through a series of adorable little towns separated by hilly green cow pastures dotted with palm trees. For reasons that are unclear to me, the houses on this stretch of road are particularly well maintained, brightly painted with well-manicured gardens. ‘What a nice place to live’ comes to mind as you drive.

Right about now everybody in the car is starting to get antsy and that’s ok because I know exactly where you need to stop. Since you missed that departure time by about an hour, it’s time for lunch anyway. As you approach the coast, you need to wind your way steeply uphill before cresting the mountain and riding downhill to the coast. As you reach the highest point of this mountain (almost definitely driving 5 miles per hour behind an enormous truck that you can’t pass), there’s a restaurant called La Roca.

I have no affiliation with La Roca. This info is all coming from the love in my heart. My family has been going there for years. Originally, it was pretty rustic, but sometime over the last few years they completely remodeled it and now it’s modern and very nice. Either way, the magic of the restaurant was, and still is, the view. It sits atop the mountain with a stunning view of the countryside below. You can even see a waterfall in the distance.

There’s a clearly marked trailhead right next to the restaurant and you can hike to the waterfall that you can see from the balcony. We always say we’ll do the hike next time and never do. Waterfall hike or not, order anything on the menu, it’s all delicious. Enjoy the view, recharge your batteries, and then pack everybody back into the car and start driving downhill to the beach.

As you arrive at the coast, you’ll hit the small beach town of Samara, which is a fun place to explore, but you’ll have to save that for another day because you’re heading to Carrillo. After Samara you only have about ten minutes left in the car. After you cross a one-way bridge over a small river, you’ll want to pull over at the little store for snacks and drinks because it’s the last one before the beach.

Fully stocked with goodies from the store, you’ll drive five more minutes until you hit Playa Carrillo. You’ll know you’ve made it when you’re driving next to an enormous beach with calm waves, the entirety of which is lined with several rows of palm trees. You can pull over at any spot you please. Throughout the entire palm tree section of the beach there are benches, tables, and grills. The vibe is laidback and local, with lots of families enjoying the shade and waves.

After several hours of fun in the sun, it’s time to pack everybody and everything back into the car and start the drive home. If your family is anything like mine, the return trip is a lot quieter than initial drive as your kids will be slouched over sleeping like a pile of puppies. So, there you have it, the perfect family beach trip. Remember, this is between me and you. I don’t want the tables at La Roca and the shady spots at the beach to be full of other people.

About the Author

Vincent Losasso, founder of Guanacaste Wildlife Monitoring, is a biologist who works with camera traps throughout Costa Rica

World.title: Costa Rica Flights to the US Back on Track as Trump Blames Biden for Ground Stop
World.content:
If you’re flying between Costa Rica and the United States today, your flight should run close to schedule. The nationwide US ground stop that froze departures on Friday afternoon ended after about four hours, and airports in Costa Rica reported operations returning to normal on Saturday.

Check your flight in your airline’s app before you leave for the airport anyway. Aeris, which runs Juan Santamaría International Airport outside San José, has asked passengers to confirm their flight status directly with their airline, since itineraries can still change. Friday’s disruption hit both of the country’s main airports. At Juan Santamaría, Aeris said 12 departures and 11 arrivals were affected, and six departures and four arrivals were canceled. The rest were moved to overnight and early Saturday slots.

In Liberia, Guanacaste Airport representative Renata González said seven flights were canceled and that operations returned to normal over the course of Saturday. The outage was not an attack. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it began during maintenance work to replace old copper wiring with fiber-optic cable, which disrupted communication with planes and radar feeds. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of hostile action.

Duffy said more than 9,000 US flights were canceled and nearly 25,000 were delayed. It was the longest nationwide ground stop in the United States in 25 years. On Sunday, President Donald Trump made his first public comments on the ground stop and blamed his predecessor. In posts on Truth Social, he called the Biden administration “an FAA disaster” and said “everything they touched turned bad.”

Trump said his administration has a plan for the flight control systems and urged Congress to approve the money quickly, saying much of the current air traffic control system is 50 years old. Efforts to modernize the FAA’s systems have spanned several administrations of both parties.

If your flight was canceled Friday and you have not rebooked, start with your airline’s website or app rather than the airport counter. If you decided not to travel at all, US rules entitle you to a refund for a canceled flight, even when the cause was out of the airline’s control. Whether a policy would have covered you is a separate question, covered in our guide to travel insurance after the ground stop.

Many US airlines fly a plane into Costa Rica and send the same jet straight back, so delays at a US hub can still ripple into a departure here, as Friday’s cancellations showed. Air traffic between the two countries has largely recovered, but the episode has renewed debate in Washington over how quickly, and at what cost, the US air traffic control system should be replaced.

World.title: Costa Rica Banks Pay as Little as 436 Colones per Dollar – Here’s How to Get More
World.content:
If you are changing dollars into colones, where you do it matters more than ever. With the dollar at a record low, Costa Rica’s banks closed Friday buying dollars for between ₡436 and ₡440 each, according to Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) data compiled by El Observador. On $1,000, the gap between the best and worst of those rates is ₡4,000, or about $9.

The dollar closed Friday at a weighted average of ₡446.10 on Monex, the foreign exchange market run by the BCCR, a new record low and the lowest level since Monex began operating in 2006. It was the eighth straight session of declines and broke the previous record of ₡446.80, set on Sept. 17. The dollar has lost 10.3% of its value against the Costa Rican currency so far this year, according to El Observador.

Bank counter rates, as reported to the BCCR on Friday, varied by up to ₡4 per dollar. Banco Cathay offered the most, buying dollars at ₡440 and selling them at ₡452.50. Banco Nacional and BAC bought at ₡439 and sold at ₡453. Banco de Costa Rica (BCR) and Banco Popular bought at ₡438 and sold at ₡452. BCT paid the least, buying at ₡436 and selling at ₡454. The BCCR’s official reference rate in effect for the weekend is ₡442.56 for buying and ₡448.34 for selling.

Every bank pays less than the market rate when you sell it dollars. At BCT’s ₡436, changing $1,000 brings in ₡10,100 less than the Monex average, about $23. For a retiree converting a $2,000 monthly pension, choosing the best counter rate over the worst is worth about ₡8,000 a month. Changing money twice costs even more. At Banco Nacional’s rates, converting dollars to colones and back again loses ₡14 on every dollar, or roughly $31 on $1,000.

The BCCR publishes the buying and selling rate of every bank and exchange house each business day on its website, so you can compare before you go. Rates posted on Friday afternoon generally carry through the weekend, but they will move again when Monex reopens on Monday. If you already bank in Costa Rica, ask whether your bank applies a different rate to conversions made through online banking than at the teller window.

If you are paying with a foreign card, choose colones when a card terminal or ATM offers to charge you in dollars instead. That on-the-spot conversion, known as dynamic currency conversion, usually uses a less favorable rate than your card network applies. Shops, restaurants and tour operators that accept cash dollars set their own exchange rate, so it is worth checking it against the bank rate before you pay.

The Central Bank has been buying heavily without stopping the slide. On Friday it bought $41.8 million, or 84.8% of the $49.3 million traded on Monex, including $32.3 million in purchases meant to stabilize the market, according to El Observador. Its stabilization purchases total $1.39 billion so far in 2026, with no stabilization sales recorded. Specialists have said the dollar’s decline tends to deepen toward the end of the year, particularly in November, as companies pay year-end aguinaldo bonuses and taxes in colones.

For residents whose income arrives in dollars, including retirees, remote workers and landlords who charge rent in dollars, the slide has meant a steady loss of purchasing power. By early November, each $1,000 bought 46,810 fewer colones than in January, and the weak dollar has also hit businesses that earn in foreign currency, from exporters to Costa Rica’s medical tourism industry. With no sign yet that the slide is ending, the few colones you gain by shopping around for a rate are among the only savings within your control.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves to Demolish Narco Airstrips Without a Conviction
World.content:
Costa Rican authorities could destroy clandestine airstrips used by criminal groups without waiting for a final court ruling, under a bill that cleared a key legislative committee this week with unanimous support.

The Security and Narcotrafficking Committee approved the bill on Thursday. It is titled the Law to Sanction and Disable Clandestine and Unauthorized Airstrips and Allow the Confiscation of Assets Linked to Illicit Activities. The bill now goes to the full Legislative Assembly for a first-round vote and is not yet law.

President Laura Fernández submitted the measure in June as one of six bills in her administration’s package against organized crime. It is the fourth of the six to clear the committee. Under the bill, the Civil Aviation Directorate (DGAC) would declare an airstrip, airfield or helipad clandestine or illegal through a reasoned administrative resolution. Owners, tenants and administrators would first get a 10-business-day hearing to present evidence.

Once that resolution is final, the Public Security Ministry’s Air Surveillance Service could disable, demolish or destroy the site, with help from other agencies and municipalities. The rules would cover facilities used for drug trafficking, money laundering, human trafficking and organized crime.

Prosecutors could also ask a criminal judge to freeze the property in the National Registry, which would block its sale, donation, transfer or mortgage while the measure is in force. Machinery, vehicles and aircraft used to build or operate the strips could be seized and later permanently forfeited. The Costa Rican Drug Institute (ICD) would administer them.

The bill raises the prison sentence for building, enabling, facilitating or allowing a clandestine airstrip from the current three to eight years to five to 10 years. Owners, tenants or administrators who rebuild, rehabilitate or reuse a strip that authorities have already closed or destroyed would face 10 to 15 years.

Fines for operating aircraft at unauthorized facilities would double, from 20 to 40 base salaries. Deputy Kattia Calvo of the governing Pueblo Soberano party said changes were added to guarantee due process, including a way for property owners to present evidence of their innocence. Social Christian Unity Party deputy Abril Gordienko backed the bill, noting that clandestine strips can also enable crimes beyond drug trafficking.

Frente Amplio caucus leader José María Villalta said it was the first bill the committee had discussed that could truly hit organized crime, because it targets the assets criminal groups use to operate. He also raised procedural concerns. He warned that a separate bill on tourist airparks could create conflicting rules on air surveillance.

Costa Rica already allows the Air Surveillance Service to identify, declare illegal and disable clandestine strips under Law 9902, in force since 2020. According to the new bill’s statement of purpose, that law has no specific tools to act on the assets used to build or maintain the strips.

How many strips exist is unclear because they are built to go unnoticed. Fernández has said there are close to 200. The Public Security Ministry’s last official figure, from 2020, put the number of identified unauthorized strips at more than 140, and at least 20 were reported destroyed between the law’s entry into force and the end of 2024.

Some legal analysts have questioned whether the property freeze adds much to existing organized crime and registry security laws. They have also warned that a landowner may not know a strip is operating on their land. The bill now awaits a first-round vote in the full Assembly.

World.title: Italian Wanted in 2021 Santa Cruz Killing Extradited to France
World.content:
Costa Rica extradited two men to France on Thursday afternoon. One of them is an Italian national investigated in connection with the 2021 shooting death of a French citizen in Santa Cruz, Guanacaste. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) identified the men as Gianni Marco Basile, 68, and Iván Javier Pablot Martínez, 48, a Colombian-born naturalized Costa Rican.

French authorities want them in separate cases. Basile is sought on suspicion of aggravated homicide and extortion, and Pablot on international drug trafficking charges. Agents from the OIJ’s Special Tactical Response Service (SERT) escorted both men from La Reforma prison to Juan Santamaría International Airport in Alajuela. There they were handed to French officials and flown on a commercial flight to Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris.

INTERPOL’s National Central Bureau in San José coordinated the transfer, and the Public Prosecutor’s Office directed the case. Attorney General Carlo Díaz said the extraditions are part of the international judicial cooperation mechanisms through which Costa Rica responds to requests from other countries.

According to the OIJ, Basile is investigated for his alleged role in the killing of Pierre Claude Gazel, a French citizen who died on Oct. 5, 2021. The agency said Gazel was shot in front of his home in Santa Cruz at around 6:40 a.m., and the gunman fled on a motorcycle with another person.

The OIJ said French investigators identified prior conflicts and communications between Basile and Gazel. Because the victim was French, authorities in France chose to prosecute the case there. A judicial authority in Paris issued an international arrest warrant for Basile on Feb. 14, 2025.

OIJ INTERPOL agents tracked Basile for about two months before finding that he lived in Escazú, west of San José. They arrested him on Nov. 7, 2025, while he was driving in Curridabat. A criminal court in San José’s Third Judicial Circuit authorized his extradition on June 3, 2026. Pablot was detained in September 2025 by OIJ agents who specialize in organized crime. French authorities allege he belonged to a network that shipped drugs from Colombia to France and other European countries.

The case dates to Nov. 22, 2011, when French customs officers in Marseille arrested two Colombians carrying 29 kilograms (64 pounds) of cocaine. Investigators found the group allegedly used a company that sold wooden houses as cover for moving drugs into Europe. French authorities linked Pablot to the group, where he allegedly worked with a man known as “El Viejo.”

Case documents cited in local reports indicate that a criminal court in Marseille sentenced Pablot to nine years in prison on drug trafficking charges. A San José criminal court authorized his extradition on in April and an appeals court later upheld the decision. The OIJ described Pablot’s case as one of the first extradition proceedings coordinated with France over international drug trafficking. A second man detained with Pablot and named in the same French case, Hamilton Fernando Restrepo Osorio, has not yet been extradited.

Both cases now pass to the French courts. The transfers add to a growing number of extraditions out of Costa Rica this year, as the country handles more requests from abroad tied to violent crime and drug trafficking.

World.title: Prosecutors Say They Found Signs of Abuse at Costa Rica’s New Megaprison
World.content:
Costa Rica’s attorney general said prosecutors found signs of possible torture, abuse of authority and human rights violations at the country’s new maximum-security prison, setting off a sharp public clash with the Justice Ministry. Attorney General Carlo Díaz led a surprise inspection on Friday, at the High Containment Center for Organized Crime (CACCO) in San Rafael de Alajuela.

He was joined by Ombudsman Angie Cruickshank, sentence enforcement judges, the director of the Public Defender’s Office and officials from the National Mechanism for the Prevention of Torture. The Public Prosecutor’s Office said the visit aimed to examine the conditions in which inmates are held and to determine whether any situation could amount to a human rights violation or a crime.

The inspection followed complaints of alleged torture and abuse of authority inside the facility.Díaz said inmates showed him bruises and other marks that appeared to come from penitentiary police officers, and described one guard squad as more violent than others. He said he also saw signs of injuries from when inmates’ heads were shaved.

Díaz remarked on the irony that inmates whose convictions prosecutors had sought were now turning to the prosecutor’s office for help. He said prosecutors need no permission to inspect prisons and will keep making unannounced visits. Inmates listed several complaints, according to the attorney general.

They included what they called systematic rights violations, beatings by penitentiary police squads and a single doctor for 1,200 inmates. They also cited cameras in bathrooms, unwashed uniforms, phone calls allowed only until Nov. 12, denial of education and work programs, and violations of their right to a defense.

Díaz also said public and private defense lawyers could not enter the prison on Thursday because an influencer was filming inside. He said he was told inmates reacted to that visit and were then attacked. The Ombudsman’s Office reported three areas of serious concern. It said inmates described a specific squad of officers entering dormitories at set hours to beat them, and that inspectors saw people with injuries on various parts of their bodies.

The office said the allegations must be investigated as several inmates, including chronic patients and people with conditions such as cancer, told inspectors they had not been evaluated or treated, the office said. Inspectors also found no way for inmates to contact the Ombudsman’s Office or file complaints.

The office reminded prison authorities that any persecution or retaliation against inmates interviewed by oversight and judicial bodies is prohibited. It said the situations it found will be investigated and analyzed. Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar criticized the inspection on Facebook, saying the delegation arrived without prior coordination with the Ministry of Justice and Peace. He asked whether the visit amounted to obsessive persecution and a political show.

Acting Justice Minister Nils Ching said it was the first time the attorney general had visited the prison system. He called the human rights allegations irresponsible, arguing that the people held at CACCO are among the most dangerous in Costa Rica. Penitentiary Police Director Pablo Bertozzi Calvo acknowledged that the law allows the institutions involved to inspect prisons.

He said, however, that the surprise visit was not properly coordinated and disrupted daily operations, and he asked the institutions to follow the coordination process used in the past. Lucrecia Tejada Cordoncillo, director general of Social Adaptation, said Cruickshank threatened, intimidated and shouted at her in front of inmates. Tejada also said the attorney general had to be repeatedly reminded to stay within the established security perimeter.

CACCO opened in October and has five modules, the first of which is nearly full. The dispute is the latest in a series of confrontations between the executive branch and the judicial and oversight institutions that monitor it, coming as prosecutors also warn that budget cuts will slow complex criminal investigations.

World.title: The Local Pharmacy and the Surprises of Costa Rica Life
World.content:
Your local neighborhood pharmacy is a one-stop-for-all-your-health-needs institution. Last year, a law passed requiring a doctor’s prescription for many types of antibiotics and other stronger drugs. Before that, you could self-medicate with your choice of uppers, downers, painkillers and plain old antibiotics if you knew which pharmacy to frequent.

I knew a guy who walked into one with the word ‘clonazepam’ written on a piece of paper and told the person at the counter that he was a truck driver in the states, and this was prescribed it for his insomnia, and wouldn’t you know it, he was suffering from the same sleep issue here and could anyone help? They could. A few minutes after a brief consultation with the pharmacist, he walked out with a bottle of high potency valium.

My first experience with a pharmacy took place in a back room. I knew I wasn’t in the US anymore when the pharmacist led me behind the counter, closed the door, instructed me to drop my trousers, and injected me in the thigh with a shot of epinephrine ( better known as adrenaline).

The reason for the shot was that I had been hit with asthma so severe that every breath sounded like I had just tried to run to the top of Chirripo. I’d spent a sleepless Saturday night seated in a rocking chair as I was unable to breathe lying down. It was rainy season and I was living in a half finished cabina that provided little protection from the elements. A tropical front had arrived, the rain came down in torrents, wind howled off the nearby Fila Tinamastes, and I was no match for the elements.

Sunday morning I was driven to a pharmacy half an hour away. Every shallow wheezing breath felt like it could be the last. The jab of the pharmacist’s needle brought instant relief. I had received this same injection as a teen, for the same reason. There it was done by a doctor, and I still remembered the doctor’s instruction to remain seated for several minutes after the injection as there is risk of a sudden drop in blood pressure.

The pharmacist here gave me no such instruction. He was not a medical doctor after all, just a guy who could measure out the proper dosage and give an injection. I stayed put in the back room, puzzling the pharmacist. Many pharmacies now have a doctor on duty during business hours, in order to write the antibiotic or clonazepam prescription that is no longer available over the counter. Still, I am always surprised by what is available without a doctor.

A while back I pinched a nerve in my upper back and the pain ran from my neck down to the fingers on my left hand. I was about to leave for a visit stateside and needed relief. My stepson is an RN in the local hospital and he gave me a list for purchase from the pharmacy. I bought a syringe and several ampules of painkiller. My stepson injected me at home. No doctor or prescription necessary.

There remain smaller mom and pop pharmacies in Costa Rica that don’t have a doctor on duty but will prescribe medication based on your symptoms. They are worth finding if you trust your self-diagnoses and don’t feel the need for a middleman with MD after the last name. And those back rooms? They are still open if an injection is necessary.

World.title: Costa Rica Falls 2-0 to Ecuador in Quito as the Bryan Ruiz Era Begins
World.content:
Costa Rica opened the Bryan Ruiz era with a 2-0 loss to Ecuador on Friday night in Quito. The team finished the friendly with 10 men and lost a defender to a knee injury, four days before it faces Argentina. Jordy Caicedo put Ecuador ahead in the first half. Moisés Caicedo, the Chelsea midfielder and Ecuador captain, sealed it from the penalty spot late in the second half at Estadio Olímpico Atahualpa, which sits about 2,850 meters (9,350 feet) above sea level.

The result gave Argentine coach Marcelo Gallardo his first win in charge of Ecuador. It was Ruiz’s first match as Costa Rica’s permanent head coach. The former national team captain won both of his games as interim coach, against Nicaragua and Haiti in the Concacaf Nations League, before the Costa Rican Football Federation gave him the job.

Costa Rica set the early tempo. The visitors pressed high and won the ball back quickly in the opening minutes. Striker Manfred Ugalde, back with the squad after serving a suspension, forced a save from Ecuador goalkeeper Hernán Galíndez around the ninth minute. Ecuador struck midway through the half. Jordy Caicedo, who plays for Argentine club Huracán, ran onto a long ball from Piero Hincapié. He went around goalkeeper Patrick Sequeira and finished with his left foot for his fifth international goal.

Costa Rica came closest to an equalizer early in the second half. Andrey Soto shot after a pass from Carlos Mora, and Ecuador defender Jackson Porozo cleared the ball off the line. Ruiz made four changes shortly before the hour mark. Alexis Gamboa, Celso Borges, Josimar Méndez and Kenyel Michel came on for Francisco Calvo, Roan Wilson, Soto and Josimar Alcócer. The changes quickly turned costly.

Gamboa went down after a collision with Ecuador’s John Yeboah a few minutes after coming on and was carried off on a stretcher. The federation said he has a left knee injury and will return to Costa Rica on Saturday for further tests, which rules him out against Argentina. Diego Mesén replaced Gamboa around the 65th minute in his first appearance for the national team. He was sent off a few minutes later for a foul on Jordy Caicedo.

Playing a man down at altitude, Costa Rica could not hold on. Ecuador was awarded a penalty for a foul on Yeboah in the box, and Moisés Caicedo converted with less than 10 minutes left. Ruiz said after the match that he left Quito satisfied with what he saw. He said many of the things the coaching staff asked for were carried out and the team showed personality, and he called the result secondary to what the squad learned. He also acknowledged that the game became an uphill battle and said the team’s style of play still needs fine-tuning.

Gallardo said Ecuador grew into the match after an uncomfortable start and called it a constructive performance. He added that the win was a good way to reconnect with the home crowd. The loss extended Costa Rica’s winless run against Ecuador, which dates back to 1992. Ecuador has now won six straight meetings, including a 3-0 win at the 2006 World Cup in Germany and a 3-1 friendly win in Chester, Pennsylvania, in June 2023.

Costa Rica plays Argentina, the 2026 World Cup runner-up, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes in Córdoba. It is the team’s last match of the year. The federation tried to call up Kendall Waston as cover, but Saprissa said the veteran defender is still recovering from an injury and will not travel.

For a team rebuilding after missing this year’s World Cup, the night in Quito showed what Ruiz has to work with. There were early signs of the aggressive approach he wants, but also how quickly a thin squad can come apart. Tuesday’s game against the world’s runner-up will show how much of that can be fixed in four days.
