World.title: Which company is the best employer in Jamaica?
World.content:
JACKSON… chairman of the Award Selection Committee

Ten of Jamaica’s most worker-centric companies have been nominated for the inaugural Gordon “Butch” Stewart Business Leader Award.

The programme, which is being staged under the theme ‘Business Leader: Employer of Choice’, will highlight the success that many of the country’s forward-looking boardrooms have had in introducing global best practices culture to their workforce.

The Jamaica Observer Media Group, which promotes the award project will, within the next few days, begin publishing stories on the firms that made the final list of 10 nominees. These institutions were trimmed down from an initial group of 60, then 40 which were further culled to 25. From this list, the final 10 nominees ultimately floated to the top

— separated in part by the compelling responses they submitted to an exhaustive and multifaceted questionnaire that, in its totality, teased out the most telling aspects of their industrial relations ethos and practices.

“All the companies that participated in the survey dedicated valuable executive time to provide granular details of their industrial relations practices,” said Moses Jackson, chairman of the Award Selection Committee.

“This was an unusually competitive group that all deserve to be nominated and to have their stories shared with Jamaica,” Jackson noted. “Even though they didn’t make it to the nomination stage, they contributed to the invaluable insight that the committee gained into the global best practices trend that Jamaica must continue to embrace so as not to fall behind. But the 10 nominees in particular are at the forefront of a positive transformation now underway at our workplaces.”

These nominees represent a wide range of industries — though not the country’s full breadth. From BPOs to financial services, manufacturing, utilities and tourism, the group of 10, both individually and collectively, present a leading-edge profile of modern management practices within corporate Jamaica.

But there are notable absences — not the least of which is the zero representation of private security services, one of the largest employers of labour in the country.

According to Jackson, that’s in part because while employers in this sector tend to lean disproportionately into contract employment, the award programme has a strong bias towards companies that offer permanent, full-time engagement. The job security and clear pathway to upward mobility that are fundamental features of this latter business model is a central value of the award programme.

To qualify for nomination, companies must have a minimum permanent staff count of 300, Jackson added.

“The Business Leader Award is by design a big business programme,” he explains. “We are interested in critical mass and the ability of employees to climb up a well-defined corporate ladder and organisations that can offer meaningful careers at scale.”

The Observer will chronicle the industrial relations successes of the 10 nominees in both its printed and electronic platforms.

However, readers will have to wait until Sunday, December 13 to learn which company in Jamaica is deemed the Employer of Choice — at least in large measure by the evaluation of the six independent individuals who make up the Award Selection Committee.

Five of the six committee members are themselves past nominees for the award. They are:

Ambassador Audrey Marks, founder and principal of Paymaster Ja;

Audrey Hinchcliffe, founder, principal and chair of Manpower and Maintenance Services Ltd;

Gassan Azan, founder, principal and chairman of MegaMart and Bashco Ltd;

Charles Ross, principal and chairman of Sterling Asset Management Ltd; and

Fred Smith, principal and chairman of Tropical Tours Ltd.

Ian Neita, former managing director of Yellow (Pages) Ltd, stands as the sole committee member who was never nominated for the award.

Importantly, employee voices will also be heard in the voting process; they will be polled to render their own verdict of the quality of the work environment that their bosses provide for them.

The award presentation and dinner will take place at AC Hotel Kingston on Lady Musgrave Road. In this regal setting the Gordon “Butch” Business Leader for 2026 will be announced as one of the final acts of an event that will begin with cocktail reception at 4:30 pm followed at 6:00 pm by the formal presentation and dinner.

The Business Leader Award is celebrating its 30th year to the very month, since its first staging in December 1996. It was branded then and up until days ago as the Jamaica Observer Business Leader Award. Earlier this month the Stewarts — family members of Sandals/ATL/Observer late patriarch Gordon “Butch” Stewart — consented to have the award renamed as a permanent tribute to their father. The rebranding was announced at a press conference at the Jamaica Observer headquarters in St Andrew.

Butch Stewart, as he was affectionately called, was known to have revered the award programme, viewing it as a vital and effective platform for the encouragement of business growth in Jamaica, and the direct promotion of local entrepreneurs.

This is the first time that the award is recognising businesses specifically for the quality of the work environment they provide staff — a particular corporate feature for which Butch Stewart was famous within the enterprises he founded and chaired. In fact, this point was emphasised by his son Brian Jardim who spoke at the press conference to announce the rebranding.

Jardim recalled his father’s obsession with staff welfare, and noted the convergence of this philosophy with the theme of the award that bears his name: Gordon “Butch” Stewart Business Leader: Employer of Choice.

World.title: Bad roads hurting south coast tourism
World.content:
HENZELL...we have had to refund many guests based on the fact that our website is saying it takes between two to two and a half hours from Montego Bay and, in some cases, now it is taking three to three and a half hours Photo: Kasey Williams

TREASURE BEACH, St Elizabeth — Tourism stakeholders in Treasure Beach on Jamaica’s south coast are demanding urgent repairs to the main road linking the area to Montego Bay via eastern Hanover and southern St James, warning that its deplorable condition is already driving a spate of booking cancellations ahead of the crucial winter tourist season, which runs from mid-December to April.

The section of the main road badly scarred with potholes stretches from the Westmoreland/Hanover border through Ramble to Anchovy in St James.

Well-known hoteliers Jason Henzell and David Folb, as well as Transport Manager Darin James last Wednesday expressed frustration over the deplorable road.

Henzell, who operates highly acclaimed Jakes Hotel and Jack Sprat with 125 staff in Treasure Beach, said the situation is dire.

“We have had to refund many guests based on the fact that our website is saying it takes between two to two and a half hours from Montego Bay and, in some cases now, it is taking three to three and a half hours,” Henzell told the Jamaica Observer.

“It has been very costly to us. Guests who have written about the conditions of the road also deter potential guests from coming, so it has been an extremely costly situation for not only Jakes, but all of the operators along the south coast,” added Henzell.

Folb, owner of the popular high-value Lashings Boutique Hotel and Villas and Lashings Beach Club in Treasure Beach with 10 full-time staff and more than 20 linked leased businesses, shared a similar sentiment.

“The [bad] roads are causing a monumental problem. People don’t want to come. I literally spoke to a friend of mine today who is thinking about coming here in a group of six people for Christmas and they said oh, we have spoken to such and such, ‘if the roads are going to be that bad then we will go to Barbados’,” Folb told the Sunday Observer.

“It is affecting our business drastically. There are actually people who are cancelling, because of the roads… There was a famous cricketer a few weeks ago who had to leave very early because he didn’t want to chance going back on those roads on the day of his flight,” added Folb.

James, the transportation manager at Jakes hotel and Lashings Boutique Hotel, suggested that the road be patched until a permanent fix can be done.

“That road, especially out from Ramble to Montpelier, is a total disgrace. The road has been like that for almost three years. Even if they have plans to do a major reconstruction of the road, just patch the areas until then. These potholes are so wide and deep. I have the biggest vehicle in our fleet and I don’t want to drive through that bad road,” he said.

He said utilising Norman Manley International Airport in Kingston is not a viable option as that is more costly.

“It is more expensive to travel from Kingston to Treasure Beach than from Montego Bay, even though it might be quicker, but it is twice the distance in mileage, so you are burning more gas and paying tolls. With my class three vehicle, to and from Kingston with four tolls, is over $12,000,” said James.

The effect the bad road is having on the tourism industry was also highlighted by reports that last week visitors travelling to Negril from Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay had to endure a six-hour bus ride.

Last week, Opposition Member of Parliament for St James Southern Nekeisha Burchell, in whose constituency the Anchovy main road is located, posted on her Instagram account that drain cleaning and preparation for asphalt laying commenced there on Tuesday.

“After more than a year of representations work has finally begun on Anchovy main road. I’m grateful to the [National Works Agency] and contractors for getting started, and to the residents who stopped to share their appreciation. I understand the frustration with the traffic; I use this road too. Crews will continue clearing drains and preparing the road for asphalt over the coming weeks, so please take care around them. I’ll keep following up and sharing updates,” the post read.

On Thursday the National Works Agency said temporary repairs are being done to the corridors pending a major project to repair critical sections of the main roads now in the procurement phase.

Henzell said he is eagerly awaiting further updates regarding the completion date for the now under-construction Long Hill bypass, which is to be connected to the Montego Bay Perimeter Road.

“I have been trying to get onto people about the Montego Bay bypass, which apparently is going to open shortly, I don’t know if the bypass includes the exit to the south coast road,” he said.

“I am pleased that there was a meeting at Pier One and there seems to be some movement and solutions happening for Negril, but as it pertains to the south coast now, I really am interested when the ramp to the Long Hill bypass will be activated,” added Henzell.

The perimeter road is slated for completion in December. The perimeter road is complemented by the Long Hill Bypass, a 10.5-kilometre corridor upgraded from its original two lanes to four lanes with Jersey barriers. The Long Hill Bypass is slated for completion in 2027.

World.title: Crowning controversy
World.content:
Shenseea

In 2021, when Shenseea’s Trending Gyal freestyle sent social media into a frenzy and prompted many listeners to hail her as the next queen of dancehall, the entertainer was flattered by the recognition but made it clear that wearing the crown was not particularly high on her list of priorities.

At the time, the Sheng Yeng leader insisted that her focus was simply on making music, enjoying the creative process, and allowing her work to speak for itself rather than becoming consumed by the expectations that came with a coveted title.

“I’m honoured that they [the fans] see me as such [the next dancehall queen], but it wasn’t a title I’ve always wanted. I want to do music and enjoy it for the fun, not because it is expected of me to do so,” she told local media back then.

Five years later, however, the Grammy-nominated entertainer appears to have had a change of heart.

In a recent interview that has been gaining considerable traction across social media, Shenseea expressed confidence that her accomplishments have now earned her the right to claim the dancehall crown.

Pointing to current statistics as the basis for her position, the

Alpha artiste suggested that she has done enough to warrant recognition as the genre’s leading woman.

Her declaration has once again stirred the long-running conversation about dancehall’s royalty, particularly as veteran entertainer Spice remains widely regarded as Jamaica’s reigning queen of dancehall.

But while Shenseea’s international profile and commercial achievements have undoubtedly strengthened her standing in the global music industry, whether those accomplishments are enough to displace an artiste whose legacy has been built over decades is another matter.

For entertainment publicist and digital media consultant Toni-Ann Kelly, of Black Butterfly Media, Shenseea has not yet earned the crown. While acknowledging the entertainer’s commercial achievements and impressive streaming numbers, Kelly questioned whether such statistics were enough to justify her claiming the throne.

“Where she loses me is how we get from streaming and YouTube and figures like that to her being the queen of dancehall,” Kelly argued. “Beenie Man is a good example of why I say that. Sean Paul’s international reach deserves every bit of respect, and anybody can make a case for Vybz Kartel’s influence, but I still give Beenie Man the title of king because, to me, he lives and breathes dancehall… You feel how much he enjoys the music, how well he knows his audience and how much he cares about what happens to the culture. I get that same sense of commitment from Bounty Killer and Sean Paul. I hold a queen to that same standard.”

Drawing comparisons with some of the genre’s most recognisable female figures, Kelly argued that international reach must be complemented by an unmistakable musical identity and a genuine connection with the culture.

“Lady Saw was hard to miss and harder to mistake. So is Spice. With Shenseea, I find the opposite happens too often. Everybody knows her name, yet on too many records her personality gets lost in the mix,” she said.

For Kelly, being a contender for the crown requires the kind of individuality that allows audiences to immediately recognise an artiste through her delivery, writing, and stage presence.

“For somebody claiming to be the woman who captivates this space, she’s still a little too easy to miss in it,” she continued. “All the kings and queens of dancehall were captivating in every era and there was none that was or is missed.”

Entertainment publicist, media practitioner, and director of communications at Prism Marketing Consultants Raymond “Shadow” Small offers a somewhat different perspective.

He told the Jamaica Observer that he believes Shenseea has established herself as a legitimate contender, even if that does not automatically make her the rightful successor to Spice.

Small acknowledged her impressive catalogue, international collaborations, Grammy recognition, performances on major stages, and ability to reach audiences beyond traditional dancehall markets. However, he cautioned against confusing international popularity with cultural leadership.

“Being internationally successful does not automatically mean that an artiste has inherited the crown. Spice’s position was established through years of consistency, hit records, commanding performances, cultural influence and her contribution to creating opportunities and visibility for female dancehall artistes,” he said. “Shenseea has a strong argument based on her current commercial success, but Spice has an established legacy that cannot simply be displaced by streaming statistics.”

Still, Small believes the genre has enough room for both women to establish their own legacies without one having to surrender her position for the other to thrive.

“Shenseea should not have to wait for Spice to become inactive before establishing her own legacy. Both women can dominate different periods and represent different dimensions of the genre without one having to diminish the other,” he said.

World.title: ‘Fix our roads properly’
World.content:
Motorists manoeuvring the Shettlewood to Mackfield main road in the vicinity of Ramble in Hanover on Friday. Garfield Robinson

ANCHOVY, St James — Residents and business operators along the Anchovy to Shettlewood and Mackfield main roads spanning southern St James and eastern Hanover are cautiously optimistic about the longevity of road repairs now being done a few weeks ahead of the winter tourist season.

Last Thursday, the National Works Agency said temporary repairs are being done to the corridors pending a major project to restore critical sections of the main roads now in the procurement phase.

On Friday, the Jamaica Observer saw marl being utilised on sections of the thoroughfare at Chester Castle in Hanover. A few kilometres east in Anchovy, St James, residents and business operators there said they are eagerly awaiting the completion of the Long Hill bypass, but are also hoping for a permanent fix to their main road amid ongoing works there.

“When the bypass is done and I am going into Montego Bay I won’t be going down Long Hill. I will be using the bypass 24/7. You can a go down Long Hill and there is a sudden breakaway and you gone a gully and dead. I just want them to finish the work on the bypass. It would be the best thing for everybody, but for now we need a good fix to the main road, it is what we have now to use everyday,” said a welder in Anchovy who gave his name only as Massop.

The Long Hill and Anchovy to Savanna-La-Mar main road is one of the main corridors connecting the island’s north and south.

“This road is very important. There are people who use this road to get to the airport and even work in Montego Bay coming from as far as Mandeville. They are coasters from Mandeville to Montego Bay,” he added.

He pointed to the daily struggle commuters face with delays.

“Every morning there is traffic from the south-west heading into MoBay because of the road condition. A contractor is doing some scraping on the bad part of the road and I hope that they will properly fix the road. The little scraping makes a big difference with the traffic flow. The bad road goes all the way towards Savanna-La-Mar at Mackfield,” Massop told the Sunday Observer.

“Just recently people blocked the road at Ramble on the Hanover side. The bad roads go through Hanover at Chester Castle, Bethel Town, Montpelier, all of these roads are no good…The little scraping, I hope they will fix the roads properly with quality work,” he added.

He recalled the distress one motorist experienced in Ramble when his vehicle was stuck in a pothole.

“You see right at Burn Ground [Ramble], I remember the road was being fixed one morning with patching and in the afternoon rain came and washed out everything and ever since that has been a recurring problem in Burn Ground. The road patching was poor and rain just washed it out after. Hurricane Melissa came and made it worse,” Massop said.

Category 5 Melissa unleashed extensive damage to roads, buildings, infrastructure and lives on October 28, 2025.

“I saw a car on the Burn Ground road go into a pothole and people had to use another vehicle to pull it out,” he added.

Residents from Mount Carey are also hoping that the road works will last.

“From Montpeiler to Mount Carey is a good road, but the rest of the road is bad, so now that they are doing work on it, please do it properly. When the road work doesn’t last we as taxpayers lose,” said Mount Carey resident Denise.

Anchovy vendor Tadge Jones is also calling for quality work to be done.

“We want the work to be done quickly, because the traffic is terrible, but, at the same time, we want it to be done properly,” he said.

Granville Wright, a resident of Shettlewood in Hanover, complained that the bad roads are costly to motorists.

“Is the first time from the storm blow some work is being done. You see the problem is, when they are to put three inches of asphalt they put one and a half and then we the motorist suffer,” he claimed.

“Me nuh stop buy front-end parts and all sorts of rubbers in order to get my car to drive good,” he added.

World.title: MORE THAN A GAME
World.content:
Reggae Girlz team manager Crystal Walters.

For Crystal Walters, the journey from the football field to the administrative corridors of the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) has been defined by unexpected opportunities, quiet determination, self-respect, and an unwavering belief in women’s football.

It is a journey that, in some ways, mirrors the evolution of the women’s game in Jamaica — significant breakthroughs born out of perseverance and a continuing fight for recognition.

Today, as Reggae Girlz team manager and an emerging figure in safeguarding within Jamaican football, Walters occupies a position of considerable responsibility. But hers is more than a story of professional advancement. It is about a young woman, who has experienced the sport from almost every perspective and is determined to ensure others benefit from the opportunities afforded to her.

“I never imagined being actively involved administratively at the senior level, but there is always a saying that the youths just need an opportunity, and I got that and made use of the opportunity,” Walters told the Sunday Observer.

Like many aspiring Jamaican footballers, she developed her talents within the school system, moving from Jonathan Grant High to St Jago High, where she shared the field with a young Khadija “Bunny” Shaw.

Walters later represented Harbour View and The University of the West Indies in the Women’s Premier League before moving to Shortwood Teachers’ College, where her playing career blossomed.

There, she collected several accolades, including the Principal’s Award, became the institution’s first female footballer to score 10 or more goals in a season, and helped Shortwood capture the intercollegiate title in her first year.

It was also at Shortwood that she received her first national call-up, although an opportunity away from the field would ultimately reshape her future.

While still a player, Walters began assisting with administrative duties, including helping members of the national programme complete health insurance documentation. The late Jean Nelson recognised her potential and increasingly entrusted her with assignments involving the Reggae Girlz.

“She would oftentimes call me in to assist her with paperwork or even drive to Shortwood to drop off documentation for the Reggae Girlz for me to complete,” Walters recalled.

With Nelson’s assistance, another opportunity emerged, setting Walters on a path that would lead to the JFF.

She joined the federation as an intern during the historic 2019 Women’s World Cup qualification campaign, working her way through the programme as Jamaica prepared for its first appearance at the global showpiece.

Following that campaign, she continued working within the federation, assisting with marketing responsibilities, while developing the administrative skills that would eventually see her entrusted with managing the senior women’s national team.

Her progression through the various levels of Jamaican women’s football has been remarkable, but Walters admits it has been anything but straightforward.

“It has not been easy. It has been a rough journey in terms of just looking back on all that I have experienced in terms of pushback and challenges,” she acknowledged.

“It was important for me to stand firm as a woman and maintain my discipline. If it wasn’t for passion and discipline, I probably would have walked away already.”

Those experiences have strengthened her conviction that women deserve greater opportunities to contribute to football beyond their playing careers, while reinforcing the importance of maintaining her values.

“It’s never easy as a female, but it’s the respect that you put out there for yourself, you will get it back in return.”

For Walters, increasing female representation in football administration is essential to the sport’s development.

“I definitely think we need more women administrators,” she said, pointing to the increasing emphasis being placed on female involvement in women’s football programmes by international governing bodies.

“Beyond a few women that are behind the scenes, you don’t really have much involvement.”

She is particularly interested in creating pathways for former players to transition into administration, recognising that their experience and understanding of the game can be invaluable.

Plans are already being explored for workshops and consultations to strengthen women’s participation in the sport’s administrative structures.

“I am looking forward to mentoring a few women, whether past players who want to be a part of sport administration, especially football,” she shared.

“It is important for me after this campaign to see how best I can mentor, to see how I can share that wealth of knowledge to strengthen what we currently have.”

Walters is equally conscious of the responsibility attached to representing one of Jamaica’s most recognisable sporting brands.

“I represent a big brand — the Reggae Girlz, a pool of players that are elevated, educated, and are doing so much for themselves and their country,” she said.

“The onus is on me as the team manager to elevate myself. No one can do that for me except me.”

That commitment to personal development extends beyond her immediate responsibilities with the national team.

While helping Jamaica secure another World Cup appearance in 2027 remains her priority, Walters is also seeking to make a lasting contribution through safeguarding.

Having completed specialised training in Zurich, Switzerland, she has assumed a lead safeguarding role within the JFF, helping to promote safer and more respectful environments throughout the sport.

“Taking on the FIFA safeguarding lead for the JFF, it means helping to create a safer environment for our youth, administrators, everyone involved in the sport,” she explained. “How do we make it a safe space, a comfortable space for everyone to experience the love, camaraderie, but in a safe and respectful way?”

Her work addresses concerns ranging from bullying and intimidation to sexual misconduct and other threats to athlete welfare.

Walters has already led two internal safeguarding sessions involving JFF staff and conducted engagements with the St Catherine Football Association and club administrators. She has also engaged with the national Under-17 programme.

A formal safeguarding policy is being developed with FIFA’s support, subject to JFF approval.

For Walters, whose own career was transformed when someone recognised her potential and extended an opportunity, the ambition is now to help create a better environment for those following in her footsteps.

And perhaps that will ultimately prove to be one of her most meaningful contributions to Jamaican football; not simply helping the Reggae Girlz reach another World Cup, but ensuring that the next generation of women has a clearer, more welcoming and safer pathway to positions of influence.

World.title: Chuck admits JLP has communication problem
World.content:
Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Delroy Chuck delivers the keynote address at the Commissioning Ceremony for Justices of the Peace for St Catherine at Lighthouse Assembly in Spanish Town, St Catherine, on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Photo: JIS

The governing Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) enters its 83rd annual conference on Sunday against the backdrop of concern that it has a communication problem.

Last Thursday, that anxiety was highlighted in a blunt, public admission by one of its senior members, Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Delroy Chuck in an address at the commissioning service for justices of the peace (JPs) at Lighthouse Assembly at Garbally Drive in Spanish Town, St Catherine.

Chuck spoke to the issue against the backdrop of members of the party having been forced in recent weeks to focus attention on deflecting and correcting what they deem to be lies and misinformation circulating in the public space, particularly on social media, about the Government.

A war of words has erupted between senior members of the Government and deejay Beenie Man following controversial remarks he made in the British media about how Hurricane Melissa relief money has been handled. Several other entertainers have since taken sides with Beenie Man.

“The challenge the Government has is one of communication; how do you explain really complex matters to the people? It’s one thing to say, ‘Spend di money, man’ but the consequences [for doing so] are great,” Chuck argued. “How do we say to them, we have to spend within our means.”

He told the JPs that any family that spends more than it earns knows the consequences of doing so.

“Before you know it, the bank going to foreclose on everything; [the furniture company] come tek weh yuh furniture, the mortgage company come and tek weh yuh house. That’s the consequence for a family that spends more than what it earns, but it is even worse for the country because we could be downgraded, inflation could go out of sight, the dollar could go out of sight. You would see empty shelves before you know it because we wouldn’t have money to buy anything,” said Chuck.

According to the Chuck, “Governments have done it in the past, and we have seen the consequence.” He reiterated that “the real challenge for the Government is to ensure that we can explain to the people why we have to take tough decisions in order to move forward and to survive”.

Jamaica Observer sources say Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, the leader of the JLP, is expected to dedicate a portion of his speech at today’s annual conference in Montego Bay, St James, to do just that.

Chuck acknowledged that questions have been raised about the pace of recovery following Hurricane Melissa, which hit sections of the island in October 2025, and how the Administration has spent relief money. The Government has also been accused of reacting poorly to criticism. But Chuck hit back at people whose purpose, he said, is to tear the Government down.

“There are people on social media who’re trying to increase the misery index of the country. They misinform, they lie…[they say] the Government get money and tief it, all di ministers dem put di money inna dem pocket. Yuh see it on social media, enuh,” said an exasperated Chuck.

He argued that few countries have had to deal with two “greatest crises” like Jamaica has faced with the COVID-19 pandemic and Hurricane Melissa. Regarding the pandemic, Chuck noted that the country “lost a huge amount of revenue and commercial activity”.

“Last year Melissa damaged a third of the island, the damage to the revenue and the economy is still being assessed,” he stated.

“We received donations of about US$1.4 million, and people say, ‘Weh di money deh?’ ” he said, referencing the now all-out war between the Government and Beenie Man, who has since penned a recording titled Weh Di Money Deh.

On Friday, Beenie Man, a known supporter of the Opposition People’s National Party, used colourful language to describe Local Government Minister Desmond McKenzie. This, after McKenzie, while addressing the annual JLP West Kingston Constituency Conference on Thursday night took a jab at the entertainer declaring, “Dat deh record nah sell at all, nobody nah buy it.”

Suggesting that Beenie Man was seeking relevance, McKenzie said, “Yuh have a certain deejay, fi di last 20 years him cyaan mek a number one hit song. And all of a sudden, him cyaan mek it locally cause him nah say nutten. [So] him lef di shores of Jamaica an gone out deh go talk about ‘weh di money deh…Government hold on pon di money”.

Chuck sought to explain why much of the money was not utilised to provide relief, stating that, “We have to account for how the US$1.4 million was spent.” He pointed out that nearly $70 billion has been spent by the Government to fix schools, hospitals, and roads damaged by the hurricane. He also pointed to the nearly $20 billion being spent on the Restoration of Owner or Occupant Family Shelters (ROOFS) Programme, noting that this was separate from the more than US$6.5 billion the Government expects to spend through the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) to rebuild the country.

“That US$6.5 billion don’t start spend yet, enuh, but people are asking, ‘Weh di money?” said Chuck.

He lamented that the Government has failed to communicate its priorities, pointing out that Jamaicans living in the western end of the island, where the hurricane caused most damage, want their roofs fixed as a matter of urgency, while elsewhere, pothole-riddled roads are the greatest priority.

“There are others who say, ‘Spend di money, man, there’s misery.’ So how yuh spend di money?” Chuck asked. He posited that, “You can run wid it, you can borrow, or you can print money,” but warned that each choice has consequences.

“If you run wid it or yuh borrow or yuh print money…yuh feel good [in the moment]. Everybody say di Government great. Yuh doing a fantastic job for about a year or two and then after two years, dawg nyam wi supper. Inflation could be 20 or 50 per cent or [like in] the 1990s, 100 per cent. The dollar would move from $150 or $160 to $500. Can you imagine the consequence?”

He defended the Government for being fiscally prudent, arguing that, “If we were ever fiscally irresponsible the consequences are dire.” Chuck said if the Government started running huge budget deficits, “the rating agencies could downgrade us, and if they downgrade us then we would have to borrow money, not at single digit [interest] like we’re doing, but at double digit — 15 and 20 per cent. It would hurt us; the debt would climb from 67 [per cent of gross domestic product], where it is now, back up to 120 per cent”.

The senior minister said the Government has been trying its best to be fiscally prudent while asking Jamaicans to “bear as much as possible the inconvenience, the discomfort”.

World.title: Preserving The Jamaican Interior Vernacular
World.content:
One of Jamaica’s luxurious properties, Round Hill Hotel and Villas. (Round Hill Hotel and Villas)

We are all affected by our physical environment whether they make us feel safe, vulnerable, inspired or at peace, and sometimes even nostalgic. One of the things that Jamaicans are proud of is our culture, our sense of belonging to something that cannot be replicated or taken from us. Although Jamaicans are spread across every corner of the globe, we are united by a common thread, the thing that makes us one of the most beloved cultures on the planet: Our ‘Jamaican-ness’ is what we’ll call it.

There are a few things that immediately give us a sense of pride and identity. Bob Marley, our pristine beaches, Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, a cold Red Stripe, to name a few.

But how about many of the iconic architectural and design elements we grew up with?

A gingerbread style/or chattel home (which are still very much celebrated and maintained in other islands like Barbados)

A colourful corner shop/coconut jelly stall

Dark mahogany wood furniture

Beaded doorways

Red clay or wooden floors

Tapestry upholstered sofas and Rooms styled with antique heirlooms

These images evoke a sense of nostalgia for many of us. They are all iconic, cultural elements that have slowly faded from our identity as Jamaicans (and yes, some of them are relics of our colonial ties), but nevertheless, we made them our own.

Technological advancements have rendered many things obsolete, but that is a product of our development as a nation, and we are proud of that, but I encourage us to look at some of the ways in which we have traded our Jamaican-ness to blend in with the rest of the world, to keep up with design trends and create more affordable buildings and interiors, and, is there a way to adapt to modern systems and materials without losing our sense of self?

The choice between a solid wood kitchen and one made from engineered wood has become more difficult in recent years, due to an increase in global production of ready to instal medium density fibreboard (MDF) cabinets. Although solid wood cabinets still lead in popularity, MDF has outpaced traditional solid wood in annual growth, securing its position as the fastest-growing material segment in the kitchen cabinet market with a 6.2 per cent compound annual growth rate. And while there is a strong argument for the cost benefit and overall efficiency of prefabricated millwork, how are we incorporating the ‘Land of wood and water’ into the spaces we design if we continue to substitute the elements that add texture for materials that merely mimic texture?

I have been to many estate sales, mostly because I love looking at antiques, and one thing I have noticed, is that the whatnot and the breakfront are always the last to leave the lot. Again, these pieces originated in Europe and were adopted by Jamaica, but they were also adapted! Historically, it wasn’t as seamless as it is now to import furniture, so we were forced to fabricate our own. In doing this, we were able to create versions of these pieces that were unique to Jamaica.

Local furniture designers, sculptors and cabinet makers like Burnett Webster, Alvin Mariott and Ralph Turnbull swapped the typical soft woods used in the European versions of these furniture pieces for heavier, stained solid mahogany, cedar and blue mahoe native to Jamaica, carvings of pineapples and banana leaves were incorporated into the designs, and upholstery was often substituted for cane/wicker which were breathable and better suited for the tropics. We used the resources readily available to us to create solid pieces of furniture that could withstand hurricanes, mould, and importantly, time. Solid wood furniture was currency and passed down as heirlooms. Today’s mass-produced furniture could never keep up with the longevity of a Jamaican whatnot.

There was a time when, to live in a Jamaican home was to be surrounded by texture. Caning or wicker were used frequently for rugs and furniture. Many of our material choices were not simply for aesthetics. Beaded doorways and cotton window treatment facilitated airflow throughout the home. Today, we use roller shades and solid doors and wonder why the house is always hot. Now, let us have a moment of silence for louvred windows. A highly functional architectural element that we have replaced with glass casement windows that can offer neither the privacy nor natural airflow that Jalousie windows/ louvres were designed to facilitate. Vernacular architecture, designed for the Jamaican climate like verandas, homes elevated on stone or wooden pillars, pitched roofs and fretwork all served to cool homes naturally. Now we simply buy ceiling fans and airconditioning units and blame El Nino.

Change is good, development is good, globalisation is good and access to affordable material is critical. In 2025 Statin reported Jamaica’s import spending at US$7.5 billion, 85-90 per cent of our furniture and building finishes (outside of paint and cement) is imported. We are at the mercy of shifts in design trends and global innovation standards that aren’t often best suited for our climate or our cultural identity. But this is the world we live in. The questions is, how do we maintain our Jamaican-ness and profit from it?

Three of Jamaica’s most internationally recognised luxury properties are Round Hill Hotel and Villas, GoldenEye and Half Moon. This is not by coincidence. All of these properties utilise many of the architectural and design elements mentioned earlier that form part of our traditional design identity. Ralph Lauren and Chris Blackwell had a choice; they could have renovated their establishments into ultra-modern concrete structures with prefabricated furniture but chose to lean into our Jamaican-ness. Too often, we tend to lean out.

Industry leaders can find ways to incorporate the Jamaican vernacular into our designs by simply adding a few solid wood pieces of furniture, utilising local art, and even repurposing an old breakfront or heirloom instead of dismissing it as not trendy. Incorporating materials like limestone, which was once manufactured in Jamaica with varieties such as Hellshire marble and Serge Island Green Marble, not only adds texture but utilises a material that represents approximately 70 per cent of the island’s surface. I am not advocating for Jamaican homes to become museums, or that we reinstall red clay floor tiles, but I am asking for us to understand the principles behind the vernacular and reinterpret them. That might look like, one beautifully made local piece of furniture, contemporary shelving inspired by a whatnot, and blending traditional Jamaican elements comfortably beside modern finishes.

Hurricane Melissa taught us how vulnerable we are, but it also taught us how loved we are by so many people around the world. We are loved for our Jamaican-ness, and if we channel our creativity and resilience into preserving all the things that make us unique, we may very well see not only the social, but also the economic benefits of that shift. Imagine reviving our local furniture industry to its glory days (when manufacturing peaked at 27.3 per cent of GDP with furniture as a massive mainstay subsector). Imagine a renewed interest among our youth in millwork and carpentry as viable paths to wealth creation. Imagine incorporating our architecture and design into our tourism product by offering tours dedicated to that discipline. Imagine introducing specific building codes, aesthetic zoning or charters that preserve the architecture in specific zones, like those that exist in parts of Europe, Latin America and Morocco.

An article recently described a project on the north coast as a Miami-style development, and it prompted me to ask, when we modernise Jamaica, what are we aspiring to look like? Is it Miami? What does it say about the visual identity we’re assigning to Jamaican development? Design is so much more than maximising square footage and choosing the path of least resistance; it is a representation of our island, our people and our identity. Let us strive to be cultural stewards, and design spaces that celebrate our Jamaican-ness.

— Joelle Smith

CEO/lead designer, If Walls Could Talk

Photos courtesy of Pinterest, David Skinner Antiques, Julia Lynn Photography, If Walls Could Talk, Kelee Fabre Photography, Round Hill Hotel and Villas, and Half Moon Resort

World.title: Security Sunday: Der lange Weg zum Frieden in der Ukraine – mit Claudia Major
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Die diplomatischen Bemühungen um ein Ende des Ukraine-Kriegs laufen auf Hochtouren. Doch wie realistisch ist ein Frieden wirklich, wenn bei den zentralen Fragen völlig gegensätzliche rote Linien aufeinanderprallen?

Darüber spricht Rixa Fürsen im Security Sunday mit der Sicherheitsexpertin Claudia Major vom German Marshall Fund. Die beiden ordnen ein, was die Gespräche in Abu Dhabi gebracht haben: einen großen Gefangenenaustausch, aber keine Einigung zu Feuerpausen für Energieinfrastruktur und Schwarzmeer-Schifffahrt.

Sie fragen, warum Russland derzeit kaum Anreize für Kompromisse sieht und welche Hebel Europa wirklich in der Hand hat.

Und es geht darum, was die Ukraine jetzt braucht, um durch den Winter zu kommen, kurz vor dem Treffen der Koalition der Willigen in Berlin.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

World.title: Estonia to close border with Russia after ‘sabotage attack’ on defense firm
World.content:
He added: "Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered."

Threod's security staff stopped the attack before it could cause significant damage, authorities said. Eight suspects, all residents of neighboring Latvia, were detained. Five have been remanded in custody.

Estonia's Internal Security Service, known as KAPO, said intelligence gathered by its officers showed the attack was commissioned by Russia's GRU military intelligence agency. Threod makes long-range reconnaissance and attack drones.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Sunday: "This is part of Russia’s broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia. We will not be intimidated."

The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs has been contacted for comment on the allegations.

The latest attempt follows an August arson attack on Milrem Robotics, which supplies unmanned ground vehicles to Ukraine. Estonian authorities formally blamed Russian intelligence for that incident in September.

KAPO has warned that Russia is increasingly targeting European defense manufacturers to disrupt military production and deliveries to Ukraine. The investigation into Saturday's attempted attack remains ongoing.

This article has been updated.

World.title: Romania slams ‘unacceptable’ drone strikes on Black Sea ships
World.content:
The Greek-flagged oil tanker Evia Petrol V was struck just after 9 p.m., followed 35 minutes later by a strike on another ship, the Marsol, according to a statement from Romania's defense ministry published on its Facebook page.

“In both cases, the fires were extinguished by the ships' crews. No casualties were reported,” the ministry said.

A third vessel, the Ali Najafov, also reported being struck overnight. It remains unclear who launched the drones.

Romania's military detected aerial targets on radar and sent F-16 fighter jets into the air. Authorities also issued warnings to residents near the coast about possible drone threats.

The attacks came after another commercial ship, the Larissa 1, was reportedly hit by a drone near Romania's coast on Friday.

Romanian Defense Minister Ștefan-Radu Oprea said Sunday he would raise the incidents with allied counterparts in Brussels. “We need the solidarity of our allies,” he said, calling for more surveillance aircraft and equipment to defend against drones.

Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the EU will help finance some Black Sea security costs following recent attacks on commercial shipping.

In October, at least seven commercial vessels were struck by drones in the Black Sea close to NATO and EU members Romania and Bulgaria, leaving more than 20 sailors dead and dozens missing.

World.title: Israel kills Hamas commander in Gaza strike
World.content:
According to the Israeli military, Abu Younis previously served as deputy commander of the brigade and led its Tel al-Sultan Battalion.

The IDF accused him of directing attacks against Israeli civilians and soldiers, as well as working to rebuild Hamas’ military capabilities.

“The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed,” the military said.

Writing on Telegram, Hamas’s Al-Qassam Brigades said Abu Younis had been involved in “numerous high-profile operations” and was “one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the October 7th attack.”

Abu Younis succeeded Nael Abu Obeid, who was killed by Israel on Sept. 15, making him the latest in a series of Hamas commanders targeted by Israeli forces.

The killing comes amid a fragile ceasefire that took effect in Oct. 2025, ending major fighting but failing to stop Israeli strikes in Gaza. U.S. President Donald Trump’s broader peace plan remains stalled over disagreements about Hamas’ disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has insisted that Hamas surrender its weapons before Israeli troops withdraw, rejecting a proposed phased approach that would see both steps take place in parallel.

World.title: Ukraine claims thousands of Russian casualties and a slowing Kremlin advance
World.content:
Russian casualties are rising, according to the commander and to NATO officials.

“In the past few months, Russia has been losing more than 40,000 troops — killed or seriously wounded — every month. The United States in 14 years, in Vietnam, lost 56,000. Here in one month, Russia, dead or seriously wounded, 40,000. And in October, early reporting indicates this number may have climbed to over 50,000,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said this week.

Neither Ukraine nor Russia publishes their exact military losses.

The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies this summer estimated that Russian forces had suffered about 1.4 million casualties, including 400,000 to 450,000 fatalities, from the start of the full-scale invasion through June 2026. It estimated Ukrainian casualties at 525,000 to 625,000, including 125,000 to 150,000 fatalities, over the same period.

Despite rising casualties, the Russian military continues to press forward but is making few lasting gains, Apostol said. He estimated that Ukrainian forces had retaken more than 800 square kilometers from Russian forces this year as the result of two local counteroffensive operations.

Ukraine’s offensives have both a military and a political meaning as they show Kyiv is successfully resisting Russian pressure, Apostol said.

World.title: EU reiterates ‘grave concern’ over Gaza humanitarian crisis as winter approaches
World.content:
Kaja Kallas speaks to the press ahead of an EU summit in Brussels on Oct. 16, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

The bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has called on Israel to allow more humanitarian aid into Gaza as weather worsens living conditions.

Europe’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has called on Israel to protect civilians in Gaza as severe flooding batters the enclave, saying an airstrike on the Nasser Hospital on Thursday was “deeply alarming.”

“The severe flooding and winter conditions that have struck Gaza are further aggravating the living conditions of an already exhausted population, exacerbating unsafe conditions and human suffering,” Kallas said in a statement Saturday.

Kallas also called on Israel to comply with international law and allow the United Nations and humanitarian organizations unimpeded access and to reopen all border crossings into Gaza.

World.title: Italy hits Meta with €805M fine over privacy law violation
World.content:
The investigation, launched in 2025, established that access to a user's camera roll is requested with a single permission for the entire app, which the authority said covers multiple features with different needs. The authorization request was preceded by a generic warning that didn't allow users to understand that they were authorizing picture and video suggestions, the authority said.

"If granted in full, this type of permission allows the app to read the device's entire photo archive, usually permanently, without the user or the authorities being able to verify which information is actually being used,” the statement reads.

The authority also said it "rejected the objection of lack of jurisdiction raised by the company in favor of the Irish authority, because the ePrivacy regulation does not provide for the 'one-stop-shop' mechanism."

Meta has 60 days to get consent separately and specifically for the feature, clearly explain what it does and how it can be disabled, the authority said. It also must be disabled by default, including for those who have already authorized it.

Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. It has the right to appeal the decision.

World.title: Nearly €20m in cash found buried, hidden in Hungary corruption case
World.content:
The money — more than 5 billion forints, €2.6 million and €1.2 million — was found across locations in Budapest, Pest, Békés and Nógrád counties, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, an anti-corruption body, said in a statement.

“This officially marks the end for the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” Magyar posted on Facebook, originally in Hungarian, in reference to Orbán’s government.

It took 12 Treasury staff eight hours to tally the cash using 5 counting machines, Finance Minister Kármán András said.

The announcement comes after Hungarian authorities detained Aron Orbán, the former prime minister’s brother, as part of an investigation into people smuggling. The former prime minister said on social media that the move, announced by Magyar on Monday, was part of a “political witch-hunt” to get him.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reacted wryly to the latest announcement, referring to the arrest of Orbán’s brother and the cash discovery on X.

“Dear Victor, I’ve always been an admirer of your creativity, but now I must say I’m impressed as never before,” he wrote.

World.title: 19 slow worms mistaken for vipers rescued from water meter chamber
World.content:
Just under two dozen slow worms, initially mistaken for venomous vipers, were found in a water meter chamber in southern Poland.

 

Wildlife rehabilitation centre Leśne Pogotowie received a report that venomous vipers had taken refuge in the underground chamber. However, rescuers found 19 slow worms sheltering from the cold weather instead.

The chamber provided ideal conditions, with its cool, damp environment protecting the worms' winter torpor, and the concrete structure offering protetion from freezing temperatures.

The smooth, vertical walls of the chamber meant the slow worms easily descended down into the space, but had no way of climbing back to the surface.

After being rescued from the chamber, the slow worms could be not be released straight back into nature. Instead, they were taken to the animal rehabilitation shelter.

At this time of year, the reptiles were already in a state of winter torpor. Releasing them in cold conditions would leave them with little time to find a new shelter.

At the centre, the slow worms will be provided with the right conditions to spend the winter. A stable, low temperature allows them to remain in hibernation and reduces the risk of unnecessary waking.

The slow worms will only be returned to the wild in spring, when temperature are high enough.

What is a slow worm?

With their serpentine appearance, slow worms are often mistaken for snakes. In reality, they are actually legless lizards.

They are non-venomous and do not pose a threat to humans. In fact, the creatures are beneficial garden residents, as they feed on snails, earthworms and other small invertebrates.

Poland is home to two species of slow worms, the common slow worm and the eastern slow worm. The two species are very similar, but differ, among other things, in the structure and arrangement of their scales. Many males of the eastern slow worm have characteristic blue spots on their backs.

They can be mainly found in the south eastern region of Poland.

World.title: Hundreds of thousands in Prague protest Czech government's public media funding plans
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Prague on Sunday to defend the independence of public television and radio and oppose the government's plans to change their funding system. The demonstration was organised by the civic organisation Million Moments for Democracy. Its slogan, "Never again 4:36", refers to the time when the government majority pushed through a controversial amendment to the law in the Chamber of Deputies at first reading in mid-October. The vote took place in the early hours of Saturday morning, after the majority cut short the plenary debate, denying more than 60 opposition MPs the opportunity to speak.

 

At Letná, Prague's largest square, an estimated 350,000 to 400,000 people took part in the protest against the government's plans and policies, according to media reports on Sunday afternoon.

Protesters who had come from many parts of the country sharply criticised the government's policies and demanded that the coalition party Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD), led by Tomio Okamura, the speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, withdraw from the government.

While the two public service broadcasters are currently funded by the population through compulsory monthly subscription fees, the government wants to finance them from the state budget in future. The proposal has provoked significant public resistance, as many fear that the government could exert influence over the editorial independence and impartiality of the two broadcasters.

According to publicly available data, this future state subsidy would be much lower than the current licence-fee revenues of public television and radio.

The opposition, the press and a significant part of public opinion also oppose the changes because they fear that state funding of public service media would restrict their freedom.

At the demonstration, student organisations at universities and colleges in the Czech Republic, dozens of Czech theatres, writers, numerous top athletes, churches, healthcare workers and representatives of international journalists' organisations also expressed their support for public television and radio.

Speakers repeatedly stressed at the protest that public service media cannot be the property of politicians, the government or the state, but belong to everyone and must reflect the views of all significant sections of society. They also called for independent and free public media.

In the Czech Republic, every household that owns a television or radio is required to pay a monthly fee of 150 koruna (2,400 forint) for television and 55 koruna (880 forint) for radio. This year, Czech Television's revenue from these fees amounts to 6.73 billion koruna (107.68 billion forint), while Czech Radio receives 2.47 billion koruna (39.52 billion forint).

The Babiš government has announced that it would abolish the household fees and instead fund the two public service broadcasters through the state budget. The Prague demonstration was broadcast live by the public news television channel, the CTK news agency and a few independent media outlets. Radek Vondráček of the strongest governing party, Elégedetlen Polgárok Akciója (ANO), condemned the organisers of the protest and the organisation Million Moments for Democracy in a television debate programme, calling them "an association of professional agitators".

According to police reports, the demonstration proceeded without incident until early evening, and there were no disturbances.

World.title: UK: London's Santa School trains Father Christmas performers for 2026
World.content:
With Christmas approaching, dozens of Father Christmas impersonators swapped their festive grottos for classroom desks in south London on Thursday 12 November, attending a training session designed to make their encounters with children as magical as possible. Dressed in their familiar red suits, the Santas practised saying "Merry Christmas" in sign language, studied the latest toy trends and learned how to respond to unexpected questions from young visitors.

 

Organised by the Ministry of Fun, Santa School is now in its 28th year, preparing performers for appearances in shopping centres, department stores and festive attractions across the UK and beyond. The lessons also cover more sensitive situations, such as children wishing for separated parents to reunite or sick relatives to recover, where kindness and careful listening matter more than promises.

The training also featured the Ministry of Fun's annual State of Santa report, which offers a glimpse into changing Christmas traditions. According to the organisation's research, bookings for Mrs Claus have risen by 32%, while 60% of children still send physical letters to Father Christmas. Mince pies remain the favourite Christmas Eve offering, appearing on 77% of plates, although kombucha has made its debut on 2% of tables. The report also suggests that a typical visit to Santa lasts just three minutes and 45 seconds, leaving performers little time to create a memorable experience. For veteran Santas, the challenge is not simply knowing the latest toys, but making every child feel heard and preserving the magic of Christmas.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 15th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Australia and Philippines sign new defence pact amid South China Sea tensions
World.content:
Australia and the Philippines signed a defence agreement on Sunday to make joint patrols, military exercises and disaster relief operations easier to organise, Philippine officials said.

 

Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr and Australian Ambassador Marc Innes-Brown signed the agreement in Manila, with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese attending the ceremony during his visit for regional summits.

The Defence Cooperation Arrangement updates a 1995 agreement. It builds on a separate visiting forces agreement, in force since 2012, which already allows troops from each country to train on the other’s territory.

Teodoro said the new arrangement would simplify the procedures for carrying out joint activities.

“Rather than 100 steps to do a single thing, it will just now take 10,” he told reporters, according to Reuters.

He said closer cooperation between the countries’ naval, air and ground forces would help the Philippines deter threats, including in the South China Sea.

Australia said the agreement covered information sharing, military planning and training, monitoring activity at sea and developing defence infrastructure.

Asked whether the pact was intended to counter China, Albanese said: “This isn’t aimed at any one country. This is about supporting sovereignty of every country.”

He said most Australian trade passed through the South China Sea and stressed the importance of keeping shipping routes open.

Australia also announced additional funding for its Southeast Asia Maritime Partnerships programme. It will provide regional partners with aerial and surface drones, secure communications equipment and training to help detect and respond to threats at sea and cyberattacks. The announcement did not give a funding figure.

Manila expands its defence partnerships

The agreement follows several recent steps by the Philippines to strengthen military ties with its partners.

On 9 November, Japan agreed to supply coastal radar and surveillance drones to the Philippine military under a 4.3 billion yen (€24 million) grant. The equipment is intended to help monitor ships in waters around the country.

In a statement released on 10 November, Australia, Japan, the Philippines and the United States also committed to a joint military coordination centre in the Philippines. They agreed to coordinate defence investments and expand joint exercises.

China’s claims in the South China Sea overlap with those of the Philippines and several other Southeast Asian countries. Beijing has previously criticised Manila’s joint military activities with its partners, saying they increase regional tensions.

An international tribunal ruled in 2016 that China’s claims of historic rights to resources had no legal basis where they exceeded the rights granted by the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Beijing rejects the ruling.

World.title: Megaspeed says alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, left company last year
World.content:
Megaspeed has confirmed that Alice Huang, accused of spying for China and linked to an alleged affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, left the Singapore-based data center company in August 2025.

 

The company, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, is currently conducting an internal probe over the scandal.

US intelligence authorities suspect that Alice Huang had links to China's Ministry of State Security and may have been recruited as an intelligence asset.

Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs has, however, explicitly stated that Alice Huang was not investigated for espionage. In a statement published on November 12, the ministry said that the investigation into Huang concerned suspected offences relating to the purchase and export of servers, and not alleged links to Chinese intelligence.

The ex-Nvidia CEO is alleged to have had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang. On November 8, Jensen Huang admitted having an affair although Ms. Huang is not mentioned by name. Nvidia, the American multinational tech company, has lost nearly $2tn in value since the story became public, although a direct link remains unclear.

According to a statement published by Megaspeed, Alice Huang “left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company”. Ms. Huang had been serving as the controlling shareholder of the company since March 2023.

Singaporean authorities are continuing their investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals, while the company is also under scrutiny in the US over alleged export control violations.

According to media reports, Megaspeed is alleged to have supplied high-end AI chips to China through a network of shell companies and false declarations. The allegations have not been proven, and Singaporean authorities are continuing their investigation.

Nvidia had been working with Alibaba, the Chinese e-commerce giant. Ms. Huang is said to have deepened commercial ties between Nvidia and Alibaba.

Nvidia has defended its commercial operations. In a statement published last week, the company’s board stated it had no reason to believe that US national security or confidential Nvidia trade secrets were compromised.

Huang, a former journalist for Chinese state media, worked at HSBC Hong Kong and CITIC Securities and Hexi Capital where she met her husband Kang Wei. Mr. Wei later introduced Huang to the former Nvidia CEO. Jensen Huang is accused of taking part in further extra-marital affairs.

World.title: Mysterious object in space: Could it be a Soviet probe missing for 40 years?
World.content:
A mysterious object speeding through the Solar System has shown unusual acceleration, raising speculation that it could be a spacecraft from the former Soviet Union that went missing nearly 40 years ago.

 

Known as 1998 KY26, the object is an 11-metre-wide body passing near Earth. Scientists have noticed that its trajectory cannot be fully explained by the gravitational pull of the Sun or Earth.

This unusual behaviour is known as "non-gravitational acceleration", meaning that forces other than gravity are influencing the object's path and speed.

NASA chief Jared Isaacman said on Thursday that the agency is monitoring KY26 but stressed there is no reason for concern. He reassured the public that the object poses no known threat to Earth and that there is no evidence it could collide with our planet.

Has Phobos 1 been found?

A group of researchers has put forward an unusual explanation. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and two colleagues, Adam Hibberd and Adam Crowl, believe KY26 could be Phobos 1, an unmanned Soviet spacecraft launched on 7 July 1988. The probe lost contact with Earth while on its way to Mars.

The researchers built a simplified model of Phobos 1 and compared how it would reflect sunlight as it rotated with observations of KY26. They found that the model closely matched eight separate sets of observations of the object.

KY26 reflects almost 52% of the sunlight that hits it and completes one full rotation every 5.35 minutes. Loeb and his colleagues argue that these characteristics are consistent with their hypothesis that KY26 could be an artificial object.

New study challenges the dark comet theory

One explanation, first proposed in a 2023 study, is that KY26 is a so-called 'dark comet' containing trapped water that turns into gas, creating thrust as the object moves through space. However, astronomers have not detected the cloud of gas or tail normally associated with comets.

A separate scientific study has offered a contrasting explanation. Researchers concluded that 1998 KY26 is most likely a dehydrated asteroid. This would mean that water ice is unlikely to be responsible for its unusual acceleration, as temperatures are too high for sufficient ice to survive over an extended period.

Another possible explanation is solar radiation, which can exert pressure on the object's surface and slightly alter its trajectory.

Other observations also point towards a natural, rocky asteroid rather than an old spacecraft. A study published in the journal Nature Communications in 2025 estimated its diameter at just 11 metres.

Japanese spacecraft could solve the mystery

A Japanese space mission could eventually provide important answers. The Hayabusa2 spacecraft is due to reach 1998 KY26 in July 2031 and study it at close range. It would be the first mission to directly investigate an asteroid of this tiny size.

Images and measurements taken during the encounter could reveal whether the object is indeed a natural rocky body or potentially something artificial.

Until then, Avi Loeb's suggestion remains a fascinating but unproven theory. The Harvard astrophysicist has even joked that Hayabusa2's cameras might discover a label reading "Made in the U.S.S.R." rather than a block of ice.

World.title: "Dans Gaza" wins best documentary at Montreal's Cinemania festival
World.content:
This award shines a light on the work of those who have continued to inform the world from Gaza.

 

The documentary "Dans Gaza", directed by Hélène Lam Trong (source in French), was awarded on Saturday 14 November the prize for best documentary film at the Cinemania Francophone Film Festival in Montreal. Over 72 minutes, the film follows four Agence France-Presse journalists: Mai Yaghi, reporter, Adel Zaanoun, Gaza bureau coordinator, and photojournalists Mahmud Hams and Mohammed Abed.

The documentary portrays the first seven months after the Hamas attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023. With free access to the enclave blocked, international media then relied on Palestinian journalists on the ground to document the conflict.

For more than 200 days, these four reporters worked under bombardment, despite the danger, while facing the same shortages as the rest of the population. At the same time, they had to protect their families, who were directly exposed to the war.

A film made without ever being able to enter Gaza

A journalist for around twenty years, Hélène Lam Trong gradually shifted towards documentary filmmaking. She notably directed "Daech, les enfants fantômes", which earned her the Albert Londres audiovisual prize in 2023.

For "Dans Gaza", she was approached by AFP in January 2024, three months after the start of the war.

Yet the director was never able to travel to the Palestinian enclave. Free access for the international press was banned there by the Israeli army.

The four reporters had agreed to testify, but no one knew whether they would ever manage to leave Gaza. When they were eventually evacuated with their families through Egypt, the director met them in Cairo. The film was built from their accounts and above all from the footage they themselves had shot as part of their work for AFP. Nearly 85% of the documentary is based on their own images.

In Montreal, it was Adel Zaanoun who accepted the prize (source in French) on behalf of the team. He dedicated it to the journalists killed in the war in Gaza, but also to those who continue to work in the field, "without food, without water, without internet, without anything".

Heading for the Oscars?

Made in 2025, "Dans Gaza" is a Franco-Belgian co-production bringing together Factstory Docs, AFP's documentary subsidiary, ARTE France and RTBF.

The film had already been recognised at Sunny Side of the Doc in La Rochelle, before winning in April 2026 both the Grand Prix and the Audience Award at FIGRA, then two prizes in July at the Doc Edge festival in New Zealand, for best international documentary and best editing.

A trajectory that now opens the way for a possible nomination at the 2027 Oscars in the best documentary category.

World.title: Turkey talks green at COP31 while cracking down on activists
World.content:
As the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya co-hosts the COP31 climate conference with Australia, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is using the global spotlight to promote his country’s climate ambitions. But his green image is being challenged at home by environmentalists, who say they face an intensifying government crackdown.

Advertising

The summit opened with a cinematic video highlighting the growing threat of global warming. “When did you decide to look at nature as if it’s not your nature?” a narrator asked during the opening presentation.

Addressing world leaders, Erdogan stressed Turkey’s determination to tackle climate change and presented Antalya’s ancient, multicultural history as fitting for its role as host.

Three-quarters of world's displaced people 'on frontlines of climate crisis'

“At the centre of our civilisations lies respect for nature,” he said. “The earth is a sacred trust that must be protected and guarded. We are a nation that considers even harming an ant a violation of rights, and that embraces the principle of planting the last sapling in your hand even if you know the apocalypse will come tomorrow.”

A different reality

The COP31 summit gives Erdogan a prominent international stage, but human rights campaigners warn of a very different reality outside the conference halls.

Last month, the US-based Human Rights Watch raised the alarm over a widening campaign against Turkey’s environmental movement. The report’s author, Deniz Bayram, said activists face a growing wave of arrests, fines and intimidation.

“People told us that when they protested, they faced police violence and abusive tactics by security officers, as well as legal harassment through unfair criminal investigations with no criminal evidence,” Bayram said.

She said the authorities had also put pressure on demonstrators through their families. In the eastern Black Sea region, security officers contacted the adult sons of women protesters who lived in other cities and told them to stop their mothers attending further rallies, according to Bayram.

“Women told us that they are not really afraid of facing such violence from the authorities, but they are having a hard time with these family matters with their own relatives,” she said. “So these abusive tactics create a chilling effect, preventing people from attending further demonstrations.”

Tear gas and court cases

Police intervention at environmental protests has become routine across Turkey, where local demonstrations have surged since the government relaxed restrictions on gold and coal mining.

Suheyla Dogan, a retired civil engineer who has become a leading voice in protests against gold mines, has repeatedly rallied villagers against mining projects. She said the personal cost of activism was rising sharply.

“If we take any direct action, we are punished; they open court cases against us,” said Dogan, who faces four separate legal cases. “At the demonstrations, we have faced a lot of tear gas, water cannon, beatings and so on.”

Ahead of a planned demonstration in Antalya during the climate summit, Dogan said, several organisers were detained by police and released a day later. She believes the move was intended to deter people from turning up, even though the rally had not been banned.

African push to triple climate adaptation finance left off Cop31 agenda

Legal experts warn that a climate of fear is deepening as pre-trial detention becomes standard practice, leaving activists in jail for weeks before their cases are heard, often only to be released later. The government maintains that the right to protest remains protected, but environmental lawyer Ismail Hakki Atal said lawyers defending activists were increasingly being targeted too.

Atal represented villagers fighting to protect the Akbelen Forest near the south-western town of Milas, where he alleges that the government-backed conglomerate Limak breached Turkey’s Olive Law by cutting down olive trees and dumping rubble on olive groves.

“Because I exposed this in a live news broadcast, police detained me twice within five days, even though I was acting as the villagers’ lawyer,” Atal said. “The ruling AKP has effectively established a judiciary in Turkey capable of having anyone it wishes arrested. The judicial system currently hangs over us like the Sword of Damocles and is used as a stick when necessary.”

Retirees on the front line

Dogan acknowledged that the mounting pressure was beginning to sap the movement’s strength, particularly among younger people.

“People are now more afraid to join us. Villagers are more afraid because if they protest and are taken to prison, they stay there for a long time,” she said. “When we call people on to the streets, they ask: ‘How are you going to protect us if something happens to us?’ Young people who have jobs and children are especially afraid.”

World set to breach 1.5C warming limit as UN warns time is running out

With fewer people of working age willing to risk their jobs and their freedom, the burden of frontline protest is increasingly falling on retirees such as Dogan.

“I am retired, I have my pension, and I don’t have a job to lose,” she said. “Maybe retired people are now more willing to be on the streets than young working people. I see it as my duty; I have to do it.”

For now, Turkish environmentalists say they refuse to be silenced. They have vowed to make their voices heard on the sidelines of COP31, as an older generation steps forward to keep the movement alive.
