World.title: Police arrest anti-Pax Silica protesters as ASEAN Summit opens in Manila
World.content:
PAX SILICA PROTEST. Militants gather at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila on November 15, 2026, to protest the proposed Pax Silica initiative and US President Donald Trump’s visit to the 49th ASEAN Summit.

At least 11 protesters were arrested by police within the freedom park, according to Manila Police District Spokesperson Philip Ines

MANILA, Philippines – Police clashed with protesters at Liwasang Bonifacio on Sunday morning, November 15, as activists opposing Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump tried to march toward the ASEAN Summit venue.

The protesters were trying to reach the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC), the venue of the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Police blocked the protesters from proceeding to the summit venue. Some of the protesters managed to slip through several layers of policemen armed with shields. The cops, however, managed to block the protesters again.

ASEAN PROTEST. Protesters scuffle with police officers in Manila on November 15, 2026, during a protest against US President Donald Trump’s upcoming visit and participation in the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) President Jerome Adonis said police told them they could not hold a street protest because they did not have a permit.

After nearly an hour of attempts to march to PICC, the protesters retreated to Liwasang Bonifacio. Despite this, at least 11 protesters were arrested by police within freedom park, according to Manila Police District Spokesperson Philip Ines.

Ines said at least 16 personnel from the Manila Police District were injured.

Cops dragged protesters into a police vehicle. Some officers were seen slapping, kicking, and punching one activist as they took him away.

Adonis questioned the legality of the arrests, saying they were made inside a freedom park.

ASEAN PROTEST. Police arrest a protester in Liwasang Bonifacio on the opening of the ASEAN Summit in Manila, on Sunday, November 15. Photo by Patrick Cruz/Rappler

“Ang gulo ho nanggaling sa pulis. Hindi po galing sa amin. Nagdedepensa lang kami ng hanay namin,” he added. (The trouble started with the police, not us. We were only defending our ranks.)

Rappler asked the Manila Police District why the protesters were arrested, but it had yet to respond as of writing.

Under the Revised Penal Code, a person arrested without a warrant should be brought to court within a maximum of 36 hours, and that is for grave violations.

Police also towed the truck that protesters had used as a makeshift stage. Adonis accused police of puncturing their vehicles with nails.

In Liwasang Bonifacio, where the protesters plan to camp out, human manure was scattered in front of the statue of Andres Bonifacio, the “father of the Philippine revolution.”

ASEAN PROTEST. Personnel from the Manila Department of Environment and Public Service clean the human manure scattered in front of the statue of Andres Bonifacio, in Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila, on Sunday, November 15. Photo by Patrick Cruz/Rappler

Bayan Muna Chairperson Teddy Casiño, who was also at the protest, claimed that the police were behind this.

“Isang malaking ka-hipokrituhan ang ginagawa ng gobyerno. Nagpapakita ng hospitality sa mga dayuhan pero binabastos ang kanyang mga mamamayan,” Casiño said. (The government’s actions are widely hypocritical. It shows hospitality to foreign visitors while disrespecting its own people.)

Personnel from the Manila Department of Environment and Public Service later cleaned the human manure.

Concerns over Pax Silica

Protesters have raised concerns that Pax Silica could displace Indigenous peoples and farming communities in the planned 4,000-acre industrial hub in New Clark City, Tarlac.

Pax Silica is a US-led initiative that seeks to strengthen supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors through partnerships with other countries. The signing of the Pax Silica agreement had reportedly been targeted for November, coinciding with Trump’s visit to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit.

Trump is expected to arrive in Manila on Tuesday, November 17, for the Special ASEAN-US Summit.

However, Department of Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo clarified that the Philippines would not sign the agreement during the 49th ASEAN Summit.

“We do not want to distract attention or take away attention from the regional initiatives that ASEAN and the Philippines are proposing,” Rodolfo told reporters on Tuesday, November 10.

Despite the delay, the Philippines eyes to sign the deal with the US before the year ends, Rodolfo said.

Amid the protests, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro appealed to the public to reconsider holding demonstrations during the summit.

“Whatever their demands may be, I hope these are not pursued through protests, although I recognize that this is their right. In these times, however, it would be better to have more in-depth discussions about whatever concerns the students may have,” Castro said during a press briefing on Saturday, November 14.

Prior to the Sunday protest, thousands of students also protested against Pax Silica. – Rappler.com

World.title: Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN struggles
World.content:
Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled it

When Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III sold his family’s shares in the main Lopez holding company in August, he said the move would allow his family to “channel our family’s resources into businesses aligned with our personal mission,” adding that more announcements would come in due time.

Three months later, his new game plan is clear. It centers on two companies that serve everyday Filipinos: ABS-CBN and Rockwell Land.

On Thursday, November 12, First Philippine Holdings Corporation (FPH), led by Gabby’s cousin, Federico “Piki” Lopez, agreed to sell its 90.74% voting stake in Rockwell Land. The buyer is Gabby’s and his siblings’ private firm, Crème Investment Corporation, and the price tag is P15.92 billion.

This completes a 94-day asset swap that began on August 10. Back then, Crème sold its 25.68% share in Lopez Inc. to San Miguel boss Ramon S. Ang for about P11 billion. Lopez Inc. was originally built as the untouchable top holding company meant to protect the family empire from outside takeovers. (READ: The secret to the Lopez family’s enduring control of ABS-CBN)

THEN…The Rockwell property with the old Meralco power plant (upper right) in Makati City. Rappler/Rockwell brand rap file image

For decades, Rockwell Land has been the Lopez Group’s luxury lifestyle and consumer jewel. Started in 1995 on the site of an old Meralco power plant in Makati, Rockwell turned an industrial lot into Rockwell Center, which is now home to Power Plant Mall, high-end condos, serviced apartments, and offices.

…AND NOW. Bird’s eye view of Rockwell Makati with Power Plant Mall at the center. Courtesy of Rockwell Land

This focus on everyday consumers is a natural fit for Gabby who spent his career in TV, entertainment, and public-facing brands. Just two days after the August sale, Gabby and his cousins pledged P2.2 billion of their own money to help rebuild ABS-CBN. He explained why: “ABS-CBN has been part of this family for generations. The mission our family set out to pursue remains the heartbeat of this family—to be in the service of the Filipino. We are putting our own money behind this conviction.” (READ: Gabby Lopez: Man on a mission)

This is a sharp contrast from Piki Lopez’s world at FPH and First Gen, an ascetic, heavy-infrastructure universe of geothermal steam fields, gas turbines, and pumped-storage hydropower projects that require tens of billions of pesos and years, sometimes decades, of engineering before they make money. At the 2026 annual stockholders’ meetings of FPH and First Gen, Piki repeatedly framed his leadership around the “compounding” value of long-term choices, and that “direction over speed” matters more. In other words, a slow-and-steady approach built for power grids rather than quick profits.

Gabby does not seem to be retreating from the family business. Instead, he is separating the group’s lifestyle and media brands from FPH’s power business and bringing them under his own control.

BOSS. Ambassador Manuel “Manolo” Lopez speaks at a corporate event following Rockwell Land Corp.’s listing on May 12, 2012, in Rockwell Power Plant Mall’s premises in Makati City. Courtesy of Rockwell Land FB

Rockwell also has deep ties to Gabby’s late uncle, Manuel “Manolo” Lopez. Manolo ran Meralco for over 30 years and was deeply disappointed when the family and business group, both led then by his older brother Oscar, the father of Piki, forced FPH to let go of Meralco in 2009 to pay off First Gen’s geothermal debts. Manolo was quoted then saying, “Meralco would have been my parents’ legacy.” In March and April 2026, Manolo’s children joined Gabby and other cousins in publicly challenging Piki’s leadership. Buying Rockwell brings a business closely linked to Manolo’s side of the family under Crème’s direct control.

Beyond family history and culture, this deal solves a major money problem for Gabby’s branch: ABS-CBN needs cash, and Rockwell makes it.

In 2025, Rockwell earned P4.73 billion. ABS-CBN lost P4.72 billion. Crème has already pledged P766.7 million to ABS-CBN’s P6-billion fundraising drive. Buying Rockwell gives Gabby’s family an established, profitable company that brings in its own money. (READ: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way)

CASH COW. Rockwell Land’s 2025 earnings. Courtesy of Rockwell Land website

Where the dividends went

Before losing its broadcast franchise in 2020, ABS-CBN was a reliable cash machine for its parent firm, Lopez Holdings, former Benpres Holdings and one level below Lopez Inc in the Lopez group shareholder tree. ABS-CBN paid Lopez Holdings P447 million in dividends in 2018 and P269 million in 2019. Once the network went off the air, those payouts vanished. From 2020 to 2025, ABS-CBN racked up about P45.5 billion in losses. (READ: ABS-CBN is now 84% content — and still losing money. Can P6 billion fix it?)

With ABS-CBN out of cash, Lopez Holdings had to lean almost completely on FPH, which owns the group’s power and property businesses. From 2021 to 2025, FPH paid Lopez Holdings a flat P567 million a year in dividends. After Lopez Holdings paid its bills and shared profits with public stockholders, only about P247 million actually reached Lopez, Inc. in 2025.

FPH’s own financial records show where that money came from. In 2025, subsidiary Rockwell paid FPH roughly P630 million in dividends. Meralco—where FPH still owns a 3.95% stake—paid another P1.115 billion. Together, those two companies gave FPH P1.75 billion in cash dividends. That is more than triple the P567 million FPH sent up to Lopez Holdings.

FPH didn’t just hoard the extra cash. As a public company, it had debts, operating costs, outside shareholders, and massive power projects to pay for. First Gen and its subsidiary, Energy Development Corporation, were pouring money into geothermal drilling, hydropower, and battery storage while paying off loans. First Gen President and COO Giles Puno noted at this year’s annual meeting that while the company aims to pay out 30% of its yearly recurring profit, those payouts depend on spending needs, growth plans, and debt payments. To save cash, First Gen cut how much it paid as yearly dividend to its parent FPH from P0.90 per share in 2024 to P0.80 in 2025.

So most of the Piki-led power group’s profits stayed locked inside the operating companies. For family members at the very top of the corporate ladder, including Gabby and the heirs of Manolo, that meant waiting years for bigger payouts. Buying Rockwell lets Crème skip all those corporate middlemen. Instead of waiting for cash to trickle up through FPH, Lopez Holdings, and Lopez, Inc., Gabby’s firm can soon collect dividends straight from the source as Rockwell’s main owner.

What Rockwell brings Gabby

Rockwell’s net profit for parent shareholders climbed from P3.11 billion in 2023 to P3.71 billion in 2024, reaching P4.73 billion in 2025. The 2025 number got a boost from a one-time gain after buying Alabang Commercial Corporation. Even without that extra boost, Rockwell still earned about P4.1 billion.

Its cash flow has grown right along with its profits. Rockwell brought in P2 billion in cash from daily operations in 2025, up sharply from P144 million in 2024, even though real estate requires heavy upfront spending on land and construction. Its regular dividends grew steadily too, rising from P0.0752 per share in 2023 to P0.1018 in 2024, and hitting P0.1212 in 2025. Renting out commercial spaces gives Rockwell a steady safety net beyond just selling condos. Power Plant Mall in Makati, its office buildings, and its December 2025 purchase of Alabang Commercial Corporation—which added Alabang Town Center and a nearby office tower—bring in reliable rental cash.

Of course, Rockwell has big bills of its own. Its P21.6-billion Alabang deal is being paid in installments through December 2027, and it raised P10 billion in retail bonds in March 2026 to fund active projects. It can’t pay dividend to its owners every single peso it makes. Still, it gives Gabby a healthy business that makes money rather than drains it.

Rockwell’s ties to ABS-CBN

Rockwell and ABS-CBN share more than just the Lopez family name. Over the last four years, Rockwell has been one of the main buyers of the real estate ABS-CBN sold to raise cash.

In 2022, Rockwell bought properties from ABS-CBN for P786 million, followed by another P733 million deal in 2023. Those sales gave the network profit gains of P246 million and P232 million. In 2024, Rockwell bought more ABS-CBN land for about P679 million—booking a P223.1-million gain for the broadcaster—and agreed to buy ABS-CBN’s Iloilo property for P91.4 million. Later company filings showed even more property deals between the two firms.

Their shared history goes back even further. Before Rockwell went public in 2012, its housing arm built the 53 Benitez condos in Quezon City on the site of an old movie studio. Lopez Holdings, then known as Benpres Holdings, also owned 24.5% of Rockwell directly before selling it to FPH in August 2009.

Smaller day-to-day ties are still in place. ABS-CBN Holdings Corporation, which handles the network’s depository receipts, keeps its main office at Rockwell Business Center Sheridan in Mandaluyong. Lopez Holdings also pays office rent to Rockwell.

No merger or money-sharing plan between Rockwell and ABS-CBN has been announced, and they remain completely separate companies. Still, Rockwell has repeatedly stepped in to buy the properties ABS-CBN needed to sell, and now Gabby is taking over Rockwell itself.

From minority shareholder to controlling owner

Until August, Crème’s 25.68% share in Lopez Inc. gave Gabby’s family a small, indirect piece of several businesses, but very little control over dividend payouts.

Under the P15.92-billion deal approved by FPH on November 12, Crème will buy 86.58% of Rockwell’s common shares, plus voting preferred shares that raise its total voting power to 90.74%. Once regulators approve the deal and Crème makes a required buyout offer to the remaining public stockholders, it becomes the controlling owner. That gives Crème a direct say over Rockwell’s board and dividend payouts, within the limits of corporate law, loan rules, and minority shareholder rights.

If Rockwell keeps paying its 2025 dividend rate of P0.1212 per share, Crème’s incoming block of 5.30 billion common shares would bring in about P642 million a year before taxes. Future payouts aren’t guaranteed—they will depend on Rockwell’s profits, spending needs, and board votes.

Three months after leaving Lopez, Inc., Gabby Lopez’s new game plan is clear. He has fresh cash for ABS-CBN, the network he spent his life building, and direct control of Rockwell Land, a profitable lifestyle developer that already makes money. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

Part 3 on Monday, November 16 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

World.title: Maria Ressa speaks at 2026 ASEAN Business and Investment Summit
World.content:
Artificial intelligence can reproduce ‘the worst of who we are,’ says Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa

MANILA, Philippines – Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa warned that artificial intelligence deployment by the private sector has outpaced regulation and control by the government.

Ressa delivered a keynote speech and joined a fireside chat on “Trust in the Age of AI,” at the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit in Parañaque City on Sunday, November 15.

She noted that because AI models scrape training material from the internet, it can reproduce “the worst of who we are.”

“It can work for you the same way social media works for content creators, but it is a Faustian bargain if you do not look at the design,” Ressa said during the fireside chat, hosted by veteran journalist Karen Davila.

The two-day business summit, happening on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, ends on Sunday. – Rappler.com

World.title: US floated idea of Ukraine ceding Donbas for NATO membership, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
TALKS. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy meets with US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, on the day of the European Political Community summit, following Kushner's trip to Russia, in Dublin, Ireland, on November 12, 2026.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv would not concede territory but would put the question to a national referendum if Ukraine received security guarantees, a right to a strong military, and reconstruction funds

KYIV, Ukraine – US negotiators have floated the idea of Ukraine’s potential withdrawal from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, following the latest round of peace talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi.

This is the first time the question of linking NATO membership to territorial concessions has been raised during the talks, Zelenskyy said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday, November 14.

“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?” he said.

“That is why I believe NATO is back on the agenda. But you have also heard [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation.”

Putin has long said Ukrainian membership of NATO is a red line for Moscow, citing the issue as one reason for launching Russia’s full-blown invasion in 2022.

Zelenskyy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a national referendum.

‘This war must be ended first’

Echoing comments made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, November 13, Zelenskyy dismissed Russia’s call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine.

“We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first,” he said.

US President Donald Trump‘s envoy ‌and son-in-law Jared Kushner said on Saturday that the two sides had set out “maximalist positions” in the talks this week, but in private discussions both “understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war.”

“Serious and constructive work continues among those of us committed to finding solutions,” Kushner said in a social media post.

Zelenskyy also dismissed Putin’s suggestion for a local humanitarian ceasefire in Kostiantynivka, a hotly contested city in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, saying it reflected Moscow’s inability to take the city by force. Civilians there have already had the opportunity to evacuate, he added.

“Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” he said.

Ukraine has given a list of seven or eight other frontline settlements where civilians, including children, are trapped for a potential humanitarian truce but Russia prefers to use them as military targets, Zelenskyy said.

Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians in the war.

Large prisoner exchange agreed

The two days of US-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia concluded on Wednesday in the Emirati capital without a major breakthrough, though the sides agreed to a prisoner exchange that will involve more than 1,000 people, Zelenskyy said.

The final numbers for the prisoner swap were still under discussion, he added.

Kushner and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff had pledged to raise an energy ceasefire with Putin at a meeting in Moscow on Thursday, Zelenskyy said, but there was no news of any progress after their talks.

“Putin personally does not support a ceasefire,” he said.

Zelenskyy met Witkoff and Kushner on Thursday in Ireland after their talks in Moscow. He said the US negotiators had told him that all sides had agreed for Europe to have a seat at the negotiating table in forthcoming peace talks.

In Abu Dhabi, delegates from Europe — which is now Ukraine’s largest financial and military backer — had talks with US and Ukrainian officials but did not sit at the table with Russia.

At the summit in Ireland, EU leaders agreed that Europe’s team for any Ukraine peace talks would comprise five major military powers — non-EU member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland — as well as EU officials.

Kushner said the US focus was now on “facilitating direct engagement between Moscow and European partners and preparing the agenda for the next round of trilateral talks.” – Rappler.com

World.title: After midterm sweep, Democrats split over Trump, cost-cutting agenda
World.content:
TRUMP. United States President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media after disembarking Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, October 10, 2026.

US President Donald Trump retains significant executive authority to block much of the Democrats' agenda, complicating the party's efforts to lower costs, the central issue voters gave Democrats control of Congress to fix

Fresh from a midterm election landslide, Democrats met in Denver this week united in wanting to deliver voters relief from high costs, but split over how to achieve that, what lessons to draw from their victory and how combative they should be toward President Donald Trump.

Despite the celebratory mood after the November 3 rout of Republicans, tensions between moderates and a restive progressive wing surfaced at the party’s first major gathering since its victory, along with anxiety that the party could squander the opportunity voters had handed it.

The gathering offered an early glimpse of the battle to define its future as prospective 2028 presidential candidates and senior leaders debated how to turn electoral success into a governing agenda while navigating long-standing ideological and generational divides.

The conference, hosted by Majority Democrats, a group that advocates for younger party leaders and against left-wing activism, offered a forum for the jockeying now underway as Democrats debate what lessons to draw from their midterm win and begin the search for a 2028 White House standard-bearer.

Speakers disagreed over whether to embrace a bolder progressive agenda or tack toward the center, exposing competing approaches to lowering food, healthcare and housing costs, while working alongside Trump, who retains veto power for two more years.

California Representative Ro Khanna, a progressive and potential presidential candidate, urged Democrats to stop chasing the political center and embrace a bolder agenda, including universal healthcare, a wealth tax, a $25 federal minimum wage, deep Pentagon cuts and abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

By contrast, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, a moderate and another potential 2028 contender, argued the party should move beyond ideological litmus tests, saying voters “don’t give a damn” about such debates and care instead about whether Democrats can deliver results.

The breadth of the Democratic victories has allowed moderates and progressives to argue that voters have endorsed their vision for the party’s future.

“It’s to be expected that there will be a big debate because the Democratic victory was so broad it swept in centrists, southern Democrats and more progressive and left-wing Democrats,” Democratic strategist Elaine Kamarck told Reuters.

Trump retains significant executive authority to block much of the Democrats’ agenda, complicating the party’s efforts to lower costs, the central issue voters gave Democrats control of Congress to fix.

Democrats are projected to hold at least 255 seats to ​Republicans’ 169 in the US House, with 12 contests still ​undecided. In the Senate, the breakdown will be ⁠at least 55-44, with Democrats possibly gaining one more seat in Alaska when vote-counting is completed.

Work with Trump or fight him?

One of the most striking debates in Denver centered on how to govern with Trump still in the White House.

James Talarico, the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from Texas since 1988, urged Democrats to work with Trump.

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” Talarico said, drawing tepid applause. “We’re tired of being pitted against each other.”

He found an ally in Iowa Governor-elect Rob Sand, who said he encouraged Democrats at campaign events to applaud Republicans and that partisan warfare will not deliver results.

“The only way we’re going to fix that is by fixing it together,” Sand said.

Minutes later, US Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Eric Holder, who was attorney general in the Obama administration, largely rejected accommodation with Trump.

Raskin, expected to become chairman of the House Judiciary Committee in January and oversee investigations of Trump next year, said the Republican Party had become an authoritarian cult of personality.

“We’re going to reassert all of the powers of Congress that have been surrendered and abdicated by the MAGA Congress to King Trump,” Raskin said. “We’re going to enforce the Constitution against him.”

Holder warned Democrats against pursuing bipartisanship.

“If we retreat into caution, if we operate out of fear, if we take refuge in the niceties of the old Washington and seek approval from those who have been and are actively dismantling our institutions, we will fail.”

There has been a long-simmering debate inside the party over whether to move further left or pursue a more centrist agenda, and this election has only intensified those tensions.

Competing visions for governing

Almost everyone who spoke at the conference agreed the party’s top priority was lowering costs and improving life for working families.

It was a theme echoed by New York Representative Hakeem Jeffries, set to become US House Speaker, and several prospective 2028 presidential candidates, including Shapiro, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and Khanna.

But splits emerged over how to achieve that.

Jeffries, a moderate, was heckled by a group of protesters, who accused him of being too timid to deliver change and called for a House leader who embraced a more populist progressive agenda.

Khanna and Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, another progressive who this week challenged more centrist Senator Chuck Schumer of New York for the party’s top leadership job in the Senate, called for populist, government-funded economic solutions.

Don’t blow it

There was a collective anxiety among the speakers that the party might squander one of the biggest victories it has achieved in a generation.

Many speakers described the win not as an enduring mandate, but rather a temporary opportunity voters had given them to fix the country’s problems.

Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego, another potential presidential contender, noted that many Hispanic voters who voted for Trump in 2024 backed Democrats this month.

“It was not, though, a love letter to the Democratic Party,” Gallego said. “It is a short-term loan that we need to keep paying, or we will lose it.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Candon cops hold school safety drills on shooting incidents
World.content:
Police personnel from the Candon City Police Station conduct a school safety drill on active attacks and shooting incidents at Parioc Elementary School in Candon City, Ilocos Sur, to familiarize teachers and pupils with emergency procedures and strengthen their readiness for possible security threats. (Photo courtesy of Candon CPS)

SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — Police personnel conducted safety drills on active attacks and shooting incidents in four schools in Candon City to strengthen emergency preparedness among teachers and pupils.

The activities were carried out by personnel of the Candon City Police Station (CPS) under the supervision of its officer-in-charge, Police Lt. Col. Zaldy C. Fuentes.

The drills were held at Oaig Daya Elementary School, Saint Cecilia Early Learning Center Inc., Parioc Elementary School and San Andres Adventist Elementary School, Candon CPS said in a report on Friday, Nov. 13.

Article continues after this 

The exercises aimed to assess and strengthen existing emergency protocols, improve participants’ readiness and familiarize school personnel and pupils with the proper safety procedures during an active attack, shooting incident or other security threats within school premises.

Police said the activity was intended to help schools respond appropriately and protect the lives of pupils and personnel in the event of an emergency. /ms

World.title: Bukidnon cops nab 10 wanted persons in manhunt ops
World.content:
Bukidnon map. INQUIRER FILES

MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — In a series of coordinated law enforcement operations conducted across the province from November 12 to 14, police units apprehended 10 wanted individuals, highlighted by the capture of a provincial topmost wanted person.

The operations were executed by various municipal police stations, including Manolo Fortich, Impasugong, San Fernando, Quezon, Valencia City, Malaybalay City, Don Carlos, Lantapan, and Libona, operating in close coordination with the Provincial Intelligence Unit and provincial mobile force companies.

Among those arrested was 22-year-old Marco Pagar Ochate—listed as a Provincial Level Top 5 Most Wanted Person—who was collared in Manolo Fortich on Nov. 14 for violating the New Anti-Carnapping Law (R.A. 10883).

Article continues after this 

Other arrested suspects faced outstanding warrants for multiple offenses, including frustrated homicide, robbery, acts of lasciviousness, estafa, and illegal gambling.

All apprehended suspects are currently detained under police custody across respective municipal stations for proper documentation and legal disposition. /ms

World.title: Over 22 journos covering Asean protests subjected to police harassment
World.content:
A police barricade resulted in an altercation between protesters and police officers, with the two sides violently pushing and shoving each other, during a rally staged on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, in time for the opening of the 49th Asean Summit. —Photo by Zacarian Sarao (INQUIRER.net)

MANILA, Philippines—The National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) documented at least 22 media workers who reported experiencing police harassment during the demonstrations on Sunday amid the 2026 Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit.

“The arrests, attempted arrests, and harassment of protesters and journalists constitute violations of the people’s right to peaceful assembly and the media’s freedom to report on matters of public interest,” the NUJP said in a statement on Sunday.

Among those affected were campus journalists from the University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) Perspective, UPLB The Staple, UP Philippine Collegian, and City College of Calamba The Sentinel.

Article continues after this 

A campus journalist from the Philippine Collegian and a reporter from Southern Tagalog Exposure were also arrested, according to the NUJP.

NUJP said they were covering Lakbayan of Southern Tagalog delegates and were present when the Philippine National Police arrested approximately 300 delegates in Sucat, Muntinlupa.

Read: Police arrest 300 protesters in Muntinlupa City

For its part, the Southern Police District earlier told the Inquirer that police arrested over 200 individuals because they did not conduct a rally at a freedom park and lacked a permit.

At Liwasang Bonifacio, two campus journalists from University of the Philippines Tinig ng Plaridel and a journalist from Altermidya said that police attempted to arrest them.

Article continues after this 

The incident happened during the All Workers Unity protest march from Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila toward the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay, the venue of the 49th Asean Summit and Related Summits.

Read: UP CMC condemns attempted arrest of student-journos covering protest

Article continues after this 

“We are also following up on reports from two other media workers who allegedly experienced physical violence at the hands of the police during the dispersal,” said the NUJP.

The NUJP cited the account of Atlermidya’s Adrian Puse, who said a Manila Police District officer grabbed him from behind and forcibly restrained both his arms despite his clearly marked media uniform and identification.

Puse managed to free himself after identifying himself as a journalist.

“The right to protest is a fundamental democratic right that must be respected and protected,” the NUJP said.

Your subscription could not be saved. Please try again. Your subscription has been successful. Subscribe to our daily newsletter SIGN ME UP

“Equally, journalists must be allowed to exercise their duty to cover public events, document abuses, and report the stories of those who take to the streets,” they added. /atm

World.title: UP CMC condemns attempted arrest of student-journos covering protest
World.content:
The police barricade resulted in an altercation between protesters and police officers, with the two sides violently pushing and shoving each other. (Photo by Zacarian Sarao)

MANILA, Philippines — The University of the Philippines College of Media and Communication (UP CMC) and its official student publication, Tinig ng Plaridel (TNP), have condemned the attempted arrest of two student-journalists while covering a workers’ protest march in Manila.

In a joint statement, the college and publication said the two staff members were documenting Manila Police District (MPD) officers carrying a protester to a police station at around 11 a.m. on Sunday, when they were allegedly subjected to verbal intimidation and attempts to apprehend them.

The incident occurred as the student-journalists covered the All Workers Unity protest march from Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila to the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay, where the 49th Asean Summit and Related Summits is held.

Article continues after this 

“We demand that the police refrain from hampering the work of and intimidating student journalists reporting on the protest actions in the exercise of their role as campus journalists,” said UP CMC and TNP.

“We also demand that authorities recognize citizens’ constitutional right to participate in protest activities and report on them,” they added.

One of the student-journalists sustained minor abrasions during the incident, according to the statement.

The UP CMC and TNP said police also confiscated the student’s cellphone which contained video footage of the protest and arrests, but eventually the device was returned.

According to the college, they would hold the Philippine National Police (PNP) accountable if its students were harmed while performing their duties as campus journalists or participating in peaceful protests.

The Inquirer sought comment from the PNP but had yet to receive a response as of posting time. /ms

World.title: San Juan City, Tieza break ground for P17.1-M tourist center
World.content:
Tieza COO Mark Lapid (left) and San Juan City Mayor Francis Zamora lead the groundbreaking ceremony of the ₱17.1-million Pinaglabanan Tourist Center and Souvenir Shop at the historic Pinaglabanan Shrine on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. —Photo from the San Juan City government

MANILA, Philippines — San Juan City Mayor Francis Zamora and Chief Operating Officer Mark Lapid of the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (Tieza) led the groundbreaking ceremony of the Pinaglabanan Tourist Center and Souvenir Shop on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at the historic Pinaglabanan Shrine in San Juan City.

The ₱17.1-million tourism infrastructure project is a joint initiative of the San Juan and Tieza, which is aimed at further strengthening the city’s position as a premier historical and cultural tourism destination in Metro Manila.

The project involves the construction of a two-storey tourism facility featuring a visitor information center, pasalubong and souvenir shop, coffee shop, indoor and al fresco dining areas, and accessible visitor amenities.

Article continues after this 

READ: Experience unique flavors of San Juan

Strategically located at the historic Pinaglabanan Shrine, the facility is envisioned to serve as a welcoming hub for local and international tourists, providing convenient access to tourism information, locally made products, refreshments, and other visitor services.

The project will also complement San Juan City’s existing heritage attractions, including the Museo ng Katipunan, Museo El Deposito, and the historic El Deposito Underground Reservoir, further enhancing the overall visitor experience within the city’s heritage tourism district.

READ: DOT rolls out dashboard tracking Philippine tourism data

The groundbreaking marked another milestone in the partnership between San Juan City and Tieza in advancing heritage conservation, tourism development, and local economic opportunities. /atm

World.title: Some unused vaccine funds diverted to patient aid – Deputy Speaker Garin
World.content:
Department of Health. INQUIRER FILES

MANILA, Philippines — Billions of pesos in unused vaccine funds prompted the House of Representatives to redirect part of the proposed 2027 immunization budget to medical assistance for patients.

Garin, a former health secretary, said funds for influenza and pneumococcal vaccines remained unused despite the urgent need to protect Filipinos against preventable diseases.

“For example, the flu vaccine budget was not touched. The 2025 funds have not been used. The 2026 funds have not been used,” Garin said in Filipino during the “Saturday News Forum” at Dapo Restaurant in Quezon City, referring to unused funds for flu and pneumococcal vaccines for children.

Article continues after this 

READ: Garin backs 2027 medical aid shift, cites 11% fund use

According to Garin, Health Secretary Edwin Mercado had taken steps to use the available funds, with vaccine deliveries expected to begin before the end of 2026 and continue throughout 2027.

“In other words, those that they bought last week and those they will still buy, their delivery will be actually at the end of this year and will spill over to the whole of 2027,” she said.

The House version of the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget reduced funding for family health, immunization and nutrition commodities by about P4.87 billion.

Garin said the realignment was intended to address rising medical costs while allowing the government to use previously approved funds for vaccine procurement.

READ: Cost, not fear, keeps Filipinos away from vaccines

“That’s why Congress decided to put the funding for immunization into the medical assistance program. Why? So many are getting sick. Health expenses are rising,” she said.

Article continues after this 

She said medical assistance benefits both patients and hospitals by helping cover treatment costs and sustain hospital operations.

Garin stressed that the government must ensure that appropriated funds are actually spent on health services rather than left unused. /atm

World.title: Abandoned motorcycle leads cops to judge’s slay suspects
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

PAGADIAN CITY — A motorcycle abandoned in Barangay Maasin, Zamboanga City has led police investigators to the suspects in the ambush of Judge Joseph Wee Sit early on Thursday.

On Saturday afternoon, the police had filed criminal complaints against three suspects before the Zamboanga City Prosecutor’s Office.

Lt. Col. Shellamie Chang, spokesperson of the Police Regional Office 9 (PRO 9), said investigators were able to establish the identity of one suspect, who was the alleged gunman.

Article continues after this 

Two others remain unidentified as of Saturday; one served as driver of the alleged gunman while the other drove a support getaway vehicle, Chang added.

Chang said the filing of criminal complaints followed sustained case build-up by the Special Investigation Task Group (SITG) “Wee Sit,” backed by judicial affidavits alongside documentary and forensic evidence gathered by investigators.

Wee Sit was driving past 6 a.m. on Thursday to the Zamboanga City port to cross the sea to Isabela City, Basilan where he is presiding judge of Regional Trial Court Branch 2.

A motorcycle pulled up near his vehicle in Barangay Tumaga, opened fire and then fled.

Rescuers who responded to the scene first revived Wee Sit, who suffered six gunshot wounds, then rushed him to a local hospital where he later died.

Article continues after this 

On Friday, SITG investigators spotted a white Yamaha NMAX motorcycle abandoned in Maasin, some 13 kilometers away from the crime scene in Tumaga where scene-of-the-crime operatives recovered eight fired cartridge cases of caliber .45 handgun.

Chang said probers were able to piece together information from closed-circuit television footage and eyewitness accounts to establish the relation of the abandoned vehicle to the ambush of Wee Sit.

Article continues after this 

Investigators earlier said the perpetrators were two individuals riding a white Yamaha NMAX motorcycle, both wearing jackets and helmets.

Brig. Gen. Elmer Ragay, PRO 9 director, said the filing of criminal complaints demonstrates the police force’s commitment to pursuing justice through diligent, evidence-based investigation and close coordination among concerned units.

World.title: Protesters, police clash in Manila during Asean Summit protest
World.content:
Photo by Zacarian-Sarao

MANILA, Philippines — What was meant to be a peaceful protest coinciding with the start of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit on Sunday escalated into a tense confrontation between rallyists and police, with protesters claiming that authorities were trying to sabotage their program.

The protests were slated to start as early as 7:30 a.m. as various groups, under the collective All Workers Unity, planned to gather at the Liwasang Bonifacio freedom park in Manila for a march towards the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC) — the main venue for the 49th Asean Summit.

But after their arrival, protesters said the Liwasang Bonifacio grounds were covered with what they claimed were human feces.

Article continues after this 

“Nagkalat sila ng dumi rito sa Liwasang Bonifacio para pigilan ang mga mamamayan magtipon dito,” said Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) chairperson Teddy Casiño in an interview with reporters.

(They spread excrement at Bonifacio Plaza to prevent citizens from gathering here.)

“Talagang amoy na amoy ‘yung dumi ng tao na ikinalat dito, mula doon sa paanan (ng rebulto) ni Andres Bonifacio hanggang sa may bangketa,” he added.

(The human waste that was spread here really stinks, from the foot of the statue of Andres Bonifacio to the sidewalk.)

The groups were protesting the government’s alleged anti-worker policies, the arrival of US President Donald Trump, and the proposed establishment of a Pax Silica hub in New Clark City.

Article continues after this 

Labor leader Jerome Adonis said they received information that it was the Philippine National Police (PNP) who ordered unidentified individuals to spread feces around the park. However, the PNP has denied this.

This issue forced the groups to gather at the back portion of the park, before they officially began marching around 10 a.m.

Article continues after this 

However, as soon as the protesters reached the main road in front of Liwasang Bonifacio, police immediately set a barricade to prevent them from marching further.

The police barricade resulted in an altercation between protesters and police officers, with the two sides violently pushing and shoving each other. (Photo by Zacarian Sarao)

Police said they were blocking the protesters from marching as they lacked the necessary permit to hold one, ordering them to stay within the premises of Liwasang Bonifacio, which as a freedom park, is a designated public space where citizens can hold political demonstrations without needing the government’s authorization.

Protesters initially tried to evade the police barricade, but this resulted in a violent pushing and shoving between both sides.

Adonis said they attempted to negotiate with the police during the scuffle, but the authorities maintained that they will not allow the protesters to proceed any further.

Due to this, protest organizers yielded to the police’s orders, stating that they will postpone their march for today to avoid the situation from escalating further.

“Ayaw namin makipagsakitan so kami na ‘yung sumunod sa kanilang pakiusap, so umatras kami ng mapayapa,” said Adonis.

(We didn’t want to fight, so we followed their request and withdrew peacefully.)

But just shortly after protesters began returning to the park, tension once again erupted after authorities suddenly attempted to seize one of the vehicles being used by the rallyists for their sound system.

This resulted in another violent jostle between both parties.

Police once again attempted to confiscate the vehicle, this time successfully, resulting in another violent confrontation. (Photo by Zacarian Sarao)

The confrontation later reached a standstill, but only until the police moved to seize the vehicle once more, this time managing to successfully take it.

The chaos that ensued right after resulted in several arrests, with protest organizers claiming that a total of nine participants were nabbed by cops—several of whom suffered injuries.

Protest organizers then maintained that it was the police who were repeatedly instigating the disorder, describing the arrests and violent clashes as illegal and invoking the protesters’ constitutional right to peaceful assembly.

“Pagpapakita po ito kung gaanong karahas ang kapulisan laban sa mamamayan na nagpoprotesta para i-raise ang iba’t ibang issues [na kinahaharap ng bansa],” said Adonis.

(This shows how violent the police are against citizens who are protesting to raise various issues the country is facing.)

“Violation din po ito lalo na doon sa pagpasok nila sa loob ng freedom park,” he added.

(This is also a violation, especially when they entered the freedom park.)

Under the Public Assembly Act of 1985, law enforcement agencies are generally not allowed to interfere with or enter the immediate area of a peaceful public assembly held in a designated freedom park.

Meanwhile, Adonis said they are continuing to monitor the status of its arrested members.

“Dapat i-release lahat ang iligal na inaresto na kinaladkad nila,” said Adonis, citing one of the arrests where an unconscious protester was allegedly kicked multiple times and was then sent to the Manila Police District instead of a hospital.

(All those illegally arrested and dragged away must be released.)

The police barricade resulted in an altercation between protesters and police officers, with the two sides violently pushing and shoving each other. (Photo by Zacarian Sarao)

Meanwhile, in a separate interview with reporters, PCPT Atty. Felino Nebato, chief district legal officer of Manila, asserted that the protesters were arrested as they were already outside the bounds of Liwasang Bonifacio.

He also explained that the vehicles used by the protesters were confiscated as it was obstructing traffic around Liwasang Bonifacio.

“Hindi naman lugar ito ng sasakyan, pang-tao ito … andoon din kasi ‘yung paraphernalia nila,” said Nebato.

(This isn’t a place for cars, it’s for people… their paraphernalia is there too.)

“Nakailang warning na kasi na paalisin, eh talagang ayaw umalis, pinipilit nilang doon along the street,” he added.

(They’ve already been warned several times to remove it, but they really did not want to and were forcing it to stay along the street.)

When asked what specific violations the arrested protesters committed, Nebato said authorities were still in the process of determining which laws and ordinances they actually violated.

Nebato then denied allegations that it was the PNP who ordered the use of feces in the vicinity of Liwasang Bonifacio, stating that they too tried to apprehend the suspects behind it.“Hindi naman gawain ng PNP manira at mamerwisyo ng tao, we always maintain peace and the protection of our citizens,” he asserted.

Police attempted to seize one of the vehicles used by the protesters, but to no avail as rallyists gathered around the vehicle. (Photo by Zacarian Sarao)

(It is not the job of the PNP to destroy and harm people, we always maintain peace and the protection of our citizens.)

March on Tuesday, Nov. 17 to 18, to continue

Meanwhile, despite the violent demonstration on Sunday, Bayan president Renato Reyes Jr. told Inquirer that the scheduled march from Liwasang Bonifacio to PICC on Tuesday, Nov. 17 and to Mendiola on Wednesday, Nov. 18 will still continue.

“Oo tuloy pa rin, pero bukas dito lang kami,” he told Inquirer.

Asked whether the groups would secure a permit for the march, Reyes said there would be no point in doing so.

Until the march, protesters will stake out at Liwasang Bonifacio as part of its protest demonstrations. /ms

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation. The Myanmar side discussed boosting exports of Myanmar’s agricultural and fishery products to five post-Soviet states, and invited investment from the countries in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in southern Myanmar.

Simultaneously, an EEC sub-delegation led by Dmitry Fesenko, head of the industrial development monitoring and analysis department, met with Deputy Industry Minister Dr. Aung Zeya to discuss technical cooperation regarding micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and agro-based industries.

The EAEU—comprising Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia—represents a critical bloc of junta allies. Naypyitaw initiated multi-sector dialogue with the EAEU and EEC in 2022, signing memorandums of understanding for closer cooperation in 2023.

Trade between Myanmar and the EAEU member states more than tripled between 2019 and 2024, surpassing US$1.5 billion, according to EAEU data released last year. Myanmar’s primary exports to the bloc include rice, coffee, palm oil and cocoa beans, while it imports EAEU fertilizers, consumer goods, machinery, metals, cement and pharmaceuticals. The official trade figures exclude weapons and military equipment supplied to the regime by Russia and Belarus, both major arms suppliers.

Despite these figures, regional analysts argue the junta’s Eurasian pivot is driven more by diplomatic survival than viable economic strategy.

“Compared to neighbors like China and Thailand, trade and investment from these [EAEU] countries is worlds apart. Even under the previous governments of U Thein Sein and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, how much investment actually came from them?” an analyst pointed out.

“If the regime wants to do business, it has a massive ASEAN market to tap. The regime’s focus on those faraway markets suggests its motivations are far more geopolitical than economic. They desperately want to join the Russian-led geopolitical bloc.”

Regime chief Min Aung Hlaing, who has publicly condemned major powers for utilizing economic sanctions and political pressure as violations of global norms, personally attended the 4th Eurasian Economic Forum in Belarus last year. During the summit, he made an urgent appeal for Myanmar to be granted EAEU observer status—a demand his foreign minister aggressively reiterated during Imanaliev’s visit this week.

Naypyitaw’s push to integrate into Moscow’s economic architecture mirrors the generals’ broader strategy to embed an isolated regime in non-Western multilateral organizations; in May 2023, Myanmar was formally recognized as a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), led by China, Russia and India.

World.title: Myanmar’s Dwindling Debt to China, Scammers Nabbed in Shan, and More
World.content:
China no longer Myanmar’s biggest creditor

China is no Myanmar’s principal creditor, even though the military regime is bound for life and beyond by the money and favors it owes its protector. On paper at least, Japan is now Myanmar’s largest foreign government lender, while Beijing’s focus has shifted from extending new loans to managing existing debts.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics, Myanmar’s public and publicly guaranteed external debt stood at US$10.34 billion last year, down from around US$13.5 billion in 2021. Country-to-country debt accounted for $5.68 billion, with Japan holding $3.86 billion. China was owed only around US$1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s creditor-by-creditor breakdown.

Prior to the political opening in 2011, China was effectively Myanmar’s only major lender, at interest rates as high as 4.5 percent. But after reforms began, Myanmar regained access to financing from institutions and partners including the Asian Development Bank and the Japan International Cooperation Agency on far more favorable terms.

“Myanmar will not borrow money from China any more if interest rates remain high,” then-deputy finance minister Maung Maung Win pledged in June 2020.

An AidData assessment released in May shows that China committed $14.7 billion in development finance to Myanmar between 2000 and 2023 through 505 projects. Nearly 92 percent took the form of loans, mainly from the Export-Import Bank of China and China Development Bank.

But AidData estimates that Myanmar’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors had fallen to around US$1.7 billion by the end of 2024 or just about 19 percent of its external public debt.

The loans from China simply stopped. AidData found that China Eximbank, historically the largest lender, has not issued a new loan since 2019. While it was the COVID-19 pandemic that initially slowed lending, the trend has continued throughout the post-coup period.

The reason seems to be that the operating environment in Myanmar is deteriorating. Many planned Chinese-backed projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are in conflict areas or regions entirely beyond the putschist regime’s control. Key trade routes, resource projects and infrastructure investments increasingly depend on arrangements with ethnic armed groups rather than Naypyitaw alone.

Bangladesh ties Rohingya crisis to Beijing’s Indian Ocean ambition

Dhaka has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) that rules most of Myanmar’s Rakhine State as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis—and that could force China’s hand in dealing with the new reality there.

At stake for Bangladesh is the burden of hosting over 1 million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled the military’s brutal 2017 clearance operations. And since the AA controls entire Bangladeshi border with Myanmar, including Paletwa Township in neighboring Shin State, Dhaka has opened pragmatic dual-track discussions, engaging both the AA and the military regime after Naypyitaw’s repeated failures to facilitate the repatriation.

China, meanwhile, remains focused on its multi-billion-dollar projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). The key project—a deep-sea port and special economic zone in Kyaukphyu—is designed to solve Beijing’s “Malacca Dilemma” by giving it maritime access to the Indian Ocean. Kyaukphyu also serves as the terminus for the twin oil and gas pipelines currently pumping energy to Yunnan Province. Yet the port project remains stalled, with Kyaukphyu under AA siege.

Dhaka is increasingly looking to China for leverage. During Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Beijing in June—which closely followed a trip by Myanmar regime chief Min Aung Hlaing—Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed a tripartite China–Myanmar–Bangladesh economic corridor. That would provide Beijing with an alternative overland route to the Indian Ocean while Kyaukphyu remains in limbo.

In July, China’s ambassador to Bangladesh explicitly tied this proposed corridor to resolving the refugee crisis, suggesting it could facilitate Rohingya repatriation.

International scrutiny of the western front is intensifying. UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie is currently in Bangladesh to assess the armed conflict in Rakhine and the deteriorating situation in the refugee camps. Yet Beijing’s diplomatic shield of the military usurpers in Naypyitaw remains firmly in place. Addressing the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in late October, China’s representative reiterated that the crisis must be resolved bilaterally between Myanmar and Bangladesh, free from Western interference, a process China insists it is facilitating.

The International Court of Justice will rule next week whether the Myanmar military’s crackdown against the Rohingya people constituted a genocide.

No end to arrests of Chinese scammers in Shan

Some 759 foreigners were arrested between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31 for alleged involvement in scam operations in Shan State, and 502 were Chinese, regime media report.

Another 15 Chinese scammers were arrested on Monday in rural parts of Kyethi Township, southern Shan State. The township lies in an area that is contested by two rival ethnic armed groups: the Restoration Council of Shan State (RCSS) and the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), whose headquarters are in nearby Wan Hai.

After a Chinese-led crackdown on industrial-scale scam compounds in the Kokang region of northern Shan State in late 2023, operations scattered across at least 17 townships in southern and eastern Shan, including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse. Others famously relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy Township on the Thai border.

In other words, the syndicates adapted, their units becoming smaller and more nimble across scattered locations and moving further inland from prying eyes on the international border. Now they settle in places like Kyethi, where they can exploit lawlessness and administrative vacuums or collaborate with junta-aligned militias and armed groups.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: ASEAN Should Accept Myanmar Back at Diplomat Level: Bangkok
World.content:
BANGKOK—Myanmar’s foreign minister should be allowed back into meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) regional bloc, Thailand’s top diplomat said on Thursday after a visit to the war-torn country.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said his meetings with regime leader Min Aung Hlaing and others had revealed “a desire on the part of Myanmar to engage, to return to ASEAN.” But he said there was no talk of specific steps.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level meetings of the 11-nation ASEAN since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize ties since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president earlier this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

“For Thailand, we believe that the next step is to have the foreign minister of Myanmar participate in the ASEAN meetings at the level of foreign minister,” Sihasak told reporters.

His comments came ahead of a meeting of ASEAN leaders starting Sunday in the Philippines.

Sihasak said he had also raised the “very urgent problem” of water pollution among tributaries of the Mekong River, which straddles five Southeast Asian countries and China, saying a working group would meet later this month.

Last week, authorities in northern Thailand suspended tap water production after arsenic levels at the waterworks intake was found to be 30 times higher than the safety standard. More than a dozen villages were affected by the suspension.

A subsequent field sample from the nearby Sai River measured arsenic at 25 times the safety standard, the government said.

Thai officials previously pinned the toxic sediment on wastewater from mining activity upstream in Myanmar.

Sihasak said he also raised the issue of a spillover of violence into Thailand.

World.title: Myanmar Faces Year of Blackouts as Regime Admits 30% Power Shortfall
World.content:
Myanmar’s rotating power cuts will remain in place through 2027, with generation expected to meet only 70 percent of national demand, Deputy Energy Minister Aye Kyaw announced Wednesday.

Addressing the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament, he said next summer’s 24-hour electricity demand is forecast at 5,010 MW, while generation capacity is only 3,540 MW.

“That’s why we need to continue the load shedding measures,” he said.

Despite having the poorest electricity access in the region, Myanmar made significant progress in grid connectivity under the National League for Democracy’s 15-year National Electrification Plan in 2015. By 2020, more than half of households had electricity access, and the NLD’s World Bank-backed plan aimed to achieve nationwide electrification by 2030.

However, the plan was scrapped after the 2021 coup, and regime mismanagement has since triggered rolling power outages across the country.

The World Bank says reliable supply has dropped sharply since the military takeover, affecting nearly half of connected households — with 41.6 percent receiving only enough electricity for basic lighting and phone charging, and 9.1 percent getting no electricity at all.

It blames the deepening generation crisis on the suspension of LNG power plants, declining domestic gas production, hydropower stress, infrastructure damage, and stalled investment.

In response, the regime reintroduced nationwide rolling blackouts, leaving residents in even major cities struggling to manage households and livelihoods.

“We have to be ready to fill up the water, cook meals, and iron our clothes the moment the power comes back on,” Ko Thant Zin from Insein Township in the suburbs of Yangon told the Irrawaddy.

He said the electricity supply rotates between four hours on and four hours off.

“Under the civilian government, the roads were bright with lights. Now, I have to open my eyes wide to see the way ahead while driving at night,” he commented.

The deputy energy minister told citizens to install solar panels if they want a reliable supply. However, import curbs and surging prices have put solar options out of reach for most urban residents.

“Forget about solar panels, most people can’t even afford a portable power pack,” a resident of downtown Yangong’s Botahtaung Township told The Irrawaddy. “Prices have been skyrocketing because of import restrictions.”

He added that power cuts would cause major suffering during the El Niño heatwave forecast for November through January.

“I can’t imagine how we will get through next summer,” he said, reacting to the rationing announcement. “It will be especially tough for young children and the elderly.”

Demand driven by outages has seen the price of solar panels surge to a record high. Yangon residents said a household solar power system now costs at least 10 million kyats (around US $4,760), putting it beyond the reach of ordinary families.

Last month, Yangon City authorities mandated that all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar power systems to operate elevators and emergency lighting, as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

The World Bank says chronic power shortages remain one of the main constraints on Myanmar’s economy, limiting its recovery and keeping poverty persistently high.

The deputy energy minister also announced plans to develop two 55 MW small-modular-reactors in cooperation with Russia’s atomic agency, ROSATOM, starting in fiscal 2028-29. The project is slated for completion in fiscal 2035-36 but locations have yet to be announced.

World.title: Three Years After Operation 1027, Hopang Transformed Under Wa Rule
World.content:
Friday marks three years since Hopang in the Wa Self-Administered Zone experienced its first taste of the joint ethnic offensive known as Operation 1027, when drones deployed by the Brotherhood Alliance bombed a monastery sheltering retreating Myanmar military personnel from nearby Kunlong base.

For the Myanmar military, which had controlled Hopang for decades, the drone strike was an early warning that its grip on the town was nearing an end. For the United Wa State Army (UWSA), it presented an opportunity to gain one of the most important towns in Wa territory without firing a shot.

Less than two months after the Nov. 13 drone attack, forces of the Brotherhood Alliance—which grouped the Arakan Army, Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA)—and allied groups entered Hopang with little resistance. Rather than holding the town themselves, they quickly handed it over to their ally, the UWSA.

Operation 1027, which inflicted one of the most devastating military setbacks in the Myanmar military’s history, had begun on Oct. 27, 2023, in Chinshwehaw, a border town just 8 km from Hopang. Just 19 km away, Kunlong, a key town on a China-Myanmar trade route, also fell after sustained drone attacks by alliance forces.

As Kunlong collapsed, its commander, officers and wounded soldiers fled to Hopang.

“A battalion commander and a soldier entered the monastery building and pleaded for shelter,” recalled a witness who was in the compound. “They told the abbot they had been under drone attacks for four days, and had only managed to retreat after receiving supporting fire.”

That same night, drones struck the monastery.

For Hopang residents, who had watched the fighting around Kunlong from hilltop pagodas, the attack on the monastery signaled that war was coming closer. By the next morning, many were fleeing the town, leaving their homes and shops behind.

Some local drivers found themselves ferrying displaced families back and forth, while others stayed behind to guard their properties. Residents feared not only a potential urban battle similar to the fighting in Kunlong, but also the prospect of Myanmar military airstrikes.

One restaurant owner recalled watching looters load crates of beer from his shop onto vehicles through CCTV cameras while he was fleeing.

Among those who fled were a monk who was injured in the November 13 drone attack, as well as health workers from a public hospital in Hopang.

Hopang was home to a military battalion and a police station, but all the surrounding towns including Kunlong and Chinshwehaw were controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance. At this point, Hopang was effectively isolated.

When MNDAA troops entered Hopang in early January 2024, the remaining military and police units reportedly surrendered with little resistance. Under a prior arrangement between the MNDAA and the UWSA, control of the town was then transferred to the Wa army.

Unlike Lashio, Laukkai, Chinshwehaw or Kunlong, Hopang largely escaped major battle damage. Yet residents say the town has since undergone a different kind of transformation, one increasingly shaped by Chinese capital and Wa administration.

The ethnically diverse town, home to Shan, Wa, Bamar, Kachin, Ta’ang and other communities, was once known for its Buddhist, Christian and traditional ethnic festivals. Today, residents say casinos, bars, hotels, massage parlors and prostitution-related businesses funded by Chinese investors have proliferated.

Some residents also complain of heavy taxation and a justice system that includes public executions, practices rarely seen under previous administrations.

The yuan now dominates much of the local economy, with residents increasingly pricing goods in the Chinese currency rather than kyats. In the healthcare arena, expensive Chinese-run private hospitals have emerged alongside the only public hospital.

Over the past three years, rumors have repeatedly surfaced that the UWSA will return Hopang to the regime. Residents say they see no sign that this is imminent, however.

The town, which participated in the 2010, 2015 and 2020 elections, did not take part in the regime-organized 2025 poll and is absent from the list of constituencies scheduled to be put to a vote in additional elections scheduled for April 2027.

Recently, regime Defense Minister and peace negotiator Lieutenant General Yar Pyae visited Panghsang, the UWSA headquarters. There was no indication that Hopang’s status was discussed during his meetings with Wa leaders, however.

While the UWSA remained officially neutral during Operation 1027, it emerged among the campaign’s biggest beneficiaries. Without openly joining the offensive, it gained full control of Hopang and Panlong, while also securing partial control along with the Myanmar military over Tangyan, a strategically important town on the route to Lashio, the largest town in northern Shan.

Three years after the first drone bombs fell on Hopang, the town has changed beyond recognition for longtime residents.

During Operation 1027, the MNDAA and TNLA went on to seize almost the whole of northern Shan State including the capital Lashio and all vital trade routes with China.

However, under strong Chinese pressure, in 2025 the ethnic armies were forced to halt fighting the Myanmar military and hand back several liberated towns to the regime.

World.title: Myanmar’s Coup President Barred From Upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit
World.content:
The Philippines announced Wednesday that Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from joining the 49th ASEAN summit and high-level meetings in Manila from November 15 to 17, upholding a ban imposed after the 2021 military coup.

Myanmar will instead be represented by the Director-General of its ASEAN affairs department, according to a statement issued by Manila’s Department of Foreign Affairs.

“We welcome this official confirmation that there is no place [at the summit] for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing,” Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights foundation, told The Irrawaddy.

“ASEAN made the right decision in line with its principles. We have been demanding that no junta member be permitted to join the summit.”

She added that ASEAN would have sacrificed its credibility and responsibility to the people of Myanmar by inviting the junta leader, who faces a genocide ruling at the international court later this month.

Confirmation that the ban remains in place came after domestic and international rights groups warned the regional bloc against legitimizing a regime that is intensifying violence against civilians.

On Monday, the Special Advisory Council for Myanmar (SAC-M) and ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights urged regional leaders “to immediately confirm” that Min Aung Hlaing and his junta cohorts would be excluded from the summit.

It also called on ASEAN leaders to adopt “measurable benchmarks for compliance” with the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC), along with “a series of escalating punitive steps” if the junta continues to defy the peace plan.

Regime leaders were barred from regional summits for failing to implement the April 2021 consensus, including an immediate end to violence and constructive dialogue with the opposition.

The regime largely ignored the 5PC before formally rejecting it in a July 2026 vote by its rubber-stamp parliament. However, it continues to pay lip service to the plan.

During his latest talks with ASEAN special envoy Theresa Lazaro in Naypyitaw in October, Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe claimed the regime was implementing the 5PC “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives.”

The UN reports that at least 8,384 civilians have been killed by regime forces since the coup, in an escalating military campaign that has also left over 4 million displaced. Meanwhile, nearly 23,000 political prisoners remain in detention, including deposed democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

However, ASEAN members began bilateral engagement with the regime after it rebranded in civilian clothing in April following elections widely condemned as a sham. Since then, coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been invited on official visits to bloc members Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Malaysia.

Both Malaysia—once a vocal critic of the regime—and Thailand drew widespread condemnation from rights groups for hosting the junta leader.

Both nations defended the visits as pragmatic re-engagement in search of solutions to challenges they face, such as refugee repatriation for Malaysia and transborder issues for Thailand.

Critics have warned that bi-lateral engagement may sway a collective ASEAN decision to reintegrate the regime.

However, the move to uphold the summit ban marks a major setback for a junta desperate for legitimacy on the international stage.

“This is a huge blow to the junta. I am sure it has not expected this kind of decision,” Khin Ohmar commented. “It also signals that the junta’s election farce failed to confer legitimacy, since even those advocating its return to the international stage want to avoid being seen as complicit in its violence.”

World.title: Myanmar Junta Seeks Record Military Budget as Millions Struggle With Poverty
World.content:
The Myanmar regime plans to increase the military budget to a record high for the 2026-27 fiscal year, even as approximately one-third of the country’s population lives in poverty.

Since 2021, the regime has been waging war against several established ethnic armed organizations as well as newly emerged resistance forces, including the People’s Defense Force, across the country, spending a large portion of its budget on military expenses.

Last Thursday, the regime’s rubber-stamp Union Parliament (Pyidaungsu Hluttaw), where the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and its allies hold a majority of seats, debated a supplementary budget allocation bill.

The proposed allocation would bring total defense spending to 10.53 trillion kyats (US$5.01 billion), combining the initial 2026-27 fiscal year estimate of 7.95 trillion kyats with a supplementary grant of 2.58 trillion kyats.

Chit Swe, an Upper House lawmaker representing Ayeyarwady Region’s Constituency No. 11 and first deputy chair of the Joint Public Accounts Committee, urged parliament on November 5 to approve the regime’s proposed budgets, including the record-high military budget.

He said the committee had only eight days to verify the budget, with some items requiring ground observation, and that at least two weeks would be needed for verification.

If the supplementary allocations are approved, the budget deficit is projected to surge from 8.98 trillion kyats to 11.41 trillion kyats, he stated.

The military budget has surged continuously since the coup.

Under the last civilian government, led by ousted democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, defense expenditure for the 2020-21 fiscal year stood at just 3.4 trillion kyats.

In the 2023-24 fiscal year, it increased to over 5.6 trillion kyats. Although defense expenditures for the remaining years were not officially released, the current budget figures show that spending has nearly doubled compared to 2023-24.

Meanwhile, approximately 17.9 million people are “multidimensionally poor”, while two-thirds of the population are either poor or at risk, according to a UN Development Programme (UNDP) report published on October 8.

After five years of military regime rule, Myanmar people continue to suffer from soaring prices of basic goods and living costs amid the civil war, and face personal safety and security concerns.

Although the budget is still in draft form, the proposed military expenditure has drawn widespread criticism from the public.

“The budgets that should be spent on the country’s education, health, social welfare and nation-building are instead being used to kill the people,” said Naung Yoe, a military defector who now works with the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute (MDSI), a research institute.

According to the MDSI, the Directorate of Defense Industries, which manufactures ammunition and aerial bombs used in the regime’s indiscriminate attacks, has consumed the largest share of the military’s budget since the coup.

“It is deeply tragic and unfortunate,” he said.

World.title: Mideast Crisis Fuels Oil Conflict in Myanmar’s Heartland
World.content:
Myanmar’s small-scale oil prospectors are under fire from all sides as rebels and the military battle to capture a cottage industry that is becoming increasingly lucrative amid the ongoing Middle East crisis.

“As long as we work here, bad luck can kill us,” said Htun Aung, a worker on an oil well in Myanmar’s arid heartlands.

“But if the reality of death is hard to face, then making a living is even harder,” said the 52-year-old, speaking under a pseudonym for security reasons.
