World.title: Special forces officers convicted of assaulting protesters jailed for five years each
World.content:
Special forces officers jailed for assaults

A court has sentenced special forces officers convicted of physically assaulting journalist Guram Rogava and protester Zviad Maisashvili during demonstrations in November and December 2024 to five years in prison each.

The special forces officer convicted of assaulting Guram Rogava, a journalist with Formula TV, was also banned from professional duties for three years. Lasha Gamkrelidze, the new prosecutor in the case, informed the journalist of the verdict by telephone.

According to Formula, Rogava had expected to testify as a victim during the trial. However, the prosecutor explained that his testimony was unnecessary because the court and the defence had accepted the charges as undisputed. Rogava himself believes that the person who directly assaulted him remains at large.

Two other special forces officers arrested in connection with the assault on Zviad Maisashvili were each sentenced to five years in prison. Lawyer Dimitri Mchedlishvili confirmed the information to Tabula.

On 30 November 2024, at around 06:30, special forces officers kicked Zviad Maisashvili in the face during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, causing him to lose consciousness. Footage of the assault circulated on social media.

On 7 May 2026, Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office announced that it had identified and detained five people in connection with assaults on Rogava, Maisashvili and opposition politician Levan Khabeishvili.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, four of those detained were current or former special forces officers, while the fifth was a serving officer with the Interior Ministry’s Security Police Department. Two of the suspects were already serving prison sentences at the time of their arrest.

Prosecutors said that on 29 November 2024, during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, an officer from the Interior Ministry’s Special Tasks Department assaulted Guram Rogava while the journalist was carrying out his professional duties.

The detainees were charged under Article 333(3) of the Criminal Code with abuse of official powers involving violence. The officer detained in connection with the assault on Rogava also faced an additional charge of unlawfully obstructing a journalist’s professional activities.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office’s initial statement, the charges carried prison sentences of five to eight years.

Maisashvili said both special forces officers detained over the assault on him had admitted their guilt and apologised to him.

Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili

Background

The assaults on Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili were among several high-profile incidents of police violence during pro-European protests in Tbilisi in November and December 2024.

The protests began on 28 November 2024, after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that the government would take the issue of opening EU accession talks off the agenda until the end of 2028.

In the following days, law enforcement officers used water cannon, tear gas and other crowd-control measures against protesters on Rustaveli Avenue and near the parliament building. Numerous incidents of physical violence against demonstrators, journalists and human rights defenders were documented.

Both protesters and members of the media sustained injuries during the demonstrations. The assault on journalist Guram Rogava attracted particular attention. On 29 November 2024, a special forces officer attacked Rogava while he was reporting live from Rustaveli Avenue, leaving him seriously injured.

Media representatives and human rights organisations called for investigations into these incidents. On 30 November 2024, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) said the police’s use of water cannon, pepper spray and batons, including against peaceful demonstrators and journalists, had been disproportionate.

According to Georgia’s Public Defender’s 2024 report, the ombudsman and his representatives visited 624 people who had been detained or injured during protests between 15 April 2024 and 1 March 2025. Of those, 360 reported ill-treatment.

The report also noted that no police officers had been held accountable for violence committed by law enforcement personnel during that period.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office statement of 7 May 2026, more than 550 witnesses were questioned and thousands of investigative and procedural actions were carried out as part of the investigations into the cases involving Zviad Maisashvili, Levan Khabeishvili and Guram Rogava.

The Prosecutor’s Office said the investigations would continue to identify other possible perpetrators and bring them to justice.

World.title: Weekly review of prices for Azeri Light, Dated Brent, and Urals
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. This week (November 9-13), average prices for Azeri Light (CIF), Azeri Light (FOB Ceyhan), Urals, and Dated Brent crude decreased.

According to Trend’s calculations, based on data from oil market participants, the average price of Azeri Light (CIF) crude, produced at the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli field in Azerbaijan, fell by $9.51, or 8.6%, compared to the previous week, to $100.70 per barrel.

According to the report, the highest price for this grade of crude oil during the week was $102.68 per barrel, while the lowest was $99.40.

The average price of Azeri Light crude on a FOB basis at the Turkish port of Ceyhan was $96.53 per barrel, which is $6.99, or 6.7%, lower than the previous week’s figure. During the week, the maximum price was $98.79 per barrel, and the minimum was $95.13.

The average price of Urals crude dropped by $7.01, or 9.2%, compared to the previous week, to $69.31 per barrel. During the week, the highest price was $72.20, and the lowest was $67.30.

Dated Brent crude averaged $92.64 per barrel, down $7.82, or 7.8%, from the previous week. During the week, the price reached a high of $96.11 per barrel and a low of $90.56.

World.title: Azerbaijani gymnast wins bronze medal at World Championships in China
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. Azerbaijani gymnast Ammar Bakhsaliyev has achieved a historic success at the World Junior Trampoline Gymnastics Championships, currently being held in Nanjing, China.

According to the Azerbaijan Gymnastics Federation, the Azerbaijani representative, competing in the individual event, scored 54.850 points in the qualification round and advanced to the final in sixth place.

Ammar Bakhsaliyev continued his successful performance in the final, scoring 55.450 points to claim the bronze medal. The gold medal was won by a gymnast from Japan, while the silver went to a representative of Türkiye.

This result marks a milestone in the history of Azerbaijani trampoline gymnastics. Ammar Bakhsaliyev has thus become the first Azerbaijani trampoline gymnast to win an individual medal at the World Junior Championships.

World.title: Tajikistan’s CO2 emissions rise 14.2% in 2025 - Eni
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. Tajikistan’s carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions increased by 14.2% in 2025, while the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over the 2015–2025 period stood at 8.6%, according to Italian energy company Eni’s World Energy Review 2026.

Eni’s data show that the country’s CO2 emissions amounted to 4.2 million tonnes in 2015 and 6.9 million tonnes in 2019. Emissions then rose to 7.3 million tonnes in 2020, 7.4 million tonnes in 2021, 7.6 million tonnes in 2022 and 7.8 million tonnes in 2023, before reaching 8.9 million tonnes in 2024. The company did not provide an absolute figure for 2025.

For comparison, the regional indicator for Russia and Central Asia rose by 3.1% in 2025, with a CAGR of 1.8% for 2015–2025, according to Eni.

Regional CO2 emissions amounted to 1,941 million tonnes in 2015 and 2,025 million tonnes in 2019. They then declined to 1,963 million tonnes in 2020, before rising to 2,151 million tonnes in 2021 and 2,153 million tonnes in 2022. Emissions kept rising, reaching 2,208 million tonnes in 2023 and 2,276 million tonnes in 2024. Eni did not provide an absolute figure for 2025.

Eni also reported that Tajikistan’s population reached 10.8 million in 2025, compared with 10.6 million in 2024. The country’s population increased by 1.8% year-on-year, while its CAGR for 2015–2025 was 2.2%.

According to the report, Tajikistan’s population stood at 8.6 million in 2015 and 9.5 million in 2019. It then rose to 9.7 million in 2020, 10 million in 2021, 10.2 million in 2022 and 10.4 million in 2023, before reaching 10.6 million in 2024 and 10.8 million in 2025.

World.title: Kakadu artist's 'rock art' paintings in high demand
World.content:
Sitting at a table in a tiny art gallery nestled inside Kakadu National Park, Blaldja artist Ivan Namarnyilk slowly paints precise, thin strokes with his manyilk, a traditional brush made of sedge grass.

But before Namarnyilk even has the chance to finish his pieces, tourists visiting the Marrawuddi Arts and Culture Centre in Jabiru are asking to buy them.

"I'm not a machine," he jokes.

"You gotta be patient, no rushing. We gotta be steady."

Ivan Namarnyilk says his art is "like the country, the animals, the people, everything has connection". (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Taught by his father, a fellow prominent artist at Mudginberri Station, Namarnyilk has been painting "rock art" on paper since he was a teenager.

More than three decades on, Namarnyilk is keeping his culture alive by passing it on to the next generation.

"My art is really, really special," he says.

"It's really special for me and for my future kids.

" Today we [are] using all this new, modern style but the original was like the rock art. "

Known for his detailed, x-ray style works, Namarnyilk mainly uses ochre to paint or scratch-draw local animals and cultural totems before applying his signature, mouth-blown clay handprint.

Ivan Namarnyilk’s art uses natural ochres along with his signature hand print. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"We use natural colour like red ochre, white clay, yellow ochre," he says.

"I like painting spirit man, kangaroo, echidna, turtle, fish like barramundi or black bream.

"We respect our totems — my father's totem is irritja [wedge-tailed eagle] and my mother's is duwa [mud crab]."

In August, Namarnyilk sold thousands of dollars worth of his art at his first solo exhibition during the Mahbilil Festival in Jabiru.

Ivan Namarnyilk held his first solo exhibition at the Mahbilil Festival in August. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

He says sharing his pieces was "really special" and vital for helping to financially support his family.

"I like helping my community," he says.

" I like painting; it's really, really important because to me, it's like the country, the animals, the people, everything has connection [in] our culture. "

A different style

Over the past 25 years, more than 500 West Arnhem Indigenous artists have sold pieces at the Marrawuddi Arts and Culture Centre.

Business manager Caron Farrell says the gallery buys artwork "up-front" from about 30 regular makers, with 40 per cent of sales proceeds going towards keeping the centre open.

Caron Farrell says "visitors are quite taken aback to the different styles" on display. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"This space does all of West Arnhem so it's really important for the artists to be able to bring their art here in all different forms," she says.

" A lot of the artists are a long way from us, so the art will be brought in by plane or by family members. The regular artists that live within Jabiru or Mudginberri, they will come here and paint. "

Ms Farrell says it's a treat for holiday-makers passing through Jabiru to watch the artists paint, scratch, draw and weave onsite, before taking the pieces back to their homes all around the world.

Demand for Ivan Namarnyilk’s pieces has never been higher, with the proceeds helping to support his family and the gallery. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"It's really important for Jabiru to get the tourists in and keep this place going for that art to be in homes," she says.

"I think they get a bit shocked of how much there is and how vast the art is, like [it's] a little bit different say to central desert, the style.

"Obviously, West Arnhem, it's art that you see on all the rock formations, compared to say, central desert, where it's the dot painting.

"You find visitors are quite taken aback to the different styles that are here."

World.title: Worrying signs as Wallabies leave it too late to fire in Scotland defeat
World.content:
It might be unfair to be overly critical about the Wallabies' latest defeat, this time to Scotland at Murrayfield.

Its narrow nature, 15-12, is one aspect.

The conditions too have to be considered.

Scotland beat Wallabies in desperate, dour Murrayfield arm-wrestle The Wallabies fall to a fourth straight defeat as Scotland claims a 15-12 victory in a dour display at Murrayfield.

This was an afternoon of such monochrome dreariness that even Scotland couldn't muster much of their usual attacking verve, dank and grey, the lingering firework smoke above the playing surface reminiscent of some primordial Celtic realm

It was far removed from the bright lights of Friday night in Paris or Saturday afternoon in Cardiff.

Opposing skippers Rory Darge and Harry Wilson both referred to the game as descending into an arm-wrestle, though at times the contest we witnessed was so bad that calling it as such would almost be cruel to practitioners of that maligned pastime.

But then again, autumnal Scottish afternoons are just not what the proponents of free-flowing, attacking rugby union had in mind as ideal conditions for their craft.

Les Kiss said as much to UK broadcaster ITV, describing the game as "turgid".

"I think [Gregor Townsend] and I both would have preferred some drier weather," he added.

Both teams struggled to hold onto the ball in cold and wet conditions. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Undoubtedly, the conditions were reflected in the Scottish play as the hosts produced a litany of errors, most of which were a by-product of a series of over-complicated running lines that looked perfect when drawn up in the dryness and warmth of the training rooms, but less so when countered by the freezing rain and fast-pressing Wallabies defence.

That defence is worth pointing out as a positive.

The Wallabies had conceded seven tries in each of its previous three games, letting 138 points be scored against them. Shipping just two against Scotland marked a huge improvement.

But neither side hit the attacking heights both are capable of — a familiar failing of this Wallabies team at present.

Where the Scots limitations seemed a result of over complication, the Wallabies' attacking limits were self-imposed by the bland simplicity of their game plan.

Things started relatively well despite the tricky conditions.

Scotland barged their way up to the Wallabies line and spun the ball wide to an unmarked Matt Fagerson to open the scoring.

Matt Fagerson scored the opening try. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol)

The Wallabies went up the other end and hit back immediately, Harry Potter finishing a move started by Carter Gordon's driving surge.

This was what the Wallabies didn't have against England; the fly half taking charge, double-pumping the pass as he approached the line before releasing Jeremy Williams, Len Ikitau and finally Potter to score.

A solid move, well constructed, well finished.

It took the best part of an hour before we saw anything of the like again from the men in gold.

Between times, fans were subject to a dour attacking display whenever the Wallabies had the ball in hand, the visitors relentlessly forced to retreat back up field before either kicking the ball away or flat-out losing it.

One-out runners with no passing, no speed in the back line movement, no width, no use of the thrilling attacking talents at their disposal, no way through the walls of Scottish defenders.

One of the most desperate passages came with about quarter of an hour remaining.

The Wallabies had forced a line out just outside the Scotland 22, a rare attacking chance. But through 18 phases of bland hit ups with little to no imagination the Wallabies went backwards a handful of metres, and then lost the ball to a Scotland turnover.

A kind observation would have been that the Wallabies were being patient, taking their time to find an opening in a Scottish defence that had significantly tightened its leash.

A less kind one would be that it was clueless and uninventive, destined to fail.

The Wallabies struggled to make anything happen with the ball in hand. (AP Photo: Scott Heppell)

Neither side had anything like clean ball, a litany of errors plaguing the contest in the loose, with the chaotic breakdown simply adding to the confused display from both teams.

But the Wallabies showed they can attack when they want to, adding to the frustration of what had gone before.

Ben Donaldson came onto the field, shifting Gordon to centre and immediately made an impact, passing wide and giving the visitors the impetus to attack.

With almost his first phase of play, Donaldson immediately looked to move the ball wide, moving laterally at pace to open the Scotland defence — perhaps running himself into a starters spot in Cardiff next week.

Later, Donaldson spun the ball wide to Williams, whose flick pass out the back of the hand released Jorgensen to scoot down the line and score.

As the clock ticked into the red, the ball was again spun wide, Tate McDermott and Harry Wilson releasing Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, almost a non-entity both this week and last in an attacking sense but finally running with the ball in hand.

Jorgensen and Tom Wright were both involved before the later was bundled into touch, the gun-shy Wallabies now firing from the hip with alacrity.

Suaalii. Jorgensen. Wright. These names had barely been mentioned all game.

Tom Wright and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii were barely seen in an attacking sense. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol)

By the time they were, it was far too late.

Again, perhaps it's unfair to judge the Wallabies too harshly for a sour outing in which both teams struggled to rouse themselves from their mutual stupor.

So attention should shift to Wales, who now awaits inside the Principality Stadium next Sunday (AEDT).

The roof in Cardiff means "conditions" is not an excuse that can be laid down in case of another attacking no-show.

But Wales's defence may yet be just as stingy as it was against the All Blacks, where the Welsh made a stunning 346 tackles.

For reference, Scotland (154) and the Wallabies (194) combined to make 348 at Murrayfield.

The Wallabies have one more chance to prove they are moving in the right direction.

They would do well to find a way to unleash their attacking weapons before it's too late.

World.title: Labor urged to address fire station delays months before fatal blaze
World.content:
The Geelong council wrote to the state government just months before a fatal Armstrong Creek house fire, urging it to take greater responsibility for delays in delivering a promised fire station for the major growth area.

On Saturday, an Armstrong Creek house fire killed a 65-year-old man, eight years after the state government pledged to build a new fire station in the area as "an absolute priority" following a fatal house fire in the suburb in 2017.

Police officers and an SES vehicle near the scene of the fatal weekend house fire. (ABC News)

The latest death came just days after the ABC questioned the state government about the failure to deliver the promised fire station.

An unattributed response from the government last week claimed progress on the development of the station was "facing delays due to council and service authorities approval" at the government's preferred Boundary Rd site.

But a letter seen by the ABC shows City of Greater Geelong CEO Ali Wastie wrote to the emergency services minister in June urging the government to take responsibility for delays.

City of Greater Geelong CEO Ali Wastie urged the Victorian government to take responsibility for the fire station site. (ABC News: Jedda Costa)

"The Victorian government's decision to acquire and seek to develop this land significantly ahead of neighbouring properties has created foreseeable and well understood constraints, most critically, the absence of coordinated servicing infrastructure, including drainage," Ms Wastie wrote.

"The Victorian government has elected to purchase and pursue development of a site that was not yet ready for delivery.

"It is therefore neither accurate nor appropriate to suggest that the city is responsible for the consequences of that decision."

Ms Wastie wrote the letter responding to government assertions the City of Greater Geelong was responsible for delays in delivering the project.

"The city categorically rejects these claims," Ms Wastie wrote. "It is essential that public commentary reflects the reality of the situation and that accountability sits where responsibility properly lies."

Geelong CEO and mayor call for action

Just two days before the weekend's fatal house fire, Premier Ben Carroll was questioned about undelivered election promises — including the fire station — during a visit to Geelong.

Mr Carroll travelled to Geelong on Thursday for a transport announcement, where the ABC was able to directly ask why Geelong residents should trust that the latest round of election promises would be kept.

Ben Carroll was questioned about the fire station and undelivered promises just days before the fatal fire. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

"I'm asking the people to look at what I've delivered in three months," Mr Carroll said, before spruiking his delivery of the Big Build Royal Commission.

"Yes, we could always do better. We can always do more.

"But I've made it very clear that I'll be a financially responsible premier, socially progressive and also deliver services that I know that people of Geelong need."

Speaking on Sunday, Ms Wastie said she felt the government's blaming of the city for delays to the project had "been inherent for some time".

Ms Wastie said a lack of funding for the project in the state government's latest budget was particularly concerning.

"Council officers have met with Fire Rescue Victoria (FRV) officers as recently as last month and they confirmed at that meeting that they have no budget to deliver a fire station at Armstrong Creek," Ms Wastie said.

"We're not interested in blaming anyone, we just want to make good on this progress for a fire station in Armstrong Creek.

"These assets need to come on in a timely way, and for this one that needs to be an absolute priority for the incoming government."

Geelong Mayor Stretch Kontelj said he wanted it to be clear that the city was not holding the project up.

Stretch Kontelj says the new fire station will save lives. (ABC News)

"The government bought land in a paddock that hadn't yet been developed, and hasn't got all the services, or hasn't got any services in it, and as far as I understand that land hasn't been settled as far as the purchase is concerned yet," Cr Kontelj said.

"They can't be blaming council for that [delay]."

Cr Kontelj said it was time to "put the blame game to one side" and get the fire station built.

"We all recognise that that fire station needs to be built as soon as possible, Armstrong creek is the fastest growing area of Geelong, and it's a facility that literally will help save lives," he said.

"We just need to take the politics out of it and get it done … because we know that lives are at risk as long as it's not built."

Emergency services outside an Armstrong Creek on Boxing Day 2017, following a fatal house fire. (ABC News)

The ABC on Sunday sent questions to the state Labor Party regarding the delivery of the fire station.

A comment attributed to a Labor spokesperson was supplied.

"This was a tragic incident and our thoughts are with this man's family and friends," the spokesperson said.

Further unattributed comments noted the party's belief Armstrong Creek was "well served and well protected" by nearby CFA and FRV brigades.

Peter Marshall says plans for the Armstrong Creek station have been repeatedly delayed. (ABC News: Leanne Wong)

United Firefighters Union (UFU) secretary Peter Marshall said fire crews were paged to attend the Armstrong Creek house fire at 2.54am on Saturday morning, with a CFA crew from neighbouring suburb Grovedale arriving at 3:05am — 11 minutes later.

An FRV crew from Belmont arrived at 3:07am, he said.

"Where the fire station was supposed to be built is only four-and-a-half kilometres away from this particular event," Mr Marshall said.

" One can only conclude the outcome would have been very different. "

A fire truck is currently parked behind temporary fencing across the road from the Armstrong Creek land earmarked for the new station, in what has been referred to as a makeshift fire station.

World.title: Live: Wall Street slides as Nvidia pulls down tech stocks, ASX treading water
World.content:
Wall Street's third quarter results season has almost wrapped up — bar two of the most significant events in recent times.

Nvidia, the erstwhile "most valuable" company on the planet — around which the fortunes of so many AI players orbit — is spinning a bit off its axis and the market is hoping things will stabilise with a strong result on Tuesday.

On Thursday, trading in Claude chatbot creator Anthropic is expected to begin, setting up a real-time barometer for sentiment on the AI trade.

"The market has rose-coloured glasses on almost all the risks," including inflation and the war in Iran, in addition to uncertainty over AI, Wells Fargo investment boss Sameer Samana.

Mr Samana said disappointments this week "could finally kind of wake investors up from this ability to look at every glass as half full."

The twin worries of Nvidia's position at the heart of the AI's circular and massive investment boom and the departure of its polestar/rock-star CEO Jensen Huang in rather unseemly circumstances has seen the chipmaker's value fall from about $US5.8 trillion in early October to $US3.9 trillion as of Friday.

Analysts expect earnings growth of 90% on revenue of $109 billion in the company's fiscal third quarter. If that's not at least met, then stand clear.

Anthropic's initial public offering is set to value the company at up to $US1.4 trillion, as the AI lab and some of its investors aim to raise up to $US64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares.

Anthropic's Nasdaq listing comes on the heels of the high-profile June IPO for Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $US75 billion at a nearly $1.75 trillion valuation.

Big retailers will also feature this week with Walmart, Target, Home Depot and Lowe's all posting results will give insights into how consumer spending is holding up in the face of mounting inflation.

With Reuters

World.title: Data centres become dirty word as rollout faces rising opposition
World.content:
Data centres store and process information.

But right now they're doing much more: they're at the centre of concern about how much their construction is stoking inflation.

And, they're a lightning rod for communities rising up against what they feel is the cost of rapid growth.

"Over the last year, we've obviously seen an absolute explosion in our pipeline," IBISWorld research analyst Andrew Ledovskikh says.

His research has found Australia currently has about 2.3 gigawatts (GW) worth of power capacity in 79 data centres.

That's enough to power about 1.5 million homes, depending how you work the numbers.

Planned projects would give Australia capacity estimated to be more than 10 times that — between 23 and 67GW — according to the Australian Energy Market Operator.

Not all projects make it, and Commonwealth Bank research forecasts 9GW of capacity by 2035.

Data centre capacity is expected to grow rapidly. (Supplied: AEMO/CBA)

"We really are just at the beginning. This is the moment where the water sort of recedes back into the beach and everything's calm before the tsunami hits," Mr Ledovskikh said.

For advocates such as Belinda Dennett, it's an "enormous opportunity", with a construction timeline supporting our economy.

Belinda Dennett believes building data centres can help transform Australia's economy. (ABC News: Jack Ailwood)

Lamenting that "we've missed other global technology waves", Ms Dennett said this boom was a chance to "build on our advantages in cheap renewable energy".

"That comes at a $4.1 billion opportunity a year," she said.

"We can transform our economy and ensure Australia's future prosperity."

For opponents such as Judy Gunson, however, the mushrooming sites are an "invasion" of neighbourhoods.

" It's very obvious that the people doing this don't care about local communities," she said. "We want a pause. "

Issue rockets onto political radar

In recent years, data centres have become a magnet for controversy in Europe and the US over the impact of noise, light and sheer size of the centres on neighbouring properties.

Then there are environmental and economic concerns, because they use, and drive up, the cost of water and power.

Opponents are winning new fights:

More than 40 proposals against data centres were on the ballot in the US midterms, and the overwhelming majority passed.

The Victorian planning minister failed to approve or deny nine new data centre projects before the government went into "caretaker" mode ahead of this month's election, meaning "no decision" was the decision.

Communities in New South Wales have stopped two large data centre proposals in recent months.

US-based political scientist David McCuan has seen this issue take off, and quickly.

"They've caught fire across the country," he said.

" You would not have expected this issue to be on the radar more than a year ago. "

An expert in political science at Sonoma State University, Professor McCuan said the backlash to the rapid growth of the centres meant there was "bipartisan" opposition in recent elections.

Anti-data centre demonstrators have had significant success in the US. (AP: Marc Levy)

Anti-data centre measures were on the ballot in more than 40 different jurisdictions in the midterms.

A temporary ban, called a moratorium, is in place in New York and Texas has paused connections to the electricity grid — effectively stopping development.

"The battle that we see going on over data centres and AI, that unites both [political] sides," Professor McCuan said.

"They've affected a governor's race in Texas, they've affected local issues in zoning for what's going on in Ohio or in the Midwest. That's not something we would have forecast, say, eight, 10, 12 months ago."

That speed is being replicated in Australia.

Communities protest as data centres rise

Judy Gunson is fired up about the energy use of data centres.

"It just filled me with terror, actually," she said.

"The potential to derail any slow progress we're making towards reducing [carbon] emissions by this rollout, which is using extraordinary amounts of power."

We're standing in the shadow of the Westgate Bridge, next to Melbourne's busy container port.

What used to be the printing plant for the Herald Sun newspaper is being cleared for a massive data centre, to be built by NEXTDC.

Judy Gunson is a spokeswoman for the Port Melbourne data centre action group. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

The community activist is protesting the build, concerned about the speedy pace and enormous scale of data centre construction.

" This one's gonna be eight storeys tall … The one in Plumpton [Melbourne's north-west] is 3 kilometres square. "

Communities in Sydney and Launceston are just some of those that have objected to development of the centres.

And it's having an effect.

A dispute about power poles hit plans for the expansion of an existing NEXTDC site in the inner-west of Melbourne.

The fight wiped $3 billion off the listed company's value when the share price cratered 42 per cent in one day. The share price recovered after a rival company bought up a huge amount, cheaply.

Fears economy is importing inflation via AI

Then there is the problem of interest rates.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is currently attempting to "cool" the Australian economy by lifting interest rates.

The aim is to lower the speed of prices rising, a force called inflation. Consumer prices are going up by 4.3 per cent annually at the moment.

Along with rocketing fuel prices due to war in the Middle East, the rapid construction of data centres and spending on artificial intelligence (AI) is often slated for overheating our economy and driving up inflation.

An internal RBA note suggests local data centre operators have raised record capital of at least $35 billion so far this year, fuelling rapid construction of AI infrastructure.

That's 46 per cent more than the 2025 figure, and even the central bank thinks it is a conservative guess.

Michele Bullock believes data centre technology is not currently putting pressure on the country's economy. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

In a press conference after the most recent rate hike, RBA governor Michele Bullock said a huge proportion, "maybe 70 per cent", of data centre technology was imported, so was "not putting pressure on the Australian economy and Australian goods and services".

Where it does, she said, is in pushing up prices for scarce construction materials and skilled labourers.

"There is a chunk and it's related to building the warehouses and getting electricians to come in and install the servers and all those sorts of things.

"That does put pressure on Australian resources, and that's where it might be putting inflationary pressure in."

Ms Bullock said the hope was that, over time, data centre investment would lead to gains in productivity, which would ultimately lower inflation.

Loading...

Political problems growing, not fading

For a long time, data centres looked like warehouses and were set in industrial areas.

The hyper-scale push means they're growing far larger and are increasingly encroaching on residential and farming land, which brings developers into conflict with the communities around them.

The Victorian government went into a caretaker period ahead of this month's election, before Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny made a decision on nine contentious data centre projects that had been "fast-tracked" to her office.

People power costs NEXTDC A neighbourhood dispute over power poles has wiped $3 billion from a listed company in a day and made the AI boom a little shakier.

A statement from a Labor spokesperson, after the deadline, said all proposals went through a "rigorous planning process":

" We welcome the jobs and investment data centres bring to Victoria — but we're putting sensible guardrails in place as the industry grows. "

The spokesperson pointed to a policy that required new developments to source their own renewable power and not be near schools.

World.title: Giant hail, heavy rain and damaging winds possible for south-east Qld
World.content:
Severe thunderstorms could bring giant hail, heavy rain and destructive winds to south-east Queensland from midday today, the Bureau of Meteorology warns.

Meteorologist Robert Urbaniak said areas south of Hervey Bay down to the Gold Coast and west towards Toowoomba could be in the firing line.

Giant hail, heavy rain and damaging winds are possible. (ABC News: Charmayne Allison)

"There is a chance for giant hail, which is bigger than 5 centimetres, and intense rainfall and destructive winds greater than 125 kilometres an hour," he said.

"So that's a big storm day; that's pretty impactful."

The bureau said the severe storms were expected to hit from midday and peak between 2pm and 5pm.

"Regular thunderstorms are possible most other places other than the far south-west," Mr Urbaniak said.

Severe heatwave conditions are expected to persist over the coming days. (ABC News: Miriam Mazurek-Kaminska)

Severe heatwave warning continues

A severe heatwave warning remains in place for the Cape York Peninsula, North Tropical Coast and Tablelands districts.

Weipa has recorded its longest stretch of days with temperatures above 36 degrees Celsius, with 41 days as of Sunday.

Mr Urbaniak said this was expected to continue into the coming weekend.

"By the end of the week it might have recorded 48 days with consecutive daily temperatures above 36 degrees, which is absolutely crazy," he said.

A severe heatwave warning is in place for parts of north Queensland. (ABC News: Miriam Mazurek-Kaminska)

Meanwhile in southern parts of the state, temperatures are expected to drop midweek.

"Temperatures will go down to sort of the mid-20s by late this week," Mr Urbaniak said.

Wet and stormy weekend for Qld

The latest forecasts come after a weekend of wet and stormy weather across parts of the state.

Severe storms hit late on Friday and into Saturday morning, particularly around the eastern Darling Downs and near Gatton.

Areas south-west of Toowoomba were drenched by up to 80 millimetres in two hours, with up to 60mm in half an hour near Gatton.

On Sunday, severe storms affected several different regions, including South East Queensland, the Darling Downs, Maranoa and Warrego, Central Highlands and all the way in the state's North West.

Severe storm risks are expected to clear south-east Queensland from Tuesday. (ABC News: Charmayne Allison)

Storms expected to clear SEQ from Tuesday

Mr Urbaniak said severe thunderstorm risks were expected to clear south-east Queensland from Tuesday.

The focus is then expected to shift to the Capricornia Coast and Northern Queensland on Tuesday and Wednesday.

A new trough is forecast to sweep into far-western Queensland on Thursday and Friday.

The bureau said this would bring widespread showers and thunderstorms from the Gulf Country through to Charleville, Augathella and Cunnamulla.

World.title: The US flight saga looked like a clown show. Are there any adults in the room?
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House The US flight saga looked like a clown show. Are there any adults in the room? Michael Koziol November 16, 2026 — 7:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: One of the first stories I covered after Donald Trump’s inauguration was the devastating crash of American Airlines Flight 5342, which collided with a Black Hawk army helicopter on approach to Washington’s city airport. All 67 people on both aircraft died. While bodies and debris were still being pulled from the water, Trump called a news conference and speculated without evidence that diversity, equity and inclusion policies could be to blame. It was premature, reckless, insensitive and wrong. Passengers wait at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as flights are delayed. AP The president took an entirely different approach to the nationwide ground stop that halted air traffic across the US on Friday and is still playing out with delays and cancellations 48 hours later. He did not say anything publicly throughout the crisis, instead posting about the boat crash in New Orleans, California Governor Gavin Newsom, and, most of all, about the redevelopment of a Washington golf course.



It was only on Sunday morning (US time) that Trump commented on the airspace incident, writing on Truth Social that Congress must approve “desperately needed” funding to build a new air traffic control system. As the crisis unfolded, the president had his inexperienced homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, in front of the cameras explaining that “this is not another 9/11”, and scolding reporters for not adopting Trump’s rebranding of AI (“We call it SI, remember,” he told a journalist). Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in the White House briefing room. AP Later, when Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy appeared in the White House briefing room for a news conference on which millions of Americans and others were hanging, it felt as though their main mission was to praise Trump and demand money from Congress. “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” Mullin said. “We’re built to handle crises like this.” Would that it were true.



It took more than five minutes to get to the actual nub of what happened – a router that was playing up and giving inconsistent data, leading technicians to shut down the system. And it took 10 minutes to get to the announcement that the ground stop had actually been lifted. “What is Duffy doing?” observed conservative columnist and former Bush administration speechwriter Marc Thiessen on X. “No one cares about political responsibility right now. They want to know what’s happening, when it will be fixed, and when planes will be flying again!” Loading Things didn’t get off to a great start the next day either. Duffy’s morning-after news conference began late, and the microphones didn’t work properly. He and other officials had to stand around for minutes while tech staff resolved the issue. Steve Bannon, the MAGA commentator and former Trump strategist, was scathing on his TV show as he watched the mess unfold live. “Let me be blunt – when you step up to the mic, the mic’s got to work,” he said.



“People are going to say, ‘Hey, why should we get on planes? We can’t even get the sound right’. We’re about to go through a shredding machine with the Democrats in charge, and people better be on point. Related Article Aviation An old copper wire in the bush: why the US had to shut down its airspace “When you say 10.30[am], stick the landing – let’s have it at 10.30. When you come out, have the sound ready to work. Because now this is going to be the meme.” It looked like a clown show. But tech issues are a small thing. The more sinister part is that it’s difficult to trust anything these administration officials say because their instincts are to praise the leader and deflect blame to others. That’s not what people need in a crisis.



Duffy, when asked why the White House couldn’t get the money for system upgrades from a Congress that has been controlled by Republicans for two years, went down the Trump route and asked the reporter which news outlet she was with. And on Saturday, Duffy was quick to point the finger at telecommunications network owner L3Harris, which performed the maintenance work. That may be the case but, as Duffy himself points out, it is successive US governments that have let the network remain this antiquated for this long. On Sunday, he was asked on CNN why Trump does not speak publicly about air traffic control upgrades as much as, say, his White House ballroom or the Washington golf course, if the issue was so important. Duffy said the president constantly talked to him about it in private. Trump “loves the airspace”, he told CNN. “This is the first president we’ve ever had who cares this much about modernising the airspace.” You can see why Americans might find that difficult to believe. Last year, Trump was blaming DEI hires for air crashes hours after they occurred, and his Department of Government Efficiency was sacking technicians from air traffic control in a cost-cutting exercise. Now he is demanding $US50 billion ($74 billion) for critical upgrades.



Related Article On the ground

Airports Love? No, just thousands of dispirited, stranded passengers, actually Everybody agrees that US air traffic control, radar and weather systems – which still use floppy discs for some functions – need to be modernised. It’s an awful lot of money, but in Duffy’s telling, it would essentially mean building an entire new bespoke system. This is a great test for a president who says that he wants to do deals with the incoming Democratic Congress. It could even be done before the new lawmakers take their seats. It’s on Democrats, too, not to play politics and to engage with the administration in good faith, if that is what’s on offer. But on too many occasions, this is an administration elevates politics and propaganda above competence and compromise. The clowns must become the adults in the room. TechnologyExecutive shake-up Jensen Huang discusses Nvidia return: report Kevin Whitelaw November 16, 2026 — 7:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Ousted Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang is discussing a possible comeback to the company just days after the board of directors pushed him out, the Financial Times reported. Huang, who admitted having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and was reported to have another with an Nvidia vice president, has been discussing the idea of returning as several Silicon Valley allies have begun lobbying for him to come back, the newspaper reported. The Nvidia scandal has just taken another turn. Bloomberg via Getty Images In a social post late last week, Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time” and the uncertainty created by his departure in urging the board to take a “slow, measured, and deliberate” approach to Nvidia’s future leadership. That should include “the potential return of Jensen Huang,” Altimeter’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides’ Gavin Baker wrote in a letter to Nvidia’s board posted on X.



Prior to Huang’s resignation, a longtime Nvidia engineer had urged the board in an internal post to consider employee sentiment before taking any action, according to Wired. The post has since drawn thousands of comments, with several urging the board to find a way to bring Huang back, the technology news platform said, citing internal correspondence it reviewed. Nvidia has about 42,000 employees worldwide. Billionaire Elon Musk separately said on X that a petition was underway to reinstate Huang and that he would sign it. It was not immediately clear whether Musk was referring to the internal effort reported by Wired. Elon Musk said Nvidia would lose “critical” deals without Huang at the helm. AP On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Fox News’s Sunday Morning Futures that Nvidia needs a “dramatic shakeup” in leadership and should go outside the company to find new leadership after a series of accusations that the company facilitated sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese entities. Meanwhile, it was reported that Nvidia’s board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Huang.



Related Article Updated

Billionaires The superchip genius or the big name wildcard? Eight contenders to replace Huang as Nvidia’s CEO Haas’ name has been making the rounds among analysts since Huang’s exit. He spent seven formative years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He is among several candidates being considered and there is no guarantee he will be offered the job or accept it, the FT reported. Nvidia’s finance chief Colette Kress is currently interim CEO. Nvidia’s board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the CEO role and had not formally engaged any potential candidates. “Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature,” the board said in a statement.

Warning: Graphic content London: The British government will discuss plans for a “staggered” age of consent that would stop men of a certain age from having sex with much younger women after the conviction of celebrity Russell Brand for rape. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and colleagues will consider changing consent laws that allow men of any age to have sex with girls over 16, a cabinet minister confirmed, after a judge sentenced Brand to a decade in prison for rape and sexual assault. Russell Brand outside court during his trial. AP Photo/Alberto Pezzali The move also follows allegations against Little Britain comedian and children’s book author David Walliams, who is accused of preying on teenagers and young women. He denies the claims and is facing a police investigation.



The cabinet discussion heightens the national debate over predatory conduct after one of Brand’s accusers called for the law to be changed to make it a criminal offence for a man over 30 to have sex with a girl under the age of 18. Work and Pensions Minister Pat McFadden confirmed that the issue would be discussed in cabinet given the concerns about the treatment of women. David Walliams is being investigated over allegations he preyed on teenagers and young women. He denies the claims. Getty Images “The whole country, last week, has been appalled by the abuse of power by powerful men, and a big age gap can be part of that, can be a factor in that,” he told Sky News on Sunday (UK time). “We probably will consider it, but I can’t give you a result of that at the moment. What we will definitely do is think about whatever we can do to help people at the wrong end of these abuses of power.”



Asked about the issue on the BBC on Sunday, he said: “It’s certainly a question that has been raised and will be discussed.” The government has already pledged to change the law on non-disclosure agreements after some of Walliams’ accusers said they had received threatening legal letters that stopped them warning others about him. Mia Latter has accused Russell Brand of rape. Getty Images for Academy Museum of Motion Pictures Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones said last week it “should not be possible” for people in positions of power to use injunctions or NDAs to prevent people going public to reveal abuse. Consent laws in the UK were changed in 1885 to raise the age of consent for girls from 13 to 16. Later changes brought the age into line for males and females, as well as for gay and straight sex.



Brand was sentenced to nine years in prison after a jury found him guilty of raping a 21-year-old woman at his home in 2009, when he was 34. The woman told Southwark Crown Court that they had begun having consensual sex but that he had “flipped” her over and anally raped her despite her telling him to stop. Brand was also found guilty of three counts of sexual assault, taking his prison sentence to 10 years and six months, and he was acquitted of two charges of rape. View post on X The Metropolitan Police confirmed last week they were investigating other claims against Brand, including some aired by the Sunday Times and Channel 4 in 2023. The women who testified in the court case were separate from those in the 2023 reports. One of those who spoke to the media three years ago, Mia Latter, chose to waive her anonymity on the weekend by telling the Sunday Times of her claims against Brand.



Latter said she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and he was 30 after she had met him and gave him her number while shopping in Leicester Square in central London. Related Article Graphic content

Courts More women accuse Russell Brand of sexual misconduct as police pursue fresh allegations She said she told him her age, but he invited her to dinner and referred to her as “the child” in front of his entourage. “He was a very successful man who had a lot of power and sway in the industry,” she told the Sunday Times. “Whereas I was a 16-year-old with no life experience, no sexual experience and no prior relationships. What was my level of maturity meant to be?”



Latter, now 37, said she =suffered as a mother and sister as a result of Brand’s conduct. She was known as “Alice” when she spoke to the media three years ago. Related Article Courts Police investigating children’s author and Little Britain star David Walliams for sex offences “I don’t want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other,” she told the newspaper. “If you’re between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. “But… if you’re in your thirties, forties and fifties and you’re trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence.”

World.title: Huge pop stars lived in my suburb, but there are other reasons to love it
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Come walk with me through Scarborough, as blissful a place as you might find. It won’t take long, for it’s not a huge slab of land. It’s actually only a fragment of the larger Redcliffe Peninsula, the seaside locale to Brisbane’s north-east where two bridges – one named for the famed engineer Manuel Hornibrook, the other for the WWI veteran Ted Smout – shoot across Hays Inlet in Bramble Bay. Like any peninsula, Scarborough has water on three sides, with the ceaseless ripples of Moreton Bay kissing its beaches. In earlier days, no Scarborough building was taller than the Norfolk pines. Morgan Roberts Scarborough Marina. Morgan Roberts As majestic as that sounds – and there’s plenty of natural beauty to celebrate in this part of the world – it would be folly to ignore the humans who have called it home. Think footballers like Artie Beetson, Bunny Pearce and Petero Civoniceva, and actor William McInnes. Then there’s the Bullivants, Vaughan and Carmel – once owners of the Nature’s Own vitamin and supplements business. They built neighbouring his and hers mansions on Prince Edward Parade after amalgamating a few smaller allotments on one of the suburb’s more salubrious boulevards, with its groves of towering Moreton Bay figs.



Forgotten shoes on the foreshore. Morgan Roberts The “Gollum Tree” in Scarborough Beach Park. Morgan Roberts Snoops were often seen snapping photos of the homes, one an ostentatious triple-storey structure, and the other more like a doll’s house on steroids, where life-sized animals appeared to cavort in a lush, poolside garden. If Scarborough has celebrity runs on the board though, it’s mainly courtesy of the Bee Gees. The suburb of Redcliffe to the south even has a laneway named after them, decorated with statues of brothers Barry, Maurice and Robin Gibb. But it was in Scarby, as some locals call it, that the siblings (including youngest brother Andy, a star in his own right) actually lived. When the Gibb clan migrated from England in 1958, they moved into a guest house in Oxley Avenue then settled in Fifth Avenue. Imagine being a neighbour to their early rehearsals for gigs at Redcliffe Speedway and Queensland coastal resorts, before the trio decamped to the Gold Coast, and then Sydney in 1963. Putting all that aside, there’s plenty to love about Scarby: clean air, friendly residents who are passionate about the district, accessible and safe beaches, good schools and shops, and a low crime rate.



The house on Fifth Avenue where the Bee Gees lived as young teens. Morgan Roberts Bee Gees Way in Redcliffe. City of Moreton Bay Barry Gibb visits the Redcliffe Peninsula in 2015. Chris Hyde I’ve lived in Scarborough for the past two years, but my connection stretches back to the ’70s when my parents moved from Brisbane’s inner north with my youngest brother and me in tow. Sadly, mum and dad have checked out, but both are interred on the peninsula, as are an aunty and uncle. As your guide, I’ll first lead you east along Eversleigh Road, beginning where it intersects with Ashmole Road, virtually in the shadow of Kayo Stadium, where the Dolphins rule. The road is mysteriously wide, the architecture eclectic. Where Eversleigh Road bisects Scarborough Road, we avoid a left turn, where we would catch sight of the sprawling Southern Cross Catholic College campus. Beachside living at its finest. Morgan Roberts Dog walking on the promenade. Morgan Roberts



The gentle swoosh of ripples breaking the shore are the soundtrack to our life. Morgan Roberts Instead, we stay true to our course and walk by the suburb’s eponymous primary school and then on to Queens Beach, a sliver of paradise where pooches run free and kite surfers defy gravity as they race past Drury Point towards Scarborough Beach. Now watch your step, because this is where the magic happens. Scarborough Beach Park abuts Moreton Bay on its eastern flank and to the west, Landsborough Avenue, which zigs one way, then zags another. I walk this way every day accompanied by my better half and our dog. The birdsong, the gentle swoosh of ripples breaking the shore, and countless greetings from passers-by are the soundtrack to our life. Council workers tend to the park as if it were their own, cleaning public areas with almost military precision, much to the appreciation of visitors, who descend on the area each weekend and holiday period with the type of zeal a chip-hungry seagull could admire. Grab a picnic table or spread a blanket and watch as boats bob along between the shore and Moreton Island. Morgans Seafood. Morgan Roberts Overlooking Deception Bay. Morgan Roberts



Some residents yearn for quieter days when Scarborough was still a secret, its streets were less cluttered, and no building was taller than any of the Norfolk pines, standing to attention where grass gives way to sand. The aroma of coffee rides the breeze from Landing, a family-run cafe on the ground level of The Oscar, a multi-rise residential and commercial development on the former site of the movie theatre. With its oxide-coloured tables, Landing pays homage to the red cliffs that James Cook noticed in 1770, and its designer sausage rolls are next level. Not to mention the Breton buns, the croissants and brownies. Related Article Opinion

Life in the ’burbs Soldier crabs and sunset walks: Why nobody wants to leave this seaside suburb Kate Wild Contributor Scarborough is awash with dining options. Choose between any number of Asian or continental-themed restaurants, including Vietnamese, Indian, Japanese and Italian. Drop by the Friendly Grocer and they’ll prove the name is not misused. Wander further around to Thurecht Parade, where sunsets roll on forever. Morgans offers muddies, sweet lip and prawns so fresh, it’s easy to think these little treasures should still be swimming. Dine in alongside the trawlers, or skip across to Jamieson Park, where Deception Bay reveals itself, and breathe in the beauty. Drop by the Scarborough Harbour Brewing Company and quench your thirst. I can vouch for each and every one, which probably explains my expanding girth. The Bee Gees’ old wooden house on Fifth Avenue is still standing, and Barry Gibb returned for a nostalgic visit as recently as 2024. “We fell into paradise when we got off that ship,” Gibb said at the time. “We didn’t know what hit us.”

World.title: Lack of training, funding hindering GP-led adult ADHD care: study
World.content:
NationalQueenslandDoctors at work Lack of training, funding hindering GP-led adult ADHD care: study Courtney Kruk November 16, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Medicare rebates should be increased and more training provided for Queensland doctors treating adults with ADHD, a new study has found. The research by the University of Queensland was conducted nearly a year after GPs were given the power to diagnose and prescribe medication for adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, a condition marked by symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity. Queensland was the first Australian jurisdiction to embrace the expansion but, unlike other states, GPs aren’t required to undertake mandatory ADHD-specific training. Assistant Professor Dr Sidd Sarmah is a Gold Coast-based GP and practice owner, and chair of AMA Queensland’s General Practice Committee. PhD candidate Benjamin Johnson, from UQ’s National Centre for Youth Substance Use Research, said Queensland doctors needed better training to avoid misdiagnosis.



“Even though many GPs have experience with treating childhood ADHD, adult ADHD can be quite tricky to diagnose, which is why there needs to be more education and compulsory training,” Johnson said. Related Article Healthcare ADHD treatment cheaper, easier as GPs get green light to prescribe drugs “For example, someone experiencing burnout can present with similar impairments to ADHD, such as inattention and forgetfulness, but their treatments are very different. “That’s why it’s really important to be able to differentiate between situational factors and a long-term developmental disorder.” Best practice ADHD diagnosis typically requires two to three hours over several sessions to cover developmental history, collateral reports, screening for co-occuring health conditions and shared decision-making.



Before the expansion into GP-led care, adults seeking diagnosis had to visit a specialist, usually a psychiatrist. Such appointments could cost upwards of $1000 and incur waiting periods of up to a year, making care inaccessible for many people. While expanding GP authority had relieved strain on the system, Johnson’s research found current Medicare funding arrangements do not support longer consultations, and rebates should be reviewed to ensure GPs are not financially penalised for providing comprehensive care. Ritalin is the most common medication prescribed to treat and manage ADHD. Assistant professor Dr Sidd Sarmah, a Gold Coast-based GP, agreed with the need for current Medicare funding arrangements to be reviewed, but said doctors are well-placed to provide adult ADHD care and didn’t necessarily need compulsory training. “I support training and GPs should have access to good education [and] shared care pathways with psychiatrists and paediatricians,” Sarmah said.



“GPs have been able to take on this new challenge very well, primarily because our fellowship involves rigorous specialist training, and we manage quite a few complex chronic conditions, and most adult mental health problems. Related Article Queensland Health LNP drags feet on ‘sorely needed’ health workforce plan “It was a breath of fresh air [when the changes were announced] because the real alternative to that was actually no care because access [for adults seeking ADHD assessment] was a big problem at that point in time.” Sarmah noted GPs have been managing ADHD for children between the age of four and 17 since 2017, and said some have chosen not to broaden their services to adults after the changes came into effect in December last year. “I do a lot of skin cancer work, a few GPs [at my practice] do mental health work,” he said.



“They wouldn’t necessarily want to get involved from an interest point of view in ADHD management because it is a very complex condition [and] Medicare rebates do not reward long and complex consultations, which is a paradox.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The superchip genius or the big name wildcard? Eight contenders to replace Huang as Nvidia’s CEO
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesBillionaires The superchip genius or the big name wildcard? Eight contenders to replace Huang as Nvidia’s CEO Wyatte Grantham-Philips Updated November 16, 2026 — 5:41am ,first published November 13, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Nvidia chief Jensen Huang has resigned from his top post at the chipmaker he co-founded, after reports of the tech titan’s extramarital affairs came into the spotlight this week. One of those relationships has raised national security concerns. The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with a businesswoman US intelligence suspects to be a Chinese spy, which Beijing denies. Separately, the outlet and later others found Huang was said to have had another affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him directly – compounding calls for him to step down. Reports of a third affair, this time with another Nvidia employee, emerged on Friday following his resignation. Jensen Huang turned Nvidia into one of the biggest companies in the world before a dramatic fall from grace. Bloomberg Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation, effective immediately. The California-based company said that Colette Kress – who has been Nvidia’s chief financial officer and executive vice president since 2013 – will step into the role of interim chief executive. The scandal marks the most tumultuous chapter yet for Nvidia, whose high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for artificial intelligence. Huang has become a key face in the AI race, both across the industry and often on US President Donald Trump’s side in Washington.



Here’s what we know. Who is Nvidia’s interim chief executive? Nvidia says that Colette Kress is now interim chief executive. Before joining Nvidia more than 13 years ago, Kress worked at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments in various roles, according to her executive biography on the company’s website. Colette Kress has been named as Nvidia’s interim chief executive. In a statement about her new post on Thursday, Kress said that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years”.



The company’s board of directors also said that it had named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones, an entrepreneur and venture investor. Who is Alice Huang? Over the weekend, following news reports of Huang’s relationship with a woman identified as former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, Nvidia’s then chief executive apologised for being “unfaithful to my wife”. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang pictured at a Shanghai restaurant. “My actions hurt her and our children,” Huang wrote in an email to employees, adding that his colleagues also “deserve better” from him.



Neither Huang nor Nvidia identified who he had been intimate with by name, but the apology arrived shortly after Nvidia said it was investigating whether Huang had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort”. Last month, the Times reported that US intelligence agencies discovered Nvidia’s Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who also goes by the name Huang Le – and determined she was feeding information directly to Beijing. (Huang is a common surname and the two are not related.) Who is Kimberly Powell? The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. The Times reported Huang, 63, and Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, California, hotel during an Nvidia conference in March. Both Huang and Powell are married to other people.



The New York Times reported Huang had engaged in a second affair with one of his subordinates, Kimberly Powell, who is Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Nvidia’s code of conduct instructs staff to avoid situations that could create conflict, including “personal relationships”. Who is Lori Huang? The scandal also has ramifications for Huang’s personal life. Huang’s admission has fuelled speculation about the fate of his 41-year marriage with Lori Huang, 64. She is president of the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, which had $US9 billion ($13.1 billion) in assets as of 2024, including $US6 billion in fresh funding that year. Of Jensen Huang’s 922 million Nvidia shares, more than half belong to a trust where he and Lori Huang are the co-trustees, according to financial filings. She is also the sole controller of a trust that owns about $US5 billion worth of Nvidia shares. Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, walk to the White House to attend a state dinner hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September. AP Photo/Carolyn Kaster



Lori Huang joins a small group of tech titan spouses who have had to grapple with public infidelity. The list includes MacKenzie Scott, the ex-wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Melinda French Gates, ex-wife of Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates. The succession problem: who might replace Huang? Huang co-founded Nvidia back in 1993, and had led the company ever since, with no clear successor in sight. Huang’s ouster has led to a scramble for a new permanent chief executive, and Nvidia said it was considering both “internal and external candidates”. The Financial Times reported that Arm Holdings chief executive Rene Haas has been approached about taking over. AP As well as Kress, various other names have been floated as potential successors, including Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, Nvidia executive Ian Buck – credited as the tech genius behind the CUDA software that allows developers to write code on the company’s chips, AMD chief executive Lisa Su (who is a cousin of Jensen Huang), Arm boss Rene Haas, former Google chief Eric Schmidt and Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan. The Financial Times reported that Haas has been approached about the role. US President Donald Trump made his choice clear, saying former Apple chief Tim Cook should take over.



“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump said on social media. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” he added. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent weighed in on Sunday, saying Nvidia needs to “go outside the company” as it seeks a new chief executive. Donald Trump nominated former Apple chief Tim Cook as an ideal candidate to take over as Nvidia CEO. AP “This makes me think that as the board conducts a search for a new leader that they need to go outside the company, that just (with) what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shakeup,” Bessent told Fox News’ Sunday Morning Futures show. Where investigations stand



Nvidia hasn’t provided any notable new updates in its internal review that was first announced at the weekend. At the time, the company said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. Trump was reportedly briefed about intelligence findings involving Huang well before the scandal erupted publicly. But when asked at the weekend whether he wished he had acted sooner on that information, the president said, “I don’t think so”, and maintained that Nvidia’s chief executive was an “honorable guy”. Loading Trump later said the FBI was looking into Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, although where exactly that probe stands is unclear. Meanwhile, lawmakers from both sides of the aisle on Capitol Hill are calling for further investigations. Many eyes have been on Nvidia’s ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies’ partnership on its website. Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports.



On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained that it took its obligation to comply with American export control laws “extremely seriously” – and that it was committed to working “constructively and transparently” with the US government. Singaporean authorities said they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded there wasn’t enough evidence that she had committed a crime, but suspected she provided “inaccurate information” to downplay her role at Megaspeed and barred her from returning to the country. China, meanwhile, has denied that it attempted to ensnare Jensen Huang. Its Foreign Ministry earlier this week called the spying allegations “unsubstantiated” and said they amount to a smear campaign. What is it with the leather jackets? Jensen Huang has become known for his vast collection of leather jackets. They have become a staple of his wardrobe and his persona, and were his trademark look while delivering speeches.



Huang credits wife Lori and daughter Madison with coming up with the look. He is reported to have 60 jackets in his wardrobe. A Tom Ford leather jacket worn and signed by Huang, sold in July at a Sotheby’s auction for $US960,000. The proceeds were donated to charity. Huang has become known for his leather jackets. AP Photo/John Locher Donald and Jensen’s bromance



Huang has maintained a close relationship to Trump throughout the Republican president’s second term in office. He has successfully lobbied for looser AI regulation overall – including less strict limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. And he is among tech chief executives who have dined at the White House, and even travelled on Air Force One. Trump has called Huang “smart” and “amazing”, repeatedly insisting he join him on foreign trips. After news of his resignation broke on Thursday, the president maintained that Huang had done “done a fantastic job”. Huang and Donald Trump at the US Institute of Peace in Washington. AP The entrepreneur praised Trump effusively in 2025 before a meeting. “I come with only one purpose only, which is to inform and to be in service of the president as he thinks about how to make America great,” Huang told reporters. Nvidia committed $US25 million to help fund Trump’s White House ballroom renovation, a major personal priority for the president in his second term.



Last month, Trump presented Jensen Huang with the National Medal of Science. On Friday, Trump said Huang called him and expressed remorse over what the scandal had done to his family. Trump, in a White House interview with the broadcaster Stephen A. Smith on Thursday, praised Huang just hours after his ouster. “What he’s done is incredible,” Trump said. “Nvidia is unbelievable. “I spoke to him yesterday. He’s going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That’s what he told me. He called me.” How has this affected Nvidia’s share price?



Nvidia shares closed 4.3 per cent lower and have tumbled this week, wiping nearly $US500 billion off the market capitalisation of the company. The company is now valued around $US4 trillion, having been worth more than $US5.8 trillion in early October. Nvidia’s value has plummeted this week. Bloomberg Jensen Huang’s personal net worth has fallen by about $US19 billion this week, dropping him out of the world’s top 10 richest people list, according to Forbes. He is now the 13th richest person in the world with a net worth of about $US143 billion. A new test for the AI industry The shockwaves of Huang’s exit stress just how few figures hold so much power in the AI race. Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable companies today – and Huang has risen to fame across the tech world.



Related Article Analysis

AI Jensen Huang once told me his two golden rules. He may have broken one of them Some analysts suspect that the foreign intelligence allegations will strengthen calls in Washington for stricter export controls with China, which could in turn renew trade strains overall. Others have called it a watershed moment for Nvidia, the chipmaker that has long been seen as the crown jewel for powering AI. And questions of security risks facing the companies at the forefront of this technology are piling up Stephanie Balaouras, group research director for Forrester, said Huang’s resignation from Nvidia wasn’t just a test for the company but the AI boom as a whole. “If Nvidia stabilises quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience,” she said. “If its stock, financing relationships, or ecosystem commitments remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragile side of the AI bubble ledger.” AP, Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
