World.title: Rare 1941 plane returns to Nelson skies
World.content:
Audio player for " Rare Lockheed Electra returns to Nelson skies " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/regions/2618241%2Frare-1941-plane-returns-to-nelson-skies

Rare Lockheed Electra returns to Nelson skies Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A plane that once provided Nelson's only air service during World War II has returned to the city's skies.

The restored 1941 Lockheed 10A Electra - named Kuaka - drew a crowd during a special visit to Nelson Airport.

The rare art deco airliner, with its blindingly bright chrome exterior, was last seen in Nelson when Trans Island Airways stopped its scheduled flights between Nelson and Christchurch in 1959.

The plane is one of only two still flying in the world, with the other in the Czech Republic.

Aviation historian Richard Waugh said the Lockheed Electra was a "very sophisticated, fast aircraft" that played a pioneering role in New Zealand's aviation history.

"They were the first monoplane all metal aircraft in New Zealand and, with a tailwind, capable of say 200 miles an hour, which was faster than anything the Air Force had in the late 1930s."

Aviation historian Richard Waugh and his wife Jane St George-Waugh. RNZ / Samantha Gee

During World War II, they were the only planes servicing Nelson.

"In 1937-1938 it pioneered most of the airline schedule routes in New Zealand, particularly Auckland to Dunedin, and then from 10 November 1939, it did the airline service to Nelson."

He said the Lockheed Electra was remarkably comfortable and relatively quiet, with an interior as spectacular as the exterior.

The aircraft was involved in New Zealand's first fatal accident involving passengers on a scheduled flight, when ZK-AFE 'Kereru' crashed near the summit of Mt Richmond on a flight from Wellington to Nelson on 7 May 1942.

Five occupants were killed, with the tragedy commemorated on a plaque at Nelson Airport.

There are only two Lockheed 10A Electra planes still flying in the world. RNZ / Samantha Gee

A restoration decades in the making

Kuaka is owned by Rob Mackley, who saw it advertised in the Trade-A-Plane magazine in 1996.

"I thought, wow, that's quite rare. It was an Alaskan number, so I rang them, and I said, 'is it a Lockheed 10?' And they said, 'yes, sir, it is'."

It was being sold by a museum and was not in a flyable condition, but Mackley flew to Alaska that night to take a look at it.

The restored Lockheed Electra plane, Kuaka RNZ / Samantha Gee

He said because they rarely came up for sale there was no benchmark for its worth, and despite being "young and naive" he decided to put an offer in.

"It was a sealed bid tender, so you had to just write what you wanted to pay, put it in an envelope, take it to the reception of the museum, put it in their mahogany box."

About two weeks later, to his surprise, he got a fax saying, "come and get your aeroplane".

He said it was a mission to get the plane to New Zealand, it almost didn't happen. A restoration job he thought would take three years, took almost 30.

"It's just been one of those restorations where we've tried to be as faithful on everything as we can, and that's led to multiple years more and obviously more money, and I never added it up.

Inside the 10-seater Lockheed Electra, which has been painstakingly restored. RNZ / Samantha Gee

His wife Caroline is also a pilot and Mackley said the pair loved taking people out on the plane.

"You can fly it with one, but I opt to fly it with my wife, because she's actually more qualified than me so she's always co-pilot, and then there's room for 10 passengers.

"It's not a hangar queen, we do use it, it's neat for people to be able to come and see what aviation used to be like."

No. 23 Squadron air cadet Tayla McLean said flying in the Electra was 'very cool'. RNZ / Samantha Gee

On Saturday, one of those lucky passengers was No. 23 Squadron air cadet Tayla McLean.

"It was very cool, [the flight] was way longer than I thought and the inside is very nicely decorated and we've got to go over Kaiteri and Tahuna area and circle around Nelson."

Nelson Airport chief executive Brendan Cook said the rare plane drew quite a crowd, with people young and old turning up to get a closer look at it.

"It's an absolutely amazing aircraft, only two of its kind flying in the world with a long history of aviation in Nelson through its flying career back in the 40s and 50s."

Nelson Airport chief executive Brendan Cook. RNZ / Samantha Gee

He said travelling on it offered a "bit of a look back in time as to what flying would have been like" then.

"It was unbelievably smooth and quiet, it would have been the sight of luxury back in the day."

World.title: 'Bit of a disaster': Principals brace for more NCEA glitches
World.content:
Audio player for " Papakura principal on NCEA's return to paper exams " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/education/2623142%2Fbit-of-a-disaster-principals-brace-for-more-ncea-glitches

Papakura principal on NCEA's return to paper exams Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Papakura High School will have hard copies of Monday and Tuesday's NCEA exam papers on standby following a glitch which saw students unable to access their online exams.

About 40,000 students were sitting NCEA level 2 English on Thursday - many of them online - when a malfunction disrupted the exam, forcing many to revert to using paper exams.

While many students were given additional time to complete their exams, others will now be judged on internal work or assessments throughout the year.

Papakura High School principal Simon Craggs told Morning Report it was a "bit of a disaster".

He said he had never had full confidence NZQA would be able to run exams online at scale - and his concerns had been proven correct.

Craggs said Thursday's malfunction "hit us hard".

At first, staff were running around wondering if the problem was with the school's internet.

Rather than NZQA sending a text alert out, it sent as email at 10.03am which staff didn't see straight away, he said.

It was "pretty stressful for those kids during that time".

Craggs said it's not compulsory for all exams to be completed online - and of those that they can choose to run the "old school" way with pen and paper - they do so.

"The IT infrastructure at the school, the availability of devices, the reliability of devices, all those things are really contingent on everything working and lots of variable, whereas pen and paper, you give someone a new pen if it doesn't work.

"There's a lower risk of failure."

Craggs said many students also just prefer to use pen and paper for exams.

NZQA deputy chief executive Jann Marshall earlier said despite extensive testing, the online assessment platform didn't perform as it should have.

"We are sorry for the disruption and the stress that students, as well as teachers and parents, experienced," she said.

"It's unacceptable.

"Students have worked hard for the examination and recently expected the platform to perform well."

World.title: Survey finds GP practices embracing AI amid safety, privacy concerns
World.content:
Audio player for " GP Jamie Shepherd on AI's growing role in healthcare " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/health/2619095%2Fsurvey-finds-gp-practices-embracing-ai-amid-safety-privacy-concerns

GP Jamie Shepherd on AI's growing role in healthcare Morning Report Download MP3 6m

A survey of nearly 80 GP practices owned by primary health organisation ProCare shows almost all of them are using artificial intelligence, with only 1 percent saying they don't and don't intend to.

Despite the high uptake, barriers named by respondents include safety, privacy and cost.

The survey was run by ProCare, the country's largest primary health organisation (PHO), which owns 131 practices.

Supplied

When members were asked if any of their staff were using AI in their work, 95 percent said yes. Only 5 percent said no, with 4 percent saying they were considering it, and a little over 1 percent saying they were not using it nor considering it.

Bindi Norwell, ProCare's chief executive, said the number of clinics using AI turned out to be higher than she thought.

"I think we're always going to find those practices and clinicians who just don't, [and] are not interested in using it," she said.

"What we're trying to do is just to make sure that we provide confidence and support and tools for practices to make sure they're using AI in a very safe way."

Supplied

More than 40 respondents were using free clinical scribes such as Heidi and Nabla, just under 40 were using the paid versions, and a few fewer were using free AI programmes such as Copilot and ChatGPT.

Others were using tools for patient communications, clinical decision support and administration tasks - "All of the things that take them away from patients and can help make life easier for themselves and their patients," Norwell said.

Key concerns are privacy, security and accuracy

Supplied

More than 50 of the ProCare survey's respondents named privacy and security as one of their biggest concerns, followed by the impact on clinical accuracy.

Following high-profile data hacks of [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/health/2230243/pace-of-government-digitisation-a-real-cause-for-concern-says-manage-my-health-inquiry

Manage My Health and MediMap], data security was likely front-of-mind for many, Norwell said.

"We're dealing with patient data here at the end of the day, and ... it's very, very important that we protect patient data ... with utmost care, and I guess with privacy and security," she said.

ProCare was providing training to members to help with security, she said.

"We're also looking at the ways that we can help them with doing due diligence on new tools. So really knowing the questions to ask providers about their security levels. What are they investing in? How are they keeping up with the pace of change in AI?"

Cost was also a concern, according to more than 20 percent of respondents.

"We strongly recommend for practices to always be using paid-for versions for the extra security and protection," Norwell said.

Health NZ's guidance to its staff - who are separate to ProCare's practices - is to not use unapproved large language models (LLMs) or generative AI tools for any clinical decisions or for personalised advice to patients.

"The use of free AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) for clinical purposes is strictly prohibited due to data security, privacy and accountability concerns. You are also not allowed to use AI tools to draft notes and then transcribing it to handwritten or typed notes, even if you anonymise the patient information," the guidance says.

In March, Health NZ said staff had been caught using these free tools to write clinical notes, a move it said could result in formal disciplinary action.

Most expect use to grow substantially

Many respondents considered AI's biggest potential to be reducing time spent on clinical documentation, meaning more time with patients, alongside reduced clinician burnout and workload.

"We're using it for ... speeding up efficiencies and processes, and that ultimately delivers better patient care," Norwell said.

"I do feel now it will go more widespread across practices, rather than just individual clinicians."

World.title: Cyclone Xavier to bring damaging winds to Cook Islands
World.content:
A storm warning is in place for parts of Northern Cook Islands due to Tropical Cyclone Xavier.

The storm intensified into a category 1 cyclone on Sunday night.

The Cook Islands Meteorological Service says a storm warning is in force for Manihiki and Rakahanga, and the warning has been cancelled for Penrhyn.

Manihiki and Rakahanga can expect damaging gale-force winds up to 85km/h with wind gusts of up to 120km/h.

These are set to increase to 95km/h with gusts up to 130km/h later on Monday night.

Heavy rain and thunderstorms are also forecast.

World.title: Scotland beat Wallabies in desperate, dour Murrayfield arm-wrestle
World.content:
The Wallabies have delivered another woeful display on their spring tour, falling to a 15-12 defeat against Scotland at Murrayfield.

The defeat was the Wallabies' fourth in a row and piles the pressure on new coach Les Kiss after another display of limited attacking rugby.

A dour contest never really ignited was always destined to be close, with both teams struggling to get their attacks working on a freezing Edinburgh afternoon.

"I thought there were some really nice attacking moments from us," Les Kiss said post-match.

"Our defence definitely turned up.

"Our physicality overall was right up, which was pleasing.

"A couple of moments, that try in the corner with the maul, probably a couple of discipline moments that gave them easy yards just put us on the back foot.

"Full of fight, that's for sure. But you want to win those ones."

In the sort of dank, drizzly conditions that a Scottish autumn is famous for, the match descended into a gruelling arm-wrestle.

With the pre-match fireworks still hovering above the playing field, Matt Fagerson opened the scoring for the hosts inside the opening 10 minute, finishing off a spell of dominant possession in the corner.

The Wallabies hit back straight away, Harry Potter contorting himself to reach over and finish a rare flowing move sparked by the returning Carter Gordon in midfield.

Harry Potter scored for the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Liam Chester)

That was the end of any real attacking impetus for the Wallabies for almost an hour though as the team fell into the habit of one-out hit ups and box kicks.

As the two sides grappled with close-contact battles, former Wallaby Jack Dempsey burrowed over to score, the last points before a 45-minute scoreless spell that stretched deep into the second half.

The Wallabies felt they had hit back just before half time when Ryan Canham dived over from a rolling maul, but it was bought back by the TMO for obstruction by Jeremy Williams.

"It was a tough one," Wilson said.

"They're really trying to crack down on that at the moment and that was probably a really big moment in the end, because 14-all at half time we might have had them there.

"We've got to be better at icing those big moments."

Former Wallaby Jack Dempsey scored for Scotland in the first half. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Neither side could get going in the second half, the Wallabies defence standing tall despite Billy Pollard sin binning just after the break.

A Russell penalty looked to have sealed the game for the Scots, before Max Jorgensen scored a brilliant try in the final minute, an attacking raid of such class it raised questions as to why there had been no go-forward before then.

The Wallabies even had one chance to win the game late when Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii made a line break and Tom Wright was freed down the right wing.

However, he was bundled into touch and the Scots held on.

The Wallabies next head to Cardiff to take on a Wales team buoyed by beating the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years.

Look back on how all the action unfolded from Murrayfield in our live blog.

World.title: Shark attack hero breaks through for Iron Series win
World.content:
An emotional Charlie Verco has described his journey from a shark-attack rescue to a maiden Iron Series win as a "roller coaster".

Five months after saving Leah Stewart at Coogee Beach, Verco claimed the third round of the series by prevailing in a sprint finish in Sunday's race at Thirroul Beach.

In June, the 25-year-old paddled towards the danger and pulled the unconscious woman from the surf.

This shark attack hero believes Olympic inclusion could save lives The top seed in this year's Iron Series, who made headlines by helping save a shark attack victim earlier this year at Coogee, says having surf life saving in the Brisbane Olympic Games would help raise the profile of the sport.

After 12 days in a critical condition in hospital and a series of surgeries to amputate her arm, Stewart woke from an induced coma and was reunited with her daughter.

"Being able to manage the ups and downs of it, like the stressful rescue with Leah — I'm so happy that she was able to be alright," Verco said.

"It meant that I was able to keep focused on what I love, which is the sport.

"But realistically, we all do this sport as part of surf lifesaving. It certainly doesn't feel like we were doing a race like that.

"It feels like we're all just really wanting to win and compete against each other.

"But I like that we have the skills to be able to go and help people when they need it."

Verco beat home Ethan Callaghan and Henry Simpson in a breakthrough victory, which comes after the 25-year-old had entered this year's Iron Series as the top seed following the legendary Ali Day's retirement.

"It is a step up to try and put yourself at the front of the race as opposed to just being happy that you're here," Verco said.

"And for so long that was my goal, was just to get here. It's all about confidence.

"I've spent a long time doing races trying to get myself comfortable being at the front and setting my own pace, and I think that definitely helps."

Naomi Scott took out the women's event, with the Northcliffe athlete pipping Emma Woods in a sprint up the beach.

Before the Iron Series heads to Newcastle in January, Scott will travel to South Africa next week to defend her global Ironwoman title at the world lifesaving championships.

World.title: Chapman hat-trick fires Jillaroos to Rugby League World Cup glory
World.content:
The Jillaroos have defended their Rugby League World Cup title, dominating New Zealand 34-10 in the tournament decider at Lang Park.

The victory was all but assured after a commanding first half, with winger Jaime Chapman crossing for a hat-trick in sweltering Brisbane heat.

The win saw Australia claim a fourth-straight crown in the fifth-consecutive final featuring the Trans-Tasman rivals.

Rugby League World Cup finals live: Look back on all the action in our blog.

Chapman, whose treble brought her World Cup tally to 13, told ABC Sport it was a dream afternoon for her side.

"I feel over the moon. There's no better feeling than winning a World Cup on your turf, against the Kiwis as well.

"We knew it was coming. It was a really hard, tough game in this heat and super proud of our team and proud of our girls."

Chapman scored a stunning treble in sweltering Brisbane heat. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Lessons seemingly learnt from a lethargic start to their semifinal win over Fiji, the Jillaroos were dominant from the first minute in the tournament decider.

It took Chapman just two minutes to score the first try of the day by breaking wide, stutter stepping and rampaging through the New Zealand defence, allowing for the recalled Jesse Southwell to nail a difficult conversion.

A spectacular dive and one-handed putdown saw Chapman cross for her second in the 14th minute, before the winger put on the afterburners to complete her treble with a scintillating breakaway effort.

By half-time, Australia had run in six tries to the Kiwi Ferns' one, with Shaylee Best, Jess Sergis and Tamika Upton having also registered four-pointers, and Southwell having nailed all but one of the conversions.

Sergis's effort came after a breathtaking breakaway, while Upton completed some neat interplay with Abbi Church to compound New Zealand's misery in the shadows of half-time.

Shannon Mato's 23rd-minute converted effort was the Kiwi Ferns' only contribution to a 34-6 half-time scoreline.

Only a try-saving tackle prevented the Jillaroos from going further ahead five minutes after the break, but the Australians struggled for any cut through in an energy-sapping second half in which the still taxing conditions restricted the quality of play.

New Zealand winger Mackenzie Wiki was denied a late score thanks to a try-saving Isabelle Kelly tackle, but proceeded to find the only points of the second period by diving over with the full-time siren seconds from sounding.

Their 4-0 second-half scoreline meant the Kiwi Ferns went the entire tournament without conceding a point after half-time.

World.title: After tragically losing a mate, Herbert is helping businesses with his shirt
World.content:
Golfer Lucas Herbert has returned to Australia on a mission to use his platform to help those struggling in the tough economic climate.

Herbert has played in this week's NSW Open at the Hunter Valley, finishing in a tie for third.

But Herbert, fresh off the collapse of LIV Golf, entered this week's tournament without something synonymous with professional sport: sponsorships.

The end of LIV Golf brought an end to many commercial arrangements Herbert had, meaning he entered this week's NSW Open with his clothing as a blank canvas.

But Herbert decided he wanted to use his platform to help, following the tragic death of a mate earlier this year.

The 30-year-old from Bendigo put a call out to small businesses in the lead-up to the tournament, offering to promote them on his clothing.

He said small business owners were doing it tough, and said he wanted to help out.

He told golf journalist Tom Hobbs earlier this week that he was inspired to help small Australian businesses following the passing of a friend.

"Just seeing local business getting destroyed over here makes me sad," he said.

"One of my good friends took his own life in January because he was a small business owner and couldn't take the pressures of working 60 hours a week to keep the lights on any longer.

Lifeline on 13 11 14

"I thought it would be better than coming home wearing blank hats and clothes."

A mental health charity, electrical and a lawn care business were among the sponsors Herbert carried on his clothing this week.

Herbert will also be part of the Australian Open and Australian PGA Championship during this golf season.

World.title: Aussies crashes to record ODI loss against England after top order collapse
World.content:
Australia's top-order batters have crashed spectacularly as England romped to a record 135-run win to level their one-day international series 1-1.

England opener Tom Banton clubbed 121 runs from 99 balls as the tourists posted 6-355 — their highest ODI total in Australia — after being sent in at Adelaide Oval on Sunday.

The hosts were bowled out for 220 in 44.3 overs as England achieved its biggest winning runs margin in an ODI in Australia.

Australia's run chase started horribly with three batters — Travis Head (7), Cooper Connolly (0) and captain Mitchell Marsh (2) — caught at slip in a six-ball span.

The rapid-fire dismissals left the hosts reeling at 3-13 after 3.2 overs as England set course to level the series ahead of Wednesday's decider in Hobart.

It could have been worse for the Australians, who were 4-29 before England dropped two regulation catching chances from the bats of Matthew Renshaw, on 27, and Cameron Green, on 7.

The reprieves allowed Renshaw (63 from 74 balls) and Green to pause the rot with a 98-run partnership.

Green top-scored with 64 from 82 balls but the early damage inflicted chiefly by England paceman Gus Atkinson, who snared 3-22 from his initial seven overs, was irreparable.

Atkinson finished with 4-28 from 10 overs, his best ODI figures, and Sam Curran (2-38) and spinner Liam Dawson (2-41) also claimed multiple wickets.

Earlier, Banton, Jordan Cox (67 from 49 balls), Joe Root (62 from 68) and Will Jacks (54 not out from 40) dominated.

Banton and Root took control with a 137-run partnership from 136 balls for the second wicket, taking England to a powerful position of 1-156 in the 28th over.

Somerset batter Banton, 28, reached his second ODI ton from 86 balls before Cox and Jacks combined for a 102-run stand in less than 12 overs as England accelerated to an imposing total.

Tom Banton led from the front as England posted 6-355 in its innings. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Mark Brake)

Paceman Xavier Bartlett (3-72 from 10 overs) was the only Australian to take multiple wickets before a crowd of 31,412, the fifth-highest ODI attendance at Adelaide Oval.

Australia rested paceman Mahli Beardman, two days after his stunning one-day international debut of 6-24 in a seven-wicket win in Perth.

Beardman was replaced by Riley Meredith, who was punished in taking 1-75 from 10 overs.

Bartlett, Meredith, Spencer Johnson (1-61 from eight overs) and Jack Edwards (0-73 from nine) all conceded more than seven runs per over.

AAP

World.title: Aussie quick says 'everyone knew' about sandpaper, as Warner doubles down
World.content:
Former Australian cricketer Chadd Sayers, who played his lone Test after Sandpapergate on the infamous 2018 South African tour, has said he is comfortable stating he believed everyone in the team knew about ball-tampering.

The notorious Cape Town Test match, where Cameron Bancroft was filmed using sandpaper on the cricket ball, was thrust into the spotlight this week after Usman Khawaja in his memoir, Sabr, claimed ball-tampering was commonplace and the entire team needed to take responsibility.

The memoir has caused a rift in Australian cricket.

David Warner, who was suspended with Cameron Bancroft and then-captain Steve Smith over the incident, backed Khawaja's account in Sabr, saying it was "100 per cent accurate".

Meanwhile, Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Sayers, who was part of the Australian touring squad in 2018, said ahead of Australia's second ODI against England in Adelaide on Sunday that he was comfortable saying every member of the team knew sandpaper was being used.

"I'm comfortable saying where I'm sitting now that everyone knew what was going on [in South Africa in 2018]," Sayers said on the SEN broadcast.

"It [sandpaper] was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in change rooms … I'm not taking sides; it's just my recollection of what took place."

Sayers also said there was a meeting held in the wake of the team being caught with sandpaper, which lasted between 60 and 90 minutes.

Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball during the Test match in Cape Town, with an investigation determining he, Smith and vice-captain Warner were responsible for the ball tampering.

The trio was suspended, while the bowlers in that Test have always denied knowledge that sandpaper was being used on the ball.

In his memoir, Khawaja claimed he knew sandpaper was being used on the ball and told Bancroft to be careful.

Khawaja also said ball-tampering was commonplace in cricket.

Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Cummins hits out at Khawaja Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

"When he says 'we all knew', if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins said on Friday.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years; I did not know that was happening.

"But I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper; that's complete and utter nonsense.

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper. That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman that has been part of the team that's helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years, and the Usman that would have stopped that from happening there and then.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations. In his book Ussie's been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell a story, 100 per cent. I'm really glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Warner doubles down on Cricket Australia on social media

David Warner has hit out at Cricket Australia as Sandpapergate continues to dominate headlines. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

David Warner has made another statement on social media, claiming he was not aware of all the facts before taking the brunt of punishment for Sandpapergate.

On Saturday, Warner accused Cricket Australia of a potential cover-up by claiming he believed the bowlers were not interviewed by the organisation about the incident.

Cape Town inquiry spoke to all Aussie bowlers, ABC understands Sources connected to the Australian bowling group say they all spoke to investigators as part of the inquiry into Cape Town ball tampering, which runs counter to claims by David Warner.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," he wrote on Instagram.

"If that's correct then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning … ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

Multiple media outlets, including ABC Sport, have reported the bowlers were interviewed by Cricket Australia.

On Sunday, Warner then doubled down on his criticism of Cricket Australia and supported his previous post.

Loading Instagram content

"Just to clarify 'As far as I am aware' was the POINT," he wrote.

"I was never told the bowlers had been interviewed or provided statements.

"That information would've been pretty useful when I was forced to make decisions back in 2018.

"Why weren't we given all the evidence by CA?"

World.title: Tedesco calls time on international career after World Cup final cameo
World.content:
James Tedesco has confirmed his retirement from all representative football after a shock World Cup cameo completed a dream Test farewell.

The NRL premiership captain and long-time NSW fullback was a late addition to the bench for Sunday's Brisbane final after Latrell Mitchell was ruled out with illness.

He then enjoyed a cameo in the final minutes of Australia's 32–12 defeat of New Zealand before announcing his retirement plans.

"That's me for any rep footy; I'm done with rep footy now," the 33-year-old told AAP after adding a World Cup to his Origin series and NRL premiership this year.

"It's a good way to end it … it's been a long season, definitely ready for a break now and I'm pretty proud of it."

Australia claimed the men's and women's titles, both for the fourth straight time, after the Jillaroos took down the Kiwi Ferns 34–10 in the earlier women's decider in searing heat.

Tedesco captained Australia to the World Cup title four years ago and started at fullback against Fiji — his first Test since 2023 — in this tournament.

But with No.1 Reece Walsh in brilliant form he was content to watch from the sidelines, until Mitchell's sickness opened up a spot on the bench.

"Things happened and I get five minutes or whatever it was; it's special for me," he said.

The Kangaroos dominated from literally the opening minute. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"It was always the goal to get back into the jersey [in this tournament], whatever that looked like."

Tedesco was player of the match in the Blues' series-opening defeat of Queensland this year before producing a handful of sensational game-saving moments in the decider.

A veteran of 26 Origin appearances, Tedesco was also forced to pry his way back into the Blues' No.1 jersey after Dylan Edwards's ascension in 2024 and 2025.

Tedesco, who kept his retirement plans quiet, said without the rigours of representative duties he hoped to squeeze out two more NRL seasons.

"I didn't tell anyone; I didn't want to make it about me, that was important," Tedesco said of his call.

Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters insisted he was not aware of Tedesco's plans and that his decision to bring the veteran on was not a retirement gift.

"He didn't tell me. The reason he got on … I respect him as a person and I thought he needed to get on the field," Walter said.

"I didn't know it was his last game for Australia, but I'm so glad that happened now.

"He forced his way into the squad. You can only have one fullback, but James, the season he's had … it was just reward for him tonight."

Look back at all the action from both games in our live blog below.

World.title: How Swim GP may have given a glimpse of the future of para-sport
World.content:
Swim GP's made for TV, all-action racing format has proven a hit with swimmers and spectators alike.

But the biggest benefit may well be the innovations that placed para-swimmers front and centre of the competition at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatics Centre.

In front of a sold-out crowd, four teams: Kraken, Wahoo, King Tide and Tsunami, competed in a variety of races ranging from skins events through to mystery medley relays.

Times are not important. It's all about who touches the wall first.

"It is an opportunity for our athletes, our Paralympic team and our Olympic team, to come together and really showcase what they do," Swimming Australia Paralympic head coach Mel Tantrum said ahead of Saturday's evening events.

"This is about building the brand, building the profile of the athletes, swimming in prime time in preparation for the next six years."

The Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre was sold-out for day two. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swim GP is not a new idea, and indeed has built on the concepts reintroduced at last year's Australia vs the World in Brisbane.

However, crucially, Swim GP has seen para-swimmers take a leading role.

Swimming Australia chief executive Rob Woodhouse told ABC Sport that involving the para-swimmers "was one of the most important factors" and a "no-brainer" in Swim GP's planning for a couple of reasons.

"Both our head coaches, Mel Tantrum and Rohan Taylor, they absolutely want a packed stadium for our trials, ideally Sydney next year, but particularly the Olympic/Paralympic trials in '28 in Chandler, one of the reasons being, for the Olympics, SoFi Stadium, with 40,000 screaming Americans and Long Beach for the Paralympics," Woodhouse said.

"Some of those [para-]athletes do have sensory issues, so for them to have some experience coming out to all of that noise and those bright lights, the flashing lights and all those sorts of things is really, really important.

"So there's quite an important benefit from Swim GP for those para-athletes that do have to deal with those things to get more accustomed to a noisy venue, to a bright flashy venue and things like that.

"[Also] that aspirational view that these athletes can provide, whether they're para-athletes or able-bodied athletes, to the young kids at home, and there's a lot of kids with various disabilities that don't have opportunities to get into a pool or to even just get involved in the other sports. So, just being able to showcase our amazing para-athletes and what they do is a really critical factor."

A big atmosphere is vital for Australia's swimmers to prepare for LA Olympic Games in 2028. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Tantrum agreed, saying integrating the two programs was vital.

"Swimming Australia is really inclusive in terms of the parity between Olympic and Paralympic programs and making sure our swimmers across both programs are really profiled and really supported," Tantrum said.

"The athletes are loving being part of a bigger team. Those sort of innovative, creative competitions make the athletes feel they're part of an elite team.

"It's not just para, it's not separate, it's part of being the Australian Dolphins swim team and both programs coming together.

"The athletes are fully integrated team members. They don't sit separately. They've got the same uniform, same bleachers, same team meetings.

"And I think that's, for the athletes, it's a chance for them to really showcase their athleticism.

"It's not about, oh, you're a para-athlete, it's about elite swimming at its best.

"The world's best swimmers are here in the pool. And yeah, whether you're Olympic or Paralympic, you know, able-bodied or have a disability, it doesn't matter. You're an elite athlete first and you're here to perform."

New tech bringing para-sport into the mainstream

Victoria Belando Nicholson (right) was a member of the King Tide team. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

One of the biggest challenges in para-sport when there are a limited number of athletes, is integrating multiple classifications and how to accurately, and fairly, ensure a level playing field.

In a standard multi-class meet, swimmers with varied impairments all start their races at the same time, with the winner determined by how close a swimmer gets to the world record in their particular classification.

That's all well and good but, for spectators, it can get confusing as to who as actually won because the winner does not always touch the wall first.

Swim GP gets around this by having a staggered start, with lights on the blocks for each swimmer.

The time-gap is determined based on a swimmer's season best in a particular distance and should result in a blanket finish — far more appealing for spectators.

"I think it's a really good idea to then see everyone come up towards each other and finish pretty closely," Paralympic legend Lakeisha Patterson told ABC Sport.

"It makes it an exciting race, I think, towards the end.

"I think for an event that isn't preparing for a world champs or a major international meet, this is really good for fans to see how multi-class swimming works."

Lakeisha Patterson said she was nervous before her race, perhaps made more so when Ben Hance literally ripped the shirt off his back when walking out. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Patterson competed in, and won, Saturday night's opening race, a multi-class, mixed 100m event where each swimmer swam a different stroke, with Patterson unusually swimming butterfly, which she noted "definitely" won't be on her program for next year's world championships.

Perhaps she should reconsider. Patterson, who is classified as an S9 swimmer, swam a PB to blitz the field, although the other three swimmers; Tim Hodge (S9), Ben Hance (S14) and Keira Stephens (S10), were far closer together.

"It doesn't matter what their classification is and, in some cases, what their gender is," Tantrum explained.

"It's some new tech that we're trialling for the first time on the block so that athletes, no matter what their class or their gender, they can race together.

"With this [Swim GP] format, it's basically who touches the wall first is the winner.

"These staggered starts and close finals make the crowd get right into it. It makes it exciting if someone's got a 20-second stagger to catch up on in 100 metres. It makes for exciting racing, and the crowd really got into that last night and you could feel the crowd lift.

"That's what swimming should be, right? It should be exciting."

The future of para-sport?

Lakeisha Patterson (right) and Rowan Crothers (second right) were key members of Team Tsunami. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Patterson noted that giving para-swimmers the same platform was crucial for the development of the sport.

"I think it's incredibly important to showcase that our athletes aren't just here for participation," she said.

"We are athletes showcasing what is possible, and I think Australia is leading the way in that inclusion space and how we can involve our entire team.

"Leading into Brisbane we can really build on that and hopefully have all of Australia behind us, and showing to the people watching at home that they may have a space in Paralympic sport as well."

Fully integrated competitions remain a rarity for para and able-bodied sporting events, the Commonwealth Games being a notable exception.

Given the success of this format, Tantrum said that innovations like the staggered starts seen in Swim GP could inspire more innovation elsewhere, perhaps even adding more athletes to future Commonwealth Games fields.

"If we could influence Commonwealth Games Federation … we could potentially have a greater number of athletes and a greater number of classes competing together," Tantrum said.

"We left a number of athletes at home [from the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games] because they simply didn't have events for those classes.

"So something that is more of a multi-class format for Commonwealth Games would be a great innovation to at least consider.

What should the future of para sport look like? Birmingham 2022 celebrated the largest para sport program in history, but there's still a large gap between wealthy and developing nations. What should integration look like?

"There's potential there that we could make this more integrated, fun, with exciting finishes and more athletes involved from Australia."

Perhaps even other sports could take note?

"Our immediate purpose is to showcase swimming," Tantrum said.

"But you know, if we can lead other sports and things like track and field to follow a similar format, where the para-athletes are standing alongside their Olympic athlete colleagues?

"You know, it's humans, right? It's human story, it's humans doing the best that they can do.

"If other sports such as athletics or cycling, want to come in and do what we're doing, if we're the trailblazers of that space, we'd love others to join in as well."

Tech.title: Congress wants to tighten export rules on AI chips after Nvidia spy scandal
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Unsurprisingly, following the scandal involving now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is looking to further restrict exports of AI chips. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already said that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee.

Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act, first introduced in the House in April 2025 but stalled in the Senate, are receiving renewed interest. While that specific bill might not become law, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China,” according to Reuters. Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

Tech.title: Fanttik’s S1 Pro electric screwdriver is $40 off in the run-up to Black Friday
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon’s early Black Friday promos are already underway, and we’ll be highlighting some of our favorites over the next few days on our Shopping page. Among them is the Fanttik S1 Pro Cordless Electric Screwdriver, which is currently matching its all-time low of $39.99 ($40 off) at Amazon for a limited time.

Fanttik’s rechargeable tool is designed to make everyday household repairs and DIY projects easier, and it does a good job. Verge commerce editor Brandon Widder once called it his go-to electric screwdriver, noting he’s used it to assemble a bed, tighten bike seats, and perform other small- to medium-sized tasks around the house. It offers three adjustable torque settings, so you can use a gentler setting for more delicate jobs like electronics and more power for tougher projects.

Beyond being a capable electric screwdriver, the Fanttik also comes equipped with a few extra conveniences. For example, it features a built-in LED light to help you see screws in darker spaces, such as under a desk or inside a cabinet. The screwdriver also comes with 16 S2 hardened steel bits, including flathead and Torx bits, all of which fit inside an included magnetic storage case. The rechargeable 2,000mAh battery should handle up to 340 screws on a single charge, too, and it supports USB-C so you can quickly charge it between projects.

Tech.title: Apple’s first smart glasses are coming together
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple’s smart glasses are among the worst-kept secrets in the tech world. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says the company’s first model, which will lack augmented reality features, will be announced at June’s WWDC next year. They likely won’t ship right away, however, with Gurman saying only that “glasses shipments would begin before the end of the year.”

Key to their success will be the newly revamped Siri AI, which is adding fine-grained control over apps. By adding those features now and letting developers add support on the iPhone first, it’s hoping that its smart glasses will be able to hit the ground running.

The prototypes, dubbed N50, are currently running a pared-down version of visionOS and a new processor based on its older smartwatch chips. They also have a MagSafe-like charger Gurman describes as “flat, rectangular” and “roughly the size of a Tic Tac,” which can be used even while still wearing the glasses.

In addition to Apple putting an emphasis on style, privacy, and audio quality, the company is also hoping that Wi-Fi connectivity will grant them a certain amount of freedom, despite relying on an iPhone to actually execute many tasks:

The glasses have Wi-Fi, allowing certain functions outside of third-party apps to continue working when the iPhone isn’t nearby. Users could theoretically keep listening to audio over Wi-Fi after walking away from their phones, for instance, though the eyewear won’t operate as a fully independent device. Apple is also emphasizing the sound quality, which employees have said is industry-leading, with support for phone calls, music playback and FaceTime audio communication.

Tech.title: Rachelle Hampton won’t admit how long she spent charting the use of ‘murmur’ in Twilight
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Rachelle Hampton is a writer and co-owner at Defector Media, and the host of Normal Gossip, a podcast of anonymous listener-submitted stories about everyday drama. Whether that’s lies about luxury wool in a literal knitting circle, the impeachment of a hypocritical HOA president, or a COVID outbreak at a destination wedding with an absurd 25 bridesmaids, each story is unique in its absurdity, yet weirdly relatable.

After years as one of the co-hosts of Slate’s In Case You Missed It, a podcast that required her to be chronically online, Hampton is enjoying being a little more unplugged these days. And she has perhaps the most interesting answer we’ve ever received to the question “what’s worth splurging on?”

What is your most indispensable tool (analog or digital, app or hardware)?

I think it has to be the Notes app. My entire life is in there! My relationship to the Notes app definitely changes depending on what’s going on in my life at the time. Sometimes I just use it to make my grocery lists, but there was also a period of time where I used it to house my weekly to-do list, so it was basically the only thing between me and destruction. I’ve started blog drafts in the Notes app, and I’ve used it to write out particularly fraught text messages. There are recipes I’ve developed in there, as well as passwords and also questions for my doctors. The first note in my phone is from 2018, so it also serves as a nearly decade-long journal, though there are definitely notes that I simply can’t decipher, like why do I have a note from July 2020 that just says “4th floor”?

Which is the most underappreciated?

I absolutely hate texting. (I write all day, I don’t want to do it in my free time!!) But as someone who also refuses to delete their texts, I have to acknowledge that my most significant personal archive is probably in my Messages inbox.

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

It’s a tie between Spotify and whatever phone game I’m currently addicted to, which for the last two years has been Township. I’ve never played Sims or Animal Crossing, but I’m told that it’s something like that. I just like planting my little crops.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

I maintain inbox zero across my entire digital life, so I close all my tabs after I finish a task. Right now I have three tabs that I will close immediately after finishing this questionnaire: the first is the Google Doc I’m typing in, the second is the landing page for this series, and the third is a Google tab where I just searched Animal Crossing to make sure I had the name right.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

It’s a tie between Reddit and YouTube. Hosting a twice-weekly podcast about the internet for three years either gave me some sort of PTSD or cured me of my social media addiction, depending on how you want to look at it. I can’t spend more than twenty minutes max on IG or X or Bluesky without feeling claustrophobic. The exception is when I’m sick, and I let my fever brain rot on IG reels. Otherwise, it just feels like too much information from too many different sources. Reddit and YouTube are both places where I feel somewhat in control of what I’m seeing.

What is your happy place online?

I don’t think I’ve ever been as happy online as I was on Tumblr between 2013 and 2016. I’m always subconsciously chasing that high.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

My older brother bought me a tabletop Klipsch Bluetooth speaker for Christmas a couple of years ago, and it’s still going strong. The sound quality is incredible, and the design is super sexy, so it doesn’t immediately read as a Bluetooth speaker, which I love. I hope I never have to replace it.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

One of the stances I’m proudest of is that I’ve never (intentionally) used ChatGPT or Midjourney or any of the other generative AI tools / large language models. It’s getting harder and harder to avoid now that Gemini is built into Google and its various products. Stop trying to write my emails, Gemini!! I’ve never been swayed away from my belief that every single AI company owes a bankrupting amount of money to the writers and artists whose work their products are built on. Until that debt is paid, there’s nothing appealing to me about talking to a chatbot or creating a shitty poster.

What creation are you most proud of?

In 2020, when I was a staff writer at Slate, I spent a [redacted amount of time] methodically charting and ranking all 349 times Stephenie Meyer used the word murmur in her iconic Twilight saga. The idea had been germinating somewhere in the recesses of my brain for over a decade, only to be released by the surprise 2020 release of Midnight Sun. Seeing this blog come to life (shout out Slate’s interactive designer Natalie Matthews-Ramo!) felt like a fever dream come true.

What is your current obsession?

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

I wish I could say something chill and zen like take a cold shower or something, but the truth is when I’m writing and feeling stuck, I usually smoke a little weed, preferably a sativa strain. Getting high gets me out of my own way, which is usually the problem when I’m feeling stuck. It particularly helps with scriptwriting for Normal Gossip because the tone is so conversational, so being a little bit high stops me from over-writing.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

My favorite coffee shop is less than 500 ft from my apartment, so I end up there without my phone at least once a week, either on purpose or by accident.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Butter! With the caveat that I live by myself and don’t bake, so butter lasts a while in my household, but good butter can change a whole meal. It makes eating toast feel like a luxury instead of a chore to be completed between meetings because I’ve forgotten to eat lunch. My floor for butter is Kerrygold, but recently I’ve been loving this French brand called Isigny Sainte-Mère.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Last to arrive, first to leave.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

Tech.title: LG’s budget-friendly B6E OLED TV is up to 50 percent off this weekend
Tech.content:
LG’s B6E was already one of the most affordable OLED TVs you could buy, but it’s an even better deal now that it’s included as part of Best Buy’s latest doorbuster event. Now through the end of today, November 15th, the 55-inch model is 50 percent off, dropping it to an all-time low of $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy. If you want a larger 4K set, the 65- and 77-inch models are also discounted, dropping them to $999.99 ($900 off) and $1,499.99 ($1,200 off), respectively.

Although it’s not as bright as LG’s pricier C6, the B6E still delivers the excellent contrast and deep blacks OLEDs are often praised for. It’s nearly identical to the standard B6, except it comes with a simpler remote that lacks the motion controls and voice features found on LG’s Magic Remote. It supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 for more lifelike colors and detail in bright and dark scenes, along with Dolby Atmos for more immersive audio. And with Apple AirPlay and Google Cast built in, you can easily stream content from your phone or tablet and access a variety of streaming apps, including Netflix, HBO Max, and YouTube via LG’s webOS platform.

The B6 also offers a lot of features gamers will appreciate. It has a 120Hz refresh rate for modern gaming consoles, which is still plenty fast even if it doesn’t rival the 165Hz refresh rate on the C6. It also offers variable refresh rate support — including Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium — to help minimize screen tearing. You also get a zippy Alpha 8 Gen 3 AI processor and four HDMI 2.1 ports, making it easy to connect multiple consoles. It may lack some of the more advanced features found on LG’s more premium OLED TVs, but at 50 percent off, the B6 is a great option if you want the benefits of OLED without spending a fortune.

Tech.title: The Sony Aibo was a robot revolution dressed like a dog
Tech.content:
In the 1990s, Sony was absolutely convinced that we were on the precipice of a robot takeover. Pretty soon, the company decided, we’d all be living among countless humanoid robots. Some would be our coworkers; others would be our friends; and at least one would be our pet. And “pet” was exactly what Sony was going for when it created the Aibo. It was supposed to be part of the family.

On this episode of Version History, we go back in time and tell the story of the Aibo. David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Victoria Song and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, and together they discuss the origins of this remarkable robot dog, and its impressive success and longevity. They also try to figure out why Aibo had such an effect on its owners, what Sony got right (and wrong) about robots, and whether the idea of a robo-pet will ever be a global phenomenon.

This is the first episode of the sixth season of Version History. We’re back! This season is all about pets: gadgets that are pets, gadgets for your pets, and one gadget called pet.
